chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 1
paragraphs: The Persians who study history say that the Phoenicians started the whole conflict. They claim that the Phoenicians originally came from the coast of the Red Sea to the Mediterranean. After settling in the land where they still live today, they quickly took up long-distance sea trading. Carrying goods from Egypt and Assyria, they visited many ports, including Argos. At that time, Argos was the leading city in what we now call Greece. When the Phoenicians arrived at Argos, they set about selling their cargo. On the fifth or sixth day, when their goods were nearly sold out, a large group of women came down to the shore. Among them was the king's daughter, whose name, as the Greeks also confirm, was Io, daughter of Inachos. The women stood near the stern of the ship, buying whatever caught their eye. Then suddenly, at a signal passed among themselves, the Phoenicians rushed at them. Most of the women escaped, but Io and a few others were seized. The Phoenicians dragged them aboard and sailed straight for Egypt.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 2
paragraphs: That is how the Persians say Io came to Egypt, though the Greeks tell it differently. The Persians call this the first wrong. After that, they say, certain Greeks—whose name they cannot report—sailed to the city of Tyre in Phoenicia and carried off the king's daughter Europa. These were probably Cretans. So they were even for the earlier offense. But then, the Persians say, the Greeks committed the second wrong. They sailed with a warship to Aia in Colchis and the river Phasis. After finishing the other business that brought them there, they carried off the king's daughter Medea. The king of Colchis sent a herald to Greece demanding compensation and the return of his daughter. The Greeks replied that since the barbarians had given no satisfaction for the kidnapping of Io from Argos, they would give none in return.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 3
paragraphs: In the next generation, they say, Alexander the son of Priam heard of these events and decided to seize a wife for himself from Greece by force. He felt certain he would not have to pay any penalty, since the Greeks had paid none for their offenses. So he carried off Helen. The Greeks first sent messengers to demand her return along with compensation. When they made this demand, the Trojans pointed to the abduction of Medea. They argued that the Greeks now wanted justice from others, though they had given none themselves and had refused to hand over the woman when asked.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 4
paragraphs: Up to this point, the Persians say, there had been nothing more than the carrying off of women on both sides. But after this, the Greeks were greatly at fault. They were the first to launch a military expedition into Asia, before any barbarians had invaded Europe. The Persians maintain that while carrying off women by force is certainly wrong, it is foolish to obsess over revenge for it. The wise response is to pay the matter no mind. After all, the women would never have been carried off if they had not been willing to go. The Persians claim that the people of Asia took no great notice when their women were seized. But the Greeks, on account of a single woman from Sparta, assembled a vast army, invaded Asia, and destroyed Priam's kingdom. From that time on, the Persians say, they have always regarded the Greek race as their enemy. The Persians claim Asia and its barbarian peoples as their own domain, while they consider Europe and the Greeks to be separate from them.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 5
paragraphs: That is what the Persians say. They trace the beginning of their quarrel with the Greeks to the fall of Troy. As for Io, the Phoenicians disagree with the Persian account. They deny that they took her to Egypt by force. Instead, they claim that while they were in Argos, she became intimate with the captain of their ship. When she realized she was pregnant, she was too ashamed to tell her parents and sailed off with the Phoenicians of her own free will, to avoid being found out. Those are the stories told by the Persians and Phoenicians. I am not going to say which version is true. Instead, I will point to the man who, to my own knowledge, first committed wrongs against the Greeks, and then continue with my story. I will give an account of cities both small and great. For those that were once great have mostly become small, and those that were great in my own time were formerly small. Knowing that human prosperity never remains constant, I will write about both alike.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 6
paragraphs: Croesus was a Lydian by birth, the son of Alyattes, and ruler of all the peoples living west of the river Halys. This river flows south between the Syrians and the Paphlagonians, then runs north into the sea called the Euxine. Croesus was the first barbarian we know of who conquered some of the Greeks and forced them to pay tribute, while winning others over as friends. He conquered the Ionians, the Aeolians, and the Dorians living in Asia. He made allies of the Spartans. Before Croesus, all Greeks were free. The Cimmerian expedition against Ionia, which came before his time, was a plundering raid, not a permanent conquest.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 7
paragraphs: The royal power that had belonged to the Heracleidai passed to the family of Croesus, called the Mermnadai, in the following way. Candaules, whom the Greeks call Myrsilos, was ruler of Sardis and a descendant of Alcaios, son of Heracles. Agron, son of Ninos, son of Belos, son of Alcaios, was the first of the Heracleidai to become king of Sardis. Candaules, son of Myrsos, was the last. The kings who ruled this land before Agron were descendants of Lydos, son of Atys, from whom the whole nation took the name Lydian—they had previously been called Maeonian. From them, the Heracleidai—descended from Heracles and a slave-girl of Iardanos—took power, appointed by an oracle. They ruled for twenty-two generations, spanning five hundred and five years, passing the kingship from father to son down to the time of Candaules, son of Myrsos.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 8
paragraphs: This Candaules was passionately in love with his own wife. Convinced that she was by far the most beautiful woman alive, he kept telling Gyges, son of Daskylos—his favorite bodyguard—about her beauty, praising it endlessly. Before long, since Candaules was fated for ruin, he said to Gyges: "Gyges, I don't think you believe me when I describe my wife's beauty. People trust their eyes more than their ears. Find a way to see her naked." Gyges cried out: "Master, what madness is this? You are asking me to look upon my queen naked! When a woman removes her clothes, she removes her modesty with them. Wise men discovered long ago certain sayings we should live by, and one of them is this: let each man look only upon what is his own. I believe she is the most beautiful of all women. Please do not ask me to do something that is not right."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 9
paragraphs: Gyges resisted with these words, afraid that some harm might come of it. But the king replied: "Take courage, Gyges. Do not fear that I am testing you, or that my wife will harm you. I will arrange everything so she never even knows you have seen her. I will place you behind the open door of our bedroom. After I go in, my wife will follow. There is a chair near the entrance where she lays her clothes as she undresses, one piece at a time. You will be able to watch her at leisure. When she turns her back and walks to the bed, slip out through the door. Make sure she does not see you leave."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 10
paragraphs: Since he could not refuse, Gyges agreed. When Candaules decided it was time for bed, he led Gyges to the chamber. Soon after, the queen arrived. Gyges watched as she came in and set down her clothes. When she turned her back to walk to the bed, he slipped from his hiding place and headed for the door. But the woman caught sight of him as he left. She understood at once what her husband had done. Though struck with shame, she did not cry out. She acted as if she had noticed nothing, intending to take her revenge on Candaules. For among the Lydians, as among most barbarian peoples, even for a man to be seen naked is considered a deep disgrace.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 11
paragraphs: For the moment she kept silent and gave no sign. But as soon as dawn came, she prepared her most trusted servants and sent for Gyges. He came to her summons without suspicion, since he had often visited the queen when called. When Gyges arrived, she said: "Two paths lie before you, Gyges, and I give you the choice. Either kill Candaules and take both me and the kingdom of Lydia, or die here on the spot—so that in the future you will not obey Candaules in everything and see what you should not. Either the man who devised this must die, or you, who have looked on me naked and done what is forbidden." Gyges was stunned at first, then begged her not to force such a choice on him. But he could not persuade her, and saw that he truly had to either kill his master or be killed by others. He chose to survive. Then he asked: "Since you force me to kill my master against my will, tell me how we shall do it." She answered: "The attack will come from the same place where he displayed me naked. We will strike while he sleeps."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 12
paragraphs: They prepared their plot. When night fell—for Gyges had no way out; he had to either die or kill Candaules—he followed the woman to the bedchamber. She gave him a dagger and hid him behind the same door. While Candaules slept, Gyges crept up and killed him, seizing both his wife and his kingdom. The poet Archilochos of Paros, who lived around that time, mentioned Gyges in a verse.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 13
paragraphs: Gyges secured his kingship through the Oracle at Delphi. When the Lydians rose up in anger over the fate of Candaules, a deal was struck between the followers of Gyges and the other Lydians. If the Oracle declared Gyges king of the Lydians, he would keep the throne. If not, he would return power to the sons of Heracles. The Oracle confirmed him as king, and Gyges reigned. But the priestess at Delphi added a warning: vengeance for the Heracleidai would fall on the fifth generation of Gyges' descendants. Neither the Lydians nor their kings paid any attention to this prophecy—until it came true.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 14
paragraphs: So the Mermnadai took the throne from the Heracleidai. When Gyges became king, he sent many offerings to Delphi. He gave more silver offerings than any other man. Besides the silver, he dedicated a vast amount of gold. Most notable were six golden mixing bowls weighing thirty talents in all, dedicated in the treasury of the Corinthians (though in truth the treasury belongs not to the Corinthian state but to Kypselos, son of Aëtion). Gyges was the first barbarian we know of who made offerings at Delphi, apart from Midas, son of Gordias, king of Phrygia. Midas dedicated the royal throne on which he sat to judge disputes—a remarkable sight, displayed in the same place as the bowls of Gyges. The gold and silver that Gyges offered is called "Gygian" by the people of Delphi, after the man who gave it.

As soon as he became king, Gyges also led an army against Miletos and Smyrna, and captured the lower town of Colophon. But he performed no other great deed in his thirty-eight-year reign, so we will say no more about him.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 15
paragraphs: I will speak now of Ardys, son of Gyges, who became king after him. He captured Priene and invaded Milesian territory. During his reign, the Cimmerians—driven from their homeland by the nomadic Scythians—swept into Asia and captured Sardis, all except the citadel.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 16
paragraphs: After Ardys had ruled for forty-nine years, his son Sadyattes succeeded him and reigned for twelve years. After him came Alyattes. Alyattes waged war against Kyaxares, the descendant of Deïokes, and against the Medes. He drove the Cimmerians out of Asia, captured Smyrna (which had been founded from Colophon), and invaded Clazomenai. From that campaign he returned not as he wished, but with heavy losses. During his reign, however, he performed other noteworthy deeds, as follows.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 17
paragraphs: He inherited a war against Miletos from his father. When he invaded their territory and besieged Miletos, he did it this way: whenever the crops in the fields were ripe, he would march his army in to the sound of pipes, harps, and flutes of both high and low pitch. Once in Milesian lands, he did not tear down the farmhouses or burn them or rip off their doors. He left them standing. But he destroyed every tree and every crop, then marched home the way he came. The Milesians controlled the sea, so a blockade was useless. He left the houses intact so the Milesians would still have homes while they sowed and worked the land—and then he could return to destroy their harvest.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 18
paragraphs: He fought them this way for eleven years. During that time the Milesians suffered two major defeats: once in battle at Limenion in their own territory, and again on the plain of the Maeander. For the first six of those eleven years, Sadyattes, son of Ardys, still ruled the Lydians. He was the one who started the war and led the invasions. For the remaining five years, Alyattes, son of Sadyattes, carried it on. As I mentioned, he inherited the war from his father and pursued it with determination. No other Ionians helped the Milesians bear this burden except the people of Chios. They came to their aid to repay a debt, since the Milesians had once helped the Chians in their war against the people of Erythrai.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 19
paragraphs: In the twelfth year of the war, the Lydian army was burning the standing grain when a strong wind drove the flames into the temple of Athena at Assessos. The temple caught fire and burned to the ground. No one thought much of it at the time. But after the army returned to Sardis, Alyattes fell ill. When the sickness dragged on, he sent messengers to consult the Oracle at Delphi—either on someone's advice or because he thought it best. But when they arrived at Delphi, the priestess refused to give them any answer until they rebuilt the temple of Athena they had burned at Assessos in Milesian territory.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 20
paragraphs: This much I know from the people of Delphi. The Milesians add that Periander, son of Kypselos, who was a close friend of Thrasybulos (the tyrant of Miletos at the time), learned about the oracle given to Alyattes. He sent a messenger to tell Thrasybulos, so that he could plan accordingly. That is the Milesian version of events.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 21
paragraphs: When Alyattes heard the oracle's answer, he immediately sent a herald to Miletos. He wanted a truce with Thrasybulos and the Milesians for as long as it took to rebuild the temple. The herald set off for Miletos. Meanwhile, Thrasybulos, who already knew the whole plan, devised a trick. He gathered every bit of food stored in the city—both his own and everyone else's—into the marketplace. Then he gave a signal for the Milesians to start drinking and feasting together.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 22
paragraphs: Thrasybulos did this so the Sardian herald, seeing a vast pile of food and people feasting, would report it to Alyattes. That is exactly what happened. The herald returned to Sardis, and the peace that followed came about solely because of this trick. Alyattes had believed Miletos was suffering terrible famine and that the people were worn to the bone. But the herald's report told the opposite story. Peace was made on the condition that they would be friends and allies. Alyattes built two temples to Athena at Assessos to replace the one destroyed, and recovered from his illness. That is how the war between Alyattes and the Milesians and Thrasybulos ended.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 23
paragraphs: Now, Periander—the man who told Thrasybulos about the oracle—was the son of Kypselos and tyrant of Corinth. The Corinthians (and the Lesbians agree) say that the most extraordinary event of his life was this: Arion of Methymna was carried ashore at Tainaron on a dolphin's back. Arion was the finest harp player of his time and was the first person, as far as we know, to compose a dithyramb, give it that name, and teach it to a chorus at Corinth.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 24
paragraphs: This Arion, who spent most of his time with Periander, decided he wanted to sail to Italy and Sicily. After earning large sums of money there, he wished to return to Corinth. Trusting the Corinthians above all others, he hired a Corinthian ship and crew. But once out at sea, the crew hatched a plot to throw Arion overboard and steal his wealth. He learned of the scheme and begged them to take his money and spare his life. They refused. They told him to either kill himself so he could be buried on land, or jump into the sea at once. Driven to desperation, Arion asked one favor: let him stand on the deck in his full musician's costume and sing one last song. He promised to kill himself afterward. The crew gladly agreed—they would get to hear the world's greatest singer. They drew back from the stern. Arion dressed in his full costume, took up his lyre, stood on deck, and performed the Orthian measure. When the song ended, he threw himself into the sea just as he was, in full costume. The crew sailed on to Corinth. But a dolphin, they say, carried him on its back and brought him safely to shore at Tainaron. From there he traveled to Corinth and told Periander everything. Periander, doubting the story, kept Arion under close watch while waiting for the crew to arrive. When they came, he called them in and asked if they had any news of Arion. They said he was perfectly well in Italy—they had left him prospering in Taras. At that moment, Arion stepped out before them in the same costume he had worn when he jumped. They were struck speechless and could no longer deny what they had done. That is the story told by both the Corinthians and the Lesbians. There is a small votive offering at Tainaron from Arion: a bronze figure of a man riding a dolphin.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 25
paragraphs: After waging war against the Milesians, Alyattes the Lydian died. He had reigned for fifty-seven years. He was the second member of his dynasty to make an offering at Delphi. He dedicated a great silver mixing bowl on a welded iron stand—a remarkable sight, the finest of all offerings at Delphi, the work of Glaucos the Chian, who was the first man ever to discover the art of welding iron.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 26
paragraphs: After Alyattes died, his son Croesus inherited the kingdom at the age of thirty-five. His first target among the Greeks was Ephesus. When the Ephesians were besieged, they tied a rope from the temple of Artemis to the city wall, dedicating the city to the goddess. The distance between the old city under siege and the temple was about seven furlongs. After the Ephesians, Croesus attacked the other Ionian and Aeolian cities one by one. He invented serious charges against those he could, and against the rest he used any trivial excuse he could find.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 27
paragraphs: After conquering the Greeks in Asia and forcing them to pay tribute, Croesus planned to build ships and attack the islanders. When his shipbuilding preparations were complete, Bias of Priene (or, by another account, Pittacos of Mytilene) arrived at Sardis. Croesus asked whether there was any news from Greece. The visitor's reply put an end to the shipbuilding: "O king, the islanders are raising a cavalry force of ten thousand to march against Sardis and fight you." Croesus, taking this at face value, exclaimed: "May the gods put it into the islanders' heads to come against the Lydians on horseback!" The visitor replied: "O king, I see you dearly wish to catch the islanders riding horses on the mainland. That makes sense. But what do you think the islanders have been praying for, ever since they heard you were building a fleet? They want nothing more than to catch the Lydians at sea and avenge the Greeks on the mainland whom you hold in slavery." The story goes that Croesus was so delighted with this logic that he abandoned his shipbuilding. Instead, he made friends with the Ionians on the islands.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 28
paragraphs: As time went on, Croesus subdued nearly every nation west of the river Halys. Except for the Cilicians and the Lycians, he brought them all under his rule: Lydians, Phrygians, Mysians, Mariandynians, Chalybians, Paphlagonians, Thracians (both Thynian and Bithynian), Carians, Ionians, Dorians, Aeolians, and Pamphylians.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 29
paragraphs: With all these peoples subdued and Croesus still expanding Lydian power, all the great thinkers of Greece who were alive at that time came to Sardis, each drawn by his own reasons. Among them was Solon the Athenian. After making laws for the Athenians at their request, he left Athens for ten years. He said he wished to see the world, but his real reason was to avoid being forced to repeal any of his laws. The Athenians could not do so themselves, since they had sworn a solemn oath to live by Solon's laws for ten years.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 30
paragraphs: For this reason, and also to see the world, Solon traveled to Egypt to visit Amasis, and then to Sardis to visit Croesus. On his arrival, he was hosted as a guest in the royal palace. On the third or fourth day, at Croesus' command, servants led Solon through the royal treasuries and showed him everything—all the wealth and magnificence. When Solon had seen and examined it all, Croesus asked him: "My Athenian guest, we have heard much about your wisdom and your travels. You have journeyed through many lands in pursuit of knowledge. So I cannot help asking: who is the happiest person you have ever seen?" He asked this fully expecting to be named the happiest man alive. But Solon, choosing truth over flattery, said: "Tellos the Athenian, O king." Croesus was taken aback. "Why do you call Tellos the happiest?" he demanded. Solon replied: "First, Tellos lived at a time when his city was thriving. He had fine sons, and lived to see grandchildren born to all of them. Second, he was well off by our standards. And his death was the most glorious of endings. In a battle between the Athenians and their neighbors at Eleusis, he charged into the fight, routed the enemy, and died a beautiful death. The Athenians buried him at public expense on the spot where he fell and honored him greatly."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 31
paragraphs: When Solon had stirred Croesus' curiosity by praising Tellos so highly, the king asked who he would rank second, fully expecting to win at least that honor. Solon said: "Cleobis and Biton. They were Argives who had enough wealth to live on and, besides that, great physical strength. Both had won prizes in the athletic games. But here is the story told of them. There was a festival of Hera among the Argives, and their mother absolutely had to be driven to the temple in an ox-cart. But the oxen had not come back from the fields in time. So the two young men yoked themselves to the cart and pulled it, with their mother riding inside, for forty-five furlongs to the temple. After this feat, witnessed by the entire crowd, they received the finest possible ending to their lives. The god made clear through them that it is better for a man to die than to go on living. The Argive men stood around praising the young men's strength, while the Argive women praised the mother who was blessed with such sons. Overjoyed by both the deed and the praise, the mother stood before the statue of the goddess and prayed that Hera would grant Cleobis and Biton the greatest gift a human being can receive. After the prayer, the sacrifice, and the feast, the two young men lay down to sleep inside the temple. They never rose again. That was their end. The Argives made statues of them and dedicated them at Delphi, honoring them as men who had proved themselves truly excellent."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 32
paragraphs: So Solon gave second place to Cleobis and Biton. Croesus grew angry and said: "My Athenian guest, do you hold our prosperity in such contempt that you rank even ordinary citizens above us?" Solon replied: "Croesus, you are asking a man who knows well that the divine is jealous and loves to upset human affairs. Over a long life, a person sees and suffers many things he would rather not. I set the limit of a human life at seventy years. Those seventy years contain twenty-five thousand two hundred days, not counting leap months. If we add one extra month to every other year so the seasons arrive on time, that gives thirty-five extra months, or one thousand and fifty more days. The total comes to twenty-six thousand two hundred and fifty days—and no single day brings exactly the same fortune as another. So you see, Croesus, human life is entirely a matter of chance. I can see that you are enormously wealthy and king of many people. But I cannot call you the happiest of men until I learn that you ended your life well. A very rich man is no happier than one who lives day to day—unless good fortune also grants him a fine death with all his blessings intact. Many wealthy men are miserable, while many of moderate means are fortunate. The rich man who is unhappy has only two advantages over the lucky poor man, but the lucky poor man has many advantages over the unhappy rich man. The rich man can better satisfy his desires and withstand great disaster. But the fortunate man, though less able to endure catastrophe or gratify every wish, is spared those trials by his good luck. He is healthy, free from disease, untouched by suffering, blessed with good children, and pleasing to look at. If, on top of all this, he ends his life well—then he deserves to be called happy. But until he dies, hold off. Call him fortunate, not yet happy. No single person can possess everything, just as no single country produces all it needs. One land has one thing, another has something else. The land with the most is the best. The same goes for people: no one is complete in himself. He has this quality but lacks that one. Whoever holds on to the most blessings and then dies a gracious death—that is the person I would call happy, O king. In every matter, we must look to the end. God gives many people a glimpse of happiness, then tears them up by the roots."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 33
paragraphs: With these words, Solon refused to flatter Croesus. The king dismissed him, thinking him a fool for ignoring present prosperity and telling people to look to the end of every matter.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 34
paragraphs: After Solon left, terrible divine punishment descended on Croesus—most likely because he considered himself the happiest man alive. A dream came to him revealing the truth: he would lose his son to the blow of an iron spear-point. Croesus had two sons. One was disabled—deaf and mute. The other, named Atys, far surpassed all his peers in every way. Terrified by the dream, Croesus immediately arranged a wife for Atys. He stopped sending his son to lead the Lydian armies, as had been his custom. He removed all javelins, spears, and weapons from the men's quarters and piled them in the inner chambers, afraid that something hanging on a wall might fall on his son.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 35
paragraphs: While Croesus was busy with his son's marriage, a man arrived in Sardis—a Phrygian of royal blood, burdened by misfortune and with blood on his hands. He came to Croesus' palace and, following local custom, asked to be ritually cleansed. Croesus performed the cleansing, which among the Lydians is much the same as among the Greeks. When the rites were done, Croesus asked who he was and where he came from: "Who are you? What part of Phrygia do you come from? What man or woman did you kill?" The stranger replied: "O king, I am Adrastos, son of Gordias, grandson of Midas. I killed my own brother by accident. My father drove me out and stripped me of everything." Croesus answered: "You are the son of men who are friends of ours. You have come among friends. You will lack nothing as long as you stay in our land. Bear this misfortune as lightly as you can." So Adrastos made his home with Croesus.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 36
paragraphs: Around this time, an enormous boar appeared on Mount Olympos in Mysia. It kept coming down from the mountain to ravage the fields. The Mysians went out against it again and again, but could never harm it—instead, it kept harming them. Finally, they sent messengers to Croesus: "O king, a monstrous boar has appeared in our land and is destroying our fields. We cannot kill it no matter how hard we try. We beg you to send your son and a band of young men with dogs to help us destroy it." Croesus, remembering his dream, replied: "Do not mention my son again. I will not send him. He is newly married and has other concerns. But I will send a picked force of Lydians with all my hunting dogs, and I will order them to do everything they can to help you rid your land of this beast."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 37
paragraphs: The Mysians were satisfied with this answer. But then Atys, Croesus' son, walked in. He had heard what the Mysians wanted, and when Croesus refused to send him, the young man spoke up: "Father, in the past, the finest and noblest thing for me was to win glory in war and the hunt. But now you have shut me out from both, even though you have never seen any cowardice or weakness in me. How am I supposed to show my face in the city? What will the citizens think of me? What will my new wife think of the man she married? Either let me go to the hunt, or convince me with a good reason why things are better this way."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 38
paragraphs: Croesus replied: "My son, I am not doing this because I have seen cowardice in you or anything else to displease me. A dream came to me in my sleep. It told me that your life would be short—that you would die by an iron spear-point. Because of that dream, I rushed your marriage and now refuse to send you on this expedition. I am trying to protect you and steal you from your fate, at least for as long as I live. You are my only real son. The other, being deaf, I do not count."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 39
paragraphs: The young man answered: "Father, I understand your fear after such a dream, and I forgive it. But you have misread its meaning, and it is right that I explain. You say the dream warned I would die by an iron spear-point. But what hands does a boar have? What iron spear-point does a boar carry? If the dream had said I would die by a tusk or something like one, you would be right to do as you are doing. But it said a spear-point. Since we are fighting a beast and not men, let me go."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 40
paragraphs: Croesus replied: "My son, you have partly won me over with your reading of the dream. I change my mind. You may go to the hunt."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 41
paragraphs: Having said this, Croesus sent for Adrastos the Phrygian and told him: "Adrastos, when you were struck by a terrible misfortune—which I do not hold against you—I cleansed you. I took you into my house and have provided for all your needs. You owe me a kindness in return. I ask you to be my son's protector on this hunt, in case bandits attack you on the road. Besides, you ought to go where you can prove yourself through your deeds. That is your family's tradition, and you have the strength for it."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 42
paragraphs: Adrastos replied: "O king, normally I would not enter such a contest. It is not fitting for a man suffering my kind of misfortune to seek the company of those who are thriving. I have no desire for it, and for many reasons I would have held back. But you press me, and I owe you a debt of kindness. I am ready. You can expect your son to come home unharmed, as far as his protector can ensure it."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 43
paragraphs: After this exchange, they set out with a band of young men and hunting dogs. When they reached Mount Olympos, they tracked down the boar. Finding it, they formed a circle and began hurling spears. Then the guest—Adrastos, the man cleansed of manslaughter—threw his spear. He missed the boar and struck the son of Croesus. The dream's prophecy was fulfilled. A runner raced to Sardis to bring Croesus the news of the battle and his son's death. Croesus was shattered. What made it even more unbearable was that his son had been killed by the very man he himself had cleansed. In his anguish, he called upon Zeus as purifier, protesting the wrong done to him by his guest. He called on the god as protector of suppliants and guardian of friendship—the same god, under different names. As protector of suppliants, because by taking the stranger into his home, he had unknowingly sheltered his son's killer. As guardian of friendship, because the man he sent as protector had turned out to be his worst enemy.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 44
paragraphs: The Lydians arrived carrying the body, with the killer walking behind. Adrastos stood before the corpse and surrendered himself to Croesus. He stretched out his hands and begged the king to slaughter him over the body. He spoke of his earlier misfortune and said that on top of it, he had now destroyed the man who had cleansed him. Life was no longer worth living. But Croesus, despite his own immense grief, pitied Adrastos and said: "Guest, I have already received full satisfaction from you, since you condemn yourself to death. You are not the true cause of this evil, except that you were its unwilling instrument. Some god is responsible—the same god who warned me long ago what would happen." Croesus buried his son with all due honor. But Adrastos, son of Gordias, grandson of Midas—the slayer of his own brother, the slayer of the man who had cleansed him—when silence had fallen around the tomb and all the mourners had left, recognizing that he was the most wretched man alive, killed himself on the grave.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 45
paragraphs: For two years, Croesus sat in mourning for his son. Then the overthrow of Astyages, son of Kyaxares, by Cyrus, son of Cambyses—and the growing power of the Persians—roused Croesus from his grief. He began to think about cutting short Persian power before it grew too great.

With this plan in mind, he set about testing the oracles: those in Greece and the one in Libya. He sent messengers in every direction—some to Delphi, others to Abai in Phocis, others to Dodona. Some went to the shrines of Amphiaraos and Trophonios. Others went to Branchidai in Milesian territory. These were the Greek oracles Croesus consulted. He also sent messengers to the shrine of Ammon in Libya. His purpose was to test the oracles' knowledge. If any proved accurate, he would send again with the real question: whether he should march against the Persians.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 46
paragraphs: He gave the Lydian messengers these instructions: from the day they left Sardis, they should count the days. On the hundredth day, they should consult the oracles with this question: what is Croesus, son of Alyattes, king of the Lydians, doing right now? Whatever each oracle answered, they should write it down and bring it back. What the other oracles said is not recorded. But at Delphi, the moment the Lydians entered the sanctuary and asked their question, the priestess spoke in hexameter verse:

"I know the number of grains of sand and the measure of the ocean. I understand the mute and hear the one who does not speak. A smell has reached me: a hard-shelled tortoise boiling in a bronze cauldron, together with lamb's flesh. Bronze lies beneath it, and bronze covers it above."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 47
paragraphs: When the priestess had spoken, the Lydians wrote down the prophecy and hurried back to Sardis. As the other messengers also returned with their answers, Croesus opened each one and read it. None of them satisfied him. But when he heard the response from Delphi, he immediately accepted it and declared that the Delphic Oracle was the only true one—because it had discovered exactly what he had done. After sending out his messengers, he had thought up something impossible to guess: he had personally cut up a tortoise and a lamb and boiled them together in a bronze cauldron with a bronze lid.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 48
paragraphs: That was the answer from Delphi. As for the oracle of Amphiaraos, I cannot say what reply he gave the Lydians after they performed the customary rites at his temple. There is no record. I can only say that Croesus believed this oracle, too, possessed true knowledge.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 49
paragraphs: After this, Croesus tried to win over the god at Delphi with enormous sacrifices. He slaughtered three thousand animals of every kind suitable for offering. He piled up couches plated with gold and silver, golden cups, and purple robes on a great pyre and burned them all, hoping to secure the god's favor. He also called on every Lydian to sacrifice whatever he could. When the sacrifices were done, he melted down a vast quantity of gold and cast it into one hundred and seventeen half-bricks, each six palms long, three palms wide, and one palm high. Four of these were pure gold, each weighing two and a half talents. The rest were gold alloyed with silver, each weighing two talents. He also had a lion of pure gold made, weighing ten talents. When the temple at Delphi later burned down, this lion fell from the half-bricks on which it stood. It now sits in the Corinthian treasury, weighing only six and a half talents—three and a half talents having melted away in the fire.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 50
paragraphs: Croesus sent all of this to Delphi, along with much more: two enormous mixing bowls, one gold and one silver. The gold one was placed to the right as you enter the temple, the silver one to the left. Both were moved after the temple fire. The gold bowl now sits in the treasury of the people of Clazomenai, weighing eight and a half talents plus twelve extra pounds. The silver one stands in the corner of the vestibule and holds six hundred amphors—the Delphians fill it with wine for the festival of the Theophania. The Delphians say it is the work of Theodoros the Samian, and I believe them. The craftsmanship is clearly exceptional. Croesus also sent four silver wine jars, now in the Corinthian treasury, and two vessels for holy water—one gold, one silver. The gold one bears the inscription "from the Spartans," who claim it as their offering. But they are wrong. This too came from Croesus. A man of Delphi wrote the inscription to please the Spartans. I know his name but will not mention it. The bronze boy through whose hands the water flows is indeed a Spartan gift, but neither of the water vessels came from them. Along with these, Croesus sent many other offerings not specially distinguished, including round silver castings and a golden statue of a woman three cubits tall, which the Delphians say represents Croesus' baker. He also dedicated the jewelry from his wife's neck and her girdles.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 51
paragraphs: Those were the gifts Croesus sent to Delphi. To Amphiaraos, having heard of his courage and his tragic fate, he dedicated a shield made entirely of gold and a spear of solid gold—shaft, blade, and both points. Both offerings were still at Thebes in the temple of Ismenian Apollo in my own time.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 52
paragraphs: Croesus instructed the Lydians carrying these gifts to ask the oracles one more question: should Croesus march against the Persians, and if so, should he seek a military ally? When the Lydians arrived and dedicated the offerings, they put the question: "Croesus, king of the Lydians and other nations, considers yours the only true oracles among men. He gives you gifts worthy of your revelations and asks again: should he march against the Persians, and should he seek allies?" Both oracles gave the same answer. They told Croesus that if he marched against the Persians, he would destroy a great empire. They also advised him to find the most powerful of the Greeks and ally with them.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 53
paragraphs: When these answers reached Croesus, he was delighted with the oracles. Fully expecting to destroy the empire of Cyrus, he sent again to Delphi. Having determined the number of citizens there, he gave each man two gold coins. In return, the Delphians granted Croesus and all Lydians priority in consulting the oracle, exemption from all fees, front-row seats at the games, and the permanent right for any Lydian to become a citizen of Delphi.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 54
paragraphs: After these gifts, Croesus consulted the oracle a third time. Once he had confirmed its reliability, he used it heavily. This time he asked whether his rule would last a long time. The priestess answered in verse:
"When a mule becomes king of the Medes, then, tender-footed Lydian, flee along the pebbly Hermos. Do not linger, and feel no shame at being called a coward."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 55
paragraphs: These lines pleased Croesus more than anything, since he assumed a mule could never become king of the Medes. He and his descendants would rule forever. He then turned to finding the most powerful Greek state to befriend. His inquiries showed that the Spartans and the Athenians held the lead—the Spartans among the Dorians, the Athenians among the Ionians. These were the two most distinguished peoples of ancient times: one originally Pelasgian, the other Hellenic. The Pelasgian race never migrated, while the Hellenic was constantly on the move. Under Deucalion they lived in Phthiotis. Under Doros, son of Hellen, they settled in the region below Ossa and Olympos called Histiaiotis. Driven out by the sons of Cadmos, they lived in Pindos and were called Macednians. They later moved to Dryopis, and from there finally to the Peloponnese, where they became known as Dorians.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 56
paragraphs: What language the Pelasgians spoke, I cannot say with certainty. But if we may judge from the Pelasgians who still survive—those at Creston above the Tyrsenians (who were once neighbors of the Dorians when the Dorians lived in what is now called Thessaliotis), those who settled at Plakia and Skylake on the Hellespont (who had formerly lived among the Athenians), and the people of various other towns that are Pelasgian in origin though they have lost the name—then the Pelasgians spoke a non-Greek language. If this is true of the whole race, then the Attic people, being Pelasgian, must have changed their language when they became Hellenic. The people of Creston do not speak the same language as their neighbors, nor do the people of Plakia. But both speak the same language as each other. This proves they preserved the language they brought with them when they migrated to those places.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 57
paragraphs: The Hellenic race, as far as I can tell, has always spoken the same language from its beginning. It started small when it first separated from the Pelasgians, but grew into a great number of peoples, mainly by absorbing many non-Greek tribes. The Pelasgians, by contrast, never grew very much so long as they remained non-Greek.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 58
paragraphs: Of these two peoples, Croesus learned that the Athenians were divided and oppressed under the tyranny of Peisistratos, son of Hippocrates. A great marvel had occurred when Hippocrates, still a private citizen, went to watch the Olympic games. After he made his sacrifice, the cauldrons standing on the hearth—full of meat and water—boiled over without any fire beneath them. Chilon the Spartan, who happened to witness this, advised Hippocrates either not to marry and have children, or if he already had a wife, to divorce her, and if he had a son, to disown him. Hippocrates ignored the advice. In time, Peisistratos was born to him. When Athens was torn by faction—the coastal party led by Megacles, son of Alcmaion, and the plains party by Lycurgos, son of Aristolaides—Peisistratos aimed at seizing power for himself by organizing a third party, the hill men. He devised this scheme: he wounded himself and his mules, then drove his cart into the marketplace, claiming his enemies had tried to kill him on the road. He asked the people for a bodyguard. He already had a reputation from commanding the war against Megara, during which he had captured Nisaea. The Athenian commons, taken in, granted him a guard—not spearmen but club-bearers, who followed him carrying wooden clubs. With their help, Peisistratos seized the Acropolis. He then ruled Athens without disturbing the existing officials or changing the laws, governing fairly and well under the existing constitution.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 59
paragraphs: Before long, the followers of Megacles and Lycurgos joined forces and drove Peisistratos out. That was how he first won and lost Athens. But the two factions that expelled him soon fell out with each other again. Megacles, harassed by the infighting, sent a message to Peisistratos: would he marry Megacles' daughter in exchange for becoming tyrant again? Peisistratos accepted. Then they devised what I consider the most foolish trick imaginable—especially since the Greeks are supposed to be cleverer than other peoples, and the Athenians the cleverest of all Greeks. In the village of Paiania lived a woman named Phya, nearly six feet tall and strikingly beautiful. They dressed her in full armor, placed her in a chariot, and coached her in how to carry herself. Then they drove to the city, with heralds running ahead and calling out: "People of Athens, welcome Peisistratos! Athena herself honors him above all men and is bringing him back to her Acropolis!" The heralds spread this message everywhere. Word reached the countryside that Athena was personally escorting Peisistratos home. The people in the city, believing this woman was the actual goddess, worshipped her and welcomed Peisistratos back.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 60
paragraphs: Having regained power this way, Peisistratos married Megacles' daughter as agreed. But since he already had grown sons and since the Alcmaionid family was said to be under a curse, he did not want children by his new wife. He therefore had relations with her in an abnormal way. The woman kept this secret at first, but eventually told her mother, who told Megacles. He was furious at the insult. In his anger, he immediately reconciled with his old political enemies. When Peisistratos learned what was happening, he fled the country entirely and went to Eretria, where he conferred with his sons. Hippias' advice prevailed: they would try to win back the tyranny. They began collecting money from cities that owed them favors. Many contributed generously, but the Thebans gave the most. To make a long story short, time passed, and everything was prepared for their return. Argive mercenaries came from the Peloponnese. A man from Naxos named Lygdamis volunteered, bringing both money and men with great enthusiasm.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 61
paragraphs: Setting out from Eretria after ten years in exile, they returned. Their first landing was at Marathon in Attica. While they camped there, supporters from the city joined them, along with people from the surrounding villages who preferred tyranny to freedom. These forces gathered, while the Athenians in the city paid no attention—not while Peisistratos was raising money, not even when he seized Marathon. Only when they heard he was marching from Marathon toward Athens did they mobilize. The two armies met near the temple of Athena Pallenis. There, moved by divine inspiration, a soothsayer named Amphilytos of Acarnania approached Peisistratos and spoke to him in verse:
"The cast has been made, the net is spread wide. In the moonlit night, the tuna will come darting through."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 62
paragraphs: Peisistratos understood the prophecy, accepted it, and led his army forward. The Athenians from the city happened to be eating their midday meal at that moment. Some had already finished and were playing dice or napping. Peisistratos' forces fell on them and routed them. As they fled, Peisistratos devised a brilliant tactic to keep them scattered and prevent them from regrouping. He sent his sons ahead on horseback. Overtaking the fugitives, they delivered Peisistratos' message: go home in peace, each man to his own house.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 63
paragraphs: The Athenians obeyed. So Peisistratos seized Athens for the third time and firmly rooted his tyranny. He secured it with foreign mercenaries and a steady flow of revenue from local sources and from the region around the river Strymon. He also took hostages—the sons of Athenians who had stayed behind rather than fleeing—and placed them in the care of the Naxians, for he had conquered Naxos too and put Lygdamis in charge. He also purified the island of Delos, following the oracles. He dug up all the dead bodies buried within sight of the temple and moved them to another part of the island. So Peisistratos became tyrant of Athens. Some Athenians had fallen in battle. Others, including the sons of Alcmaion, were in exile.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 64
paragraphs: That was how things stood in Athens at the time Croesus was gathering information. As for the Spartans, he learned that they had overcome their troubles and were now winning their war against Tegea. Under kings Leon and Hegesicles, the Spartans had succeeded in every war except the one against Tegea. Before that, they had actually possessed the worst laws of almost any Greek state, both in their internal affairs and in their refusal to deal with foreigners. Their change to good government came about through Lycurgos. When this greatly respected Spartan visited the Oracle at Delphi, the moment he entered the sanctuary the priestess spoke:
"You have come, Lycurgos, to my rich temple, beloved by Zeus and all the gods of Olympos. I am uncertain whether to call you god or man in my prophecy. But I think rather a god, Lycurgos."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 65
paragraphs: Some add that the priestess also revealed to Lycurgos the entire Spartan constitution as it now exists. But the Spartans themselves say that Lycurgos, as guardian of his nephew Leobotes (then king of Sparta), brought these reforms from Crete. The moment he became guardian, he changed every law and took measures to prevent violations. After that, Lycurgos established the military institutions: the sworn bands, the companies of thirty, and the common meals. He also created the Ephors and the Senate. With these reforms, the Spartans gained excellent laws. After his death, they built a temple to Lycurgos and worship him greatly. With fertile land and no small population, they quickly prospered. Restless and confident in their strength, they consulted the Oracle at Delphi about conquering all of Arcadia. The priestess replied:

"You ask me for Arcadia? You ask for much. I refuse. Many tough, acorn-eating men live in Arcadia. They will stop you. But I am not grudging. I will give you Tegea, beaten with dancing feet, and a fine plain to measure out and divide."

When the Spartans heard this, they left the rest of Arcadia alone and marched against Tegea. Trusting the misleading oracle and expecting to enslave the Tegeans, they brought fetters with them. But they lost the battle. Those who were captured ended up wearing the very fetters they had brought and "measuring out" the plain of Tegea as forced laborers. Those fetters were still hanging in the temple of Athena Alea at Tegea in my own time.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 66
paragraphs: In that earlier war, the Spartans had struggled constantly against Tegea without success. But in the time of Croesus, under kings Anaxandrides and Ariston, they finally prevailed. Here is how it happened. After losing repeatedly, they sent to Delphi and asked which god they should appease to win the war. The priestess told them to bring home the bones of Orestes, son of Agamemnon. When they could not find the grave, they sent to Delphi again to ask where Orestes was buried. The priestess answered:

"In Arcadian Tegea, on level ground, two winds blow together under strong compulsion. Stroke meets counter-stroke, and trouble lies upon trouble. There the earth, giver of life, holds Agamemnon's son. Bring him home and you shall be master of Tegea."

Even after hearing this, the Spartans were nowhere closer to finding the bones, despite searching everywhere—until Lichas, one of the Spartans called "Benefactors," discovered them. The Benefactors were the five eldest citizens who retired each year from the cavalry. During that year, they were required to serve as roving agents of the Spartan state.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 67
paragraphs: Lichas, one of these Benefactors, found the grave in Tegea through a mix of luck and cleverness. During a period of truce with Tegea, he visited a forge and watched the smith working iron, marveling at the process. The smith noticed his wonder and said: "Friend from Sparta, if you are amazed by ironwork, you would truly have marveled at what I once saw. I was digging a well in this yard and hit a coffin seven cubits long. I could not believe men had ever been so large, so I opened it. The body inside was the full length of the coffin. I measured it, then filled the earth back in." Lichas thought carefully about what the smith described and concluded this must be the bones of Orestes, matching the oracle's riddle. The smith's two bellows were the two winds. The anvil and hammer were the stroke and counter-stroke. The iron being worked was trouble upon trouble—since iron was invented to humanity's harm. Having worked this out, he returned to Sparta and told the Spartans everything. They brought a trumped-up charge against him and banished him. He went back to Tegea, told the smith about his misfortune, and tried to rent the yard. The smith refused at first, but Lichas eventually persuaded him. He moved in, dug up the grave, gathered the bones, and took them back to Sparta. From that point on, whenever the Spartans and Tegeans clashed, the Spartans won decisively. By now they had subdued most of the Peloponnese.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 68
paragraphs: Informed of all this, Croesus sent envoys to Sparta with gifts to propose an alliance. They delivered this message: "Croesus, king of the Lydians and other nations, says: since the god's oracle told me to make the leading Greek power my friend, and since I learn that you hold that position, I invite you to become my friend and ally, sincerely and without deceit." The Spartans, who had themselves heard about the oracle given to Croesus, were glad when the Lydians arrived and exchanged oaths of friendship and alliance. They already had a connection with Croesus from an earlier occasion: the Spartans had sent to Sardis to buy gold for a statue of Apollo, the one now standing on Mount Thornax in Spartan territory. Croesus had given them the gold as a gift.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 69
paragraphs: For this reason, and because he had chosen them over all other Greeks, the Spartans accepted the alliance. They were ready when he called, and they also had a bronze mixing bowl made for him as a return gift. It was covered with figures around the rim and large enough to hold three hundred amphors. But this bowl never reached Sardis. Two versions of why are told. The Spartans say that when the bowl was on its way and came near Samos, the Samians sailed out with warships and seized it. The Samians say the Spartans carrying the bowl arrived too late—Sardis had already fallen and Croesus was a prisoner. So the Spartans sold the bowl on Samos, and private citizens there bought it and dedicated it in the temple of Hera. The sellers probably told the Spartans back home that the Samians had stolen it.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 70
paragraphs: That is the story of the mixing bowl. Meanwhile, Croesus—misreading the oracle—was marching into Cappadocia, expecting to overthrow Cyrus and the Persians. While he was preparing, one of the Lydians, a man already known for his wisdom, offered advice that made him even more famous. His name was Sandanis. He said: "O king, you are preparing to march against men who wear leather trousers and leather everything else. They eat not what they choose but what they can get from their harsh land. They drink water, not wine. They have no figs and nothing fine. If you conquer them, what will you take? They have nothing. But if they conquer you, think how much you will lose. Once they taste our luxuries, they will cling to them and never let go. For my part, I thank the gods for not putting it into Persian heads to attack the Lydians." This advice did not persuade Croesus. It is true, though, that before they conquered the Lydians, the Persians had no luxury or fine things at all.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 71
paragraphs: The Cappadocians are called Syrians by the Greeks. Before the Persians came to power, these Syrians were subjects of the Medes. Now they were subjects of Cyrus. The boundary between the Median and Lydian empires was the river Halys. It flows from the mountains of Armenia through Cilician territory, then passes between the Matienians on the right and the Phrygians on the left. Continuing northward, it separates the Cappadocian Syrians from the Paphlagonians. The Halys thus cuts off nearly all of lower Asia in a line running from the sea opposite Cyprus to the Euxine. This strip is the neck of the whole peninsula. The journey across takes five days for a man traveling light.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 72
paragraphs: Croesus marched into Cappadocia for several reasons. He wanted the land for himself, but above all he trusted the oracle and wished to avenge Astyages against Cyrus. Cyrus, son of Cambyses, had conquered Astyages and was holding him prisoner. Astyages was king of the Medes and brother-in-law to Croesus. Here is how they became related. A horde of Scythian nomads, quarreling with their own people, had sought refuge in Median territory. Kyaxares, son of Phraortes, son of Deïokes, ruled the Medes at that time. He treated the Scythians well, even entrusting boys to them to learn archery and their language. The Scythians went hunting regularly and always brought back game. But one day they returned empty-handed. Kyaxares, who had an ugly temper, treated them harshly and abusively. In response, the Scythians decided to kill one of the boys in their care, butcher him, prepare the flesh as they usually prepared wild game, and serve it to Kyaxares as if it were ordinary meat. After delivering it, they planned to flee immediately to Alyattes, son of Sadyattes, at Sardis. This is exactly what happened. Kyaxares and his dinner guests ate the flesh. The Scythians then fled and became suppliants of Alyattes.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 73
paragraphs: When Alyattes refused to surrender the Scythians despite Kyaxares' demands, war broke out between the Lydians and the Medes. It lasted five years. Each side won as often as it lost, and they even fought a battle at night. In the sixth year, during a battle, day suddenly turned to night. Thales of Miletos had predicted this event to the Ionians, naming the very year in which it would occur. When the Lydians and Medes saw day become night, they stopped fighting. Both sides became eager for peace. The mediators were Syennesis of Cilicia and Labynetos of Babylon. They arranged both the peace treaty and an exchange of marriages: Alyattes gave his daughter Aryenis to Astyages, son of Kyaxares, since agreements without strong family ties tend not to hold. These nations swear oaths in the same way as the Greeks, with one addition: they cut the skin of their arms and lick each other's blood.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 74
paragraphs: This Astyages, then—Croesus' mother's father—had been conquered and imprisoned by Cyrus, for reasons I will explain later. This was the grievance Croesus held against Cyrus when he consulted the oracles about marching against Persia. When a misleading answer came back, he assumed it was favorable and invaded Persian territory. When Croesus reached the river Halys, he crossed it—by the existing bridges, according to my account. But the popular Greek version says Thales of Miletos got the army across. The Greeks say Croesus was stuck because there were no bridges yet. Thales, who was traveling with the army, diverted the river by digging a deep crescent-shaped channel upstream of the camp. The river split into two branches, both shallow enough to ford. Some say the original channel dried up completely. But I do not believe that—for how then did they cross on their way back?

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 75
paragraphs: After crossing the Halys, Croesus arrived at Pteria in Cappadocia, the strongest fortress in the region, situated roughly in line with the city of Sinope on the Euxine. He set up camp and ravaged Syrian farmland. He captured the city of Pteria and sold its people into slavery. He took all the surrounding towns as well, driving the innocent Syrians from their homes. Meanwhile, Cyrus gathered his own forces along with all the peoples living in between and marched to meet Croesus. Before setting out, he had sent heralds to the Ionians, trying to persuade them to revolt against Croesus. The Ionians refused. When Cyrus arrived and encamped opposite Croesus, the two armies clashed in the territory of Pteria. The fighting was fierce, with heavy losses on both sides. When night fell, neither side had won.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 76
paragraphs: The two armies had fought to a draw. Croesus was unhappy with the size of his force, which was much smaller than Cyrus'. Since Cyrus did not advance the next day, Croesus marched back to Sardis. He planned to call on the Egyptians under their treaty (he had an alliance with Amasis, king of Egypt, predating his Spartan alliance) and to summon the Babylonians (he had an alliance with their king Labynetos too). He would also send word to the Spartans to arrive at a set date. Once these allies assembled and his own army regrouped, he intended to wait out the winter and march against the Persians in spring. With this plan in mind, as soon as he reached Sardis, he sent heralds to his allies calling them to gather in five months. He disbanded his existing army of mercenaries completely. He never imagined that Cyrus, after fighting to such an even result, would actually march on Sardis.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 77
paragraphs: While Croesus was making these plans, the outskirts of the city suddenly filled with snakes. When the snakes appeared, the horses abandoned their usual pastures and came to devour them. Croesus recognized this as a portent and sent messengers to the oracle interpreters at Telmessos. The messengers arrived and learned the meaning, but could not report back in time—Croesus was captured before they returned. The Telmessians had declared that a foreign army would invade Croesus' land and subdue the native people. The snake, they said, was a child of the soil, while the horse was a foreign enemy. The Telmessians gave this interpretation after Croesus was already a prisoner, knowing nothing yet of what had happened at Sardis.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 78
paragraphs: As soon as Croesus withdrew after the battle at Pteria, Cyrus learned that Croesus intended to disband his army. He calculated that his best move was to march on Sardis as fast as possible, before the Lydians could reassemble. He acted without delay. He led his army into Lydia so swiftly that he himself was the first messenger of his own arrival. Croesus was in desperate straits—everything had gone contrary to his expectations—but he still led the Lydians out to battle. At that time, no people in Asia were braver or tougher in combat than the Lydians. They fought on horseback, carrying long spears, and were superb riders.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 79
paragraphs: The two armies met on the wide, open plain before Sardis, through which several rivers flow—including the Hyllos—all joining the largest, the Hermos, which rises from the mountain sacred to the Mother Goddess of Dindymos and empties into the sea at Phocaea. When Cyrus saw the Lydians forming for battle, he feared their cavalry. On the advice of Harpagos, a Mede, he gathered all the baggage camels from his supply train, unloaded them, and mounted men on them in cavalry gear. He ordered this camel corps to advance first against Croesus' horsemen, with the infantry behind and the main cavalry behind that. He told his men to spare no Lydian who stood in their way, but not to kill Croesus—even if he resisted capture. He used the camels because horses fear the camel: they cannot stand the sight or smell. This was a trick to neutralize Croesus' cavalry, the very force on which the Lydian king was counting most. It worked perfectly. When the two sides met and the horses caught scent of the camels, they wheeled and fled. Croesus' hopes were shattered. But the Lydians did not turn coward. When they saw what was happening, they leaped from their horses and fought the Persians on foot. Eventually, after heavy casualties on both sides, the Lydians broke and were driven behind their walls. The Persians besieged them.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 80
paragraphs: The siege was underway. Croesus, expecting it to last a long time, sent new messengers from the fortress to his allies. The earlier messengers had asked them to gather at Sardis in five months. These new ones begged them to come immediately, since Croesus was under siege.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 81
paragraphs: He sent to all his allies, including the Spartans. But the Spartans had their own problem at just that time: a dispute with Argos over the district of Thyrea. The Spartans had seized Thyrea from Argive territory. At that time, the Argives controlled the entire western coast down to Cape Malea, including the mainland regions, the island of Kythera, and other islands. When the Argives came to defend their stolen land, the two sides agreed to settle the matter by a combat of three hundred champions from each side. The losing nation's army would go home. Both main armies withdrew, leaving only the six hundred fighters. They fought and proved evenly matched. By nightfall, only three men remained alive: two Argives—Alkenor and Chromios—and one Spartan, Othryades. The two Argives, believing they had won, ran to Argos to report their victory. But the Spartan Othryades stayed on the field, stripped the Argive dead, and carried their weapons back to his own camp. The next day, both sides returned and claimed victory. The Argives said more of their men survived. The Spartans said the Argive survivors had fled while their man held the field and stripped the dead. The argument escalated into a full battle, which the Spartans won. After this, the Argives cut their hair short—whereas before they had been required to wear it long—and passed a law that no Argive man could grow his hair long or Argive woman wear gold jewelry until Thyrea was recovered. The Spartans adopted the opposite custom: from that day on they wore their hair long, which they had not done before. As for Othryades, the sole Spartan survivor, they say he was too ashamed to go home when all his comrades had fallen, and killed himself on the battlefield at Thyrea.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 82
paragraphs: That was the situation in Sparta when the herald arrived from Sardis asking them to rescue Croesus from his siege. Despite their own problems, the Spartans prepared to help as soon as they heard the news. Their ships were ready and their forces assembled. But then a second message arrived: the Lydian fortress had fallen and Croesus was a prisoner. They abandoned their efforts with deep regret, treating the news as a great calamity.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 83
paragraphs: The fall of Sardis happened this way. On the fourteenth day of the siege, Cyrus sent horsemen through his army announcing rewards for the first man to scale the wall. The army attacked but failed. After everyone else had given up, a Mardian soldier named Hyroiades attempted to climb the part of the citadel where no guard had been posted. No one had thought the fortress could be taken from there because the cliff was sheer and unassailable. The former king Meles, acting on the Telmessians' advice that carrying a lion around the walls would make Sardis impregnable, had carried the lion—born to his concubine—along every section of the wall except this one, which he skipped as too steep to need protection. It faces Mount Tmolos. The day before, Hyroiades had watched a Lydian soldier climb down that very cliff to retrieve a dropped helmet. He noted the path. Now he climbed up, and others followed. Many Persians made it up after him. Sardis was taken, and the entire city was plundered.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 84
paragraphs: As for Croesus himself, this is what happened. He had a son—the one I mentioned before—who was fine in every way but unable to speak. In his earlier prosperity, Croesus had tried everything for the boy. Among other efforts, he sent to Delphi to ask about him. The priestess replied:

"Lydian, lord of many, foolish Croesus—do not wish to hear in your halls that long-prayed-for voice of your son. Far better for you if it stayed silent. For his first words will be spoken on a day of disaster."

When the fortress was being stormed, a Persian soldier rushed at Croesus, not recognizing him, and was about to kill him. Croesus, crushed by his misfortune, saw the man coming and did not care—he was indifferent to being struck down. But his mute son, seeing the Persian charging, was seized by such terror and anguish that the bonds on his voice broke. He cried out: "Soldier, do not kill Croesus!" Those were his first words. After that, he could speak for the rest of his life.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 85
paragraphs: The Persians captured Sardis and took Croesus prisoner. He had reigned fourteen years and been besieged fourteen days, fulfilling the oracle by destroying his own great empire. They brought him before Cyrus. Cyrus had a great pyre built and ordered Croesus, bound in chains, to mount it, along with fourteen Lydian boys. Perhaps he meant this as an offering of first-fruits to some god. Perhaps he was fulfilling a vow. Or perhaps, having heard that Croesus was a god-fearing man, he wanted to test whether any divine power would save him from burning alive. Whatever his reason, that is what he did. As Croesus stood on the pyre, in the worst of circumstances, the words of Solon came flooding back to him: no living person can be called happy. He sighed deeply, groaned aloud, and after a long silence, called out the name "Solon" three times. Cyrus heard this and ordered his interpreters to ask who Solon was. Croesus was silent at first. When pressed, he said: "A man I would have given a fortune for every king on earth to meet." Since this was cryptic, they pressed further. Croesus explained how Solon the Athenian had once visited, surveyed all his wealth, and dismissed it. Everything had turned out just as Solon predicted—though Solon was speaking not about Croesus specifically, but about the human condition, and especially about those who consider themselves happy. While Croesus told this story, the pyre had been lit and the edges were already burning. When Cyrus heard the interpreters' translation, he had a change of heart. He realized that he too was a mortal, and here he was burning alive another man who had once been no less fortunate than himself. Fearing divine retribution and reflecting that nothing in life is secure, he ordered the fire extinguished immediately and Croesus brought down. But his men could no longer control the flames.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 86
paragraphs: The Lydians say that Croesus, seeing Cyrus had changed his mind but that the fire could not be stopped, cried out to Apollo. If any of his many gifts had ever pleased the god, let Apollo come now and rescue him. As he wept and prayed, the sky—which had been clear and calm—suddenly clouded over. A violent storm burst, rain poured down, and the fire was extinguished. Cyrus, now convinced that Croesus was a good man beloved by the gods, had him brought down from the pyre and asked: "Croesus, who persuaded you to invade my land and become my enemy instead of my friend?" Croesus replied: "O king, I did it to your good fortune and my own ruin. The god of the Greeks is to blame—he encouraged me to march. No one is fool enough to prefer war to peace. In peace, sons bury their fathers. In war, fathers bury their sons. But the gods, it seems, willed it so."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 87
paragraphs: Cyrus freed Croesus from his chains and seated him nearby, treating him with great respect. Everyone around marveled at the sight. Croesus sat deep in thought. Then he turned and saw the Persians plundering the city of the Lydians. He said: "O king, should I speak my mind, or should I hold my tongue in my present condition?" Cyrus told him to speak freely. Croesus asked: "What is that great mob doing so eagerly?" Cyrus replied: "They are plundering your city and carrying off your wealth." Croesus answered: "Not my city and not my wealth. I own nothing anymore. It is your property they are plundering."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 88
paragraphs: This struck Cyrus. He dismissed his attendants and asked Croesus privately what he meant. Croesus said: "Since the gods have made me your slave, I think it right to share what insight I have. The Persians are wild by nature and poor. If you let them plunder and possess great wealth, expect this: whoever seizes the largest share will rebel against you. If my advice pleases you, do this. Post guards from your personal bodyguard at every gate. Have them confiscate the loot, telling the soldiers that a tenth must be offered to Zeus. This way you will not be hated for taking the goods by force, and the soldiers will willingly give them up, recognizing the justice of it."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 89
paragraphs: Cyrus was extremely pleased. He praised Croesus warmly and ordered his guards to carry out the plan. Then he said: "Croesus, since you are ready to offer good deeds and wise advice like the king you are, ask me for any gift and you shall have it at once." Croesus replied: "Master, the greatest favor you could do me is to let me send these chains to the god of the Greeks whom I honored above all others, and ask him whether it is his custom to deceive those who serve him well." Cyrus asked what complaint he had against the god. Croesus told the whole story: his thoughts, the oracles' answers, his lavish offerings, and how the prophecy had encouraged him to attack Persia. Then he repeated his request. Cyrus laughed and said: "You shall have this and anything else you ever want from me." Croesus sent Lydians to Delphi with instructions to lay the chains on the temple threshold and ask the god whether he felt no shame for encouraging Croesus to attack the Persians, promising he would destroy an empire—and showing these chains as the spoils of that empire. They were also to ask whether Greek gods thought ingratitude was acceptable.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 90
paragraphs: When the Lydians arrived and delivered their questions, the priestess reportedly answered: "Not even a god can escape fate. Croesus has paid the debt for his ancestor in the fifth generation—that ancestor who, though a bodyguard of the Heracleidai, followed a woman's treacherous scheme, murdered his king, and seized a throne that was not his by right. Apollo had earnestly wished to delay the fall of Sardis until after Croesus' lifetime, sparing his sons instead. But he could not bend the Fates. What the Fates allowed, Apollo gave: he delayed the capture of Sardis by three years. Let Croesus know he was taken prisoner three years later than fate decreed. Furthermore, Apollo saved him on the burning pyre. As for the oracle, Croesus has no grounds for complaint. Apollo told him that if he marched against Persia, he would destroy a great empire. If he had wanted to decide wisely, he should have sent back to ask whether the god meant his own empire or that of Cyrus. He failed to understand the answer and failed to ask again. Let him blame himself. When he consulted the oracle for the last time, Apollo spoke of a mule—and Croesus failed to understand that too. The mule was Cyrus himself, born of parents from two different peoples. His mother was a Mede, daughter of Astyages, king of the Medes. His father was a Persian, a man of a subject people. He was inferior in every way, yet he was husband to his own royal mistress." The Lydians brought this answer back to Sardis and told Croesus. He acknowledged that the fault was his own, not the god's. That is how the empire of Croesus ended and how Ionia was first conquered.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 91
paragraphs: There are many other offerings by Croesus in Greece beyond those I have already mentioned. At Thebes in Boeotia, he dedicated a golden tripod to Ismenian Apollo. At Ephesus, there are the golden cows and most of the temple pillars. In the temple of Athena Pronaia at Delphi, there is a large golden shield. These were still in place in my own time. Other offerings have been lost. His offerings at Branchidai in Milesian territory were, I am told, equal in weight and similar in kind to those at Delphi. The gifts he sent to Delphi and to the shrine of Amphiaraos came from his own wealth, the first-fruits of his inheritance. But the other offerings were made from the property of an enemy—a man who had conspired against Croesus before he became king, trying to make Pantaleon ruler of Lydia instead. Pantaleon was a son of Alyattes and half-brother to Croesus, but by a different mother: Croesus was born to a Carian woman, Pantaleon to an Ionian. When Croesus won the kingdom by his father's choice, he executed his rival by drawing him across a carding comb.
