The man's property, which Croesus had earlier vowed to dedicate, he offered to the shrines I have named. That is enough about his offerings.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 92
paragraphs: The land of Lydia has no great marvels to record compared with other countries, apart from the gold dust washed down from Mount Tmolos. But it does have one structure larger than any other except those in Egypt and Babylon: the tomb of Alyattes, father of Croesus. Its base is made of enormous stones. The rest is a mound of piled earth. It was built by contributions from three groups: merchants, craftsmen, and the working girls. In my time, five boundary stones still stood on top of the monument, inscribed with how much each group contributed. By measurement, the working girls' share was the largest. The common people's daughters in Lydia all practiced prostitution to earn their dowries, continuing until they married. They chose their own husbands. The monument's circumference is six furlongs and two hundred feet. Its width is thirteen hundred feet. Beside it lies a large lake, said to never run dry, called the Lake of Gyges. Such is this monument.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 93
paragraphs: The Lydians have customs very similar to the Greeks, except that they prostitute their daughters. They were the first people, as far as we know, to strike and use gold and silver coins. They were also the first retail traders. The Lydians themselves claim that the games now played by both them and the Greeks were also their invention. They say these games were devised at the same time they colonized Tyrrhenia. Their account is as follows: during the reign of Atys, son of Manes, a terrible famine struck all of Lydia. The Lydians endured it for a while, but when it continued, they looked for remedies. Various people came up with various ideas. That is when they invented dice, knucklebones, ball games, and every other game except board games (which they do not claim). They used these games as a weapon against hunger: on one day they would play all day to forget their need for food, and on the next day they would eat. They carried on like this for eighteen years. When the famine only grew worse, the king divided the entire Lydian people into two groups, chosen by lot. One half would stay, the other would emigrate. The king placed himself over those who stayed. His son Tyrsenos led those who left. The departing group went down to the coast at Smyrna, built ships, loaded everything they owned, and sailed off in search of a new homeland. After passing many peoples, they finally reached the land of the Umbrians, where they founded cities and still live today. They dropped the name Lydian and called themselves Tyrsenians, after the prince who led them.
The Lydians, then, had been made subject to the Persians.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 94
paragraphs: Our narrative now turns to Cyrus: who was this man who destroyed the empire of Croesus, and how did the Persians come to lead Asia? I will follow the account of those Persians who want to tell the truth about Cyrus rather than glorify him. I could present three other versions of the story, but this is the one I choose.

The Assyrians ruled upper Asia for five hundred and twenty years. The Medes were the first to revolt. They fought the Assyrians for their freedom, proved their valor, cast off the yoke of slavery, and won their independence. After them, the other nations did the same. All the peoples on the continent were free for a time. But then they slid back into despotic rule, and this is how it happened.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 95
paragraphs: A man of great ability appeared among the Medes. His name was Deïokes, son of Phraortes. Deïokes wanted absolute power, and he went about getting it like this. The Medes at that time lived in scattered villages. Deïokes, already well-respected in his own village, devoted himself to dispensing justice with even more care than before—though lawlessness was rampant throughout Media and he knew that injustice always wars with justice. The Medes of his village chose him as their judge. Since he was aiming at power, he judged every case with strict fairness. His fellow citizens praised him so highly that people in other villages—who had been suffering from crooked judgments—began eagerly coming to Deïokes to have their disputes settled. Eventually, no one would trust anyone else.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 96
paragraphs: As more and more people came to him, seeing that his judgments were always fair, Deïokes refused to continue. He would no longer sit in his customary seat to hear cases. He said it was not in his interest to neglect his own affairs to spend all day judging his neighbors' disputes. With his guidance gone, robbery and lawlessness grew even worse than before. The Medes assembled and discussed their situation. The friends of Deïokes spoke persuasively: "Since we cannot live in this land under the current conditions, let us appoint a king from among ourselves. Then the land will be well governed, we can get back to work, and we will not be destroyed by lawlessness." With such arguments, they persuaded the assembly to accept a monarchy.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 97
paragraphs: When they asked who should be king, everyone proposed and praised Deïokes until they agreed he was the man. He ordered them to build a palace worthy of royalty and give him a bodyguard of spearmen. The Medes did so. They built him a large, strong palace in the location he chose and allowed him to select his guards from the entire Median population. Once in power, he compelled the Medes to build a single fortified city and focus their attention on it, paying less regard to the others. The Medes obeyed. He built great, strong walls arranged in concentric circles, each ring higher than the one outside it by the height of its battlements. The hilltop site helped achieve this effect, but it was mostly achieved by design. There were seven circles in all. Within the innermost circle stood the royal palace and the treasuries. The outermost wall was roughly the same circumference as the wall around Athens. The battlements of each ring were painted a different color: white for the first circle, black for the second, crimson for the third, blue for the fourth, red for the fifth. The last two circles had their battlements plated with silver and gold.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 98
paragraphs: Deïokes built these walls around his palace. The rest of the people were ordered to live outside the walls. When the building was complete, he established a protocol—the first of its kind. No one was permitted to enter the king's presence. All business was conducted through messengers. No one could see the king. Laughing or spitting in his presence was forbidden for everyone without exception. He wrapped himself in this ceremony so that his former companions—men raised alongside him, of equally good families and no less courageous—would not grow resentful at seeing him and plot against him. If they could not see him, they might come to think of him as a different kind of being.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 99
paragraphs: Having established these customs and secured his tyranny, Deïokes was severe in enforcing justice. People wrote down their cases and sent them into his presence. He judged them and sent his decisions back out. He also arranged a system of informers and spies throughout his entire kingdom. If he heard of anyone causing trouble, he summoned the offender and punished him as the crime deserved.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 100
paragraphs: Deïokes united the Median nation under his sole rule. The Median tribes are as follows: the Busai, Paretakenians, Struchates, Arizantians, Budians, and Magians. Those are all the tribes of the Medes.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 101
paragraphs: The son of Deïokes was Phraortes. When Deïokes died after a reign of fifty-three years, Phraortes took power. Not content to rule the Medes alone, he marched against the Persians. They were the first people he attacked, and the first he made subject to the Medes. Ruling these two strong nations, he set about conquering Asia, subduing one people after another, until finally he marched against the Assyrians—those Assyrians who lived at Nineveh. They had once ruled everything, but now their allies had all revolted, leaving them isolated, though still prosperous at home. Phraortes attacked them and was killed, along with most of his army, after a reign of twenty-two years.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 102
paragraphs: After Phraortes died, his son Kyaxares took power. He is said to have been far more warlike than his ancestors. He was the first to organize Asian armies into separate divisions—spearmen, archers, and cavalry—where before they had all been mixed together. He was the king who fought the Lydians on the day that turned to night, and who united all of Asia above the Halys under his rule. Gathering all his subjects, he marched on Nineveh to avenge his father and conquer the city. He defeated the Assyrians in battle. But while he was besieging Nineveh, a vast Scythian army invaded, led by Madyas, son of Protothyes. The Scythians had entered Asia after driving the Cimmerians from Europe. Pursuing the fleeing Cimmerians, they arrived in Median territory.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 103
paragraphs: From Lake Maeotis to the river Phasis and the land of the Colchians is a thirty-day journey for a man traveling light. From Colchis it is not far to cross into Media, since only one nation—the Saspeires—lies between them. The Scythians, however, did not enter by this route. They turned aside and took the far longer upper road, keeping the Caucasus mountains on their right. The Medes met the Scythians in battle, lost, and fell under Scythian rule. The Scythians then controlled all of Asia.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 104
paragraphs: From there the Scythians advanced on Egypt. When they reached Palestine in Syria, Psammetichos the king of Egypt met them with gifts and pleas, persuading them not to go any further. As they marched back through Syria, they passed the city of Askalon. Most of the Scythians went through without causing harm, but some stragglers plundered the temple of Aphrodite Ourania. I have learned that this is the oldest of all temples dedicated to this goddess—the temple in Cyprus was founded from it, and the one on Kythera was founded by Phoenicians from Syria. The Scythians who robbed the temple at Askalon were cursed by the goddess. She struck them and all their descendants with a disease that made them like women. The Scythians themselves admit this and say it is the reason for the affliction. Visitors to Askalon can see these people for themselves. The Scythians call them Enarees.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 105
paragraphs: For twenty-eight years the Scythians ruled Asia, and their lawlessness and reckless behavior ruined everything. They exacted whatever tribute they pleased from each nation, and on top of that, they rode through the land plundering at will. Eventually Kyaxares and the Medes invited them to a feast, got them drunk, and slaughtered them. The Medes regained their empire and all the territory they had held before. They captured Nineveh (I will describe how in another account) and made the Assyrians subject, with the exception of the Babylonian district.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 106
paragraphs: After this, Kyaxares died. He had reigned forty years, including those under Scythian rule. His son Astyages succeeded him. Astyages had a daughter whom he named Mandane. In a dream, he saw her urinate such a volume that it flooded his entire capital and all of Asia. He told this vision to the Magian dream interpreters. What they revealed frightened him. So when Mandane came of age, he refused to give her to any Mede of suitable rank. Instead, fearing the dream, he married her to a Persian named Cambyses—a man of good family but quiet temperament, whom Astyages considered far beneath even a middle-ranking Mede.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 107
paragraphs: When Mandane was married to Cambyses, in the first year Astyages had another dream. He saw a vine growing from Mandane's womb that spread over all of Asia. He reported this to the interpreters and then sent for his daughter, who was pregnant. When she arrived from Persia, he kept her under guard, intending to destroy the child. The dream interpreters had told him that her offspring would rule in his place. To prevent this, when Cyrus was born, Astyages summoned Harpagos—his most trusted kinsman, steward of all his affairs, and the most loyal of the Medes—and said: "Harpagos, whatever I ask of you, do it faithfully. Do not deceive me or side with others and bring ruin on yourself later. Take the child born to Mandane, bring it to your house, and kill it. Then bury it however you wish." Harpagos replied: "O king, you have never found any fault with me, and I will take care never to offend you in time to come. If this is your will, it is my duty to carry it out faithfully."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 108
paragraphs: When the child was handed over to him, dressed for death, Harpagos went home weeping and told his wife everything Astyages had said. She asked: "What do you intend to do?" He answered: "Not what Astyages commanded. Even if he grows more deranged than he already is, I will not do his bidding or serve him in such a murder. I will not kill this child, for many reasons: the child is my own kin, and Astyages is old and has no male heir. If the throne passes to Mandane after his death—the very woman whose son he now orders me to kill—what is left for me but the greatest danger? For my own safety, the child must die. But one of Astyages' own servants must do the killing, not one of mine."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 109
paragraphs: He immediately sent a messenger to one of Astyages' herdsmen who, he knew, grazed his cattle on the most suitable pastures in mountains full of wild beasts. The herdsman's name was Mitradates, and he lived with a woman who was also a slave of Astyages. Her Greek name would be Kyno (meaning "dog"), since her Median name, Spako, translates to the same thing—the Median word for dog being "spaka." The foothills where this herdsman kept his cattle lie north of Agbatana, toward the Euxine Sea. That part of Media, bordering Saspeiran territory, is very mountainous, heavily forested, and high, while the rest of Media is entirely flat. When the herdsman came with great speed at the summons, Harpagos said: "Astyages commands you to take this child and leave it in the wildest part of the mountains, so that it dies as quickly as possible. He told me to say this: if you do not kill the child and try to save it by any means, you will die by the most terrible death. I have been ordered to verify that it is exposed."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 110
paragraphs: The herdsman took the child and went back the way he came. When he reached his hut, it happened that his wife, who had been on the verge of giving birth for days, had delivered a child while he was away—by a stroke of providence. Both husband and wife had been anxious about each other: he worried about his wife's labor, she about why Harpagos had sent for her husband so urgently. When he arrived and she saw him, she was so relieved that she immediately asked why Harpagos had summoned him. He said: "Wife, when I got to the city I saw and heard something I wish I had never seen—something that should never have happened to our masters. Harpagos' whole house was in tears. I went in, alarmed. The moment I entered, I saw a baby lying there, kicking and crying, dressed in gold-embroidered clothes. When Harpagos saw me, he ordered me to take the child as fast as I could and leave it in the mountains, wherever the wild beasts are thickest. He said Astyages commanded this and threatened me with terrible punishment if I failed. I took the child and carried it away, thinking it belonged to one of the household slaves. I could never have guessed whose child it really was. But I was puzzled by the gold clothes and the weeping in Harpagos' house. Then on the road, the servant who escorted me out of the city told me the whole truth: the child is the son of Mandane, daughter of Astyages, and Cambyses, son of Cyrus. And Astyages commands that it be killed. Here it is."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 111
paragraphs: As he said this, the herdsman uncovered the child and showed it to his wife. She saw that it was large and beautiful, and she burst into tears. She clung to her husband's knees and begged him not to expose it. He said he had no choice. Harpagos would send inspectors to verify, and if they found the child alive, he would die the most terrible death. When she could not persuade him, his wife said: "Since I cannot talk you out of exposing a child, do this. I have just given birth, and my baby was born dead. Take our dead child and expose it. Let us raise Mandane's son as our own. That way you will not be caught disobeying our masters, and we will be well provided for. Our dead baby will have a royal burial, and the living one will keep his life."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 112
paragraphs: The herdsman thought his wife's advice was excellent, and he acted on it at once. He handed over the child meant for death to his wife and took his own dead baby. He placed it in the chest that had held the other child, dressed it in all the fine clothes, and left it in the wildest part of the mountains. Two days later, he went back to the city and told Harpagos that he was ready to show the child's body. Harpagos sent his most trusted bodyguards, who saw the herdsman's dead child and buried it. So that child was buried, while the one who would later be known as Cyrus was taken in and raised by the herdsman's wife, though she gave him some other name, not Cyrus.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 113
paragraphs: When the boy was ten years old, something happened that revealed who he was. He was playing in the village—the one with the cattle stalls—playing in the road with other boys his age. The boys chose the herdsman's supposed son to be their king. He assigned some to build houses, others to be bodyguards, one to be the King's Eye, another to carry messages—he gave everyone a role. One of the boys playing with him was the son of Artembares, a prominent Mede. When this boy refused to do what Cyrus ordered, Cyrus had the other boys seize him and beat him severely with a whip. The boy, outraged at being treated so far beneath his dignity, ran to the city and complained to his father about what Cyrus had done—though he did not call him Cyrus, since that was not yet his name, but "the herdsman's son." Artembares went to Astyages in a fury, bringing his son to show the bruises, and said: "O king, your own slave—a herdsman's brat—has treated us like this!" He bared the boy's shoulders for the king to see.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 114
paragraphs: When Astyages heard and saw this, he wanted to punish the boy to avenge Artembares' honor. He summoned both the herdsman and his son. When both stood before him, Astyages looked at Cyrus and said: "You—the son of this nobody—dared to treat the son of a man I hold in the highest honor like this?" The boy replied: "Master, I treated him as he deserved. The boys of the village chose me as their king in a game, because they thought I was the best suited for it. All the other boys did what I told them. But this one disobeyed and ignored my orders, so he was punished. If I deserve to suffer for that, here I am."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 115
paragraphs: While the boy spoke, a flash of recognition struck Astyages. The child's features seemed to resemble his own. The boy's answer was too bold for a herdsman's son. And the timing of the exposure matched the boy's age. Stunned, Astyages said nothing for a moment. When he collected himself, he wanted to get rid of Artembares so he could question the herdsman alone. He said: "Artembares, I will handle this so that neither you nor your son will have cause for complaint." He dismissed Artembares and ordered his servants to bring Cyrus inside. When they were alone, Astyages asked the herdsman: "Where did you get this boy? Who gave him to you?" The herdsman said the boy was his own, born to his wife who still lived with him. Astyages told him he was being very foolish to court severe punishment, and at the same time signaled to his bodyguards to seize him. As the herdsman was being led to the torture, he broke down and told the whole truth from the beginning. He ended by begging for mercy.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 116
paragraphs: Once the herdsman had revealed the truth, Astyages cared less about him. But with Harpagos, he was furious. He ordered his guards to summon Harpagos. When Harpagos arrived, Astyages asked: "By what death, Harpagos, did you destroy the child I gave you—my own daughter's son?" Harpagos saw the herdsman in the room and knew that lying was pointless. He said: "O king, when I received the child, I thought about how I could fulfill your wishes without being a murderer in your daughter's eyes or in your own. So I did this: I called this herdsman, gave him the child, and told him that you, Astyages, had commanded the child's death. That much was true. I gave the child with strict instructions to leave it in the wild mountains and stay nearby until it was dead. I threatened him with every kind of punishment if he failed. When he did as I ordered and the child was dead, I sent my most trusted eunuchs to verify, and they saw the body and buried it. That, O king, is how the matter was handled, and that is the death the child died."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 117
paragraphs: So Harpagos told the truth. Astyages hid the anger he felt and first retold the story to Harpagos exactly as the herdsman had told it. Then, after repeating the whole account, he concluded by saying that the child was alive and that everything had turned out well. He said: "I was deeply distressed by what I had done to this child, and my daughter's hatred of me was hard to bear. But since fortune has changed for the better, first send your own son to keep the newly arrived boy company, and then come to dinner with me. I intend to celebrate with a sacrifice of thanksgiving to the gods who deserve the honor for preserving my grandson."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 118
paragraphs: When Harpagos heard this, he bowed and considered himself fortunate that his disobedience had turned out for his benefit and that he had been invited to a celebratory dinner. He went home and immediately sent his only son, a boy of about thirteen, to Astyages' palace, telling him to do whatever the king commanded. Then, overjoyed, Harpagos told his wife what had happened. But when his son arrived at the palace, Astyages slaughtered the boy. He cut the body into pieces, roasted some parts and boiled others, and had them prepared for serving. When dinnertime came and the guests—including Harpagos—were seated, Astyages and the other guests were served lamb. But Harpagos was served the flesh of his own son—everything except the head, hands, and feet, which were kept hidden in a covered basket. When Harpagos seemed to have eaten his fill, Astyages asked how he enjoyed the meal. Harpagos said he enjoyed it very much. Then the servants who had been instructed brought in the basket containing the boy's head, hands, and feet. They stood before Harpagos and told him to uncover it and take what he wished. Harpagos obeyed, uncovered the basket, and saw the remains of his son. But he kept control of himself and did not lose his composure. Astyages asked if he knew what animal's meat he had eaten. Harpagos said he knew, and whatever the king did was well done. With this answer he took the remaining flesh and went home. After that, I believe, he gathered everything together and buried it.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 119
paragraphs: That was the punishment Astyages imposed on Harpagos. Turning his attention to Cyrus, he summoned the same Magians who had interpreted his dreams. When they arrived, he asked how they had interpreted his vision. They gave the same answer as before: the child would have become king if he had lived and not died first. Astyages replied: "The boy is alive. He was living in the countryside, and the village boys chose him as their king. He did everything a real king does—he appointed bodyguards, gatekeepers, message carriers, and all the rest. What do you think this means?" The Magians said: "If the boy is alive and has already been made king without anyone arranging it, then be reassured. The prophecy has been fulfilled. He has already reigned. The visions of dreams are sometimes satisfied by trivial events." Astyages replied: "I too lean toward this view—that since the boy was named king, the dream has been fulfilled and I have nothing more to fear from him. But think carefully and advise me: what is safest for my house and for you?" The Magians said: "O king, it matters greatly to us that your rule stands firm. If power shifts to this boy, it passes to the Persians—a foreign people—and we Medes would be enslaved and despised. But as long as you are king—one of our own—we share in power and receive great honors. So we have every reason to protect you and your throne. If we saw danger now, we would warn you. But the dream has spent itself on a trivial thing. We are reassured and advise you to be the same. Send the boy away to Persia, to his parents."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 120
paragraphs: Astyages was pleased. He called Cyrus and said: "My child, I wronged you because of a dream that came to nothing. But your own destiny saved you. Now go in peace to the land of the Persians. I will send an escort with you. When you arrive, you will find a father and mother very different from Mitradates the herdsman and his wife."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 121
paragraphs: With these words Astyages sent Cyrus away. When the boy returned to the house of Cambyses, his parents welcomed him with great joy. They had long believed him dead. They asked how he had survived, and he told them. He said he had not known the truth until recently—he had been deeply mistaken about his own identity. On the journey home, he had learned everything. He had believed he was the herdsman's son. His foster parents had told him the whole story. He said the herdsman's wife had raised him, and he praised her constantly. Kyno—"the dog"—was central to his account. His parents seized on this name and spread a story that their son, when exposed as a baby, had been nursed by a dog. That is how the legend started.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 122
paragraphs: As Cyrus grew into the most courageous and best-loved young man of his generation, Harpagos sought to befriend him. He sent gifts, because he wanted revenge on Astyages. He saw no way for a private citizen to bring down Astyages alone. But watching Cyrus grow up, he worked to make him an ally, seeing a parallel between Cyrus' injuries and his own. He had already laid groundwork: he had approached each of the leading Medes one by one and persuaded them that Astyages must be deposed and Cyrus placed on the throne. Once this was accomplished and the conspiracy was ripe, Harpagos needed to communicate his plan to Cyrus, who lived in Persia. The roads were guarded, so he devised this trick. He prepared a hare, opened its belly without damaging the fur, and tucked a written message inside. He sewed the belly shut and gave the hare to his most trusted servant, disguised as a huntsman, with a net. He sent the man to Persia with verbal instructions for Cyrus: open the hare with his own hands, and let no one be present when he does.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 123
paragraphs: This was carried out. Cyrus received the hare, cut it open, and found the letter. It read: "Son of Cambyses, the gods watch over you—otherwise you could never have come through so much good fortune. Now avenge yourself on Astyages, your would-be murderer. If he had his way, you would be dead. It was the gods who saved you—and I who saved you, for it was I who gave you to the herdsman rather than killing you as Astyages commanded. If you follow my advice, you will rule all the territory that Astyages now controls. Persuade the Persians to revolt and lead an army against the Medes. It makes no difference whether I or any other leading Mede is appointed to command the army against you—they will all defect. Everything is prepared here. Do this, and do it quickly."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 124
paragraphs: Cyrus read this and considered how best to persuade the Persians to revolt. He decided on this plan. He wrote a letter and read it aloud at an assembly of the Persians. In it he declared that Astyages had appointed him commander of the Persians. "Now," he said, "I order every one of you to come tomorrow with a sickle." The Persians are divided into many tribes. Cyrus summoned representatives of all of them: the Pasargadai, Maraphians, and Maspians (the most noble—the Pasargadai include the Achaemenid clan from which the Persian kings come), as well as the Panthialaeans, Derusiaeans, Germanians (who work the land), and the Daians, Mardians, and Dropicians (who are nomads). When they all appeared with their sickles, Cyrus put them to work.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 125
paragraphs: There was a tract of Persian land, about eighteen or twenty furlongs across, overgrown with thorns. Cyrus ordered them to clear it in a single day. They did. The next day, he told them to come back washed and clean. Meanwhile, he slaughtered all his father's goats, sheep, and cattle and prepared a feast. He also provided the best wine and bread. When the Persians arrived, he had them sit in a meadow and enjoy the banquet. After they had eaten, Cyrus asked: "Which do you prefer—yesterday's labor or today's feast?" They said today's was incomparably better. Cyrus replied: "Men of Persia, here is how things stand. If you follow me, you will have this and a thousand other good things, with no slave labor. But if you refuse, you will have endless toil like yesterday's. Follow my lead and win your freedom. I believe I was born by divine providence to take this task in hand. You are no worse than the Medes in any way, neither in war nor in anything else. Since this is so, revolt from Astyages as fast as you can."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 126
paragraphs: The Persians, who had long resented Median rule, now had a leader. They eagerly set about winning their freedom. When Astyages heard what Cyrus was doing, he sent a messenger to summon him. Cyrus told the messenger to report back that he would be with Astyages sooner than Astyages wished. When Astyages heard this, he armed the entire Median nation. As if heaven had robbed him of his senses, he appointed Harpagos as their general—forgetting what he had done to the man. When Harpagos took the field with the Median army and engaged the Persians, some of the Medes fought, but those in the conspiracy deserted to the Persians. Most of the rest, seeing what was happening, deliberately fought badly and fled.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 127
paragraphs: When the Median army had been shamefully routed, Astyages heard the news and said: "But Cyrus will not escape punishment so easily." His first act was to impale the Magian dream interpreters who had advised him to let Cyrus go. Then he armed every Mede left in the city—young and old alike—and led them out. He fought the Persians, was defeated, and was taken prisoner. His Median forces were destroyed.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 128
paragraphs: When Astyages was captured, Harpagos came to stand over him, gloating and taunting. Among other barbs, he asked how Astyages enjoyed being a slave instead of a king—referring to the banquet where Astyages had served Harpagos his own son's flesh. Astyages looked at him and asked: "Do you claim Cyrus' achievement as your own?" Harpagos said yes—he had written the letter that started the revolt, so the credit was rightfully his. Astyages replied that Harpagos was both the most foolish and the most unjust man alive. The most foolish because, if this truly was his doing, he had handed the kingship to someone else rather than seizing it for himself. The most unjust because, on account of that dinner, he had enslaved the entire Median nation. If someone else had to be king instead of Astyages, it should have been a Mede, not a Persian. But now the innocent Medes had been reduced from masters to slaves, and the Persians from slaves to masters.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 129
paragraphs: So Astyages was deposed after ruling thirty-five years. The Medes bowed under Persian rule because of his cruelty, having themselves ruled Asia above the river Halys for one hundred and twenty-eight years, not counting the Scythian period. Later they would rebel against the Persians and regain independence, but they were defeated again by Darius' forces. But at this point in time, the Persians under Cyrus rose against the Medes and from then on ruled Asia. As for Astyages, Cyrus kept him at his court and did him no further harm for the rest of his life. That is how Cyrus was born, raised, and became king. And afterward, as I have already described, he conquered Croesus, who had attacked him first. With that victory, he became master of all Asia.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 130
paragraphs: These are the customs, as far as I know, that the Persians follow. They consider it unlawful to set up statues, temples, and altars, and they criticize those who do so. This, I believe, is because they do not think of the gods as having human form, as the Greeks do. Their practice is to climb to the tops of the highest mountains and offer sacrifice to Zeus, which is the name they give to the whole vault of the sky. They also sacrifice to the sun, the moon, the earth, fire, water, and the winds. These are the only gods to whom they have sacrificed from the beginning. They later adopted the worship of Aphrodite Ourania from the Assyrians and Arabians. The Assyrians call Aphrodite Mylitta, the Arabians call her Alilat, and the Persians call her Mitra.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 131
paragraphs: This is how the Persians sacrifice to the gods I have mentioned. They build no altars and light no fire. They use no libations, no flute music, no garlands, and no barley meal. When someone wishes to sacrifice, he leads the animal to an open, clean space, sets a wreath on his cap—usually of myrtle—and calls upon the god. The worshipper may not pray for blessings for himself alone. He must pray for the welfare of all the Persians and the king, since he himself is included among all Persians. He cuts the victim into pieces, boils the meat, and spreads the softest grass he can find—preferably clover—as a bed beneath it. He lays out all the meat on this bed. When everything is arranged, a Magian stands nearby and chants a hymn about the origin of the gods, which is their form of sacred invocation. Without a Magian present, no sacrifice is permitted. After a short wait, the worshipper carries the meat away and does whatever he wishes with it.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 132
paragraphs: Of all days, Persians most honor their own birthday. On that day, they think it right to set out a larger feast than on any other day. The wealthy serve a whole ox, horse, camel, or donkey roasted in an oven. The poor serve smaller animals. They eat few main courses but many side dishes, served one at a time. Because of this, the Persians say that the Greeks leave the table hungry, since nothing worth mentioning is served after the main course. They add that if Greeks were served more dishes, they would never stop eating. Persians are extremely fond of wine. They are not permitted to vomit or urinate in another person's presence. These are strict rules. They have a habit of discussing the most important matters while drunk. Whatever they decide while drunk, the host in whose house they were drinking presents the decision to them again the next day when they are sober. If they still approve when sober, it stands. If not, they drop it. Likewise, decisions first made sober are reconsidered when drunk.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 133
paragraphs: When Persians meet on the street, you can tell whether they are of equal rank by this: instead of greeting each other with words, they kiss on the mouth. If one is slightly lower in rank, they kiss on the cheek. If one is much lower, he falls to the ground and prostrates himself. They hold no people in as high regard as those nearest to them geographically, then the next nearest, and so on, with respect diminishing by distance. They consider themselves the best of all peoples by far, and that all others share in excellence according to their proximity—so the most distant peoples are, in their view, the worst. Under the Medes, each nation ruled the one next to it in the hierarchy, and the Medes ruled them all, both directly and through this chain of command.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 134
paragraphs: The Persians are more open than any people to adopting foreign customs. They wear Median dress because they think it looks better than their own, and they use Egyptian body armor for war. They eagerly take up every kind of luxury they hear about, including Greek ones. Each Persian man has many wives and even more concubines.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 135
paragraphs: After courage in battle, the highest proof of manly excellence is to have many sons. Every year the king sends gifts to the man who can show the most. They believe that numbers mean strength. They educate their sons from ages five to twenty in only three things: riding, archery, and telling the truth. Before the age of five, a boy is not brought into his father's presence but stays with the women. The reason for this is that if the child dies in infancy, the father is not touched by grief.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 136
paragraphs: I commend this custom, and also the next: neither the king nor any other Persian may execute anyone for a single offense, nor may a master inflict severe punishment on a servant for a single wrong. Only when a man's offenses are counted and found to outnumber and outweigh his services may anger be acted upon. They claim that no Persian has ever killed his own father or mother. In every case where this has seemingly occurred, investigation has revealed the child to be a changeling or illegitimate. They say it is simply impossible for a true parent to be killed by their own child.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 137
paragraphs: Whatever it is unlawful for them to do, it is also unlawful for them to speak of. The most disgraceful thing in their view is to tell a lie. The next most disgraceful is to owe a debt—for many reasons, but especially because they say a debtor is bound to tell lies. Any citizen with leprosy or a similar skin disease is not allowed to enter the city or mix with other Persians. They say such a person has sinned against the sun. Many Persians drive any foreigner with such a disease out of the country. They apply the same rule to white doves, for the same reason. They do not urinate or spit into rivers, nor do they wash their hands in them. They do not allow anyone else to do so either. They hold rivers in great reverence.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 138
paragraphs: Here is another peculiarity the Persians themselves have not noticed, though I have. All their names, which reflect their physical stature or their high rank, end in the same letter—the one the Dorians call "san" and the Ionians call "sigma." If you look into this, you will find that every Persian name ends this way, without exception.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 139
paragraphs: This much I can say with certainty from my own knowledge. What follows is reported as a secret matter and not openly discussed: the body of a Persian man is not buried until it has been torn by a bird or a dog. I know for certain that the Magians do this, since they practice it openly. The Persians coat the body in wax before putting it in the ground. The Magians are very different from other men and from the Egyptian priests. The Egyptian priests scrupulously avoid killing any living creature except those they sacrifice. The Magians, however, kill everything with their own hands except dogs and humans. They kill ants, snakes, flying creatures, crawling creatures—everything—and regard it as a great achievement. Let this custom remain as it has always been, and I will return to my earlier narrative.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 140
paragraphs: As soon as the Lydians had been subdued by the Persians, the Ionians and Aeolians sent messengers to Cyrus at Sardis, offering to submit on the same terms they had enjoyed under Croesus. After hearing their proposal, Cyrus told them a fable. A flute player once saw fish in the sea and played his flute to them, expecting them to come ashore. When they did not, he took a net, caught a huge haul, and saw them thrashing on the beach. "Stop your dancing now," he told the fish, "since you would not dance when I played." Cyrus told this story because the Ionians and Aeolians had refused his earlier invitation to revolt against Croesus, but now that everything was decided, they were ready to submit. He was angry when he said this. When the Ionians heard this response in their cities, they each built walls for defense and assembled at the Panionion—all except the Milesians. Cyrus had already made a separate treaty with Miletos on the same terms they had held under the Lydians. The rest of the Ionians resolved to send envoys to Sparta to ask for help.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 141
paragraphs: These Ionians who meet at the Panionion had the good fortune to build their cities in the most favorable climate in the known world. Regions above and below Ionia, to the east and west, all suffer compared to Ionia—some from cold and rain, others from heat and drought. The Ionians do not all speak the same dialect but use four different varieties. Miletos lies furthest south, with Myous and Priene next to it. These are settlements in Caria and share one dialect. Ephesos, Colophon, Lebedos, Teos, Clazomenai, and Phocaea are in Lydia and share another dialect, quite different from the Carian group. Three remaining Ionian cities—two on islands (Samos and Chios) and one on the mainland (Erythrai)—share a third dialect, while Chios and Erythrai speak alike but Samos has its own.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 142
paragraphs: Of these Ionians, the Milesians were safe from danger because of their treaty. The islanders also had nothing to fear, since the Phoenicians were not yet Persian subjects, and the Persians themselves were not a seafaring people. The Ionians of the mainland had split from the others for one reason only: the Greek race as a whole was weak at that time, and the Ionians were by far the weakest and least significant part of it. Apart from Athens, no Ionian city of any importance existed. The Athenians and most other Ionians were ashamed of the name and did not want to be called Ionian. Even now, most of them seem to regard the name as a reproach. But the twelve Asiatic cities were proud of the name. They established a sanctuary called the Panionion exclusively for themselves and voted to exclude all other Ionians from it—though no one else actually asked to be admitted, except the people of Smyrna.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 143
paragraphs: This is similar to how the Dorians of what is now called the Five Cities—formerly the Six Cities—refuse to admit any neighboring Dorians to the temple of Triopion. They even excluded their own members who broke the rules. In the games held in honor of Triopian Apollo, the prizes were bronze tripods. Winners were required to dedicate these to the temple rather than take them home. A man from Halicarnassos named Agasicles won a prize and ignored the rule, taking the tripod home and nailing it to his wall. For this offense, the five remaining cities—Lindos, Ialysos, Kameiros, Cos, and Cnidos—expelled Halicarnassos from the league.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 144
paragraphs: The reason the Ionians established exactly twelve cities, refusing to admit any more, was that when they lived in the Peloponnese they had been divided into twelve parts—just as the Achaeans who drove them out are divided into twelve parts today. First is Pellene, nearest to Sicyon, then Aigeira and Aigai (where the ever-flowing river Crathis rises, from which the river of the same name in Italy takes its name), then Bura, Helike (where the Ionians fled after being defeated by the Achaeans), Aigion, Rhypes, Patrae, Pharae, Olenos (where the great river Peiros flows), Dyme, and Tritaeae—the only inland city of the twelve. These formed the twelve divisions of the Ionians in old times, and these are the twelve divisions of the Achaeans now.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 145
paragraphs: For this reason the Ionians also made twelve cities. To claim that these Asian Ionians are more truly Ionian or more nobly descended than the others is nonsense. A large number of them are Abantians from Euboea, who have nothing to do with Ionia even in name. Mixed in with them are Minyans from Orchomenos, Cadmeans, Dryopians, Phocian breakaways, Molossians, Pelasgian Arcadians, Dorians from Epidauros, and many other peoples. Even those who set out from the Prytaneion of Athens and consider themselves the purest Ionians brought no women with them to their colony. They married Carian women whose fathers they had killed. Because of this slaughter, the women established a law that they swore to by oath and passed to their daughters: they would never sit at table with their husbands or call a husband by name, because the men had killed their fathers, husbands, and sons before taking them as wives. This happened at Miletos.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 146
paragraphs: Some of these Ionians appointed Lycian kings over them, descended from Glaucos and Hippolochos. Others chose Cauconian rulers from Pylos, descended from Codros son of Melanthos. Others were ruled by princes of both lines combined. Since they cling to the Ionian name more than the rest, let them be called the pure-blooded Ionians. In truth, all who trace their origin to Athens and celebrate the festival of the Apaturia are Ionian. Everyone celebrates it except the people of Ephesus and Colophon, who were excluded because of a blood-guilt.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 147
paragraphs: The Panionion is a sacred place on the northern side of Mycale, set apart by common agreement of the Ionians for Poseidon of Helike. Mycale is a promontory of the mainland extending westward toward Samos. There the Ionians gather from their cities to celebrate the festival they call the Panionia.
Those, then, are the Ionian cities.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 148
paragraphs: The Aeolian cities are these: Cyme (also called Phriconis), Larisa, Neon-teichos, Temnos, Cilla, Notion, Aigiroessa, Pitane, Aigaiai, Myrina, and Gryneia. These are the eleven ancient cities of the Aeolians. Originally there were twelve, but the Ionians took Smyrna from them. The Aeolians had settled on land at least as fertile as that of the Ionians, though the climate was not as favorable.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 149
paragraphs: The Aeolians lost Smyrna this way. Certain men from Colophon, defeated in a civil war and driven from their city, had taken refuge in Smyrna. Later, the Colophonian exiles watched for a time when the Smyrnaeans were celebrating a festival outside the walls in honor of Dionysus. They shut the gates, seized the city, and held it. The Aeolians came to the rescue, and terms were negotiated: the Ionians would return all movable property, and the Aeolians would give up the city. The Smyrnaeans agreed. They were then distributed among the other eleven Aeolian cities and made citizens.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 150
paragraphs: Those are the Aeolian cities on the mainland, apart from the ones on Mount Ida, which form a separate group. On the islands, there are five cities on Lesbos (the sixth, Arisba, was enslaved by the people of Methymna, though all were originally kinsmen). There is one city on Tenedos and one on what are called the Hundred Islands. The Aeolians of Lesbos and Tenedos, like the Ionian islanders, had nothing to fear. The remaining Aeolian cities resolved by common consent to follow wherever the Ionians might lead.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 151
paragraphs: When the Ionian and Aeolian envoys arrived in Sparta (they had moved quickly), they chose a Phocaean named Pythermos to speak for them all. He put on a purple cloak so that as many Spartans as possible would come to hear him. Standing before the assembly, he made a lengthy appeal for help. The Spartans were not persuaded and voted against assisting the Ionians. The envoys went home. Despite this refusal, the Spartans sent a ship of fifty oars to observe the situation in Ionia and keep an eye on Cyrus. When they reached Phocaea, they sent their most prominent member, Lacrines, to Sardis to deliver a warning to Cyrus: the Spartans would not allow him to harm any Greek city.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 152
paragraphs: When the herald had spoken, Cyrus reportedly asked the Greeks in his company who the Spartans were and how many. On hearing the answer, he told the Spartan herald: "I have never yet feared the kind of men who have a special place in the center of their city where they gather to cheat each other with oaths." This was a jab at the Greeks for having marketplaces, something the Persians do not use—they never buy or sell in markets. He added: "If I stay healthy, it will be their own misfortunes they discuss, not those of the Ionians." Cyrus aimed this threat at all the Greeks, since they had marketplaces. He then appointed a Persian named Tabalos as governor of Sardis and gave a Lydian named Pactyas the task of transporting Croesus' gold. Cyrus himself marched back toward Agbatana, taking Croesus with him. He considered the Ionians too unimportant to deal with personally. Babylon, the Bactrians, the Sacae, and the Egyptians—those were his primary concerns. He intended to lead campaigns against them himself and send a subordinate to handle the Ionians.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 153
paragraphs: But as soon as Cyrus had left Sardis, Pactyas persuaded the Lydians to revolt against Tabalos and against Cyrus. He went down to the coast and, since he had all the gold from Sardis, he hired mercenaries and convinced the coastal peoples to join him. Then he marched on Sardis and besieged Tabalos in the citadel.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 154
paragraphs: When Cyrus heard this on his march, he said to Croesus: "When will this end, Croesus? The Lydians apparently will not stop making trouble—for me and for themselves. I am tempted to sell them all into slavery. It seems I have done the equivalent of killing a father and sparing his sons. I carried you off—you, who were more than a father to the Lydians—and handed the city over to the Lydians themselves. And now I am surprised that they revolt?" Croesus, afraid that Cyrus would destroy Sardis, replied: "O king, your words are reasonable. But do not give in completely to anger or destroy an ancient city that bears no guilt for the past or the present trouble. The past was my doing, and I bear it on my head. The present is Pactyas' work—he is the one you put in charge. Punish him. But spare the Lydians. To prevent future revolts, give them this command: forbid them from possessing weapons of war. Order them to wear tunics under their cloaks and soft boots. Tell them to teach their sons to play the lyre, strum the harp, and run retail shops. You will quickly see them change from men into women, O king, and you will never again need to fear a Lydian revolt."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 155
paragraphs: Croesus proposed this because he thought it was better for the Lydians than being sold into slavery. He knew that without a strong argument, he could not change Cyrus' mind. He also feared that even if the Lydians escaped this time, they might revolt again and be destroyed. Cyrus was pleased with the advice. He calmed his anger and said he would follow Croesus' suggestion. He summoned a Mede named Mazares and ordered him to tell the Lydians exactly what Croesus had recommended. He also ordered Mazares to sell into slavery everyone who had joined the Lydians in besieging Sardis—and above all, to bring Pactyas back alive.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 156
paragraphs: Having given these orders while on the march, Cyrus continued on to Persia. Pactyas, hearing that an army was approaching, fled in terror to Cyme. Mazares the Mede marched on Sardis with a detachment of Cyrus' army. Finding that Pactyas and the rebels were gone, his first act was to force the Lydians to carry out Cyrus' commands. Their entire way of life changed as a result. Mazares then sent messengers to Cyme demanding the surrender of Pactyas. The Cymeans decided to consult the god at the oracle of Branchidai for guidance.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 157
paragraphs: The men of Cyme sent messengers to Branchidai to ask the god what they should do about Pactyas, in order to please the gods. The oracle answered that they should hand Pactyas over to the Persians. When the Cymeans heard this reply, they were ready to surrender him. But one citizen, a man of good reputation named Aristodicos, son of Heracleides, did not believe the oracle and suspected the envoys had lied. He stopped the surrender and insisted that a second delegation be sent to confirm the answer.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 158
paragraphs: When the second group arrived at Branchidai, Aristodicos himself put the question: "Lord, Pactyas the Lydian came to us as a suppliant, fleeing violent death at the hands of the Persians. They demand his surrender. We fear Persian power, but we have not yet dared to hand over a suppliant until you make clear what we should do." The oracle gave the same answer: hand Pactyas over to the Persians. Then Aristodicos deliberately began walking around the temple, removing the sparrows and other birds that had nested there. As he did so, a voice reportedly came from the inner sanctuary: "Most impious of men, how dare you do this? Will you drive my suppliants from my temple?" Aristodicos was ready with his reply: "Lord, you rescue your own suppliants but tell the Cymeans to hand over theirs?" The god answered: "Yes, I tell you to do it—so that you may be destroyed all the sooner for your impiety and never again come to consult the oracle about whether to surrender suppliants."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 159
paragraphs: When the Cymeans heard this, they did not want to be destroyed for surrendering Pactyas or besieged for sheltering him. So they sent him to Mytilene. But when Mazares demanded his surrender from Mytilene, the Mytilenaeans were preparing to hand him over for a price. (I cannot say the exact amount because the deal was never completed.) When the Cymeans learned this, they sent a boat to Lesbos and took Pactyas to Chios instead. But he was dragged from the sanctuary of Athena Poliouchos by the Chians, who surrendered him. The price for handing him over was the district of Atarneus on the Mysian mainland, opposite Lesbos. The Persians received Pactyas and kept him under guard to present to Cyrus. For a long time after this, no Chian would use barley meal from Atarneus in any offering to any god, and nothing grown there was used in any sacred rite. Everything from that district was excluded from all their temples.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 160
paragraphs: So the Chians handed Pactyas over. After this, Mazares campaigned against all who had helped besiege Tabalos. He enslaved the people of Priene and overran the entire plain of the Maeander, giving it to his army to plunder. He did the same to Magnesia. Then he fell ill and died.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 161
paragraphs: After Mazares died, Harpagos came to replace him as commander. He too was a Mede—the same man whom King Astyages had served the monstrous banquet, and who had helped give the kingdom to Cyrus. Appointed by Cyrus, Harpagos arrived in Ionia and proceeded to take the cities by siege. He would drive the defenders behind their walls, then pile earthen ramps against the fortifications and storm them. The first Ionian city he attacked was Phocaea.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 162
paragraphs: The Phocaeans were the first Greeks to make long sea voyages. They were the ones who discovered the Adriatic, Tyrrhenia, Iberia, and Tartessos. They sailed not in round merchant ships but in fifty-oared warships. When they reached Tartessos, they befriended the local king, Arganthonios, who had ruled Tartessos for eighty years and lived a hundred and twenty. Arganthonios liked the Phocaeans so much that he first urged them to leave Ionia and settle anywhere in his territory they wished. When they declined, he heard about the growing power of the Medes and gave them money to build a wall around their city. He gave generously: the wall's circuit is considerable, and it is built entirely of large, well-fitted stones.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 163
paragraphs: This was how the Phocaeans built their wall. When Harpagos brought his army against them and began the siege, he offered terms: he would be satisfied if the Phocaeans would pull down one bastion of their wall and dedicate one house to the king. The Phocaeans, who detested the idea of slavery, asked for one day to deliberate. During that day, they requested that Harpagos withdraw his army from the walls. Harpagos said he understood perfectly well what they planned but would allow them their day. While the army withdrew, the Phocaeans launched their fifty-oared ships, loaded their women, children, movable property, temple images, and all other offerings except bronze and stone statues and paintings, and set sail for Chios. The Persians took possession of an empty Phocaea.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 164
paragraphs: When the Chians refused to sell them the Oenussae islands—fearing these would become a rival trading hub that would shut Chios out—the Phocaeans set course for Corsica. Twenty years earlier, on the advice of an oracle, they had founded a colony there called Alalia. Arganthonios was already dead by this time. Before departing for Corsica, they sailed back to Phocaea and killed the Persian garrison that Harpagos had left. After that, they pronounced terrible curses on any man who stayed behind. They sank a mass of iron in the sea and swore never to return to Phocaea until that iron rose to the surface. But as they prepared to sail for Corsica, more than half the citizens were seized by longing for their city and their homes. They broke their oaths and sailed back to Phocaea. Those who kept the oath sailed from the Oenussae islands to Corsica.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 165
paragraphs: When these Phocaeans reached Corsica, they lived for five years alongside the earlier settlers and founded temples. But they plundered all their neighbors, so the Etruscans and Carthaginians joined forces against them. Each brought sixty ships, making a total of one hundred and twenty against the Phocaeans' sixty. They fought a sea battle off the Sardinian coast. The Phocaeans won, but it was a hollow victory: they lost forty ships, and the remaining twenty had their rams bent and were useless. They sailed back to Alalia, picked up their women, children, and whatever possessions they could carry, abandoned Corsica, and sailed to the Italian mainland, where they founded the city of Velia.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 166
paragraphs: The crews of the forty destroyed ships were captured, mostly by the Carthaginians and Etruscans. They were taken ashore and stoned to death. After this, the people of the Etruscan city Agylla found that everything passing the spot where the Phocaeans had been killed—whether cattle, draft animals, or humans—became crippled and twisted. The Agyllans sent to the oracle at Delphi for a remedy. The priestess told them to institute funeral rites for the dead Phocaeans and hold athletic and equestrian games in their honor. The Agyllans still do this today. That is the fate of the Phocaeans.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 167
paragraphs: That is the story of Phocaea in Ionia. The people of Teos did much the same thing. As soon as Harpagos captured their wall with a siege ramp, they boarded their ships and sailed to Thrace. There they founded the city of Abdera. (A man from Clazomenai named Timesios had actually founded Abdera before them, but the Thracians drove him out. He is now honored as a hero by the Teans in Abdera.)

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 168
paragraphs: The Phocaeans and Teans were the only Ionians who abandoned their cities rather than endure subjection. The rest of the Ionians—except the Milesians, who had a treaty—fought Harpagos just as bravely as the exiles, and each people proved its valor. But they were defeated one by one. Those who remained in their homeland submitted and obeyed all orders. The Milesians, as I said, had their own agreement with Cyrus and were left in peace. And so Ionia was enslaved for the second time. After Harpagos conquered the Ionians on the mainland, the islanders, terrified, also surrendered to Cyrus.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 169
paragraphs: The Ionians were in a terrible state but continued to meet at the Panionion. Bias of Priene, I am told, gave them the most valuable advice imaginable. If they had followed it, they could have become the most prosperous of all Greeks. He urged them to sail together to Sardinia and found a single Panian city there. Freed from slavery and living on the largest island in the world, they would rule over others instead of being ruled. But if they stayed in Ionia, he said, he saw no hope of freedom. This was the advice of Bias after the Ionians were conquered. Before the conquest, Thales of Miletos—a man of Phoenician descent—had given equally good counsel: he urged the Ionians to establish a single central government at Teos, since Teos lay in the center of Ionia, while the other cities would continue to exist as independent districts.
Those were the kinds of advice offered to the Ionians.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 170
paragraphs: After subduing Ionia, Harpagos marched against the Carians, Caunians, and Lycians, taking Ionians and Aeolians along as part of his force. The Carians came to the mainland from the islands. In ancient times, as subjects of Minos, they were called Leleges and inhabited the islands. As far as I can determine from the most distant past, they paid no tribute but provided crews for Minos' ships whenever he required them. Because Minos conquered a great deal of territory and was successful in war, the Carians were by far the most prominent of all peoples at that time. The Greeks adopted three of their inventions: attaching crests to helmets, putting blazons on shields, and adding handles to shields—before this, all who carried shields used leather straps around the neck and left shoulder. Long after this, the Carians were driven from the islands by the Dorians and Ionians and migrated to the mainland. That is the Cretan account of the Carians. The Carians themselves disagree. They claim they have always lived on the mainland and have always been called Carians. They point to an ancient temple of Carian Zeus at Mylasa, which is shared by the Mysians and Lydians as kin of the Carians (for they say Lydos and Mysos were brothers of Car). These peoples share the temple, but no others, not even those who speak the same language.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 171
paragraphs: The Caunians, in my judgment, are native to their region, though they claim to have come from Crete. They have been assimilated to the Carian language—or the Carians to theirs; I cannot determine which. Their customs are very different from all other peoples, including the Carians. Their greatest pleasure is to gather for drinking parties—men, women, and children, sorted by age and friendship. They once worshipped foreign gods, but later changed their minds and decided to worship only their ancestral gods. So all the Caunian men of military age put on their armor, marched to the border, beating the air with their spears, and declared they were driving out the foreign gods.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 172
paragraphs: The Lycians originally came from Crete. In ancient times, all of Crete was inhabited by non-Greeks. When the sons of Europa—Sarpedon and Minos—quarreled over the kingship, Minos won the dispute and drove out Sarpedon and his followers. The exiles went to the Milyas district in Asia. The land that the Milyans now occupy was formerly called Milyas, and the Milyans were then called Solymians. While Sarpedon ruled, his people kept the name they had brought from Crete: Termilae. They are still called this by their neighbors. But when Lycos, son of Pandion, was driven out of Athens by his brother Aigeus and came to Sarpedon in the land of the Termilae, in time the Termilae came to be called Lycians after Lycos. Their customs are partly Cretan and partly Carian. One practice is uniquely theirs among all peoples: they take their names from their mothers, not their fathers. If you ask a Lycian who he is, he gives his mother's name and traces his ancestry through the female line. If a free woman marries a slave, the children are considered legitimate. But if a male citizen—even the most prominent—takes a foreign wife or concubine, the children have no rights.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 173
paragraphs: The Carians were conquered by Harpagos without any brilliant resistance, either from the Carians themselves or from the Greeks who lived in that region. Among the Greeks there were the people of Cnidos, settlers from Sparta, whose territory includes a promontory called Triopion, jutting into the sea. Cnidian land is almost entirely surrounded by water: to the north lies the Ceramic Gulf, to the south the sea off Syme and Rhodes. The Cnidians began to dig through the narrow neck of land—only about five furlongs across—to make their territory a true island while Harpagos was conquering Ionia. But their workers kept suffering unusual injuries from flying rock splinters, especially to their eyes. They sent to Delphi to ask what was blocking them. The priestess, they say, answered in verse:
"Do not fence your land with towers or dig through the isthmus. Zeus would have made it an island if he had so wished."
When the oracle spoke, the Cnidians stopped digging and surrendered to Harpagos without resistance.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 174
paragraphs: There were also the Pedasians, who lived in the interior above Halicarnassos. Among them, whenever disaster was about to strike either themselves or their neighbors, the priestess of Athena would grow a great beard. This happened to them three times. They were the only people in all of Caria who held out against Harpagos for any length of time. They caused him considerable trouble by fortifying a hill called Lide.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 175
paragraphs: The Pedasians were eventually conquered too. When Harpagos marched into the plain of Xanthos, the Lycians came out to meet him. Though few against many, they fought with great bravery. But defeated and driven back into the city, they gathered their wives, children, property, and slaves onto the acropolis and set it all on fire, burning everything. Then they swore terrible oaths to one another and sallied out to fight. Every single man of Xanthos died fighting. Of the Lycians who now claim to be Xanthians, most are actually immigrants, except for eighty families who happened to be away from the city and so survived. That is how Harpagos took Xanthos. He took Caunus in a similar way, since the Caunians largely followed the Lycian example.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 176
paragraphs: So Harpagos was conquering the coastal regions of Asia, while Cyrus himself was doing the same in the interior, subduing every nation and skipping none. Most of these campaigns I will pass over and tell only about those that gave him the most trouble and are most worth recording.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 177
paragraphs: After subjugating all the other mainland peoples, Cyrus attacked the Assyrians. Assyria had many great cities, but the most famous and strongest was Babylon, where the royal seat had been established after the fall of Nineveh. Babylon lies on a broad plain and forms a perfect square. Each side is about fourteen miles long, making the total circuit some fifty-six miles. No other city that we know of can match its grandeur. A wide, deep moat full of water runs around it. Inside the moat stands a wall fifty royal cubits thick and two hundred cubits high. (A royal cubit is three finger-widths longer than a standard one.)

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 178
paragraphs: I must also explain what was done with the earth from the moat and how the wall was built. As they dug the moat, they formed the excavated earth into bricks. When they had molded enough, they fired the bricks in kilns. Using hot bitumen as mortar and inserting layers of woven reed matting every thirty courses of brick, they built first the banks of the moat, then the wall itself in the same way. Along the top of the wall, on both edges, they built one-room structures facing each other, with a gap wide enough for a four-horse chariot to drive between them. One hundred gates are set in the wall, all of bronze—posts, lintels, and doors alike. (There is another city called Is, eight days' journey from Babylon on a small river of the same name that flows into the Euphrates. This river carries lumps of bitumen to the surface, and it was from here that the bitumen for Babylon's wall was obtained.)

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 179
paragraphs: Babylon was walled in this manner. The city has two halves, divided by the Euphrates, which flows through the middle. The river rises in Armenia and is large, deep, and swift. It empties into the Red Sea. The city wall on each side extends down to the riverbank. From there, a wall of baked brick runs along each bank of the river. The city itself consists of houses three and four stories high, laid out in straight streets. At the end of each street that runs to the river, the brick wall along the bank has a gate—one for each street—opening onto the river, and these gates are also made of bronze.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 180
paragraphs: This outer wall is like a suit of armor for the city. Inside it runs another wall, not much weaker but enclosing a smaller area. In each half of the city stands a fortified complex. In one half is the royal palace, surrounded by a large, strong wall. In the other half stands the temple of Zeus Belos with its bronze gates, a square enclosure two furlongs on each side that was still standing in my time. In the center of the temple precinct stands a massive tower, one furlong in length and one in width. On this tower stands another, and on that another, up to eight towers in all. A spiral staircase winds up the outside. Halfway up there is a resting place with benches. At the very top stands a great temple. Inside is a large, richly furnished couch and a golden table beside it. No statue of any kind has been placed there. No one spends the night in the temple except a single native woman, chosen by the god—or so the Chaldean priests of this god claim.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 181
paragraphs: These same priests say that the god himself comes to the temple and rests on the couch. I do not believe them. The same claim is made about the temple of Theban Zeus in Egypt, where a woman also sleeps in the temple (and both women are said to abstain from relations with men). A similar practice occurs with the prophetess of Apollo at Patara in Lycia, whenever an oracle is active there. When a prophetess is appointed, she is locked in the temple overnight.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 182
paragraphs: In the temple at Babylon there is also a lower chamber containing a great seated golden image of Zeus. A large golden table stands beside it, and both the footstool and the throne are also gold. According to the Chaldeans, the gold used for these items weighs eight hundred talents. Outside this chamber stands a golden altar. There is also a larger altar where full-grown animals are sacrificed—only newborn animals may be offered on the golden altar. On the larger altar, the Chaldeans burn a thousand talents of frankincense every year during the festival of this god. In Cyrus' time, there was also a solid gold statue twelve cubits high within the precinct. I did not see it myself—I am reporting what the Chaldeans say. Darius, son of Hystaspes, wanted to take this statue but did not dare. Xerxes, son of Darius, did take it and killed the priest who tried to stop him. Such is the splendor of this temple. There are also many private offerings.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 183
paragraphs: Babylon had many rulers who improved its walls and temples. I will discuss them in my Assyrian history. But two were women. The first, named Semiramis, ruled five generations before the second. She built remarkable embankments on the plain. Before her time, the river used to flood the entire plain.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 184
paragraphs: The queen who ruled after her, named Nitocris, was far wiser. She left behind monuments I will describe. She also saw that the Median empire was growing powerful and restless, having already captured Nineveh among other cities. She took every possible precaution against them. First, she diverted the river Euphrates, which had previously run straight through the center of the city. By digging channels upstream, she made it wind so much that it passed one particular Assyrian village three times. (The village is called Ardericca, and anyone sailing down the Euphrates from the Mediterranean still passes this village three times on three separate days.) She also raised high embankments on both sides of the Euphrates. In addition, she dug a vast lake above the city, a short distance from the river, deep enough to reach water and with a perimeter of some fifty-two miles. She used the excavated earth to raise the river embankments even higher. As the lake was dug, she had enormous stones brought to the edge. When all this was finished—the lake dug and the embankments built—she diverted the river into the new lake, filling it. While the old riverbed was empty, she accomplished two things: she lined both banks of the river through the city with baked brick, matching the riverside walls, and she built a bridge over the Euphrates from stones she had quarried for the lake, binding them together with iron and lead. During the day, square wooden platforms were laid across the stones for people to walk on. At night, the platforms were removed to prevent the inhabitants of the two halves of the city from crossing over and robbing each other. When the lake was full and the bridge finished, she turned the river back into its original course from the lake. The lake, now a marsh, served its purpose, and the citizens had a bridge.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 185
paragraphs: This same queen also contrived this trap. She had a tomb built above the busiest gate of the city, directly over the gateway itself. On the tomb she had an inscription carved: "If any king of Babylon after me finds himself short of money, let him open this tomb and take as much as he wants. But let him not open it unless he is truly in need, for opening it without need will bring no good." This tomb went undisturbed until Darius became king. He thought it absurd that a gate should go unused—for he could not pass through it with a corpse hanging over his head—and that treasure should sit idle and practically invite him to take it. He would not use that gate because the body would be above him as he drove through. So he opened the tomb. But he found no money—only the body and an inscription that read: "If you were not insatiable for money and shamefully greedy, you would not have opened the resting place of the dead." Such was the character of this queen.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 186
paragraphs: This queen's son, also named Labynetos like his father, was the king of Assyria against whom Cyrus marched. When the Great King goes on campaign, he brings carefully prepared provisions and livestock from home. He also brings water from the river Choaspes, which flows past Susa. Only from this river does the king drink. The water is boiled and stored in silver vessels. Many four-wheeled mule wagons carry it wherever the king travels.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 187
paragraphs: On his march toward Babylon, Cyrus reached the river Gyndes. This river rises in the mountains of the Matienians, flows through Dardanian territory, and empties into the Tigris, which passes the city of Opis and flows into the Red Sea. As Cyrus attempted to cross the Gyndes, which was deep enough to be navigable, one of his sacred white horses charged into the river and tried to swim across. The current swept the horse under and carried it away. Cyrus was furious at the river for this outrage. He swore he would make it so weak that women could cross it without getting their knees wet. He suspended his march on Babylon, divided his army in two, and had them dig one hundred and eighty channels on each side of the river—three hundred and sixty in all—fanning out in every direction. This vast project took the entire summer.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 188
paragraphs: After punishing the Gyndes by splitting it into three hundred and sixty channels, Cyrus resumed his march on Babylon at the start of the following spring. The Babylonians marched out and met him in battle. They were defeated and driven behind their walls. They had known for a long time that Cyrus was restless and had watched him attack one nation after another. So they had stockpiled enough food for many years and were unconcerned about a siege. Cyrus was stuck. Time passed and he made no progress.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 189
paragraphs: After punishing the Gyndes by splitting it into three hundred and sixty channels, Cyrus resumed his march on Babylon at the start of the following spring. The Babylonians marched out and met him in battle. They were defeated and driven behind their walls.
