They had known for a long time that Cyrus was restless and had watched him attack one nation after another. So they had stockpiled enough food for many years and were unconcerned about a siege. Cyrus was stuck. Time passed and he made no progress.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 190
paragraphs: Then—whether someone suggested it or he thought of it himself—Cyrus did this. He posted the main body of his army at the point where the Euphrates enters the city, and another force at the opposite end where it exits. He told his men to enter the city along the riverbed as soon as the water was low enough to wade. Then he took the non-combat troops to the lake that Queen Nitocris had dug. He did exactly what she had done with the river: he diverted the Euphrates through a canal into the lake, which was still a marsh. As the water level dropped, the riverbed through the city became fordable. The Persians posted along the banks waded in and entered Babylon. If the Babylonians had noticed or realized what Cyrus was doing, they could have destroyed the Persians completely. They could have locked all the riverside gates, climbed the embankment walls, and trapped the Persians in the riverbed like fish. But the Persians took them completely by surprise. Because of the city’s enormous size, the residents in the center did not know the outer parts had been captured. There happened to be a festival that day. They were dancing and celebrating—and knew nothing until the very end.
That is how Babylon was captured for the first time.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 191
paragraphs: As for the wealth of Babylon, I will give one example among many. The entire empire of the Great King is divided into regions that supply provisions for the king and his army, separate from the regular tribute. Of the twelve months in the year, the territory of Babylon provides for four—the remaining eight are covered by all the rest of Asia. Babylonia alone accounts for a third of Asia's resources. The governance of this region—called a satrapy by the Persians—is the richest of all the governorships. When Tritantaichmes, son of Artabazos, held it as the king's appointee, he received a full artaba of silver every day. (An artaba is a Persian measure, larger than an Attic medimnos by three Attic choinikes.) He kept a personal stable of eight hundred stallions and sixteen thousand mares, with each stallion covering twenty mares. He also maintained such a vast number of Indian dogs that four large villages on the plain were exempted from all other taxes just to feed them.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 192
paragraphs: Such was the wealth of Babylon's governor. Assyria gets little rain, but what little it gets nourishes the roots of the grain. The crops grow and ripen through irrigation from the river—not through flooding as in Egypt, but by hand and with water-lifting devices. Like Egypt, the whole region is laced with canals. The largest is navigable and runs southeast toward the Red Sea. The land is the most productive grain-growing country I know of. It does not even try to produce figs, grapes, or olives, but for grain it is so generous that yields of two-hundred-fold are normal, and three-hundred-fold in exceptional years. The leaves of the wheat and barley grow four fingers wide. As for millet and sesame growing as tall as trees—I know this is true, but I will not mention the height, since I am well aware that even what I have already said will seem incredible to people who have never visited Babylon. They use only sesame oil, not olive oil. Palm trees grow throughout the plain, most of them fruit-bearing. From the fruit they make bread, wine, and honey. The Babylonians cultivate palms the same way the Greeks cultivate figs: they tie the fruit of the wild palms to the cultivated ones so that wasps enter the dates and ripen them, preventing the fruit from falling off prematurely.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 193
paragraphs: The greatest wonder of the region, after the city itself, is this. Their boats that travel downstream to Babylon are round and entirely made of leather. In Armenia, upstream of Assyria, they cut ribs of willow and stretch hides over them to form the hull, rounding the bottom without making a distinct bow or stern. They shape the boats like shields, line them with straw, load them with cargo (often casks of palm wine), and float them downstream. Two men standing upright guide each boat with paddles. Some boats are very large, some small. The largest can carry as much as five thousand talents in weight. A live donkey travels in each boat—larger boats carry several. When they reach Babylon and sell their cargo, they auction off the willow ribs and straw and load the hides onto the donkeys to carry back to Armenia. It is impossible to sail upstream against the current, which is too strong. That is why the boats are made of hide rather than wood. When they get back to Armenia with the donkeys, they build new boats the same way.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 194
paragraphs: Their dress consists of a linen tunic reaching to the feet, a woolen garment over that, and a white cloak wrapped around the whole. They wear native-style shoes, somewhat like Boeotian sandals. They grow their hair long, wear turbans, and perfume their entire bodies. Every man has a personal seal ring and a handmade walking stick. Each stick has a carved figure at the top—an apple, a rose, a lily, an eagle, or something similar. It is not the custom to carry a stick without a device on it.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 195
paragraphs: That is their clothing. Now their customs. The wisest one, in my opinion (a custom the Eneti in Illyria also follow), is this. Once a year in every village, all the young women of marriageable age were gathered in one place. A crowd of men stood around them. An auctioneer called each woman forward, one at a time, starting with the most beautiful and selling her to the highest bidder. Then the second most beautiful was sold, and so on. All were sold as wives, not slaves. The wealthiest Babylonians competed for the most beautiful women. But the ordinary men, who cared less about beauty, actually received money to take the plainer women. After the beautiful women were sold off, the auctioneer called forward the least attractive, or any who were disabled, and asked who would marry her for the smallest payment. She went to whoever demanded the least. The money came from the sale of the beautiful women: in this way, the good-looking women provided dowries for the plain ones. No father could give his daughter to any man he chose. The buyer could not take the girl home without providing a guarantor that he would actually marry her. If the couple did not get along, the rule required that the money be returned. Anyone from any village was allowed to come and buy. This was their finest custom, but it has fallen out of use. They have recently devised a new practice instead. Since the Persian conquest brought poverty and ruin, every man of the common people who lacks a livelihood prostitutes his daughters.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 196
paragraphs: The second wisest custom is this. They carry their sick out into the marketplace, since they do not use physicians. People who pass by the sick person offer advice about the disease—anyone who has suffered the same illness or knows someone who has. They approach the sick person and recommend whatever treatment cured them or someone they know. No one is allowed to walk past a sick person in silence without asking what ails him.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 197
paragraphs: They bury their dead in honey, and their funeral laments are similar to those of Egypt. Whenever a Babylonian man has been intimate with his wife, he sits beside burning incense. His wife does the same on the other side. At dawn, they both bathe. They will not touch any vessel until they have washed. The Arabians observe the same custom.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 198
paragraphs: The most shameful Babylonian custom is this. Every woman of the country must sit once in her lifetime in the precinct of Aphrodite and have intercourse with a stranger. Many wealthy women, too proud to mingle with the common crowd, drive to the temple in covered carriages with large retinues. But most women do it this way: they sit in the sacred precinct of Aphrodite wearing a wreath of cord around their heads. There are great crowds, as women are constantly arriving and departing. Straight pathways run in every direction through the seated women, and the strangers walk along these to make their choice. Once a woman takes her seat, she cannot go home until some stranger has thrown a silver coin into her lap and taken her outside the precinct. As he throws the coin, he must say: "I summon you in the name of the goddess Mylitta" (this is the Assyrian name for Aphrodite). The amount does not matter—she has no right to refuse, since the money becomes sacred. She follows the first man who throws and rejects no one. After the act, having fulfilled her duty to the goddess, she goes home. From then on, no amount of money will win her again. The attractive women leave quickly. The plain ones wait a long time—some for as long as three or four years. A similar custom exists in parts of Cyprus.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 199
paragraphs: Those are the established customs of the Babylonians. Among them there are also three tribes that eat nothing but fish. When they catch and dry their fish in the sun, they do this: they throw them into brine, then pound them with a pestle in a mortar, and strain the result through a linen cloth. Some eat this as a paste, others bake it into a kind of bread.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 200
paragraphs: After conquering Babylon, Cyrus wanted to subdue the Massagetae. This nation is said to be large and warlike. They live toward the east and the sunrise, beyond the river Araxes and opposite the Issedonians. Some say they are a Scythian people.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 201
paragraphs: Some say the Araxes is larger than the Danube, others smaller. They say it has many islands about the size of Lesbos. The people on these islands dig up and eat various roots in summer, and store ripe tree fruits for winter. They have also discovered certain trees whose fruit, when thrown on a fire at a gathering, produces a smoke that intoxicates them just as wine intoxicates Greeks. The more fruit they throw on, the more intoxicated they become, until they rise to dance and sing. That is said to be their way of life. The Araxes flows from the Matienian mountains—the same range where the Gyndes rises, the river Cyrus split into three hundred and sixty channels. The Araxes empties through forty mouths, all but one of which end in swamps and marshes. People are said to live in these marshes, eating raw fish and wearing clothes made of sealskins. The one remaining mouth of the Araxes flows in a clear channel into the Caspian Sea.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 202
paragraphs: The Caspian Sea is a body of water by itself, connected to no other sea. The entire sea navigated by the Greeks—and the ocean beyond the Pillars of Heracles, called the Atlantic—and the Red Sea are in fact all one body of water. But the Caspian is separate. It is as long as a fifteen-day voyage under oars and as wide as an eight-day voyage at its broadest point. On its western shore rises the Caucasus, the largest and tallest of all mountain ranges, home to many diverse peoples, most of whom live entirely off wild plants. They say the trees there produce leaves that, when crushed and mixed with water, are used by the natives to paint figures on their clothing. The figures do not wash out but last as long as the wool, as if woven into the fabric from the start. These people are said to have intercourse openly, like cattle.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 203
paragraphs: To the west, then, the Caucasus borders the Caspian Sea. To the east and the sunrise, a plain stretches away beyond sight. The Massagetae occupy a large part of this great plain. It was against them that Cyrus was eager to march. Many factors emboldened him: above all, the circumstances of his birth, which seemed touched by something more than human, and also his military successes—for wherever Cyrus turned his forces, no nation could escape.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 204
paragraphs: The ruler of the Massagetae was a woman named Tomyris, who had become queen after her husband's death. Cyrus sent a message proposing marriage, pretending he wanted her as his wife. But Tomyris understood that he was wooing not her but the Massagetae kingdom. She refused. When trickery failed, Cyrus marched openly to the Araxes and began his campaign against the Massagetae. He built bridges for his army to cross the river and constructed towers on the pontoon boats.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 205
paragraphs: While he was at work on this, Tomyris sent a herald with this message: "King of the Medes, stop what you are doing. You cannot know whether this will turn out well for you. Stop. Rule your own people and let us rule ours. But I know you will not take this advice, since peace is the last thing you want. If you are truly determined to fight the Massagetae, then stop building your bridge. We will withdraw three days' march from the river, and you may cross. Or if you prefer to meet us on your side, then you withdraw the same distance." When Cyrus heard this, he called a council of the leading Persians and laid the choice before them. They unanimously advised him to let Tomyris cross and fight on Persian soil.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 206
paragraphs: Croesus the Lydian was present and disagreed. He spoke against the majority view: "O king, I told you before that since Zeus gave me over to you, I would do my best to prevent any harm from befalling your house. My own sufferings have taught me bitter lessons. If you think you are immortal and lead an immortal army, there is no point in my giving you advice. But if you recognize that you are a man commanding men, then learn this first: there is a wheel of human fortune. As it turns, it does not permit the same person to prosper forever. I hold a different opinion from these advisors. If we let the enemy onto our territory and are beaten, you lose your entire empire. Obviously the Massagetae, if they win, will not retreat home—they will march on your domains. And if we win, we win less than if we had crossed and beaten them on their own ground, where we could pursue them into their territory. I am matching one case against the other. Besides, it would be intolerable for Cyrus, son of Cambyses, to yield ground to a woman. My advice: cross the river and advance as far as the enemy retreats. Then try to defeat them with this stratagem. The Massagetae, I am told, have never experienced Persian luxuries. So let us slaughter a great number of livestock, prepare an enormous feast in our camp, and set out wine without limit and every kind of fine food. Then withdraw, leaving the weakest troops behind. When the Massagetae see the feast, they will fall on it. That gives us our chance for a great victory."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 207
paragraphs: These were the competing proposals. Cyrus abandoned his first plan and chose Croesus' advice. He told Tomyris to withdraw, as he intended to cross over to her. She retreated as she had promised. Cyrus placed Croesus in the care of his son Cambyses, to whom he was handing over the kingdom, and instructed Cambyses to honor Croesus and treat him well, in case the crossing went badly. Then he sent them both back to Persia and crossed the river with his army.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 208
paragraphs: After crossing the Araxes, night fell and Cyrus had a dream in the land of the Massagetae. He dreamed he saw the eldest son of Hystaspes with wings on his shoulders, one wing overshadowing Asia and the other Europe. (The eldest son of Hystaspes was Darius, who at that time was about twenty years old and had been left behind in Persia, being too young for the campaign.) When Cyrus woke, he considered the dream carefully. Thinking it important, he summoned Hystaspes and said privately: "Hystaspes, your son has been caught plotting against me and my empire. I know this for certain, and I will tell you how. The gods watch over me and show me the future. Last night I saw your eldest son in a dream with wings on his shoulders, one overshadowing Asia and the other Europe. This dream can only mean he is conspiring against me. Go back to Persia at once and make sure you have your son ready for questioning when I return from this campaign."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 209
paragraphs: Cyrus said this because he believed Darius was plotting against him. But in truth, the gods were showing him that he would die there and his kingdom would pass to Darius. Hystaspes replied: "O king, may no Persian ever be born who plots against you! But if one exists, may he perish swiftly. You took the Persians from slaves and made them free, from subjects and made them rulers of all. If a dream has shown you that my son is plotting, I hand him over to you to do with as you wish." With this answer, Hystaspes crossed back over the Araxes and returned to Persia to keep watch over his son Darius for Cyrus.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 210
paragraphs: Cyrus advanced one day's march beyond the Araxes and carried out Croesus' plan. He then withdrew with his best troops, leaving behind the weakest. A third of the Massagetae army attacked and wiped out the soldiers Cyrus had left. Then, seeing the feast laid out, they sat down and ate. When they had gorged themselves on food and wine, they fell asleep. The Persians returned, killed most of them, and captured even more—among the prisoners was the son of Queen Tomyris, the Massagetae commander, whose name was Spargapises.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 211
paragraphs: When Tomyris learned what had happened to her army and her son, she sent a herald to Cyrus with this message: "Cyrus, insatiable for blood, do not be puffed up by what has happened. You conquered my son not in fair battle but by the fruit of the vine—the substance that fills you Persians until you lose your minds and say shameful things as it settles in your bellies. That is the weapon you used to overpower my son, not strength in combat. Now hear my good advice. Give me back my son and leave this land unpunished, even though you savaged a third of my army. If you refuse, I swear by the sun, the lord of the Massagetae, that for all your insatiable thirst, I will give you your fill of blood."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 212
paragraphs: Cyrus ignored this message. As for Tomyris' son Spargapises, when the wine wore off and he understood his situation, he begged Cyrus to free his hands. Once unbound, he killed himself.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 213
paragraphs: That was how Spargapises died. Since Cyrus would not listen, Tomyris gathered all her forces and attacked. I judge this to have been the fiercest of all battles between non-Greek peoples. Here is how it is said to have gone. First, standing at a distance, they shot arrows at each other. When their arrows were spent, they charged and fought hand to hand with spears and daggers. They stayed locked in combat for a long time, neither side willing to flee. Finally, the Massagetae prevailed. The greater part of the Persian army was destroyed on the spot, and Cyrus himself was killed. He had reigned in all twenty-nine years. Tomyris found his body, filled a leather bag with human blood, and plunged Cyrus' head into it. Exulting over the dead king, she said: "I am alive and victorious, yet you destroyed me by capturing my son through trickery. But as I warned you, I have given you your fill of blood." Of the many accounts of Cyrus' death, this is the one I find most credible.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 214
paragraphs: The Massagetae dress like the Scythians and have a similar way of life. They have both mounted warriors and foot soldiers, both archers and spearmen. They also carry battle-axes. For everything they make, they use gold and bronze. Spear points, arrowheads, and battle-axes are all bronze. Helmets, belts, and chest armor are decorated with gold. Likewise with their horses: the breastplates are bronze, but the bits, cheekpieces, and other horse fittings are gold. They use no iron or silver at all, since neither exists in their land. But gold and bronze are available in abundance.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 215
paragraphs: These are their customs. Each man marries one wife, but they share their wives in common. The Greeks attribute this practice to the Scythians, but in fact it belongs to the Massagetae. Whenever a man desires a woman, he hangs his quiver on the front of her wagon and lies with her without shame. They set no fixed limit on life span, but when a man grows very old, his relatives gather and sacrifice him along with some cattle. They boil the flesh together and feast on it. This they consider the most blessed death. A man who dies of disease is not eaten but buried, and it is counted as a misfortune that he did not live long enough to be sacrificed. They do not grow crops but live on livestock and fish, which the Araxes supplies in abundance. They drink milk. The only god they worship is the sun. They sacrifice horses to it, reasoning that the swiftest of mortal creatures deserves to be offered to the swiftest of the gods.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 216
paragraphs: When Cyrus died, the kingdom passed to Cambyses, his son by Cassandane, daughter of Pharnaspes. Cassandane had died before Cyrus, and he had mourned her deeply, commanding all his subjects to mourn as well. Cambyses, the son of Cyrus and this woman, regarded the Ionians and Aeolians as slaves inherited from his father. When he organized his expedition against Egypt, he included them among the Greek troops he brought along.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 217
paragraphs: Before Psammetichos became their king, the Egyptians believed they were the oldest people on earth. But when Psammetichos took the throne, he wanted to settle the question of which people came first. Since then, the Egyptians consider the Phrygians older than themselves and themselves older than everyone else. Psammetichos, unable to find the answer through inquiry, devised an experiment. He took two newborn children of common parents and gave them to a shepherd to raise among his flocks. He instructed that no one was to speak a word in their presence. They were to be kept in a solitary hut with goats, and when the shepherd had fed them their fill of goat's milk, he was to carry on with his other tasks. Psammetichos did this because he wanted to hear what word the children would utter first, once they were past the age of meaningless babbling. And so it happened. After two years, when the shepherd opened the door and went in, both children reached out their hands to him and said "bekos." The first time he heard it, he kept quiet. But when the word was repeated every time he came to tend them, he told his master and brought the children before him. Psammetichos heard it for himself. He then inquired which people called something "bekos" and discovered that the Phrygians use this word for bread. The Egyptians, reasoning from this, conceded that the Phrygians were older than themselves.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 218
paragraphs: I heard this from the priests of Hephaistos in Memphis. The Greeks tell many fanciful versions, including one in which Psammetichos cut out the tongues of certain women and had the children raised by them.

That is what they told me about the rearing of the children. I also heard other things in Memphis from the priests of Hephaistos. I traveled to Thebes and Heliopolis as well, specifically to check whether their accounts agreed with those in Memphis, since the priests of Heliopolis are said to be the most learned in Egypt. The parts of their accounts that deal with the gods I am not eager to report, since I believe all people know equally little about such matters. What I do mention about the gods, I mention only when my narrative forces me to.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 219
paragraphs: On matters concerning human history, the priests agreed. The Egyptians, they said, were the first people to discover the year, dividing it into twelve parts based on the seasons. They learned this, the priests said, from the stars. Their system is wiser than the Greek one, in my opinion, because the Greeks have to insert an extra month every other year to keep the seasons aligned, while the Egyptians use twelve months of thirty days each and add five extra days every year, keeping the cycle of seasons perfectly regular. The Egyptians also said they were the first to use the names of the twelve gods, and that the Greeks adopted these names from them. They were the first to assign altars, images, and temples to gods, and the first to carve figures in stone. Most of this they demonstrated was true. They said the first human king of Egypt was Min. In his time, all of Egypt except the Theban district was marshland. None of the land below Lake Moeris existed—the lake is seven days' voyage up the river from the sea.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 220
paragraphs: I thought their account of the land was correct. It is obvious, even to someone who has not been told, that the Egypt where the Greeks sail is land the Egyptians have won from the sea—a gift of the river. The same is true of the land three days' journey above the lake. No one told me this in so many words, but it is clearly the same kind of land. Egypt's soil is black and crumbly, consisting of the mud and silt the Nile has carried down from Ethiopia. Libyan soil, as we know, is reddish and rather sandy, while Arabian soil is more clay-like and stony.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 221
paragraphs: As further evidence about this land, the priests told me that in the reign of King Moeris, whenever the river rose at least eight cubits, it flooded all of Egypt below Memphis. At the time they told me this, fewer than nine hundred years had passed since Moeris' death. Yet now, unless the river rises at least fifteen or sixteen cubits, it does not overflow. If this land continues to grow in height at the same rate, and to increase in extent in the same proportion, it seems to me that the Egyptians who live below Lake Moeris—especially those in the Delta—will eventually suffer permanent drought as the Nile can no longer reach their fields.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 222
paragraphs: From the coast, Egypt extends inland about sixty schoines as far as Heliopolis. The whole land is broad, flat, without springs, and made of alluvial mud. The road inland from the sea to Heliopolis is about the same length as the road from Athens to the altar of the twelve gods at Olympian Pisa. If you measure carefully, you find these two distances differ by only a small amount—no more than fifteen furlongs.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 223
paragraphs: From Heliopolis upriver, Egypt is narrow. On one side, the Arabian mountains stretch along it from north to south, running inland without a break toward the Red Sea. In these mountains are the quarries from which the stones for the pyramids at Memphis were cut. Here the range turns and bends south toward the Red Sea. At its widest point, the range takes two months to cross from east to west. Its eastern border produces frankincense. On the other side of the Nile, toward Libya, runs another rocky mountain range where the pyramids stand, covered in sand and extending south in the same direction as the southern portion of the Arabian range. So above Heliopolis, the land is not wide—at least by Egyptian standards. For about four days' journey the valley between these two mountain ranges is narrow. The valley floor between the ranges is at its narrowest only about two hundred furlongs wide. After that, Egypt opens up again.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 224
paragraphs: Such is the nature of this land. From Heliopolis to Thebes is a nine-day voyage upstream, a distance of four thousand eight hundred and sixty furlongs, or eighty-one schoines. To sum up the measurements of Egypt: the coastline is three thousand six hundred furlongs, as I have already stated. The distance from the coast to Thebes is six thousand one hundred and twenty furlongs. From Thebes to the city of Elephantine is a further one thousand eight hundred furlongs.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 225
paragraphs: Most of this land, it seemed to me—and the priests agreed—had been won from the sea by the Egyptians over time. The space between the mountain ranges above Memphis looked to me as though it had once been a gulf of the sea, just like the areas around Ilion, Teuthrania, Ephesus, and the plain of the Maeander—if one may compare small things to great. None of the rivers that built up those places can be compared to even one of the five mouths of the Nile. There are also other rivers, smaller than the Nile, that have achieved great things. I could name several, including the Acheloos, which flows through Acarnania and has already turned half the Echinades islands into mainland.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 226
paragraphs: In the land of Arabia, not far from Egypt, there is a gulf of the sea running in from the Red Sea. It is very long and narrow, as I will describe. In terms of sailing time, it takes forty days to cross from the innermost point to the open sea in a rowing vessel. In width, the gulf is only half a day's voyage at its widest. A tide ebbs and flows in it every day. I believe Egypt was once a gulf of exactly this kind—one running in from the Northern Sea toward Ethiopia, while the Arabian Gulf ran from the Southern Sea toward Syria. The two gulfs almost met at their inner ends, separated only by a small strip of land. Now if the Nile were to divert its course into this Arabian Gulf, what would prevent it from silting the gulf up within twenty thousand years? I would expect it to fill in within ten thousand. Is it then not perfectly reasonable that, in all the ages before I was born, a gulf even larger than this one could have been filled up by so great and so active a river?

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 227
paragraphs: I believe the Egyptian account and am thoroughly convinced of it myself, because I have observed that Egypt projects into the sea beyond the neighboring coastline. Seashells are found on the hills. A salty crust eats into the stone of the pyramids. The only sandy mountain in Egypt is the one above Memphis. The soil of Egypt resembles neither that of the neighboring Arabia, nor Libya, nor Syria (the Syrians occupy the coast of Arabia). Egyptian soil is black and crumbly—clearly river silt carried down from Ethiopia. Libyan soil, as I know, is reddish and sandy. Arabian and Syrian soil is more clay and stone.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 228
paragraphs: The priests also gave me strong proof about this land. In the reign of King Moeris, whenever the river rose at least eight cubits, it flooded Egypt below Memphis. Fewer than nine hundred years had passed since Moeris' death when I heard this from the priests. Now, if the river does not rise at least fifteen or sixteen cubits, the water does not overflow. It seems to me that if the land continues to grow in height at the same rate, and to increase in extent in the same proportion, then the Egyptians who live below Lake Moeris and in the Delta will suffer the very fate they once said the Greeks would suffer. When they learned that all of Greece depends on rain and not on rivers for irrigation, they remarked that the Greeks would one day be bitterly disappointed, meaning that if the god chose not to send rain and instead sent drought, the Greeks would perish of hunger, having no source of water except from heaven.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 229
paragraphs: The Egyptians were right about the Greeks. But let me now describe the Egyptians' own situation. If, as I said before, the land below Memphis (for that is the part that keeps growing) continues to rise at the same rate as in the past, then the Egyptians living there will certainly go hungry, since it will not rain in their country and the river will no longer be able to overflow their fields. As things stand now, no people on earth—and no other Egyptians—reap the harvest with less labor. They do not have to break the ground with a plow, or hoe, or do any of the work that other men do to grow crops. The river rises on its own, waters the fields, and then recedes. Each farmer then sows his land and turns his pigs loose on it. The pigs trample the seed into the ground. After that, he waits for the harvest. He uses the pigs again to thresh the grain, and then gathers it in.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 230
paragraphs: If we follow the Ionian definition of Egypt—that only the Delta counts as Egypt, with its coastline stretching forty schoines from the Watchtower of Perseus to the fish-curing houses of Pelusium, and extending inland as far as the city of Cercasoros where the Nile splits into two branches flowing to Pelusium and Canobos—and if we accept that the rest of Egyptian land belongs partly to Libya and partly to Arabia—then by this definition, the Egyptians had no country at all in the old days. The Delta itself, as the Egyptians say and I believe, is alluvial land that has only recently appeared. If they once had no territory, why did they waste their time on the pointless experiment of trying to find out whether they were the oldest people? They would have had no need to test the language of children raised in isolation. But in my opinion, the Egyptians did not come into existence along with the Delta. They have existed since the human race began, and as the land grew, some stayed while others gradually moved downstream. In ancient times, Thebes was called Egypt, and its total circumference is six thousand one hundred and twenty furlongs.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 231
paragraphs: If our understanding of these matters is correct, then the Ionian definition of Egypt is wrong. If the Ionians are right, I can prove that the Greeks and the Ionians themselves do not know how to count. They say the whole earth consists of three parts: Europe, Asia, and Libya. They should add a fourth: the Delta of Egypt, since they assign it neither to Asia nor to Libya. By their definition, the Nile does not form the boundary between Asia and Libya—it splits at the apex of the Delta and flows around it, leaving the Delta between Asia and Libya.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 232
paragraphs: Let us set aside the Ionian view. My own definition is this: Egypt is all the land inhabited by Egyptians, just as Cilicia belongs to the Cilicians and Assyria to the Assyrians. The only true boundary between Asia and Libya is the borders of Egypt. If we follow the Greek convention, we would have to consider all of Egypt from the Cataracts and the city of Elephantine downward as divided in two: one part belonging to Libya and one to Asia. The Nile splits from the Cataracts and flows through the middle of Egypt to the sea. Up to the city of Cercasoros it flows in a single channel. There it divides into three branches: one flowing east to the Pelusiac mouth, one west to the Canobic mouth, and one running straight through the middle of the Delta to a point on the coast called the Sebennytic mouth. Two other branches split off from the Sebennytic: the Saitic and the Mendesian. The Bolbitinic and Bucolic mouths are not natural but were dug by hand. The oracle of Ammon also supports my definition of Egypt's extent, and I learned about this oracle only after I had formed my own opinion.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 233
paragraphs: The oracle's answer supports my view that Egypt extends beyond just the Delta. The people of Marea and Apis, who live on the Libyan border of Egypt, considered themselves Libyans rather than Egyptians. They resented the religious rules about cattle and did not want to abstain from eating cow's flesh. So they sent to the oracle of Ammon and claimed they had nothing in common with the Egyptians. They lived outside the Delta and spoke a different language, and they wanted to be allowed to eat whatever they wished. But the god refused them. He said that all land watered by the Nile in flood is Egypt, and all who live below the city of Elephantine and drink the Nile's water are Egyptians. That was the oracle's answer.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 234
paragraphs: When it is in flood, the Nile overflows not only the Delta but also extends into the so-called Libyan and Arabian territory, sometimes as much as two days' journey on each side, sometimes more, sometimes less.

About the nature of the river, I was unable to learn anything from the priests or from anyone else. I was especially eager to learn why the Nile begins to rise at the summer solstice and continues rising for about a hundred days, then drops back and remains low throughout the winter until the next summer solstice. No Egyptian could tell me anything about this. I wanted to know why it is the only river on earth that sends no breezes from its surface.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 235
paragraphs: Some Greeks who wanted to be considered clever have offered three different explanations for this river's behavior. Two of them I do not think worth discussing in detail, though I will mention their nature. One theory holds that the Etesian winds cause the Nile to rise by preventing the river from flowing into the sea. But the Etesian winds often fail to blow, and the Nile rises just the same. Besides, if the Etesian winds were the cause, every other river that flows against them should behave the same way—and even more so, since they are smaller and have weaker currents. Yet many such rivers in Syria and Libya are completely unaffected.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 236
paragraphs: The second explanation is even more ignorant than the first, though more striking. It claims the river produces these effects because it flows from the Ocean, which supposedly encircles the entire earth.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 237
paragraphs: The third theory sounds the most plausible but is actually the most wrong. It claims the Nile rises from melting snow. But the Nile flows from Libya through the middle of Ethiopia into Egypt—from extremely hot regions to cooler ones. How could it flow from snow? Any thinking person would reject this. The strongest evidence against it is the winds that blow from those regions, which are always hot. Second, the land is rainless and frostless. After snowfall, rain must follow within five days; so if there were snow in those lands, there would also be rain. Third, the people there are black from the burning heat. Hawks and swallows live there year-round, and cranes migrate there from Scythia to escape winter. None of this would be true if it snowed even a little in the lands through which the Nile flows.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 238
paragraphs: As for the man who spoke of the Ocean, he has carried his tale into the realm of the unknowable, and so he cannot be refuted. For my part, I know of no river called Ocean. I believe Homer or some earlier poet invented the name and introduced it into poetry.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 239
paragraphs: If, having criticized these theories, I am obliged to offer my own opinion about this mystery, I will explain what I think causes the Nile to rise in summer. During winter, the sun is driven by storms from its usual path and moves to the upper regions of Libya. That is the whole explanation in brief. The country nearest to the sun, the country over which it passes, will naturally have the least water, since the streams that feed its rivers will be dried up.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 240
paragraphs: To explain at greater length: when the sun passes over the upper parts of Libya, this is what happens. Because the air in those regions is always clear and the land always warm—since there are no cold winds—the sun does what it normally does in summer when it moves through the middle of the sky. It draws water up. Then it pushes the moisture into the upper regions, where the winds catch it, scatter it, and dissolve it. So the winds that blow from there—the south wind and the southwest—are the rainiest of all winds. I do not believe the sun releases all the water it draws up from the Nile each year. Some stays with the sun. When winter eases, the sun returns to the center of the sky. From then on, it draws water equally from all rivers. Until then, the other rivers have been swollen by heavy rains and by streams pouring through rain-soaked land. But in summer, when the rains stop and the sun's pull is felt, they run low. The Nile, however, which gets no rain and yet loses water to the sun, naturally runs lower in winter than in summer. In summer, the sun pulls from it equally as from all other water, but in winter, the Nile alone is depleted. The sun, in my opinion, is the cause of all this.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 241
paragraphs: In my opinion, the sun is also the cause of the dry air in those regions, scorching its path through the sky. That is why summer is perpetual in the upper parts of Libya. If the positions of the seasons were reversed—if the part of the sky now occupied by the north wind and winter were occupied by the south wind and midday, and vice versa—then the sun, driven from the center of the sky by winter and the north wind, would go to the upper parts of Europe as it now goes to upper Libya. As it passed through Europe, I believe it would do to the Danube exactly what it now does to the Nile.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 242
paragraphs: As for why no breeze blows from the Nile: I think it is simply unnatural for anything to blow from very hot places. A breeze normally comes from something cold.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 243
paragraphs: Let these matters be as they are and always have been. As for the sources of the Nile, no one I spoke with—neither Egyptian, Libyan, nor Greek—claimed to know anything, except the scribe of the sacred treasures of Athena at the city of Sais in Egypt. Even he seemed to be joking when he said he knew the exact truth. He said there are two mountains with sharp peaks between the city of Syene in the Theban district and Elephantine. Their names are Crophi and Mophi. The springs of the Nile, which are bottomless, flow up from between these mountains. Half the water flows north toward Egypt and half flows south toward Ethiopia. That the springs are bottomless was tested by Psammetichos, king of Egypt, who had a rope braided thousands of fathoms long and lowered it in without reaching the bottom. If this story is true—and I suspect the scribe was not telling the truth—it merely proves that there are strong whirlpools and back-currents there, caused by the water striking the mountains, preventing a sounding line from reaching the bottom.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 244
paragraphs: From no other person could I learn anything. But this much more I discovered by traveling as far as Elephantine to see for myself, and beyond that by hearsay. Going upstream from Elephantine, the ground rises steeply. In this stretch you must tie your boat on both sides, as you tie an ox, and haul it. If the rope breaks, the boat is carried away by the force of the current. This section takes four days to navigate. The Nile here is winding, like the Maeander. There are twelve schoines of this kind that must be traversed. After that, you reach a level plain where the Nile flows around an island called Tachompso. Above Elephantine, Ethiopians already inhabit both banks. They also occupy half of Tachompso, with Egyptians on the other half. Beyond the island is a great lake. Ethiopian nomads live on its shores. After crossing the lake, you rejoin the Nile's channel, which flows into the lake at this point. Then you disembark and travel on foot along the riverbank for forty days, since sharp rocks and needle-like outcrops make the river unnavigable. After forty days, you board another boat and sail for twelve more days. Then you reach a great city called Meroe. This is said to be the mother city of all Ethiopia. The people there worship only Zeus and Dionysus among the gods. They honor these greatly and have an oracle of Zeus. They go to war whenever and wherever the god tells them through his oracle.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 245
paragraphs: Sailing on from this city, you reach the land of the Deserters in the same number of days it took to travel from Elephantine to the Ethiopian capital. These Deserters are called Asmach, which in Greek means "those who stand at the left hand of the king." They were originally two hundred and forty thousand Egyptian soldiers who defected to Ethiopia for the following reason. In the reign of Psammetichos, garrisons were posted at Elephantine facing Ethiopia, at Daphnae of Pelusium facing Arabia and Syria, and at Marea facing Libya. Even in my time, the Persians maintained garrisons in the same places. The soldiers at Elephantine were on duty for three years without being relieved. They discussed the matter and unanimously decided to revolt against Psammetichos and go over to Ethiopia. When Psammetichos heard of it, he pursued them. When he caught up, he made a long speech, begging them not to abandon their ancestral gods, their wives, and their children. One of the soldiers, so the story goes, pointed to his genitals and said that wherever these went, there would be wives and children. When they reached Ethiopia, they placed themselves at the service of the Ethiopian king. In return, he gave them the territory of certain Ethiopians with whom he was at odds, telling the soldiers to drive them out and settle the land. Through living among the Ethiopians, the soldiers adopted Ethiopian customs and became more civilized.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 246
paragraphs: So the Nile is known for a distance of four months' journey by river and land beyond Egypt. That is the total if you add up all the stages from Elephantine to the Deserters. The river flows from the west and the setting sun. Beyond that point, no one can speak with certainty, because the land is desert and burned by heat.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 247
paragraphs: But I did hear the following from men of Cyrene. They told me they had visited the oracle of Ammon and had a conversation with Etearchos, king of the Ammonians. Somehow the talk turned to the Nile and the fact that no one knows its sources. Etearchos told them that some Nasamonians had once visited him. (The Nasamonians are a Libyan people who live around the Gulf of Syrtis and a stretch of coast to the east.) When asked if they could add anything to what was known about the empty parts of Libya, they told this story. Some bold young men among them—sons of their leading citizens—had, when they came of age, devised various wild adventures. Among other things, they chose five of their number by lot to explore the Libyan desert and see if they could discover more than anyone had seen before. (For the northern coast of Libya, from Egypt all the way to Cape Soloeis at its western end, is inhabited by Libyans of many different tribes—except the parts held by Greeks and Phoenicians. Above the coast and the coastal peoples, Libya is full of wild animals. Beyond the wild animals is a ridge of sand stretching from Egyptian Thebes to the Pillars of Heracles. Along this ridge, at intervals of roughly ten days' journey, are hills of salt. At the top of each hill, cold fresh water shoots up from the salt. People live around these salt hills, at the farthest edge of the inhabited world toward the desert. The first of them, ten days from Thebes, are the Ammonians, who have a temple derived from the Theban Zeus. Then, another ten days' march, are the Augillans. Then, ten days further, the Garamantes, who have a great nation with soil they carry over the salt to plant their crops. From the Garamantes, the shortest route is thirty days to the Lotophagians; among the Garamantes are also the backward-facing cattle, who graze walking backward because their horns curve forward and would stick in the ground if they walked the normal way. They differ from other cattle in no other respect except that their hides are thicker and tougher. The Garamantes hunt the cave-dwelling Ethiopians in four-horse chariots, for the cave-dwelling Ethiopians are the fastest runners of any people we have ever heard of. They eat snakes and lizards and similar creatures. Their language is unlike any other—it sounds like the screeching of bats.) From the Garamantes, another ten days' journey brings you to another salt hill with water and people living around it. This people is called the Atarantes. They are the only people I know of who have no individual names. The tribe as a whole is called Atarantes, but no person has a name. They curse the sun when it reaches its height and heap abuse on it, because it scorches and destroys both them and their land. Another ten days' march brings another salt hill with water and inhabitants. Next to this hill is a mountain called Atlas, which is narrow and round on all sides, and said to be so high that its peaks can never be seen—clouds cover them in summer and winter alike. The locals call it the Pillar of the Sky. This people takes its name from the mountain: they are called Atlantes. They are said to eat no living thing and to have no dreams. Up to the Atlantes, I can give the names of the peoples along the sand ridge. Beyond them I cannot. But the ridge extends all the way to the Pillars of Heracles and even beyond. There are salt mines and settlements at intervals of ten days' journey all along it. The houses of these people are all built of blocks of salt. Rain never falls in this part of Libya; if it did, salt walls could not stand. The salt mined here is both white and purple. South of the ridge, the interior of Libya is desert: no water, no animals, no rain, no vegetation—nothing but sand. Now, the young Nasamonians, sent off by their peers with plenty of water and food, first crossed the inhabited zone, then the zone of wild animals, then headed west through the desert. After many days of walking through deep sand, they finally saw trees growing on a plain. They went up and began picking the fruit. While they were eating, small men—shorter than average—seized them and carried them off. The Nasamonians could not understand their language, nor could the small men understand theirs. They were led through enormous swamps and emerged in a city where everyone was the same height as their captors and black-skinned. A great river ran past the city from west to east, and crocodiles were visible in it.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 248
paragraphs: Let that much suffice of Etearchos the Ammonian's account. He also claimed, as the men of Cyrene reported to me, that the Nasamonians all returned home safely, and that the people they had reached were all sorcerers. As for the river flowing past their city, Etearchos guessed it was the Nile. And reason supports this. The Nile does flow from Libya, cutting through the middle of it. As I reason about the unknown from the known, I believe it starts at a point as far west as the Danube's source. The Danube rises in the land of the Celts near the city of Pyrene and flows through the middle of Europe, dividing it in two. The Celts live beyond the Pillars of Heracles, next to the Cynesians, who are the westernmost people of Europe. The Danube crosses all of Europe and empties into the Euxine Sea at the Milesian colony of Istria. Because the Danube flows through inhabited land, it is well known.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 249
paragraphs: No one can say anything definite about the Nile's sources, since the part of Libya it flows through is uninhabited desert. I have already reported everything I could learn about its course by inquiry and personal observation. It enters Egypt from Libya. Egypt lies roughly opposite the mountain country of Cilicia. From there, it is a five-day journey in a straight line to Sinope on the Euxine. And Sinope lies opposite the point where the Danube reaches the sea. So I conclude that the Nile, in crossing all of Libya, corresponds in length to the Danube.
That is enough about the Nile.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 250
paragraphs: About Egypt, however, I will speak at greater length, because it has more wonders than any other country and more works beyond description. For this reason, more will be said about it.

The Egyptians, in keeping with their climate, which is like no other, and their river, which behaves unlike any other river, have established customs and laws that are almost entirely the opposite of other peoples'. Among them, women go to the marketplace and trade, while men stay home and weave. Other peoples push the weft upward when weaving; the Egyptians push it down. Men carry burdens on their heads; women carry them on their shoulders. Women urinate standing up; men do so sitting down. They relieve themselves indoors but eat outside in the streets, reasoning that shameful necessities should be done in private and things that are not shameful should be done openly. No woman serves as priestess to any god, male or female. Men serve all. Sons are under no obligation to support their parents if they do not wish to, but daughters are compelled to, whether they wish to or not.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 251
paragraphs: Priests of the gods in other countries wear their hair long, but in Egypt they shave their heads. Among other peoples, it is customary for the closest mourners to cut their hair when someone dies. Egyptians, when a death occurs, let their hair grow on both their heads and chins, though they normally keep both shaved. Other peoples keep their animals separate from their living quarters; Egyptians live with their animals. Others live on wheat and barley; for an Egyptian to live on these is a deep disgrace. They make their bread from spelt, which some call "zea." They knead dough with their feet and clay with their hands. They also handle dung with their hands. Other peoples leave their genitals as nature made them, except those who learned otherwise from the Egyptians. But Egyptians practice circumcision. Every man owns two garments, every woman only one. Greeks fasten the rings and sheets of their sails on the outside; Egyptians fasten them on the inside. Greeks write and calculate from left to right; Egyptians from right to left. Yet the Egyptians say they go to the right while the Greeks go to the left. They use two kinds of writing: one called sacred, the other common.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 252
paragraphs: They are exceedingly religious, more so than any other people. Their customs include these: they drink from bronze cups, which they rinse every day—not just some of them, but all. They always wear freshly washed linen. They practice circumcision for the sake of cleanliness, preferring to be clean rather than handsome. The priests shave their entire bodies every other day, so that no louse or any other unclean thing may be on them as they serve the gods. The priests wear only linen clothing and papyrus sandals. No other garment or footwear is permitted. They bathe twice a day in cold water and twice at night. They observe countless other ritual requirements. But they enjoy great advantages: they spend nothing of their own and lose nothing. Sacred food is cooked for them. Each priest receives a generous daily ration of beef and goose meat, along with wine. Fish they may not eat. The Egyptians do not grow beans in their country at all, and any that grow wild they will not eat, either raw or cooked. The priests cannot even look at beans, considering them unclean. Each god is served not by a single priest but by many, one of whom is the chief priest. When a priest dies, his son takes his place.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 253
paragraphs: Male cattle are considered sacred to Epaphos. They are tested as follows: if the priest finds even a single black hair on the animal, it is declared unfit for sacrifice. One priest is specifically appointed to examine each bull. He inspects it standing and lying down, and pulls out its tongue to check for certain prescribed signs. He also examines the tail hairs. If the bull passes every test, the priest marks it by wrapping papyrus around its horns, sealing it with clay, and stamping it with his signet ring. It is then led away. Sacrificing an unmarked bull carries the death penalty.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 254
paragraphs: This is how the animal is tested. The method of sacrifice is as follows. They lead the marked beast to the altar and kindle a fire. Then they pour wine over the altar by the victim, invoke the god, and cut the animal's throat. After cutting the throat, they sever the head. They flay the body but pronounce a curse on the head. Where there is a marketplace with Greek merchants, they carry the head there and sell it. Where there are no Greeks, they throw it into the river. The curse they pronounce over the head is this: "If any evil is about to befall either those who sacrifice or Egypt itself, let it be turned upon this head." The customs regarding the heads of sacrificial animals and the pouring of wine are the same among all Egyptians in all their sacrifices. Because of this custom, no Egyptian will eat the head of any animal.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 255
paragraphs: But the methods of disemboweling and burning the victims differ for different sacrifices. I will describe the sacrifice to the goddess they consider the greatest, at whose festival they hold the most splendid celebration. After praying, they slaughter an ox. They remove the intestines but leave the stomach and fat inside the body. They cut off the legs, the end of the loin, the shoulders, and the neck. They stuff the rest of the body with clean bread, honey, raisins, figs, frankincense, myrrh, and other spices. Having stuffed it, they burn it, pouring a great quantity of oil over it. They fast before the sacrifice and beat their breasts while the fire burns. When the beating is done, they set out a feast from the remains.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 256
paragraphs: All Egyptians sacrifice clean male cattle and calves. But they may not sacrifice females, since these are sacred to Isis. The image of Isis is that of a woman with cow's horns, like the Greek representation of Io. All Egyptians treat cows with far greater reverence than any other animal. For this reason, no Egyptian man or woman will kiss a Greek on the mouth or use a Greek's knife, spit, or cauldron, or eat the flesh of a clean ox that has been cut with a Greek knife. They bury dead cattle as follows: they throw cows into the river, but bulls are buried at the edge of each city, with one or both horns projecting as a marker. When the bodies have decomposed and the appointed time comes, a barge arrives at each city from the island called Prosopitis in the Delta. This island has many cities, but the one from which the barges come is called Atarbechis, and it contains a great temple of Aphrodite. From this city, many people sail out in all directions to the various towns. They dig up the bones of the cattle and carry them all to one place for burial. They bury other dead animals in the same way as cattle. This is their law, for they do not kill any animals.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 257
paragraphs: All who have a temple of Theban Zeus, or who live in the Theban district, sacrifice goats and abstain from sheep. Not all Egyptians worship the same gods in the same way. The only gods universally worshipped are Isis and Osiris (whom they identify with Dionysus). Those who have a temple of Mendes or belong to the Mendesian district sacrifice sheep and abstain from goats. The Thebans and their followers explain their avoidance of sheep with this story: Heracles desperately wanted to see Zeus. Zeus did not want to be seen. Finally, when Heracles persisted, Zeus devised a plan. He skinned a ram and cut off its head. He held the ram's head before his own face and wore the fleece. Then he showed himself to Heracles. This is why the Egyptians make their images of Zeus with a ram's head. The Ammonians, who are colonists of both Egypt and Ethiopia and speak a language midway between the two, adopted this practice from the Egyptians. Even the name Ammon seems to be the Egyptian word for Zeus. The Thebans do not sacrifice rams but consider them sacred for this reason. However, once a year, at the festival of Zeus, they slaughter a single ram, skin it, and drape the fleece over the statue of Zeus as Heracles once saw him. Then they bring an image of Heracles close to the Zeus statue. After this, everyone around the temple mourns for the ram and then buries it in a sacred coffin.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 258
paragraphs: About Heracles, I heard that he is one of the twelve gods. But about the other Heracles—the one the Greeks know—I could learn nothing anywhere in Egypt. Moreover, the Egyptians did not borrow the name from the Greeks. Rather, the Greeks took it from the Egyptians—specifically, those Greeks who gave the name Heracles to the son of Amphitryon. I have much evidence for this. Both parents of the Greek Heracles, Amphitryon and Alcmene, were of Egyptian descent. The Egyptians say they do not know the names Poseidon or the Dioscuri and have never accepted these gods among their own. If they had borrowed any divine name from the Greeks, they would have taken these above all, since they were already seafaring and some Greeks were already sailors. The Egyptian Heracles is an ancient god. By the Egyptians' own account, seventeen thousand years before the reign of Amasis, the eight gods became twelve, and Heracles is one of the eight.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 259
paragraphs: Wanting to learn something certain about these matters, I sailed to Tyre in Phoenicia. I had heard there was a famous temple of Heracles there. I saw it—richly furnished with many offerings. Among them were two pillars, one of refined gold and one of emerald that shone brilliantly at night. I spoke with the priests and asked how long ago their temple had been founded. I found that they too disagreed with the Greeks. They said the temple was established when Tyre was founded, some two thousand three hundred years ago. I also saw another temple of Heracles at Tyre, called the temple of Thasian Heracles. I visited Thasos as well and found a temple of Heracles built by the Phoenicians who founded Thasos while searching for Europa. This was five generations before the Greek Heracles, son of Amphitryon, was born. My research clearly shows that Heracles is an ancient god. I think those Greeks do best who have established two separate cults of Heracles: one where they sacrifice to him as an immortal Olympian god, the other where they offer the honors due to a dead hero.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 260
paragraphs: The Greeks tell many thoughtless stories, and this one about Heracles is especially foolish. They say that when Heracles came to Egypt, the Egyptians put garlands on him and led him in a procession to be sacrificed to Zeus. He submitted quietly at first. But when they began the ritual at the altar, he turned violent and killed them all. To me, this story shows complete ignorance of Egyptian character and custom. How could people who are forbidden to sacrifice any animal except pigs, bulls, and male calves (if they pass inspection) possibly sacrifice human beings? And how could one man, a mortal by their own account, kill tens of thousands? I hope both the gods and the heroes will forgive me for saying so much about these matters.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 261
paragraphs: Now here is why the Egyptians I mentioned do not sacrifice goats, either male or female. The Mendesians count Pan among the eight gods—the gods they say existed before the twelve. Egyptian artists and sculptors make the image of Pan just as the Greeks do: with a goat's face and legs. They do not actually believe he looks like this—they think he resembles the other gods. Why they depict him this way I would rather not say. The Mendesians regard all goats as sacred, but male goats more than female. The goatherds of male goats receive special honor. One particular he-goat is held in the greatest reverence. When he dies, the whole Mendesian district goes into mourning. In the Egyptian language, both Pan and the he-goat are called Mendes.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 262
paragraphs: The Egyptians consider the pig an unclean animal. If anyone merely brushes against a pig in passing, he goes straight to the river and dips himself in, clothes and all. Furthermore, swineherds—even if they are native Egyptians—are the only people in Egypt barred from entering any temple. No one will give his daughter in marriage to a swineherd or marry a swineherd's daughter. So swineherds marry only among themselves. The Egyptians do not consider it proper to sacrifice pigs to any god except Selene and Dionysus, and to these they sacrifice pigs at the same time—at the full moon—and then eat the flesh. Why they abhor pigs at other festivals but sacrifice them at this one—the Egyptians have an explanation for this, which I know but think it more fitting not to repeat.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 263
paragraphs: For Dionysus, on the eve of the festival, each man slaughters a pig by cutting its throat at his own door, then gives it back to the swineherd who sold it, to carry away. The rest of the festival of Dionysus is celebrated by the Egyptians much as it is by the Greeks, with one exception: the Egyptians do not have choruses. Instead of phalluses, they have invented something else. Small puppets about a cubit tall, moved by strings, are carried from village to village by women. The male member nods and is nearly as large as the rest of the body. A flute player leads the way, and the women follow, singing a hymn to Dionysus. Why the male member is so large and is the only part of the body that moves—there is a sacred explanation for this.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 264
paragraphs: I believe Melampus, son of Amythaon, was not ignorant of these rites. He was the one who introduced the name of Dionysus to the Greeks, along with the manner of sacrifice and the phallic procession. Strictly speaking, he did not fully reveal the whole matter—later teachers filled it out. But the phallic procession in honor of Dionysus was introduced by Melampus, and it is from him that the Greeks learned the practice. I maintain that Melampus was a clever man who acquired the art of divination. Among many things he learned from Egypt, he brought the worship of Dionysus to Greece with only minor changes. I cannot accept that the rites of Dionysus in Egypt and Greece are merely a coincidence. If that were so, the Greek rites would be Greek in character and not recently introduced. Nor can I accept that the Egyptians borrowed the practice from the Greeks or anything else. I believe Melampus learned most of the rites of Dionysus from Cadmus of Tyre and the Phoenicians who accompanied him to the land now called Boeotia.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 265
paragraphs: Indeed, nearly all the names of the gods came to Greece from Egypt. That they came from abroad I confirm by my own inquiries, and I believe they came mainly from Egypt. Except for Poseidon and the Dioscuri (as I mentioned), and also Hera, Hestia, Themis, the Graces, and the Nereids, all the gods' names have always been known in Egypt. I am reporting what the Egyptians themselves say. As for the gods whose names they say they do not know, I believe those were named by the Pelasgians—except Poseidon, whom the Greeks learned about from the Libyans. No people have had the name of Poseidon from the beginning except the Libyans, who have always honored him.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 266
paragraphs: These observances, and others I will mention, the Greeks adopted from the Egyptians. But the custom of making images of Hermes with an erect phallus they did not learn from the Egyptians—they learned it from the Pelasgians. The Athenians were the first Greeks to adopt this practice, and from them all the others took it up. By the time the Athenians adopted it, they were already counted among the Greeks, but the Pelasgians were still their neighbors. Anyone who has been initiated into the mysteries of the Cabiri, which the Samothracians celebrate (having received them from the Pelasgians), will understand what I mean. The Pelasgians who taught the Athenians once lived in Samothrace, and it is from them that the Samothracians received the mysteries. The Athenians, then, were the first Greeks to make phallic images of Hermes, and they learned this from the Pelasgians. The Pelasgians told a sacred story about it, which is revealed in the Samothracian mysteries.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 267
paragraphs: The Pelasgians originally made all their sacrifices calling upon the gods in prayer but gave them no names or titles, for they had not yet heard any. They called them simply "gods"—"theoi"—because they had set all things in order and controlled all assignments. Then, after a long time, the names of the gods came from Egypt. (Dionysus arrived much later.) Eventually they consulted the oracle at Dodona about the names—for Dodona is considered the most ancient oracle in Greece and was at that time the only one. When the Pelasgians asked at Dodona whether they should adopt the names that had come from the barbarians, the oracle said yes. From that time on, they used the gods' names in their sacrifices. Later, the Greeks received these names from the Pelasgians.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 268
paragraphs: But where each god came from, or whether they have all existed forever, and what they look like—these things the Greeks did not know until just yesterday, so to speak. I believe Hesiod and Homer lived about four hundred years before my time, no more. These are the poets who composed a theogony for the Greeks, gave the gods their titles, distributed their honors and functions, and described their forms. The poets who are said to have preceded them actually came after, in my opinion.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 269
paragraphs: About the oracles in Greece and in Libya, the Egyptians tell this story. The priests of Theban Zeus told me that two women who served in the temple were carried off by Phoenicians. One, they learned, was sold into Libya, the other into Greece. These women, they said, were the first to establish oracles in those lands. When I asked how they could speak so confidently about this, they replied that they had searched hard for these women without finding them, but learned afterward what I have just reported.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 270
paragraphs: That is what I heard from the priests at Thebes. The prophetesses at Dodona tell a different version. They say that two black doves flew from Egyptian Thebes. One went to Libya, the other to Dodona. The dove that came to Dodona perched in an oak tree and spoke with a human voice, saying that an oracle of Zeus should be established there. The people understood this as a divine command and obeyed. The dove that went to Libya told the Libyans to establish an oracle of Ammon. That too is an oracle of Zeus. The priestesses of Dodona told me this. The eldest was Promeneia, the next Timarete, the youngest Nicandra. The other temple officials confirmed their account.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 271
paragraphs: My own view is this. If the Phoenicians truly did carry off the sacred women and sell one into Libya and one into Greece, then I believe the woman sold into Greece was sold into the country now called Greece but then called Pelasgia—specifically, into the region of the Thesprotians. Being a slave there, she established a shrine of Zeus under a natural oak tree. It made sense that she would think of the god she had served in Thebes when she came to a new land. Later, when she learned Greek, she founded an oracle. She probably also reported that her sister had been sold into Libya by the same Phoenicians who sold her.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 272
paragraphs: I think the women were called doves by the people of Dodona because they were foreigners whose speech sounded like the twittering of birds. Later, they say, the dove spoke with a human voice—meaning the woman became intelligible when she learned Greek. As long as she spoke a foreign language, she seemed to speak like a bird. How could a real dove speak with a human voice? And calling the dove black is simply their way of indicating the woman was Egyptian.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 273
paragraphs: The Egyptians were also the first people to hold religious assemblies, processions, and sacred approaches to temples. The Greeks learned all this from them. My evidence is that Egyptian celebrations have clearly been practiced for a very long time, while the Greek versions are more recent.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 274
paragraphs: The Egyptians hold their religious assemblies not once but many times a year. The largest and most popular is the festival of Artemis at the city of Bubastis. The second is the festival of Isis at Busiris, which has a very great temple of Isis in the middle of the city. The third is the festival at Sais in honor of Athena. The fourth is the festival of the sun at Heliopolis. The fifth is the festival of Leto at the city of Buto. The sixth is the festival of Ares at Papremis.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 275
paragraphs: When traveling to Bubastis for the festival, they do this. Men and women sail together, with great crowds in every boat. Some of the women play rattles, some of the men play flutes, and the rest clap and sing. Whenever they pass a riverside town, they bring the boat close to shore. Some of the women shout mocking taunts at the local women, others dance, and others stand up and expose themselves. They do this at every town along the river. When they reach Bubastis, they celebrate with grand sacrifices, and more wine is consumed at this festival than during all the rest of the year. The locals say that as many as seven hundred thousand men and women (not counting children) gather there.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 276
paragraphs: That is how they celebrate at Bubastis. I have already described the festival of Isis at Busiris. After the sacrifice, all the men and women—tens of thousands of them—beat their breasts in mourning. Whom they mourn, it would be impious for me to say. Any Carians who live in Egypt go even further: they cut their foreheads with knives, making it clear that they are foreigners and not Egyptians.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 277
paragraphs: At the festival gatherings in Saïs, on a certain night, everyone lights many lamps in the open air around their houses. The lamps are shallow dishes filled with a mixture of salt and oil, with the wick floating on top. They burn all night long. The festival is called the Festival of Lamps. Even Egyptians who do not attend the gathering light lamps on that night, so it is not only Saïs but all of Egypt that is illuminated. There is a sacred explanation for why this night receives honor and light.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 278
paragraphs: At Heliopolis and Buto, they go each year and perform only sacrifices. But at Papremis, they perform sacrifices and worship as elsewhere, and in addition, when the sun begins to set, a few priests tend the image of the god while a large crowd stands at the temple entrance holding wooden clubs. Another crowd of more than a thousand men, also carrying clubs and fulfilling vows, stands opposite them. The image, placed in a small gilded wooden shrine, is transported on the day before the festival to another sacred building. The few priests who remain with the image pull a four-wheeled cart carrying the shrine and the image inside it. The crowd at the gate blocks their entry. The vow-keepers take the god's side and fight to force their way in. A fierce club fight breaks out, heads are cracked, and I believe many die of their wounds, though the Egyptians insist no one dies. The locals say this festival was established for the following reason: the mother of the god Ares once lived in this temple. Ares was raised elsewhere and came as a grown man to visit his mother. Her attendants, not knowing him, refused him entry and kept him out. He went to another city, gathered men, overpowered the attendants, and forced his way in to his mother. That, they say, is why blows are exchanged at the festival of Ares.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 279
paragraphs: The Egyptians were the first to make it a religious rule that men should not lie with women in temples, and should not enter a temple after lying with a woman without first bathing. Nearly all other peoples except the Egyptians and Greeks are careless about this. They treat humans no differently from animals and point to the fact that animals and birds mate in temples. If this displeased the gods, the animals would not do it. That is their reasoning, but I disapprove of it.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 280
paragraphs: The Egyptians are excessively careful about ritual matters—both in general and in the practices that follow. Although Egypt borders Libya, it is not rich in animals. But every animal found there is considered sacred—both those that live with humans and those that do not. If I were to explain why they are sacred, I would be drawn into religious topics that I particularly wish to avoid. What little I have said about them was said under the compulsion of my narrative. Their customs regarding animals are as follows. Caretakers are appointed for each kind of animal—both men and women—and these positions pass from parent to child. Each caretaker in the cities fulfills vows this way: they pray to the god whose animal it is, shave all or half or a third of their child's head, weigh the hair against silver, and give the silver to the animal's keeper to buy fish to feed the animals. If anyone deliberately kills a sacred animal, the penalty is death. If the killing is accidental, the penalty is whatever the priests impose. But anyone who kills an ibis or a hawk, whether deliberately or not, must die.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 281
