paragraphs: Among the animals that live with humans, there would be far more cats if not for a curious accident. When female cats give birth, they avoid the males. The toms, wanting to mate, resort to a trick: they steal the kittens and kill them, though they do not eat them. The mothers, deprived of their young and wanting more, go back to the males, for cats are extremely fond of their offspring. When a fire breaks out, something extraordinary happens to the cats. The Egyptians, lining up at intervals, try to save the cats rather than fight the fire. But the cats slip between the men or leap over them and throw themselves into the flames. When this happens, great mourning falls upon the Egyptians. In any household where a cat dies a natural death, all the residents shave their eyebrows. Where a dog dies, they shave their entire body and head.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 282
paragraphs: Dead cats are taken to sacred buildings in the city of Bubastis, where they are embalmed and buried. Dogs are buried in each person's own city in sacred tombs. Ichneumons are buried the same way as dogs. Shrewmice and hawks are taken to the city of Buto, and ibises to the city of Hermes. Bears, which are rare, and wolves, which are not much larger than foxes, are buried wherever they are found.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 283
paragraphs: The crocodile's nature is as follows. During the four coldest months, it eats nothing. It has four feet and lives both on land and in water. It lays and hatches its eggs on land and spends most of the day on dry ground, but passes the entire night in the river, since the water is warmer than the open air and the dew. Of all mortal creatures we know of, the crocodile grows from the smallest beginning to the greatest size. Its eggs are about the size of goose eggs, and the hatchling is proportionate. But the adult grows to seventeen cubits or more. It has the eyes of a pig and great teeth and tusks proportional to its body. It is the only animal that has no tongue. It does not move its lower jaw but is unique in bringing its upper jaw down onto the lower. It has strong claws and a scaly hide that is impenetrable on its back. It is blind in the water but has very keen sight in the air. Because it lives in the water, the inside of its mouth swarms with leeches. While other birds and animals flee from it, the sandpiper lives at peace with it, because the crocodile benefits from the bird. When it climbs out of the water onto land and opens its jaws—which it usually does facing the west wind—the sandpiper enters its mouth and swallows the leeches. The crocodile enjoys this and does the bird no harm.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 284
paragraphs: Some Egyptians regard crocodiles as sacred, others treat them as enemies. Those who live around Thebes and Lake Moeris consider them most sacred. Each community raises one crocodile, trained to be tame. They put ornaments of glass and gold in its ears and bracelets on its front legs. They feed it special food and treat it with the greatest care while it lives. When it dies, they embalm it and bury it in a sacred coffin. But the people around the city of Elephantine actually eat crocodiles, not considering them sacred at all. The Egyptians do not call them crocodiles but champsai. The Ionians named them crocodiles because they thought they resembled the lizards found in their garden walls.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 285
paragraphs: There are many methods of catching crocodiles. I will describe the one I think most worth telling. The hunter baits a hook with a pig's back and lets it float in the middle of the river. He himself stands on the bank with a live pig and beats it. The crocodile hears the squealing, heads toward the sound, finds the bait, and swallows it. The hunters haul it ashore. The first thing they do is plaster its eyes with mud. Once that is done, the animal is easily handled. Without it, they would have great trouble.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 286
paragraphs: The river-horse is sacred in the district of Papremis but not elsewhere in Egypt. Its appearance is this: it has four legs, cloven hooves like an ox, a snub nose, a horse's mane, visible tusks, a horse's tail, a horse's voice, and is about the size of the largest ox. Its hide is so thick that when dried, spear shafts are made from it.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 287
paragraphs: There are also otters in the river, which the Egyptians consider sacred. Of fish, they hold the lepidotos and the eel sacred. These, they say, are sacred to the Nile. Of birds, the fox-goose is sacred.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 288
paragraphs: There is another sacred bird called the phoenix. I never saw one myself, except in paintings, for it comes only rarely—every five hundred years, according to the people of Heliopolis. They say it comes when its father dies. If the paintings are accurate, it looks like this: its plumage is partly golden and partly red. In shape and size it most resembles an eagle. They say it performs this feat, which I do not find credible. They claim it comes from Arabia carrying its father's body encased in myrrh to the temple of the Sun, where it buries him. It carries the body this way: first it molds an egg of myrrh as large as it can carry and tests its weight by flying with it. Then it hollows out the egg, places its father inside, and seals the opening with more myrrh. The egg, with the body inside, weighs the same as before. It carries this to the temple of the Sun in Egypt. That is what they say this bird does.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 289
paragraphs: Near Thebes there are sacred serpents, quite harmless to humans. They are small and have two horns on top of their heads. When they die, they are buried in the temple of Zeus, to whom they are said to be sacred.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 290
paragraphs: There is a place in Arabia, near the city of Buto, which I visited to inquire about the winged serpents. When I arrived, I saw bones and spines of serpents in quantities beyond description. Piles of spines lay everywhere—some large, some medium, some small. The place where these bones are scattered is a narrow pass between steep mountains opening onto a broad plain that connects with the Egyptian plain. Winged serpents are said to fly from Arabia toward Egypt every spring, but the ibis birds meet them at this pass and kill them all. The Arabians say the ibis is honored by the Egyptians for this very reason, and the Egyptians confirm it.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 291
paragraphs: The ibis looks like this: it is deep black all over, with crane-like legs and a very curved beak. It is about the size of a landrail. That is the black kind that fights the serpents. The more common kind, which you see everywhere among humans, has a different appearance. Its head and throat are bare of feathers. Its plumage is white except for the head, the back of the neck, the wing tips, and the end of the tail, which are all deep black. Its legs and beak are like those of the black ibis. The winged serpent resembles a water snake. Its wings are not feathered but very much like a bat's. That is enough about sacred animals.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 292
paragraphs: The Egyptians who live in the cultivated part of the country practice memory more than any other people and are by far the most learned in history of anyone I have ever encountered. Their manner of life is as follows. They purge themselves every month for three successive days, preserving their health with emetics and enemas, since they believe all human diseases arise from the food people eat. Even apart from this, the Egyptians are the healthiest people in the world after the Libyans, which I attribute to their climate and the fact that the seasons never change. Disease most commonly strikes when things change, especially changes of season. They eat bread made from spelt, which they call kyllestis. They drink a wine made from barley, since they have no grapevines. They eat fish—some dried in the sun and eaten raw, others cured in brine. Of birds, they eat quails, ducks, and small birds, also cured in brine. Other birds and fish, apart from those they hold sacred, they eat either roasted or boiled.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 293
paragraphs: At banquets of the wealthy, when dinner is finished, a man carries around a wooden image of a corpse in a coffin. It is painted and carved to look as realistic as possible, about one or two cubits long. He shows it to each guest and says: "Look at this as you drink and enjoy yourself. When you die, you will be like this." This is their custom at drinking parties.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 294
paragraphs: They follow their ancestral customs and adopt no new ones. Among their many noteworthy traditions, they have one song—the song of Linos—which is also sung in Phoenicia, Cyprus, and elsewhere. Each nation has its own name for it. It is the same song the Greeks sing and call Linos. Of all the Egyptian customs that surprised me, one was this: where did they get the name Linos? They seem to have always sung this song. In Egyptian, Linos is called Maneros. The Egyptians told me that Maneros was the only son of their first king. He died young, and the Egyptians honored him with this dirge. This was their first and, for a time, only song.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 295
paragraphs: The Egyptians share another custom with the Spartans but with no other Greeks: younger men, when they meet their elders, yield the path and step aside. When an older person approaches, they rise from their seats. But in one respect they differ from all Greeks: instead of greeting each other on the street with words, they lower their hand to their knee in salutation.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 296
paragraphs: They wear linen tunics with fringes around the legs, called calasiris. Over these they throw white woolen cloaks. But woolen garments are not taken into temples, and the dead are not buried in them. This is a religious rule. It agrees with the practices called Orphic and Bacchic, which are actually Egyptian and Pythagorean. No one initiated into these mysteries may be buried in woolen clothing. There is a sacred explanation for this.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 297
paragraphs: The Egyptians also discovered which god each month and each day belongs to, and what fortune a person born on any particular day will have—how he will die and what kind of person he will be. Greek poets have made use of these discoveries. The Egyptians have identified more omens than any other people. When a portent occurs, they write down the outcome. If anything similar happens in the future, they expect the same result.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 298
paragraphs: Divination among them is organized this way. The art belongs not to any mortal but to certain gods. There are oracles of Heracles, Apollo, Athena, Artemis, Ares, and Zeus in the land. But the oracle they honor most is that of Leto at the city of Buto. The methods of divination, however, vary from oracle to oracle.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 299
paragraphs: Medicine is specialized. Each doctor treats one disease and no more. The whole country is full of doctors. There are doctors for the eyes, doctors for the head, doctors for the teeth, doctors for the stomach, and doctors for internal diseases.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 300
paragraphs: Their customs of mourning and burial are as follows. When a man of importance dies, all the women of the household plaster their heads—and sometimes their faces—with mud. Then, leaving the body in the house, they roam through the city beating their breasts, with their clothing loosened and their breasts exposed. All the female relatives join them. The men beat their breasts separately, also with loosened garments. After this, they take the body to be embalmed.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 301
paragraphs: There are professionals who practice embalming as a trade. When a body is brought to them, they show the relatives painted wooden models of corpses. They point to the best method, which I will not name in this context. They then show a second method, less expensive, and a third that is cheapest. They explain the options and ask which the family prefers. The relatives agree on a price and leave. The embalmers, working in their shop, proceed as follows for the most expensive method. First they draw the brain out through the nostrils with an iron hook, partly extracting it this way and partly by pouring in dissolving drugs. Then with a sharp Ethiopian stone they make a cut along the side and remove all the intestines. They clean the cavity and rinse it with palm wine, then again with ground spices. They fill the body with pure ground myrrh, cassia, and every other aromatic substance except frankincense, and sew it up. After this, they cover the body in natron for seventy days—no longer. When seventy days are up, they wash the body and wrap it entirely in strips of fine linen smeared with gum, which the Egyptians use instead of glue. The relatives take the body back and make a wooden case in human shape. They place the body inside, seal it, and store it in a burial chamber, standing it upright against a wall.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 302
paragraphs: For those who want the middle option and wish to avoid the expense, the process is simpler. They fill syringes with cedar oil and inject it into the body through the abdomen, without cutting or removing the intestines. They inject it through the lower opening and plug it to prevent the liquid from running out. Then they preserve the body in natron for the prescribed number of days. On the last day, they drain the cedar oil. The oil is so powerful that it dissolves the intestines and brings them out with it. The natron dissolves the flesh, leaving only the skin and bones. They return the body to the family without any further treatment.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 303
paragraphs: The third method, used for those with the least money, is this: they flush the intestines with a purgative, preserve the body in natron for seventy days, and return it.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 304
paragraphs: The wives of distinguished men are not embalmed immediately after death, nor are exceptionally beautiful women. They are not delivered to the embalmers until three or four days after death. This is done to prevent the embalmers from having intercourse with the bodies. They say one embalmer was caught doing this with a recently dead woman, reported by a colleague.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 305
paragraphs: Whenever anyone—Egyptian or foreigner—is found to have been carried off by a crocodile or drowned by the river itself, the people of whatever city the body washes up in are required by law to embalm it, treat it with all due honor, and bury it in a sacred coffin. No relative or friend may touch it—only the priests of the Nile handle and bury it with their own hands, as something more than the corpse of a mere human being.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 306
paragraphs: The Egyptians refuse to adopt Greek customs—or, broadly speaking, those of any other people. Most Egyptians observe this strictly. But there is one large city called Chemmis in the Theban district, near Neapolis. In this city is a rectangular temple of Perseus, son of Danae. Palm trees grow around it, and the gateway is of enormous stone blocks. In front of the gateway stand two large stone statues. Within the enclosure is a shrine containing a statue of Perseus. The people of Chemmis say that Perseus often appears in their region and inside the temple. A sandal worn by him is sometimes found—two cubits long—and whenever it appears, all Egypt prospers. They also celebrate athletic games in his honor, offering prizes of cattle, cloaks, and animal skins. When I asked why Perseus appears only to them and why they alone among Egyptians hold games, they said Perseus was born of their city. They explained that Danaos and Lynkeus, who sailed to Greece, were both from Chemmis. They traced the genealogy from these two down to Perseus. They said Perseus himself came to Egypt for the same reason the Greeks give—to bring the Gorgon's head from Libya. He visited Chemmis and recognized all his relatives, having learned the name of the city from his mother before leaving Greece. They hold athletic games at his command.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 307
paragraphs: All the above customs belong to Egyptians who live above the marshes. Those in the marsh country follow mostly the same practices, including monogamy like the Greeks, but have devised some unique solutions for daily life. When the river floods and the land becomes a sea, many lilies the Egyptians call lotos grow in the water. They gather these, dry them in the sun, then pound out the seed from the center of the plant—which resembles a poppy head—and make bread from it that they bake over a fire. The root of this plant is also edible: it is round, the size of an apple, and tastes rather sweet. There is another kind of lily, resembling a rose, also growing in the river. Its fruit grows on a separate stalk from the root and looks very much like a wasp's honeycomb. Inside are edible seeds the size of an olive stone, eaten both fresh and dried. They also pull up papyrus, which grows annually in the marshes. They cut off the top (which they use for other purposes) and eat or sell the lower part, about a cubit long. Those who want to enjoy the papyrus at its best roast it in a red-hot oven. Some of these marsh people live entirely on fish. They catch them, gut them, dry them in the sun, and eat them dried.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 308
paragraphs: Fish that swim in schools are not commonly found in the rivers but are bred in the lakes. They behave as follows. When the urge to breed comes on them, they swim out in schools toward the sea. The males lead, shedding their milt, and the females follow behind, swallowing it and becoming pregnant. When they have conceived in the sea, they all swim back to their usual haunts. But the males no longer lead—the females take over. Leading the school, they do what the males did: they shed their eggs, a few at a time. The males following behind swallow them. These eggs are fish. The fish that survive and are not swallowed grow to maturity. Those that are caught on their way to the sea show bruises on the left side of the head; those caught returning are bruised on the right. This happens because as they swim down to the sea, they keep close to the left bank, and returning, they hug the same bank—brushing against it as closely as possible to avoid losing their way in the current.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 309
paragraphs: For anointing their bodies, those Egyptians who live in the marshes use oil from the castor plant. The Egyptians call it kiki. They sow these plants along the banks of rivers and lakes. The plant grows wild in Greece. In Egypt, when sown, it produces an abundant but foul-smelling fruit. They gather it and either crush and press it, or boil and skim it. The resulting liquid is thick and as useful as olive oil for lamps, though the smell is unpleasant.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 310
paragraphs: Against the gnats, which are extremely abundant, they have devised these solutions. Those who live above the marshes are helped by the towers they sleep in, since gnats cannot fly high because of the winds. Those in the marsh country have a different method. Every man has a net. During the day he uses it for fishing. At night, he drapes it over his bed, crawls underneath, and sleeps under it. If he wrapped himself in a linen sheet or a cloak, the gnats would bite through it. But they do not even try to get through the net.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 311
paragraphs: Their cargo boats are made from the thorny acacia tree, which looks very much like the Cyrenian lotus plant and produces gum. From this wood they cut planks about two cubits long and fit them together like bricks. They fasten these short planks with long, close-set pegs. When the hull is built this way, they lay crossbeams over the top. They use no ribs. They caulk the seams from inside with papyrus. There is one steering oar, passed through the keel. The mast is acacia wood and the sails are papyrus. These boats cannot sail upriver without a strong wind. They are towed from the bank instead. Downstream, they travel this way: they have a raft made of tamarisk wood, bound with rushes, and a perforated stone weighing about two talents. The raft is let out ahead of the boat on a rope, and the stone is let down behind on another rope. The current catches the raft and pulls it forward, dragging the boat along. The stone, trailing behind on the bottom, keeps the boat straight. They have many such boats, some carrying thousands of talents of cargo.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 312
paragraphs: When the Nile floods the land, only the cities are visible above the water, looking very much like islands in the Aegean Sea. The rest of Egypt becomes a sea, with only the cities rising above it. When this happens, people travel by boat straight across the plain, no longer following the river's course. On the voyage upstream from Naucratis to Memphis, you pass right by the pyramids themselves. (The normal route does not go this way but through the apex of the Delta and the city of Cercasoros.) On the voyage from the sea to Naucratis across the Delta, you pass the cities of Anthylla and Archandropolis.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 313
paragraphs: Anthylla is a notable city, specifically assigned to provide shoes for the wife of the Egyptian king. This has been the case since Egypt came under Persian rule. The other city, I believe, takes its name from Archander, son-in-law of Danaos, the son of Phthios, son of Achaios. It is called Archandropolis. There may have been another Archander, but the name is certainly not Egyptian.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 314
paragraphs: Up to this point, I have been speaking from my own observation, judgment, and inquiry. From now on, I will report the history of Egypt as the Egyptians told it to me, supplemented by what I saw with my own eyes.

About Min, the first king of Egypt, the priests said the following. He dammed off the site of Memphis from the river. The entire Nile used to flow along the sandy range on the Libyan side. Min created a great embankment about a hundred furlongs south of Memphis, diverting the river away from the old channel and sending it through a new course between the two mountain ranges. Even now, the Persians keep careful watch on this bend of the Nile. The embankment is reinforced every year, since if the river broke through at this point it would flood all Memphis. On the land reclaimed from the river, Min founded the city now called Memphis, which lies in the narrow part of Egypt. He dug a lake around the city to the north and west, fed by the river (the Nile itself bounds it on the east). He also built the great and most noteworthy temple of Hephaistos there.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 315
paragraphs: After Min, the priests read out to me from a papyrus roll the names of three hundred and thirty more kings. In all these generations, eighteen were Ethiopian, one was an Egyptian woman, and the rest were Egyptian men. The woman who became queen was named Nitocris. They said she avenged her brother: the Egyptians had killed him while he was king and then handed the kingdom to her. To avenge him, she destroyed many of them by a trick. She built a long underground chamber and invited the Egyptians she knew to be most responsible to a banquet. While they were feasting, she let in the river through a large hidden channel. That was all they told me about her, except that after this she threw herself into a room full of ashes to escape punishment.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 316
paragraphs: Of the other kings, the priests could report no great deeds or achievements, except for the last of them, Moeris. He built the northern gateway of the temple of Hephaistos and dug a lake, whose circumference I will give later. He also built pyramids in the lake. I will report their size when I describe the lake itself. These were his works. The rest accomplished nothing.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 317
paragraphs: After these came the king named Sesostris. The priests said he was the first to set out with warships from the Arabian Gulf and subdue the peoples along the coast of the Red Sea. He sailed on until the sea became too shallow for further navigation. When he returned to Egypt, he raised a great army (according to the priests) and marched across the continent, conquering every nation he encountered. When he met a people who fought bravely, he set up pillars in their land recording his name, his country, and the fact that he had overcome them by force. But when he captured a city easily and without resistance, he inscribed the pillar the same way but added a picture of female genitalia, to indicate that the people were cowards.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 318
paragraphs: Marching across the continent, he passed from Asia into Europe and conquered the Scythians and the Thracians. I believe these were the furthest peoples the Egyptian army reached, because pillars are found in their lands but nowhere beyond. From there, he turned and headed back. When he reached the river Phasis, I cannot say for certain whether King Sesostris himself detached a portion of his army and left them to settle the country, or whether some of his soldiers grew tired of the march and stayed behind on their own by the Phasis.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 319
paragraphs: The Colchians are clearly Egyptian. I noticed this myself before hearing it from anyone else. When the question occurred to me, I asked both peoples. The Colchians remembered the Egyptians better than the Egyptians remembered them. The Egyptians said they thought the Colchians were descended from the army of Sesostris. I had guessed the same thing, because the Colchians are dark-skinned and have woolly hair. That alone proves nothing, since other peoples share these features. But there is stronger evidence: the Colchians, the Egyptians, and the Ethiopians are the only peoples in the world who have always practiced circumcision. The Phoenicians and the Syrians of Palestine admit they learned the practice from the Egyptians. The Syrians around the rivers Thermodon and Parthenios and their neighbors the Macronians say they learned it recently from the Colchians. These are the only peoples who circumcise, and they all clearly do it in imitation of the Egyptians. As for the Egyptians and Ethiopians, I cannot say which learned from the other, since the practice is very ancient. That the others learned it through contact with Egypt is strongly shown by this: Phoenicians who have dealings with Greece no longer circumcise their newborns, having adopted Greek customs.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 320
paragraphs: Here is another point of similarity between the Colchians and the Egyptians. They alone work flax in the same way. Their whole manner of living and their language are alike. The Colchians' linen is called Sardonian by the Greeks, while the linen that comes from Egypt is called Egyptian.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 321
paragraphs: The pillars Sesostris set up in the various countries are mostly no longer visible. But in Syria Palestine I saw them myself, with the inscriptions and the female emblems I mentioned. In Ionia too there are two figures carved in the rock: one on the road from Ephesus to Phocaea, the other on the road from Sardis to Smyrna. In both places, a man is carved in the rock four and a half cubits tall, holding a spear in his right hand and a bow in his left. His other equipment is partly Egyptian and partly Ethiopian. Across his chest from shoulder to shoulder runs a carved inscription in Egyptian hieroglyphs reading: "I conquered this land by the strength of my shoulders." He does not say who he is or where he comes from, though he has said so elsewhere. Some who have seen these carvings guess they represent Memnon, but they are far from the truth.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 322
paragraphs: When the Egyptian Sesostris was returning home, bringing back many captives from the lands he had conquered, his brother—to whom Sesostris had entrusted the government of Egypt—invited him to dinner at Daphnae in the district of Pelusium, bringing his sons as well. Then the brother piled wood around the house and set it on fire. When Sesostris realized what was happening, he immediately consulted his wife, whom he had brought along. She advised him to lay two of their six sons across the flames as a bridge over the fire, so the rest could walk across their bodies and escape. Sesostris did this. Two of his sons burned to death, but the father and the others were saved.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 323
paragraphs: After returning to Egypt and taking revenge on his brother, Sesostris put his captives to work. They dragged the enormous stones that were transported during his reign to the temple of Hephaistos. They also dug all the canals that now cross Egypt. Against their will, they made Egypt—which had previously been entirely suited to horseback and carriage travel—unfit for either. From that time on, although Egypt is flat, it could no longer be crossed on horseback or by cart, because of the canals running everywhere in all directions.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 324
paragraphs: The reason the king cut up Egypt with canals was this. All the Egyptians whose cities were not on the river but in the interior lacked water whenever the flood receded. They had to drink brackish water from wells. For this reason, Sesostris cut canals throughout Egypt. He also divided the land among all Egyptians, giving each man an equal square plot. From these plots he drew his revenue, requiring each man to pay a fixed annual rent. If the river washed away part of anyone's plot, the owner would come and report the loss. The king would send inspectors to measure how much land had been lost and reduce the tax accordingly. This, I believe, is how the art of geometry was invented and later passed to Greece. The sundial, the gnomon, and the twelve divisions of the day were learned by the Greeks from the Babylonians, not the Egyptians.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 325
paragraphs: Sesostris was the only Egyptian king who also ruled Ethiopia. As memorials, he set up two stone statues in front of the temple of Hephaistos, each thirty cubits tall—representing himself and his wife—and four statues of his sons, each twenty cubits. Long afterward, the Persian priest Darius attempted to place his own statue in front of these. But the priest of Hephaistos refused, saying that Darius had not achieved deeds equal to those of the Egyptian Sesostris. Sesostris, the priest said, had conquered as many nations as Darius plus the Scythians—whom Darius had failed to subdue. It was therefore not right for Darius to stand before his offerings, since he had not surpassed him. Darius, they say, accepted this.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 326
paragraphs: After Sesostris died, his son Pheros inherited the throne. He conducted no military campaigns. He went blind under the following circumstances. The river flooded higher than ever before—eighteen cubits—and when it overflowed the fields, a wind struck and the river became rough. The king, in a fit of arrogance, seized a spear and hurled it into the middle of the river's whirling current. He was immediately struck blind. He remained blind for ten years. In the eleventh year, an oracle came from the city of Buto: the time of his punishment was over, and he would regain his sight by washing his eyes with the urine of a woman who had never been with any man but her own husband. He tried his own wife first. When that failed, he tried woman after woman. When he finally recovered his sight, he gathered all the women he had tested—except the one whose urine had cured him—into a single city, now called Red Clod, and burned them all along with the city. The woman who had cured him he took as his wife. After recovering his sight, he dedicated offerings at all the notable temples. The most remarkable was a pair of stone obelisks he set up in the temple of the sun—each cut from a single block, a hundred cubits tall and eight cubits wide.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 327
paragraphs: After him, the priests said, a man from Memphis succeeded. His Greek name was Proteus. There is still a beautiful, well-kept sacred enclosure of Proteus in Memphis, south of the temple of Hephaistos. Phoenicians from Tyre live in the neighborhood of this enclosure, and the whole district is called the Camp of the Tyrians. Within the enclosure of Proteus is a temple called the temple of the Foreign Aphrodite. I believe this is actually a temple of Helen, daughter of Tyndareus, because I have heard the story that Helen lived with Proteus, and because the temple is called by the name of the Foreign Aphrodite. No other temple of Aphrodite bears this title.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 328
paragraphs: The priests told me the story of Helen as follows. Alexander, having carried off Helen, was sailing from Sparta to his own country. When he reached the Aegean, contrary winds blew him off course to Egypt. The winds did not let up, so he came to land at the Canopic mouth of the Nile, in what is now called the Salt Pans. On the shore there stood—and still stands—a temple of Heracles. If a runaway slave takes refuge there and has the sacred brand marks applied to his body, dedicating himself to the god, he cannot be taken back. This law has remained the same from the beginning down to my time. Some of Alexander's servants learned of this rule and deserted. They sat as suppliants in the temple and accused Alexander, wanting to harm him. They told the whole story of what he had done to Helen and the wrong committed against Menelaos. They made these accusations before the priests and before Thonis, the warden of the Canopic mouth.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 329
paragraphs: Thonis heard their story and immediately sent a message to Proteus at Memphis: "A stranger has come, a Trojan by race, who has committed an unholy deed in Greece. He seduced the wife of his host and has come here bringing this woman and great wealth, driven to your shores by the winds. Shall we let him sail away untouched, or shall we confiscate what he brought?" Proteus sent back this reply: "Whoever this man is who has done such a wrong to his host, seize him and bring him to me so I can see what he has to say for himself."

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 330
paragraphs: Thonis arrested Alexander, detained his ships, and brought him to Memphis along with Helen, the treasure, and the suppliants. When everything had been assembled, Proteus asked Alexander who he was and where he had sailed from. Alexander gave his lineage and the name of his country. He told where he had sailed from. Then Proteus asked how he had obtained Helen. Alexander fumbled and strayed from the truth. The suppliants contradicted him and told the full story of his crime. Finally, Proteus delivered this verdict: "If I did not consider it extremely important never to kill a foreigner driven to my shores by the winds, I would have punished you on behalf of the Greek. You, the vilest of men—you enjoyed the hospitality of a man and then committed the foulest of crimes against him. You crept into the bed of your host's wife. That was not enough for you—you stirred her up and carried her off like a thief. Not even that was enough—you plundered your host's home before leaving. Now, since I consider it of the greatest importance not to kill foreigners, I will not let you take this woman or the treasure away. I will keep them for the Greek host until he comes to collect them himself. As for you and your companions, I give you three days to leave my country. After that, you will be treated as enemies."

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 331
paragraphs: This, the priests said, is how Helen came to Proteus. I believe Homer knew this story too, but since it was less suited to epic poetry than the version he chose, he deliberately set it aside, while making clear that he knew the alternative. This is shown in the Iliad, where he describes Alexander's wanderings (and never retracts the passage), telling how he was blown off course with Helen to Sidon in Phoenicia. He mentions it in the passage about the battle of Diomedes. The verses run:

"There she had richly colored robes, the work of Sidonian women, whom the godlike Alexander himself had brought from Sidon, sailing the broad sea, on the voyage when he carried off Helen of noble birth."
He also refers to it in the Odyssey:

"Such drugs did the daughter of Zeus possess, such cunning compounds, good drugs, which Polydamna, wife of Thon, had given her in Egypt, that land where the fertile soil produces drugs in abundance, many beneficial when mixed, many deadly."
And Menelaos says to Telemachos:
"The gods kept me in Egypt, though I wished to return home, because I had not performed the proper sacrifices to them."

In these lines Homer makes clear that he knew of Alexander's detour to Egypt, since Syria borders Egypt and the Phoenicians (including the Sidonians) live in Syria. By these lines it is most clearly shown that the Cyprian Epic was not written by Homer but by someone else. The Cyprian Epic says Alexander reached Troy with Helen on the third day after leaving Sparta, with a fair wind and a calm sea. But the Iliad says he was blown far off course. Let us leave Homer and the Cyprian Epic here.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 332
paragraphs: When I asked the priests whether the Greek account of the Trojan War was empty or contained truth, they gave this answer. They had the story from Menelaos himself. After the abduction of Helen, a great Greek army came to Trojan territory to help Menelaos. When they disembarked and set up camp, they sent envoys to Troy, including Menelaos himself. The envoys entered the walls and demanded the return of Helen and the stolen treasure, and satisfaction for the wrongs committed. The Trojans gave the same answer then as they would later, both on oath and without oath: they did not have Helen or the treasure. Both were in Egypt with King Proteus. The Greeks thought they were being mocked and besieged the city. When they captured it, they found no Helen. Hearing the same story repeated, they finally believed the Trojans and sent Menelaos himself to Proteus.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 333
paragraphs: This much was told by the priests. I myself agree with the story about Helen, adding this reasoning. If Helen had been in Troy, she would have been returned to the Greeks whether Alexander consented or not. Neither Priam nor his family could have been so insane as to risk their own lives, their children's lives, and the city itself just so Alexander could keep another man's wife. Even if they felt that way at first, after so many Trojans died every time they fought the Greeks—and after Priam himself lost two or three sons in every battle, if we are to trust the epic poets—surely Priam would have returned Helen to the Greeks to end such terrible suffering. The kingship was not even going to pass to Alexander, who might have made these decisions himself. Hector was his elder brother and the more competent man. Hector would have been king after Priam. It was not in Hector's interest to support his brother's wickedness—especially when it was causing such catastrophes for Hector personally and for all the Trojans. The truth is, they did not have Helen to give back. They told the Greeks the truth, but the Greeks did not believe them. The divine plan, in my opinion, ensured that the Trojans would be destroyed completely—to make it clear to mankind that when great wrongs are committed, the gods send great punishments. That is what I believe.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 334
paragraphs: When Menelaos came to Egypt and sailed up to Memphis, he told the truth about what had happened. He received not only generous hospitality but also Helen unharmed, along with all his wealth. Yet despite this treatment, Menelaos behaved unjustly toward the Egyptians. He was waiting for favorable winds to sail, but they blew against him for a long time. When this continued, he devised a monstrous act: he seized two children of the local people and sacrificed them. When this was discovered, he was hated and hunted. He fled with his ships to Libya. Where he went after that, the Egyptians could not say. They told me they learned some of this through inquiry and some from events that happened in their own country, which they knew with certainty.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 335
paragraphs: That is what the priests of Egypt told me. I agree with their account of Helen, and I add this further consideration. If Helen had been in Troy, she would have been given up to the Greeks whether Alexander wanted it or not. Priam and his kinsmen would not have been so reckless as to endanger their own persons and their children and the city just for Alexander to cohabit with Helen. Even granting they may have felt that way at first, the constant casualties in battle—with Priam himself losing sons in every engagement—would have changed their minds. Moreover, it was not Alexander but Hector, his older and better brother, who stood to inherit the throne. It made no sense for Hector to tolerate his brother's criminal behavior when it brought such disaster on everyone. The simple truth is they did not have Helen. They told the Greeks so, and the Greeks would not believe them. Divine providence, I believe, arranged it so that the Trojans' total destruction would demonstrate to all humanity that terrible crimes bring terrible punishments from the gods.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 336
paragraphs: After Proteus, the priests said, Rhampsinitos took the kingdom. He built the western gateway of the temple of Hephaistos and set up two statues in front of it, each twenty-five cubits tall. The Egyptians call the one facing north Summer and the one facing south Winter. They worship and pay reverence to Summer but treat Winter with hostility. This king, they said, had such immense wealth that no later king came close to equaling it, much less surpassing it. Wanting to store his treasure safely, he had a stone chamber built as an extension of one wall of his palace. The builder, however, devised a secret scheme. He fitted one stone so that two men—or even one—could easily remove it from the outside. When the chamber was finished, the king stored his treasure inside. Time passed, and as the builder lay dying, he called his two sons to him. He told them about the movable stone, giving precise measurements for finding it. He said he had arranged this for their benefit, so they would always be rich. After his death, the sons wasted no time. That very night they went to the palace, found the stone, removed it easily, and helped themselves to the treasure. When the king opened the chamber and noticed the treasure diminishing while the seals on the door were intact and the room showed no sign of entry, he was completely baffled. When the losses continued after two or three visits, he set traps—snares beside the vessels holding the treasure. The thieves came as before. One of them climbed in and approached a vessel. The trap caught him instantly. Realizing his predicament, he immediately called to his brother and told him to come in and cut off his head, so the body could not be identified and bring ruin on both of them. The brother agreed this was good advice. He cut off the head, replaced the stone, and went home carrying the head. At dawn, the king entered the chamber. He was stunned to find a headless body in the trap with no sign of forced entry. In his confusion, he ordered the thief's body to be hung from the palace wall and set guards, with instructions to arrest anyone seen weeping or showing grief. The mother was distraught when the body was displayed. She commanded her surviving son to find some way of recovering the body, threatening that if he did not, she would go to the king herself and reveal that he had the treasure. Despite his pleas, she would not relent. So the son devised this plan. He loaded several donkeys with skins full of wine and drove them past the guards watching the body. When he drew near, he secretly loosened the ties on two or three skins. The wine poured out, and he beat his head and cried out as if he didn't know which donkey to tend first. The guards, seeing so much wine running free, rushed out with cups and caught what they could—considering it their lucky day. The young man cursed them angrily. But as they calmed him down, he pretended to soften and forgive them. He drove his donkeys off the road, rearranged the skins, and struck up a conversation with the guards. When one of them made him laugh, he gave them an extra skin. They sat down to drink right there, invited him to join them, and insisted he stay. He agreed. As the drinking went on and they became very friendly, he gave them another skin. The guards drank so heavily they passed out on the spot where they had been sitting. Late that night, the young man took down his brother's body and—to insult the guards—shaved the right cheek of each man. He loaded the body onto his donkeys and drove home, having fulfilled his mother's demand. The king was furious when he learned the thief's body had been stolen. Determined to catch the culprit, he did something I do not believe (but the priests told it as fact): he placed his own daughter in a room and commanded her to receive all men alike, but before lying with any man, she must make him tell the cleverest and the wickedest thing he had ever done. If anyone told her the story of the thief, she must seize him and not let him go. The daughter obeyed. The thief, learning what was happening and determined to outdo the king in cunning, did this: he cut the arm off a recently dead man and carried it under his cloak. He went to the king's daughter, and when she asked the question, he said the wickedest thing he had ever done was cutting off his brother's head when it was caught in a trap in the king's treasury, and the cleverest was getting the guards drunk and recovering the body. She grabbed for him, but in the darkness he held out the dead man's arm. She seized it, thinking she was holding him, while he slipped out through the door. When this was reported to the king, he was astounded at the man's ingenuity and daring. Finally, he sent a proclamation to every city: he offered the man a full pardon and great rewards if he would come forward. The thief trusted the king and came. Rhampsinitos was so impressed that he gave the man his daughter in marriage, calling him the cleverest of all men. He said the Egyptians surpassed all others, and this man surpassed the Egyptians.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 337
paragraphs: After this, they said, the king went down alive to the place the Greeks call Hades. There he played dice with Demeter. Sometimes he won, sometimes she won. He came back with a golden napkin as her gift. From the time of his descent, the Egyptians celebrate a festival. It was still observed in my time, though I cannot say they celebrate it for this reason. The priests weave a robe in a single day. They blindfold one of themselves and lead him, wearing the robe, to the road that goes to the temple of Demeter. Then they go back. The blindfolded priest, they say, is guided by two wolves to the temple of Demeter, twenty furlongs from the city, and the wolves lead him back again to the same spot.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 338
paragraphs: As for the stories the Egyptians tell, anyone who finds such things believable may accept them. My rule throughout this work is to write down what each people told me, as I heard it. The Egyptians say Demeter and Dionysus are the rulers of the underworld. The Egyptians were also the first to teach the doctrine that the human soul is immortal: that when the body dies, the soul enters another creature being born at that moment. After passing through all creatures of land, sea, and air, it enters a human body once more. The full cycle takes three thousand years. Some Greeks have adopted this doctrine—some earlier, some later—and presented it as their own. I know their names but will not write them down.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 339
paragraphs: Until the reign of Rhampsinitos, the priests said, Egypt enjoyed perfect order and great prosperity. But under Cheops, who succeeded him, the country was plunged into misery. He closed all the temples and forbade the Egyptians from offering sacrifices. Then he compelled them all to work for him. Some were forced to drag stones from the quarries in the Arabian mountains to the Nile. Others transported the stones across the river in boats and hauled them to the Libyan mountains. A hundred thousand men labored at a time, in three-month shifts. Ten years of oppression went into building the road along which the stones were dragged—a project nearly as impressive as the pyramid itself, in my opinion. The road is five furlongs long, ten fathoms wide, and eight fathoms high at its tallest, built of polished stone with carved figures. Ten years for the road, plus the time for the underground chambers on the hill where the pyramids stand. Cheops intended these chambers as his burial vaults. He built them on a kind of island by channeling water from the Nile. The pyramid itself took twenty years to build.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 340
paragraphs: The pyramid was built in tiers, like steps—some call them rows, others call them bases. When the first tier was complete, they raised the remaining stones with machines made of short pieces of wood. They lifted each stone from the ground to the first tier. Once it was there, it was placed on another machine standing on the first tier, which raised it to the second. There was either a separate machine on each tier, or possibly a single portable machine that was moved from tier to tier as each stone was set. I describe both methods because both were told to me. The upper part of the pyramid was finished first, then the next section down, and the lowest and ground-level section was finished last. There is an inscription on the pyramid in Egyptian characters recording how much was spent on radishes, onions, and garlic for the laborers. As I well remember, the interpreter who read the inscription said the total was sixteen hundred talents of silver. If this is true, how much more must have been spent on iron tools, on food and clothing for the workers, since the construction went on for the number of years I mentioned, and other time was spent—no small amount, I imagine—quarrying and transporting the stones and building the underground chambers?

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 341
paragraphs: Cheops reached such a depth of wickedness, they said, that when he ran short of money he made his own daughter sit in a brothel and ordered her to charge a certain sum (they did not tell me the exact amount). She collected what her father demanded, but she also decided to leave a monument of her own. She asked each visitor for the gift of one stone. From these stones, they say, the middle pyramid of the three was built—the one that stands in front of the Great Pyramid. Each side is one hundred and fifty feet long.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 342
paragraphs: Cheops reigned fifty years, the Egyptians said. After his death, his brother Chephren succeeded him. He followed the same practices as Cheops. He also built a pyramid—smaller than his brother's, for I measured both. It has no underground chambers. No channel from the Nile runs into it, as with the other, where water flows through a built conduit and surrounds the island on which Cheops himself is said to lie. Chephren built the base course of Ethiopian stone of various colors and made the rest forty feet shorter than the first pyramid, which stands nearby. Both rise from the same hill, which is about a hundred feet high. Chephren reigned fifty-six years.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 343
paragraphs: Together, these two reigns count as one hundred and six years. During this time, the Egyptians suffered every kind of misery, and the temples stayed closed the entire time. The Egyptians hate these two kings so much that they are reluctant to even say their names. Instead, they call the pyramids after Philitis, a shepherd who grazed his flocks in the area at that time.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 344
paragraphs: After Chephren, Mykerinos became king. He was the son of Cheops. He disapproved of his father's deeds. He reopened the temples and allowed the people, who had been ground down to the last extreme of suffering, to return to their work and their sacrifices. He judged lawsuits more fairly than any other king. For this reason, the Egyptians praise Mykerinos above all their kings. He not only judged well but also, when any man was dissatisfied with his verdict, gave him money from his own purse to make him content. While Mykerinos was being kind to his people and pursuing this way of life, his first misfortune struck: his daughter died, the only child in his house. He was overwhelmed with grief and wanted to bury her in something beyond an ordinary coffin. So he had a hollow wooden cow made, gilded with gold, and placed his dead daughter inside it.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 345
paragraphs: This cow was not buried in the ground. It was still visible in my time, in the city of Sais, placed in a richly decorated chamber within the royal palace. Incense of every kind is burned before it daily. Each night, a lamp burns beside it all night long. In an adjacent room, there are statues that the priests at Sais told me represent the concubines of Mykerinos. Colossal wooden figures of women, about twenty in number, stand there naked. But who they really are, I can only say what I was told.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 346
paragraphs: Some tell a different story about this cow and the statues. They say Mykerinos fell in love with his own daughter and violated her. The girl hanged herself in grief. He buried her in this cow. Her mother cut off the hands of the serving women who had let the king reach her daughter. Their statues show the same mutilation suffered by the living women. But I think this is nonsense, especially regarding the hands. I saw the statues myself—the hands had simply fallen off from age and were still lying on the ground at their feet in my time.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 347
paragraphs: The cow is covered with a crimson robe, except for the head and neck, which are visible and heavily plated with gold. Between the horns is a golden disc representing the sun. The cow is not standing but kneeling. It is the size of a large living cow. Every year, when the Egyptians beat themselves in mourning for the god I will not name in this context, the cow is brought out of the chamber into the daylight. They say the dying daughter asked her father to let her see the sun once a year.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 348
paragraphs: After his daughter's death, a second misfortune struck this king. An oracle came from the city of Buto, telling him he had only six years to live and would die in the seventh. He was outraged. He sent a reproach to the oracle, accusing the god of injustice: his father and uncle, who had closed the temples, oppressed the people, and ignored the gods, had lived long lives, while he, who was pious, was to die so soon. A second message came from the oracle: it was precisely because he had been pious that his life was being shortened. He was supposed to have done what the other two kings had done. Egypt was fated to suffer for one hundred and fifty years. The two kings before him understood this; Mykerinos did not. Hearing this, Mykerinos accepted that his fate was sealed. He had many lamps made. Every evening, he lit them, drank, and enjoyed himself, never stopping day or night. He roamed the marshes and the groves and every place he heard was pleasant. His plan was this: by turning night into day, he would make six years into twelve and prove the oracle false.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 349
paragraphs: This king also left behind a pyramid, much smaller than his father's. It is square, with each side measuring two hundred and eighty feet. Half its height is built of Ethiopian stone. Some Greeks wrongly say this pyramid was built by Rhodopis, a courtesan. They clearly do not even know who Rhodopis was, or they would never have attributed to her a project that cost an immeasurable fortune. Besides, Rhodopis lived in the time of King Amasis, not in the time of Mykerinos—many generations later than the kings who built the pyramids. Rhodopis was Thracian by birth, a slave of Iadmon of Samos, and a fellow slave of Aesop the fable-writer.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 350
paragraphs: Rhodopis came to Egypt brought by Xanthes of Samos, intending to work as a courtesan. She was freed for a large sum by Charaxos of Mytilene, the brother of the poet Sappho. Once free, she stayed in Egypt and became very attractive, amassing a large fortune—for Rhodopis, at least, though nothing near enough to build such a pyramid. Anyone can see a tenth of her wealth to this day, so there is no reason to attribute great riches to her. Rhodopis wanted to leave a monument of herself in Greece—something no one else had thought of or dedicated in a temple—and offer it at Delphi. So she spent a tenth of her wealth on a large number of iron ox-roasting spits (as many as the tithe would buy) and sent them to Delphi. They still lie in a heap behind the altar that the Chians set up, opposite the temple itself. The courtesans of Naucratis seem to be especially charming, for this woman became so famous that every Greek knew the name Rhodopis. After her, another courtesan named Archidice became celebrated throughout Greece, though less talked about than Rhodopis. When Charaxos returned to Mytilene after freeing Rhodopis, Sappho sharply satirized him in a poem. That is enough about Rhodopis.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 351
paragraphs: After Mykerinos, the priests said, Asychis became king. He built the eastern gateway of the temple of Hephaistos—by far the most beautiful and largest of all the gateways. All have carved figures and elaborate architecture, but his surpasses the rest by a wide margin. During his reign, they said, money was very scarce and business was stagnant. A law was passed allowing a man to borrow money by pledging his father's corpse as security. An additional clause stated that the lender gained power over the borrower's entire family tomb. If the debtor failed to repay, he could not be buried—neither in his family tomb nor in any other—and he could not bury any of his relatives. This king, wanting to outdo all previous kings, left as his memorial a pyramid made of bricks. An inscription on it reads: "Do not compare me unfavorably with the stone pyramids. I surpass them as Zeus surpasses the other gods. They plunged a pole into a lake, collected the mud that stuck to it, made bricks, and built me."
Such were the deeds of this king.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 352
paragraphs: After him, a blind man from the city of Anysis became king. His name was also Anysis. During his reign, Sabacos the Ethiopian and his great army invaded Egypt. The blind king fled to the marsh country. The Ethiopian ruled Egypt for fifty years. During that time, he never executed a criminal. Instead, he sentenced each offender to raise the level of the embankment around his home city by piling up earth. The cities that were already elevated became even higher. They had been raised first under the reign of Sesostris, when the canals were dug, and now they were raised a second time under the Ethiopian. The highest of all Egyptian cities, in my opinion, is Bubastis, where there is a famous temple of the goddess Bubastis (called Artemis by the Greeks) well worth describing.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 353
paragraphs: The temple is arranged this way. Except for the entrance, it is completely surrounded by water. Two channels flow in from the Nile, each running along one side of the temple entrance without merging. Each channel is a hundred feet wide and shaded by trees. The gateway is sixty feet high and decorated with remarkable six-cubit-tall figures. The temple sits in the center of the city, and since the ground around it was raised but the temple was not moved, you can look down into it from every direction. A low wall with carved figures encircles it. Inside the enclosure is a grove of very tall trees surrounding the temple, which contains the god's image. The enclosure is one furlong long and one furlong wide. The road leading to the entrance runs through the marketplace toward the east, about three furlongs long and four hundred feet wide, paved with stone and lined on both sides with enormously tall trees. It leads to the temple of Hermes. That is how this temple is arranged.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 354
paragraphs: The Ethiopian king's departure happened this way. He fled because of a dream. In the dream, a man stood beside him and advised him to gather all the priests of Egypt and cut them in half. Sabacos said this dream was a trap set by the gods to lure him into sacrilege, which would then bring destruction on him from gods or men. He would not do it. Since his fated time of ruling Egypt was up anyway (he had been told by oracles in Ethiopia that he would reign fifty years), he chose to leave voluntarily. When the Ethiopian departed, the blind king returned from the marshes and resumed his rule.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 355
paragraphs: The blind king had lived in the marsh country for fifty years on an island he had built by heaping up ashes and earth. Whenever Egyptians came to bring him food (secretly, without the Ethiopian's knowledge), he asked each one to bring along a load of ashes. No one could find this island until the time of Amasis. For more than seven hundred years it remained hidden. Its name is Elbo. It is about ten furlongs across in each direction.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 356
paragraphs: After the blind king, a priest of Hephaistos named Sethos came to the throne. He neglected and disrespected the warrior class, believing he would never need them. Among other slights, he took away the twelve-yoke plots of choice land that had been granted to them by previous kings. When Sennacherib, king of Arabia and Assyria, later marched a great army against Egypt, the warriors refused to defend the country. The king-priest, stuck with no army, went into the temple and wept before the god's image, lamenting the danger. He fell asleep and dreamed the god stood over him, telling him to take courage and march against the Arabian army. The god himself would send help. Trusting the dream, Sethos gathered whatever Egyptians would follow him—not one soldier among them, but shopkeepers, craftsmen, and market people. They camped at Pelusium, which commands the entrance to Egypt. That night, field mice swarmed into the enemy camp and gnawed through their quivers, their bowstrings, and the leather handles of their shields. In the morning, finding themselves disarmed, the enemy fled, and many were killed. A stone statue of this king still stands in the temple of Hephaistos, holding a mouse in his hand. The inscription reads: "Look upon me and learn reverence for the gods."

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 357
paragraphs: Up to this point, the Egyptians and their priests were my source. They declared that three hundred and forty-one generations of men had passed from the first king to this last priest-king, and that in each generation there had been both a king and a chief priest. Three hundred and forty-one generations of men equals eleven thousand three hundred and forty years, since three generations make a hundred years. In all that time, they said, no god had appeared in human form. They did say, however, that during the period before and after this span, such things had happened four times. The sun, they said, had risen twice where it now sets and set twice where it now rises. Nothing in Egypt changed because of this—neither the crops nor the river nor disease nor death.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 358
paragraphs: When the historian Hecataeus visited Thebes and traced his ancestry back to a god in the sixteenth generation, the priests of Zeus did much the same for him as they did for me (though I did not trace my own genealogy). They led him into the great inner hall of the temple and showed him wooden statues—as many as I described. Each chief priest sets up a statue of himself during his lifetime. The priests counted and showed the statues, demonstrating that each was the son of the one before, going through all the statues from the most recent all the way back to the earliest. When Hecataeus traced his descent and connected himself to a god in the sixteenth generation, they challenged him with their own genealogy, refusing to accept that any man was descended from a god. They traced their counter-genealogy like this: each statue, they said, was a piromis born of a piromis (meaning a good and noble man). They showed three hundred and forty-five statues, each piromis descended from piromis, without ever connecting the line to either a god or a hero.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 359
paragraphs: From their declaration it followed that the beings represented by the statues were human in form and far from being gods. But they said that before these men, gods were the rulers of Egypt. They did not mingle with humans. One of them always held supreme power. The last god to rule Egypt was Horus, the son of Osiris—the god the Greeks call Apollo. He deposed Typhon and became the last divine king of Egypt. Osiris in Greek is Dionysus.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 360
paragraphs: Among the Greeks, Heracles, Dionysus, and Pan are considered the youngest of the gods. But among the Egyptians, Pan is extremely ancient—one of the eight gods they call the first generation. Heracles belongs to the second generation of twelve gods. Dionysus belongs to the third generation, descended from the twelve. I have already shown how many years the Egyptians reckon between Heracles and the reign of Amasis: seventeen thousand. They reckon Pan to be even older, and Dionysus to be the most recent of the three, yet still fifteen thousand years before Amasis. The Egyptians claim to know these figures with certainty because they have always kept careful records. As for the Dionysus said to be born of Semele, daughter of Cadmos, that was about sixteen hundred years before my time. Heracles, son of Alcmene, about nine hundred years. Pan, son of Penelope (the Greeks say he was born of Penelope and Hermes), came after the Trojan War, about eight hundred years before my time.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 361
paragraphs: Of these two accounts, each man may adopt the one he finds more credible. I have already stated my own opinion. If Heracles and Dionysus, sons of human mothers, had appeared openly in Greece and grown old there, as did Heracles the son of Amphitryon and Dionysus the son of Semele, then people would have said they were mortals named after earlier gods. But in fact, the Greeks say that Dionysus was sewn into Zeus' thigh immediately after birth and carried to Nysa in Ethiopia—above Egypt. As for Pan, the Greeks cannot say where he went after being born. It is clear to me that the Greeks learned the names of these gods later than those of all the others, and they trace the genealogy of each from the time when they first learned of them.
So far the history is told by the Egyptians themselves.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 362
paragraphs: But now I will tell what other nations also report, in agreement with the Egyptians, about what happened in this land. I will add something of my own observation as well.

After the priest of Hephaistos, the Egyptians could not live without a king. They appointed twelve kings over themselves, dividing Egypt into twelve parts. These twelve intermarried and ruled by agreement, bound by these terms: none of them would try to overthrow the others, none would seek to gain more than the rest, and they would be the closest of allies. They made these agreements and enforced them strictly because, at the very beginning of their rule, an oracle had told them that whoever poured a libation from a bronze cup in the temple of Hephaistos would become king of all Egypt. (They always assembled in all the temples together.)

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 363
paragraphs: Moreover, they decided to join forces and leave a common memorial. So they built the Labyrinth, situated just above Lake Moeris, near the place called Crocodile City. I have seen it myself, and it surpasses description. If someone gathered all the walls and great works built by the Greeks, they would be found to have cost less labor and money than this Labyrinth. Yet the temples at Ephesus and Samos are remarkable enough. The pyramids too are beyond words, and each one equals many great Greek buildings. But the Labyrinth surpasses even the pyramids. It has twelve covered courts with gates facing each other: six on the north side, six on the south, all connected. A single wall surrounds them all. There are two sets of rooms—one underground, one above ground—three thousand in total, fifteen hundred of each. I went through the upper rooms myself and saw them with my own eyes, so I speak from firsthand knowledge. The underground rooms I know only by report, since the Egyptian guards refused to show them. They said these rooms contain the tombs of the kings who originally built the Labyrinth, and also the tombs of sacred crocodiles. So I speak of the lower rooms from hearsay, but the upper ones I saw for myself and found them to surpass all other human works. The passages through the rooms and the winding paths through the courts filled me with endless wonder as I went from courtyard to room, from room to colonnade, from colonnade to more rooms, and from those back to more courts. The roof of every chamber is stone, as are the walls, and the walls are covered with carved figures. Each court is surrounded by columns of white stone, perfectly fitted. At the corner where the Labyrinth ends stands a pyramid two hundred and forty feet high, with great carved figures. The entrance to this pyramid is underground.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 364
paragraphs: Even more wondrous than the Labyrinth is Lake Moeris, beside which it stands. The lake's circumference is three thousand six hundred furlongs—sixty schoines—equal to the entire coastline of Egypt. It runs north-south, and at its deepest point is fifty fathoms. That it is artificial and dug by hand is self-evident. In the middle of the lake stand two pyramids, each rising fifty fathoms above the water, with an equal depth of construction below. On top of each sits a colossal stone figure on a throne. The pyramids are thus a hundred fathoms total. One hundred fathoms equals a furlong of six hundred feet (the fathom being six feet or four cubits, each foot being four palms and each cubit six palms). The lake's water does not come from the ground there, which is extremely dry. It comes from the Nile through a channel. For six months it flows into the lake, for six months it flows back into the Nile. During the six months when the water flows out, the lake yields a silver talent per day from the fish catch for the royal treasury. When the water flows in, it yields only twenty minas.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 365
paragraphs: The locals also said this lake has an underground outlet to the Syrtis in Libya, running westward along the mountain above Memphis. Since I could not see what became of the excavated earth, I asked the people living nearest the lake where it had been dumped. They gave me an easy answer: it was carried to the Nile. The river would dissolve and carry it away. This is plausible. I know the same thing was done at Nineveh, the Assyrian capital. Thieves decided to tunnel from their house to the royal treasury. They began digging and dumped the excavated earth into the Tigris, which flows past the city. They worked at it every night until they succeeded. The same method, I believe, was used for the Egyptian lake—except that the work was done by day, not night. The excavated earth was carried to the Nile, which would naturally scatter and dissolve it. That is how this lake was dug.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 366
paragraphs: The twelve kings continued to rule justly. But in time, the following happened. After making sacrifices in the temple of Hephaistos, they were about to pour libations on the last day of the festival. The chief priest brought out the golden cups they always used, but he miscounted and brought only eleven instead of twelve. Psammetichos, standing at the end without a cup, took off his bronze helmet and held it out for the libation. All the other kings also wore helmets that day—it was a coincidence, nothing premeditated. But the others remembered the oracle about the bronze cup and asked Psammetichos about it. When they saw he had acted innocently, they decided not to kill him. Instead they stripped him of most of his power and banished him to the marshes, forbidding him from leaving or having any dealings with the rest of Egypt.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 367
paragraphs: Psammetichos had previously been a fugitive. When the Ethiopian Sabacos had killed his father Necos, Psammetichos had fled to Syria. When the Ethiopian departed because of the dream, the Egyptians from the Saite district brought him home. Then, as king, he was exiled a second time by the eleven kings because of the helmet. Banished to the marshes, Psammetichos felt he had been wrongly treated. He planned revenge. He sent to consult the oracle of Leto at Buto, the most truthful oracle in Egypt. The answer came: vengeance would arrive from the sea, when bronze men appeared. He was deeply skeptical—bronze men from the sea seemed impossible. But not long afterward, a group of Ionians and Carians, raiding by sea, were forced ashore in Egypt. They came in full bronze armor. An Egyptian who had never seen armored men ran to the marshes and told Psammetichos that bronze men had come from the sea and were plundering the plains. Psammetichos, recognizing the oracle's fulfillment, made friends with the Ionians and Carians. With great promises, he persuaded them to join him. With their help and the support of loyal Egyptians, he overthrew the eleven kings.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 368
paragraphs: Having gained power over all Egypt, Psammetichos built the southern gateway of the temple of Hephaistos at Memphis. He also built a court for Apis, where the sacred bull is kept when it appears—a court opposite the gateway, surrounded by a colonnade and covered with carved figures. Instead of pillars, the colonnade is supported by colossal statues twelve cubits tall. Apis is Epaphos in Greek.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 369
paragraphs: To the Ionians and Carians who had helped him, Psammetichos granted plots of land on opposite sides of the Nile, known as the Camps. He gave them these lands and fulfilled all his other promises. He also placed Egyptian boys with them to learn Greek. From these boys who learned Greek descended the interpreters who exist in Egypt today. The Ionians and Carians occupied these lands for a long time. They lie near the sea, below the city of Bubastis, on the Pelusiac mouth of the Nile. King Amasis later moved them to Memphis, making them his personal bodyguard against the native Egyptians. After their settlement in Egypt, the Greeks had regular contact with them. Because of this, we have accurate knowledge of Egyptian history from the reign of Psammetichos onward. They were the first foreign-language speakers to settle in Egypt.
That is how Psammetichos became king of Egypt.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 370
paragraphs: I have already mentioned the oracle in Egypt several times. Now I will describe it, since it deserves a full account. This oracle is sacred to Leto. It is located in a great city near the Sebennytic mouth of the Nile, on the way up from the sea. The city's name is Buto, which I have mentioned before. In Buto, there is a temple of Apollo and Artemis. The temple of Leto, which houses the oracle, is itself quite large, with a gateway sixty feet high. But the most remarkable thing I saw there I will now describe.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 371
paragraphs: Of all the sights in that temple, the most wondrous is the island called Chemmis. It floats in a deep, wide lake beside the temple. The Egyptians say it is a floating island. I never actually saw it move, and I was amazed to hear that an island could float. On it stands a great temple of Apollo with three altars. Many palm trees grow on it, along with other trees, both fruit-bearing and not. The Egyptians explain its floating this way: Leto, one of the eight original gods, lived in Buto where the oracle now stands. When Isis entrusted Apollo to her care, she hid him on this island (which until then had been fixed) to protect him when Typhon came searching everywhere for the son of Osiris. They say Apollo and Artemis are the children of Dionysus and Isis, and that Leto became their nurse and savior. In Egyptian, Apollo is Horus, Demeter is Isis, and Artemis is Bubastis. It was from this tale, and no other, that Aeschylus son of Euphorion took his idea of making Artemis the daughter of Demeter. For this reason, they say, the island became a floating island.
That is their story.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 372
paragraphs: Psammetichos ruled Egypt for fifty-four years. For twenty-nine of those years, he besieged the great Syrian city of Azotos until he finally captured it. Azotos withstood a siege longer than any other city I know of.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 373
paragraphs: Psammetichos' son was Necos, and he became king of Egypt. He was the first to attempt the canal connecting the Nile to the Red Sea, which Darius the Persian later completed. The canal is a four-day voyage in length and wide enough for two triremes to be rowed side by side. The water comes from the Nile.
