The canal runs from a point slightly above the city of Bubastis, past the Arabian city of Patumos, and into the Red Sea. The first part runs along the Arabian side of the Egyptian plain, past the ridge that extends south of Memphis, where the stone quarries are. The canal follows the base of this ridge from west to east, then turns south through a gap in the hills toward the Arabian Gulf. The shortest and most direct route from the northern sea to the southern (or Red) Sea is across the strip from Mount Casion on the border of Egypt and Syria—a distance of exactly a thousand furlongs. That is the most direct route. The canal is much longer because it winds. A hundred and twenty thousand Egyptians died during the digging under Necos. He eventually stopped because an oracle warned him he was working for the benefit of a barbarian. (The Egyptians call anyone who does not speak their language a barbarian.)

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 374
paragraphs: After abandoning the canal, Necos turned to warfare. He had triremes built, some for the Mediterranean and some for the Arabian Gulf on the Red Sea. Their ship sheds can still be seen. He used these ships when he needed them. On land, Necos fought and defeated the Syrians at Magdolos. After the battle, he captured the great Syrian city of Cadytis. He dedicated the clothes he wore during these victories to Apollo, sending them to the temple of the Branchidai near Miletos. After a total reign of sixteen years, Necos died and passed the throne to his son Psammis.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 375
paragraphs: During Psammis' reign, envoys came from Elis. The Eleians boasted that they ran the Olympic games in the most fair and honorable way possible and believed that not even the wisest people on earth—the Egyptians—could improve on them. When Psammis heard why the Eleians had come, he summoned those Egyptians considered the wisest. They met with the Eleians and heard their full account of the rules. The Egyptians then asked whether their own citizens were allowed to compete. The Eleians said the games were open to all Greeks. The Egyptians replied that this was completely unfair, since it was impossible for the Eleians not to favor their own countrymen at the expense of foreigners. If they truly wanted to organize fair games, open to all, then they should exclude Eleians from competing entirely and make the games open only to outsiders. That was the Egyptians' recommendation.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 376
paragraphs: Psammis ruled Egypt for only six years. He campaigned against Ethiopia and died immediately afterward. His son Apries succeeded him. Apries became the most prosperous of all Egyptian kings before him, except for his great-grandfather Psammetichos. He reigned for twenty-five years and during that time marched against Sidon and fought a sea battle against the king of Tyre. But disaster was fated for him, and it came about through an event I will describe more fully in the Libyan narrative and only briefly here. Apries sent a great army against the Cyreneans and suffered a devastating defeat. The Egyptians blamed him for this and revolted, believing he had deliberately sent them to certain destruction so that the survivors would be fewer and easier to rule. The returning soldiers and the friends of the dead were furious and openly rebelled.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 377
paragraphs: When Apries heard of the revolt, he sent Amasis to talk the rebels down. But when Amasis arrived and was urging the Egyptians to stop, one of them came up behind him and placed a helmet on his head, declaring him king. Amasis did not resist—he accepted. Once he had been proclaimed king by the rebels, he prepared to march against Apries. Apries sent a distinguished Egyptian named Patarbemis to bring Amasis back alive. When Patarbemis reached Amasis and summoned him, Amasis—who happened to be on horseback—lifted himself in the saddle, broke wind, and told Patarbemis to take that back to Apries. Patarbemis persisted, urging Amasis to obey the king's summons. Amasis replied that he had been preparing to do just that for some time, and Apries would have no complaint—he would come in person and bring others with him. Patarbemis understood both the words and the preparations. He hurried back to report to the king. When Apries heard the report, he flew into a rage and had Patarbemis' nose and ears cut off. The rest of the Egyptians, who had until then remained loyal, saw one of their most respected citizens so horribly mutilated and immediately went over to the other side, giving themselves to Amasis.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 378
paragraphs: Apries, learning of this second defection, armed his foreign mercenaries and marched against the Egyptians. He had around thirty thousand Carian and Ionian mercenaries. His royal palace was in the city of Sais—a large and impressive building. Apries and his mercenaries marched to attack the Egyptians, and Amasis and his forces marched to resist them. Both armies came to the city of Momemphis and prepared for battle.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 379
paragraphs: There are seven classes of Egyptians. They are called: priests, warriors, cowherds, swineherds, shopkeepers, interpreters, and boatmen. These are the classes, named after their occupations. The warriors are called Hermotybians and Calasians, and they come from the following districts (since all Egypt is divided into districts).

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 380
paragraphs: The Hermotybians come from the districts of Busiris, Sais, Chemmis, Papremis, the island called Prosopitis, and half of the district of Natho. At their peak, they numbered one hundred and sixty thousand. None of them practices any trade. They devote themselves entirely to warfare.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 381
paragraphs: The Calasians come from the districts of Thebes, Bubastis, Aphthis, Tanis, Mendes, Sebennys, Athribis, Pharbaethos, Thmuis, Onuphis, Anysis, and Myecphoris (this last is on an island opposite the city of Bubastis). At their peak, the Calasians numbered two hundred and fifty thousand. Like the Hermotybians, they are forbidden to practice any trade and devote themselves solely to military training, passing the tradition from father to son.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 382
paragraphs: Whether the Greeks learned this from the Egyptians, I cannot say with certainty, since I see that the Thracians, Scythians, Persians, Lydians—and nearly all barbarian peoples—hold those who learn trades in lower esteem than other citizens. They regard those who are free from manual labor as noble, especially those who devote themselves to war. All the Greeks have adopted this attitude, the Spartans most of all. The Corinthians look down on craftsmen the least.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 383
paragraphs: The warriors enjoyed certain privileges granted to them alone, besides the priests. Each man received twelve yokes of prime land, tax-free. A yoke is a square of one hundred Egyptian cubits on each side (the Egyptian cubit being equal to the Samian). These plots were granted to all warriors, though different men held them at different times—the same man never held the same plot in consecutive years. Each year, a thousand Calasians and a thousand Hermotybians served as the king's bodyguard. While on duty, they received a daily ration of five minas of baked bread, two minas of beef, and four cups of wine, in addition to their land grants.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 384
paragraphs: When Apries with his mercenaries and Amasis with the whole body of Egyptians reached the city of Momemphis, they joined battle. The mercenaries fought well but were vastly outnumbered. They were defeated. Apries, they say, believed that not even a god could dethrone him—so firmly established did he think he was. But in that battle he was beaten, captured alive, and taken back to Sais, to his own former palace, now the residence of Amasis. Amasis kept him in the palace for a while, treating him well. But eventually, when the Egyptians complained that it was unjust to maintain a man who was their greatest enemy, Amasis handed Apries over to the people. They strangled him and buried him in his ancestral tomb in the temple of Athena—nearest the sanctuary, on the left as you enter. The people of Sais buried all the kings of their district inside this temple. The tomb of Amasis is also there, though further from the sanctuary than that of Apries—a great stone colonnade, richly decorated, with columns shaped like palm trees.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 385
paragraphs: Inside this colonnade are double doors. Behind the doors is the burial chamber. Also in Sais is the burial place of a god whose name I consider it impious to mention in this context. It is in the temple of Athena, behind and extending along the entire wall of the goddess' house. In the sacred enclosure stand tall stone obelisks. Beside them is a lake, decorated with a stone rim—beautifully finished—and about the same size, I thought, as the lake called the Round Pool on Delos.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 386
paragraphs: On this lake they perform by night the drama of the god's sufferings. The Egyptians call these performances Mysteries. I know the full details of how they are conducted, but I will say no more. Similarly, about the rites of Demeter, which the Greeks call the Thesmophoria, I will keep silent—except for what may be spoken without impiety. The daughters of Danaos brought this ceremony from Egypt and taught it to the Pelasgian women. Afterward, when the Dorians drove out the entire population of the Peloponnese, the rite was lost, except among the Arcadians, who were not driven out and remained.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 387
paragraphs: After Apries was overthrown, Amasis became king. He came from the district of Sais, from the city of Siuph. At first, the Egyptians despised him and held him in low regard, since he had been a commoner and came from an undistinguished family. But Amasis won them over by cleverness rather than force. Among his countless treasures was a golden foot-basin in which Amasis himself and all his dinner guests used to wash their feet. He had this melted down and made into a statue of a god, which he placed in the busiest spot in the city. The Egyptians thronged to worship it. When Amasis learned what had happened, he called the Egyptians together and revealed that the statue had been made from the foot-basin—the very basin in which they had formerly vomited, urinated, and washed their feet, and which they now worshipped. He said his own case was much the same. He may once have been a commoner, but now he was their king, and they should honor and respect him.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 388
paragraphs: In this way he won the Egyptians over. His method of governing was this. In the early morning, until the marketplace filled up, he dealt energetically with whatever business was brought to him. After that, he drank and joked with his companions, being playful and not at all serious. His friends were troubled by this and reproached him: "O king, you do not conduct yourself properly by indulging in trivial amusements. You should sit solemnly on your throne all day and attend to business. That way, the Egyptians would know they are governed by a great man, and your reputation would improve. What you are doing now is not kingly at all." Amasis replied: "Men who own bows string them when they need to use them and unstring them when they are done. If a bow were kept strung all the time, it would break and be useless when needed. The same is true of people. If someone devoted himself entirely to serious business and never relaxed into play, he would go mad or have a stroke without even noticing. I know this, and I give each its proper share of my time."

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 389
paragraphs: They say Amasis was a drinker and a joker even as a private citizen, with no serious inclinations at all. Whenever his funds ran dry from drinking and high living, he would steal. When people accused him of having their property and he denied it, they would take him to the nearest oracle. Sometimes the oracle convicted him, sometimes it acquitted him. When he became king, he treated the temples of gods who had acquitted him with contempt—not caring for them or contributing to their upkeep. He considered them worthless and their oracles false. But the temples of the gods who had convicted him of theft he treated with the greatest respect, considering them genuine and their oracles truthful.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 390
paragraphs: First, in Sais, he built and completed for Athena a temple gateway that is a great marvel, far surpassing all others in height and size, with stones of exceptional quality. He also dedicated colossal statues and enormous human-headed sphinxes. He brought other enormous stones for repairs as well. Some were quarried from the quarries near Memphis. Others—the truly gigantic ones—came from the city of Elephantine, which is a twenty-day voyage from Sais. But what amazed me most was a single-stone chamber he brought from Elephantine. It took two thousand men (all boatmen) three years to transport. The outer dimensions of this chamber are twenty-one cubits long, fourteen cubits wide, and eight cubits high. The inner dimensions are eighteen cubits and one hand long, twelve cubits wide, and five cubits high. It stands beside the entrance to the temple. They did not actually drag it inside, they say, because as they were hauling it in, the master builder sighed heavily, weary of the long labor. Amasis took this as a bad omen and would not let the stone be moved further.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 391
paragraphs: Amasis also dedicated remarkable works at all the other important temples. At Memphis, in front of the temple of Hephaistos, he set up the enormous reclining statue that is seventy-five feet long. Two statues, each twenty feet tall, stand on the same base—one on each side—carved from the same block of stone. There is another stone statue of similar size at Sais, reclining in the same position as the one at Memphis. Amasis was also the one who built the great and remarkable temple of Isis at Memphis.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 392
paragraphs: In the reign of Amasis, Egypt is said to have been more prosperous than at any previous time, both from what the river gave to the land and from what the land gave to its people. The country at that time contained twenty thousand inhabited cities. It was Amasis who established the law that every Egyptian must appear once a year before the governor of his district and declare his means of livelihood. Anyone who failed to do so, or could not prove he lived by honest means, was punished by death. The Athenian Solon brought this law from Egypt and established it at Athens. It is an excellent law, and I hope it stays in force forever.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 393
paragraphs: Amasis became a friend of the Greeks. Among other tokens of friendship, he granted the city of Naucratis to Greeks who came to Egypt, giving them a place to live. For those who did not wish to settle but came on trading voyages, he set aside areas where they could erect altars and sacred precincts to their gods. The largest, most famous, and most used of these is called the Hellenion. It was founded jointly by the following cities: of the Ionians, Chios, Teos, Phocaea, and Clazomenae; of the Dorians, Rhodes, Cnidos, Halicarnassos, and Phaselis; of the Aeolians, Mytilene alone. The Hellenion belongs to these cities, and they are the ones who appoint the market supervisors. Other cities that claim a share have no right to one. Separately, the Aeginetans established a precinct of Zeus, the Samians one of Hera, and the Milesians one of Apollo.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 394
paragraphs: In ancient times, Naucratis was the only port of entry in Egypt. Anyone who arrived at any other mouth of the Nile was required to swear he had not come there intentionally. Having sworn his innocence, he had to sail his ship to the Canobic mouth. If contrary winds made this impossible, he had to transport his cargo by barge around the Delta to Naucratis. Such was the privileged status of Naucratis.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 395
paragraphs: When the Amphictyons contracted the building of the current temple at Delphi (the previous one had burned down) for three hundred talents, the people of Delphi had to raise a quarter of the cost. They traveled from city to city collecting contributions. From their visit to Egypt they received a large donation. Amasis gave them a thousand talents of alum, and the Greeks living in Egypt gave them twenty minas.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 396
paragraphs: Amasis also made a pact of friendship and alliance with the people of Cyrene. He decided to take a wife from there—either because he wanted a Greek wife, or simply out of friendship for Cyrene. He married a woman named Ladice, said by some to be the daughter of Battus, by others of Arcesilaus, and by still others of Critobulos, a prominent citizen. When Amasis lay with her, he found himself unable to consummate the marriage, though he had no trouble with his other wives. After this continued for some time, Amasis told Ladice he believed she had used witchcraft on him, and that nothing could save her from the worst death of any woman. Ladice denied everything, but Amasis was unmoved. So she silently vowed to Aphrodite that if Amasis lay with her successfully that night, she would send a statue to the goddess at Cyrene. Immediately after the vow, Amasis was able to perform. From then on, every time he came to her, he succeeded. He loved her very much after that. Ladice fulfilled her vow and sent the statue, which was still in good condition in my time, set up facing outward from the city of Cyrene. When Cambyses conquered Egypt and learned who Ladice was, he sent her home to Cyrene unharmed.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 397
paragraphs: Amasis also dedicated offerings in Greece. At Cyrene, he gave a gold-plated image of Athena and a painted portrait of himself. At the temple of Athena at Lindos, he gave two stone statues and a remarkable corselet of linen. At the temple of Hera on Samos, he gave two wooden portraits of himself, which were still standing in my time in the great temple, behind the doors. He made these gifts to Samos because of the friendship between himself and Polycrates, son of Aeaces. His gifts to Lindos were not because of any friendship but because the temple of Athena at Lindos was said to have been founded by the daughters of Danaos, who landed there while fleeing the sons of Aegyptus. Those were the offerings of Amasis. He was the first man to conquer Cyprus and compel it to pay tribute.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 398
paragraphs: Against this Amasis, then, Cambyses the son of Cyrus was marching, bringing with him Ionians, Aeolians, and other subject Greeks alongside his Persian forces. The cause of the expedition was this. Cambyses had sent an envoy to Egypt demanding the daughter of Amasis in marriage. He did this on the advice of an Egyptian doctor who bore a grudge against Amasis. Amasis had sent this man away from his wife and children to Persia when Cyrus requested the best eye doctor in Egypt. The doctor, resenting this, urged Cambyses to ask for Amasis' daughter, knowing that Amasis would be distressed whether he gave her up or refused. Amasis, afraid of Persian power, could neither give his daughter nor refuse. He knew Cambyses wanted her as a concubine, not a wife. So he dressed up the tall, beautiful daughter of his predecessor Apries—the only surviving member of that royal house—named Nitetis, and sent her as his own daughter. But when Cambyses greeted her as the daughter of Amasis, the girl said: "O king, you do not realize you have been deceived. Amasis dressed me up and sent me as his own daughter, but I am actually the daughter of Apries, his former master, whom he overthrew." This revelation and this cause of anger drove Cambyses against Egypt.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 399
paragraphs: That is the Persian account. But the Egyptians claim Cambyses as one of their own, saying he was born of this very daughter of Apries. They say it was Cyrus, not Cambyses, who sent for Amasis' daughter. But they are wrong. They know Persian customs perfectly well—the Persians never allow an illegitimate son to rule when a legitimate one exists, and they know that Cambyses was the son of Cassandane, daughter of Pharnaspes, not of any Egyptian woman. But they twist the truth to claim kinship with the house of Cyrus.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 400
paragraphs: There is yet another story, which I do not believe. They say that a Persian woman visited the wives of Cyrus and saw Cassandane's tall, handsome children standing beside her. The visitor praised them extravagantly. Cassandane, who was Cyrus' wife, replied: "Even though I am the mother of such children, Cyrus dishonors me and gives all his attention to the woman he brought from Egypt." She spoke bitterly about Nitetis. Her eldest son, Cambyses, then said: "Mother, when I am grown, I will turn Egypt upside down." He was about ten years old when he said this, and the women were amazed. But he remembered it, and when he became a man and took the throne, he made the expedition against Egypt.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 401
paragraphs: Something else contributed to the expedition. Among the foreign mercenaries of Amasis was a man from Halicarnassos named Phanes. He was capable and brave in battle. This Phanes, having some complaint against Amasis, escaped from Egypt by ship, intending to get an audience with Cambyses. Since he was a man of standing among the mercenaries and had detailed knowledge of Egyptian affairs, Amasis pursued him vigorously. He sent his most trusted eunuch after him in a trireme. The eunuch caught him in Lycia, but could not bring him back, since Phanes outwitted him. He got his guards drunk and escaped to Persia. Cambyses was eager to march against Egypt but was uncertain about the route through the waterless desert. Phanes arrived, told him all about Amasis' affairs, and also showed him the route. He advised Cambyses to send a message to the king of the Arabs asking for safe passage.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 402
paragraphs: This is the only known entrance to Egypt. From Phoenicia to the borders of the city of Cadytis belongs to the Syrians called Palestinians. From Cadytis, which I estimate is a city not much smaller than Sardis, the trading posts along the coast down to the city of Ienysos belong to the Arabian king. From Ienysos the coast belongs to the Syrians again as far as Lake Serbonis, along which Mount Casion runs down to the sea. From Lake Serbonis, where Typhon is said to be hidden, Egypt begins. The entire area between Ienysos, Mount Casion, and Lake Serbonis—no small stretch, some three days' journey—is utterly waterless desert.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 403
paragraphs: I will now mention something that few travelers to Egypt have noticed. Twice a year, earthenware jars full of wine are imported to Egypt from all parts of Greece and from Phoenicia. Yet you almost never see an empty wine jar anywhere in Egypt. What happens to them all?

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 404
paragraphs: I will explain. The head man of each town must collect all the jars from his district and send them to Memphis. The people of Memphis fill them with water and transport them to the waterless parts of Syria. So every jar of wine that enters Egypt is emptied and sent on to Syria to join the others.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 405
paragraphs: The Persians provided this water supply route through the desert after they conquered Egypt. But at the time of Cambyses' invasion, when the route had no water stations, Cambyses took Phanes' advice and sent a messenger to the Arabian king to request safe passage, giving and receiving pledges of friendship. No people revere the oath of friendship more than the Arabs. When two men wish to make a pledge, a third man stands between them. Using a sharp stone, he makes a cut on the inside of each man's palm near the base of the middle fingers. He takes a thread from each man's cloak, dips it in blood, and smears seven stones placed between them, invoking Dionysus and Ourania. When this ceremony is complete, the man who made the pledge introduces the foreigner (or fellow citizen, if the pledge is between citizens) to his friends, and they too consider themselves bound by the oath. The Arabs recognize only two gods: Dionysus and Ourania. They say they cut their hair in the same style as Dionysus, shaving it in a circle around the head and cutting the temples short. They call Dionysus Orotalt and Ourania Alilat.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 406
paragraphs: When the Arabian king had exchanged pledges with Cambyses' envoys, he devised this plan. He filled camel skins with water and loaded them onto the backs of all his living camels. Then he drove them into the desert and waited for Cambyses' army. That is the more credible version. But since there is a less credible story too, I should tell it. There is a great river in Arabia called the Corys, which flows into the Red Sea. They say the Arabian king made a pipe from stitched raw oxhides long enough to reach from this river to the desert. He brought the water through the pipe and had large cisterns dug in the desert to store it. It is a twelve-day journey from the river to the desert. They say he brought the water through three separate pipes to three different spots.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 407
paragraphs: Meanwhile, Psammenitos the son of Amasis was camped at the Pelusian mouth of the Nile, waiting for Cambyses. Cambyses did not find Amasis alive when he invaded Egypt. Amasis had died after a forty-four-year reign, during which he had suffered no great misfortune. When he died, he was embalmed and placed in the tomb he had built for himself in the temple. During the reign of his son Psammenitos, the Egyptians witnessed the greatest portent ever seen: it rained in Egyptian Thebes. Rain had never fallen there before that time, and has not fallen since, according to the Thebans themselves. In upper Egypt, rain simply does not fall. Yet on this occasion, it rained in Thebes—a drizzle.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 408
paragraphs: When the Persians had crossed the waterless desert and were camped near the Egyptians in preparation for battle, the Greek and Carian mercenaries of the Egyptian king devised a cruel revenge on Phanes for leading a foreign army against Egypt. Phanes had left his sons behind in Egypt. The mercenaries brought the boys to the camp, in full view of their father. They set up a large mixing bowl between the two armies. Then, one by one, they brought Phanes' sons to the bowl and cut their throats over it. When all were dead, they poured wine and water into the bowl of blood, and every mercenary drank from it. After that, battle was joined. The fighting was fierce, and many fell on both sides. But the Egyptians were routed.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 409
paragraphs: I witnessed a remarkable thing there, which the locals told me about. The bones of those who fell in this battle lay scattered on the field, each side's dead lying separately just as they originally fell. The skulls of the Persians are so thin that you can pierce them by throwing a mere pebble. The Egyptian skulls are so tough that you can barely crack them with a heavy stone. The Egyptians, they told me, shave their heads from childhood. The sun bakes the bone and hardens it. This is also why Egyptians do not go bald—you see fewer bald men in Egypt than anywhere else. The Persians have weak skulls because they always wear felt caps and shade their heads from the sun. I saw this myself, and I saw the same thing at Papremis among those who fell with Achaimenes, son of Darius, when he was defeated by Inaros the Libyan.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 410
paragraphs: The Egyptians, fleeing from the battlefield in disorder, shut themselves inside Memphis. Cambyses sent a Mytilenean ship up the river with a Persian herald to invite them to surrender. But when the Egyptians saw the ship enter Memphis, they swarmed out, destroyed the ship, tore the crew limb from limb, and carried the pieces inside the walls. After this they were besieged and eventually surrendered. The neighboring Libyans, terrified by what had happened in Egypt, submitted without a fight. The Cyrenaeans and Barcaeans, equally frightened, did the same, sending gifts. Cambyses graciously received the Libyan gifts but was displeased with those from Cyrene—I think because the amount was too small (they sent five hundred minas of silver). He grabbed the coins and flung them with his own hands to his soldiers.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 411
paragraphs: On the tenth day after receiving the surrender of Memphis, Cambyses placed the Egyptian king Psammenitos—who had reigned only six months—in the outskirts of the city to humiliate him, along with other Egyptians. He tested his spirit as follows. He dressed the king's daughter as a slave and sent her out with a water pitcher, along with other noble daughters similarly dressed. As the girls passed their fathers on their way to fetch water, the fathers cried out and wept. Psammenitos saw his daughter and understood, but he only bowed his head. After the water-carriers had passed, Cambyses next sent the king's son, along with two thousand other young Egyptian men of the same age, all with ropes around their necks and bridles in their mouths. They were being led out to be executed in reprisal for the Mytileneans who had been destroyed with the ship at Memphis. The royal judges had decreed that for each man killed, ten noble Egyptians should die. Psammenitos saw them being led past and recognized his son at the head of the procession going to his death. But though the other Egyptians around him wept and showed their anguish, Psammenitos did the same as when he saw his daughter: he only bowed his head. When these too had passed, it happened that a man from his drinking circle—an older man who had been stripped of all his possessions and reduced to begging from the soldiers—walked past. When Psammenitos saw him, he burst into loud weeping. He struck his head and called his friend by name. Guards were there to report each of his reactions to Cambyses. Cambyses was surprised by this and sent a messenger to ask: "Your master Cambyses wants to know, Psammenitos, why you did not cry or mourn for your daughter being enslaved or your son going to his death, but you honor this beggar who, they tell him, is not even a relative." Psammenitos answered: "Son of Cyrus, my own misfortunes are too great for tears. But my companion's grief deserves weeping—a man who has fallen from great wealth to beggary at the threshold of old age." When this reply was reported, Cambyses and all those around him thought it was well spoken. Croesus, who had accompanied Cambyses to Egypt, wept at hearing it. So did the Persians present. Even Cambyses felt some pity. He ordered Psammenitos' son to be reprieved from execution and Psammenitos himself to be brought from the outskirts into his presence.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 412
paragraphs: Those who went for the son found he was already dead—he had been the first to be killed. But Psammenitos was brought before Cambyses and lived with him for the rest of his days, receiving no further ill treatment. If he had known enough to keep out of politics, he could have recovered Egypt and governed it as a vassal. The Persians customarily honor the sons of kings and give kingdoms back to the sons of those who have rebelled. There are many examples of this custom. But Psammenitos plotted revolt and paid the price. He was caught trying to stir up the Egyptians and, when Cambyses discovered this, he drank bull's blood and died on the spot. That was his end.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 413
paragraphs: From Memphis, Cambyses went to the city of Sais with the specific intention of doing what he did. When he entered the palace of Amasis, he ordered the body of Amasis dragged from its tomb. When this was done, he commanded them to whip the corpse, pluck out its hair, stab it, and heap every kind of abuse on it. When they were exhausted from this—since the embalmed body resisted and would not fall apart—Cambyses ordered it to be burned. This was an impious command, since the Persians consider fire to be a god. Neither the Persians nor the Egyptians believe in burning the dead. The Persians object because they think it wrong to give a human corpse to a god. The Egyptians consider fire to be a living beast that devours everything it catches and then dies with its meal. Their law forbids giving the dead to beasts. That is why they embalm their dead—to prevent them from being eaten by worms. So Cambyses was ordering something forbidden by the customs of both nations. The Egyptians say, however, that it was not really Amasis who was mistreated but another Egyptian of similar build, whom the Persians abused thinking it was Amasis. They say Amasis had learned from an oracle what would happen after his death. To prevent it, he buried the substitute body—the one that was whipped—just inside the door of his tomb, and ordered his son to place his own body in the deepest corner of the burial chamber. I do not believe these commands of Amasis actually happened. I think the Egyptians invented the story to make themselves look better.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 414
paragraphs: After this, Cambyses planned three military expeditions: one against the Carthaginians, another against the Ammonians, and a third against the Long-lived Ethiopians who dwell in the part of Libya along the Southern Sea. He decided to send his navy against Carthage, a land force against the Ammonians, and spies to the Ethiopians first—ostensibly to bring gifts to the Ethiopian king but really to observe conditions. The spies were also to check whether the so-called Table of the Sun really existed.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 415
paragraphs: The Table of the Sun is said to be this: a meadow outside the city, filled with the boiled meat of every kind of four-footed animal. The city's officials place the meat there at night. During the day, anyone who wishes may come and eat. The locals say the earth itself produces the food each night. That is the account of the so-called Table of the Sun.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 416
paragraphs: When Cambyses decided to send spies, he immediately summoned the Fish-eaters from the city of Elephantine—those who understood the Ethiopian language. While they were being fetched, he ordered his navy to sail against Carthage. But the Phoenicians refused to go. They said they were bound by solemn oaths to the Carthaginians and would be committing an impious act by attacking their own offspring, since Carthage was a Phoenician colony. Without the Phoenicians, the rest of the fleet was not strong enough. So the Carthaginians escaped Persian subjection. Cambyses chose not to use force against the Phoenicians, since they had voluntarily submitted to Persia and the entire navy depended on them. The Cyprians had also volunteered and took part in the Egyptian campaign.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 417
paragraphs: When the Fish-eaters arrived from Elephantine, Cambyses sent them to the Ethiopians with instructions on what to say. He gave them gifts to bring: a purple robe, a twisted gold necklace, bracelets, an alabaster box of myrrh, and a jar of palm wine.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 418
paragraphs: The Fish-eaters arrived and presented their gifts to the Ethiopian king. They said: "Cambyses, king of the Persians, wishes to become your friend and ally. He has sent us to converse with you and brings you these gifts—the things he himself takes most pleasure in." The Ethiopian king, understanding that they were spies, answered: "The king of the Persians did not send you with gifts because he values my friendship. You have come to spy on my kingdom. Your king is not a just man. If he were just, he would not have coveted a land that is not his, nor would he be trying to enslave people who have done him no wrong. Give him this bow and tell him: the king of the Ethiopians advises the king of the Persians to attack the Long-lived Ethiopians when the Persians can draw a bow this size as easily as I do. Until then, let him thank the gods for not putting it into the minds of the Ethiopians to conquer lands beyond their own." Having said this, he unstrung the bow and handed it to the envoys.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 419
paragraphs: Then he took the purple robe and asked what it was and how it was made. When the Fish-eaters explained about the dye and the dyeing process, the king said the people were deceitful and so were their garments. He asked about the gold necklace and bracelets. When the Fish-eaters explained they were jewelry, the king laughed and said he had stronger chains than those in his own country. He asked about the myrrh. When they explained how it was used as perfume, he made the same remark as about the clothes. But when he came to the wine and learned how it was made, he was delighted with the drink. He asked what the Persian king ate and what was the greatest age a Persian man could reach. They told him about bread, explaining how wheat was grown, and said that eighty years was the longest any Persian could expect to live. The Ethiopian king said he was not surprised they died so young, since they lived on dung (meaning the wheat). They would not even reach that age if they did not have the wine to sustain them—and he acknowledged that in this one thing the Persians surpassed his people.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 420
paragraphs: When the Fish-eaters asked the king about his own people's lifespan and diet, he said most of them reached a hundred and twenty years, with some exceeding even that. They ate boiled meat and drank milk. When the spies expressed amazement at such long lives, the king led them to a spring. After bathing in it, they found their skin became sleek and shining, as if the water were oil. They said it smelled of violets. The water of this spring, the spies said, was so light that nothing would float in it—neither wood nor anything lighter than wood. Everything sank. If this water really is as they describe, then using it for everything might be the reason these people live so long. They also have a remarkable prison: all prisoners are bound with golden chains, since bronze is the rarest and most precious metal among the Ethiopians. After the spring, they visited the prison and saw these golden fetters.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 421
paragraphs: Last of all, they saw the Ethiopian coffins. These are said to be made of crystal, in the following way. They dry the corpse—either in the Egyptian manner or some other way—and coat it entirely with plaster. Then they paint it to look as much like the living person as possible. They place the body in a hollow column of crystal, which is mined in great quantities there and is easy to work. The corpse is visible through the column, and it gives off no unpleasant smell or any other disagreeable effect. It looks exactly like the person did in life. The closest relatives keep the column in their house for a year, offering it first-fruits and sacrifices. After that, they carry it out and set it up near the city.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 422
paragraphs: After seeing everything, the spies returned. When they reported back, Cambyses was furious. He immediately set out to march against the Ethiopians, without ordering provisions or considering that he was about to campaign at the ends of the earth. Being out of his mind—truly insane—he marched as soon as he heard the Fish-eaters' report. He ordered the Greek troops with him to stay behind and took only his land army. When he reached Thebes on the march, he detached fifty thousand men and sent them against the Ammonians, with orders to enslave the population and burn the oracle of Zeus. He himself continued the march toward Ethiopia with the rest of his army. Before they had covered a fifth of the journey, all the food they had brought was gone. After the food, the pack animals were eaten. If Cambyses had seen reason at this point and turned back, he would have been a wise man despite his initial error. But he paid no attention and kept going. As long as the soldiers could find plants, they survived by eating grass. But when they entered the desert, some of them did a terrible thing. They drew lots, choosing one man out of every ten, and ate him. When Cambyses heard about this, he was terrified by the cannibalism and abandoned the Ethiopian expedition. He turned back and reached Thebes with his army greatly reduced. From Thebes, he went down to Memphis and let the Greeks sail home.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 423
paragraphs: That was the fate of the Ethiopian expedition. As for the force sent against the Ammonians, they set out from Thebes with guides. They are known to have reached the city of Oasis, which is inhabited by Samians said to belong to the Aeschrionian tribe. This place is seven days' march from Thebes through the desert. In Greek it is called the Island of the Blessed. The army is said to have reached this point. But after that, no one knows what happened except the Ammonians themselves and those who have heard from them. They never reached the Ammonians and never returned. The Ammonians tell this story: after leaving Oasis and crossing the desert toward them, when the army was roughly halfway between Oasis and their territory, a great and violent south wind rose while the men were eating their midday meal. It carried vast quantities of sand and buried them all. That is how the Ammonians say they disappeared.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 424
paragraphs: When Cambyses arrived at Memphis, the sacred bull Apis appeared to the Egyptians. (The Greeks call him Epaphos.) As soon as Apis appeared, the Egyptians put on their finest clothes and began celebrating. Cambyses saw the Egyptians feasting and assumed they were celebrating his military disasters. He summoned the officials of Memphis and demanded to know why the Egyptians had held no festivities when he was in Memphis before but were doing so now, when he had returned with a diminished army. They told him that their god had appeared—something that happened only after long intervals—and that it was customary for all Egypt to celebrate when he came. Cambyses said they were liars and sentenced them to death for lying.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 425
paragraphs: After executing them, he called the priests. The priests gave the same answer. Cambyses said that if a tame god had come to the Egyptians, it would not escape his attention. He ordered the priests to bring Apis. They went and brought him.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 426
paragraphs: This Apis (or Epaphos) is a calf born of a cow that can never conceive again. The Egyptians say a bolt of light strikes the cow from heaven and she conceives Apis. The calf they call Apis has these marks: it is black, with a white square on its forehead, the image of an eagle on its back, double hairs in its tail, and a scarab mark under its tongue. When the priests brought Apis, Cambyses—half mad as he was—drew his dagger and aimed for the bull's belly but struck its thigh. He laughed and said to the priests: "Wretched people, are these your gods—creatures of flesh and blood that feel the blade? This is a god worthy of the Egyptians. But you will not laugh at me and get away with it." He ordered the priests to be whipped and any Egyptian caught celebrating to be killed. So the festival was broken off. The priests were punished. Apis, wounded in the thigh, lay in the temple, weakening.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 427
paragraphs: When Apis died from the wound, the priests buried him secretly without Cambyses' knowledge. Cambyses, the Egyptians say, immediately went completely mad—though they claim he had never been entirely sane. His first monstrous act was to kill his own brother Smerdis, born of the same father and mother. He had sent Smerdis back to Persia from Egypt out of jealousy, because Smerdis alone of all the Persians could draw the Ethiopian bow—pulling it about two finger-widths—which the Fish-eaters had brought back. After Smerdis returned to Persia, Cambyses had a dream in which a messenger arrived from Persia saying that Smerdis was sitting on the royal throne with his head touching the sky. Fearing his brother would kill him and seize power, Cambyses sent Prexaspes—his most trusted Persian—to Persia to murder Smerdis. Prexaspes went to Susa and killed him. Some say he took Smerdis hunting and killed him during the hunt. Others say he led him to the Red Sea and drowned him.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 428
paragraphs: They say this was the beginning of Cambyses' evil deeds. Next he killed his sister, who had accompanied him to Egypt and whom he had also married—she was his full sister, same father and same mother. He married her in the following way. Before that time, it had not been the Persian custom to marry sisters. Cambyses fell in love with one of his sisters and wanted to marry her. Since this was unprecedented, he summoned the royal judges and asked whether there was any law that permitted a man to marry his sister. The royal judges are specially chosen Persians who serve for life or until caught in some wrongdoing. They settle disputes and interpret ancestral customs. Their decision carries great weight. When Cambyses put his question to them, they gave an answer that was both cautious and truthful: they found no law permitting a brother to marry his sister, but they found another law stating that the king of Persia might do whatever he wished. So they did not violate the law out of fear of Cambyses, but in order to protect themselves they found a different law that supported the king's desire. Cambyses married the woman. Not long after, he married another sister as well. It was the younger of the two who accompanied him to Egypt and whom he killed.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 429
paragraphs: About her death, two stories are told. The Greeks say Cambyses matched a lion cub against a puppy. His wife was watching. When the puppy was being overpowered, another puppy—its brother—broke free from its chain and joined the fight. Together the two puppies beat the lion cub. Cambyses was pleased, but his wife, sitting beside him, wept. Cambyses asked why she was crying. She said watching the puppy defend its brother made her think of Smerdis—there was no one to defend him. The Greeks say Cambyses killed her for this remark. The Egyptians tell a different story. They say the two were sitting at dinner when the wife picked up a head of lettuce and stripped off the leaves. She asked her husband whether the lettuce looked better stripped or full. He said full. She replied: "Yet you have stripped the house of Cyrus just as I stripped this lettuce." He flew into a rage and kicked her. She was pregnant. She miscarried and died.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 430
paragraphs: These were the mad acts of Cambyses against his own family, whether driven mad by Apis or by some other cause, since many afflictions strike mortals. Cambyses is said to have had epilepsy from birth—a serious disease. It would not be strange if his mind was affected when his body was not sound.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 431
paragraphs: His acts of madness against other Persians were these. He said to Prexaspes—the man he honored above all, who carried his messages, and whose son served as Cambyses' cupbearer (also a high honor)—he reportedly said: "Prexaspes, what sort of man do the Persians think I am, and what do they say about me?" Prexaspes answered: "O king, they praise you highly in everything, but they do say you are too fond of wine." This report about what the Persians said enraged Cambyses. He replied: "So the Persians say I drink too much wine and have gone mad? Then their earlier words were false." (On a previous occasion, when Cambyses asked Croesus and the Persian counselors who was the greater man—he or his father Cyrus—they had answered that he was greater than Cyrus, since he held everything his father had possessed plus Egypt and command of the sea. But Croesus, dissatisfied with this answer, had said: "Son of Cyrus, I do not consider you equal to your father. For you do not yet have a son such as he left behind in you." Cambyses was pleased with this and praised Croesus' judgment.)

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 432
paragraphs: Remembering this conversation, Cambyses said angrily to Prexaspes: "Learn for yourself whether the Persians speak the truth or whether it is they who are mad when they say this. If I shoot at your son standing over there by the entrance and hit him right through the heart, the Persians will be proved liars. If I miss, then they are right and I am out of my senses." He drew his bow and shot the boy, who fell. Cambyses ordered the body cut open. When the arrow was found in the heart, he laughed with delight and said to the boy's father: "So you see, Prexaspes, that I am not mad—the Persians are. Now tell me: has any man in the world ever shot so true?" Prexaspes, seeing the man was deranged and fearing for his own life, answered: "O king, I think not even the god himself could have shot so well." That was one occasion. On another, for no reason at all, Cambyses arrested twelve Persians of the highest rank and buried them alive head-first.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 433
paragraphs: While he was doing these things, Croesus the Lydian thought it right to advise him: "O king, do not give way entirely to your youthful passions. Restrain yourself. Self-control is a good thing. Foresight is wisdom. You are killing your own countrymen for no reason. You are killing children. If you go on like this, beware that the Persians revolt. Your father Cyrus urged me repeatedly to advise you and suggest whatever I thought was best." This was friendly counsel. But Cambyses answered: "You dare advise me? You managed your own country so well! And you gave my father such good advice when you told him to cross the Araxes and attack the Massagetae—when they were willing to cross over to our side! You destroyed yourself by governing Lydia badly, and you destroyed Cyrus by persuading him to cross. But you will not get away with it. I have been looking for an excuse to deal with you." He snatched up his bow to shoot Croesus, but Croesus jumped up and ran out. Since Cambyses could not shoot him, he ordered his servants to catch and kill him. The servants, knowing Cambyses' temperament, hid Croesus. They calculated that if Cambyses later regretted it and asked for Croesus, they could produce him and receive a reward. If the king never regretted it and never asked, they could always kill him then. Not long afterward, Cambyses did want Croesus back. The servants told him the Lydian was alive. Cambyses said he was glad Croesus was alive—but the servants who had saved him would not go unpunished. He had them executed.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 434
paragraphs: Many such mad acts Cambyses committed against Persians and allies while staying in Memphis. He opened ancient tombs and examined the dead bodies. He also entered the temple of Hephaistos and mocked the god's statue. (The image of Hephaistos closely resembles the Phoenician Pataici—the figures Phoenicians carry on the prows of their warships. For anyone who has not seen these: it looks like a pygmy.) He also entered the temple of the Cabiri, which no one is allowed to enter except the priest. He burned the images after thoroughly mocking them. These images also resemble Hephaistos. They say the Cabiri are the sons of Hephaistos.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 435
paragraphs: It is clear to me from every piece of evidence that Cambyses was thoroughly insane. Otherwise he would never have mocked sacred rites and customs. If you asked all the peoples of the world to choose which customs are best, each would—after examining the options—choose its own. Everyone believes their own traditions are far superior. So it is natural that only a madman would make fun of such things. There is ample proof that all people hold this view. One example: when Darius was king, he summoned certain Greeks in his court and asked them what price would make them willing to eat their dead fathers. They said no amount of money could persuade them. Then Darius called in some Indians called Callatians, who do eat their parents. In the Greeks' presence, through an interpreter, he asked the Callatians what price would make them willing to burn their dead fathers. The Callatians cried out in horror and begged him not to say such blasphemous things. That is how firmly customs are held. And I think Pindar was right when he said: "Custom is king of all."

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 436
paragraphs: While Cambyses was campaigning in Egypt, the Spartans launched their own expedition against Samos and against Polycrates, son of Aeaces, who had seized power there. At first Polycrates had divided the state into three parts and shared rule with his brothers Pantagnotos and Syloson. But later he killed one brother, banished the younger one, Syloson, and held all Samos for himself. He made a guest-friendship pact with Amasis of Egypt, exchanging gifts. In a very short time, Polycrates' power grew rapidly. His fame spread throughout Ionia and the rest of Greece. Wherever he directed his forces, he was victorious. He had a hundred fifty-oared ships and a thousand archers. He plundered and raided everyone without distinction, saying he would please a friend more by giving back what he had taken than by never taking it in the first place. He captured many islands and many mainland cities. Among others, he defeated the Lesbians in a sea battle—they had come out in full force to help the Milesians—and captured them. The prisoners dug the entire moat around the walls of Samos in chains.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 437
paragraphs: Amasis was well aware that Polycrates was extremely lucky. This concerned him. When Polycrates' good fortune continued to grow, Amasis wrote him a letter: "Amasis says this to Polycrates. It is pleasant to hear of a friend's success. But your great good fortune does not please me, since I know the gods are jealous. For myself, I would prefer that I and those I care about succeed in some things and fail in others, living life with alternating fortune, rather than succeeding in everything. I have never heard of anyone who prospered in all things and did not end badly. Take my advice: think of what you value most, the thing whose loss would hurt your heart the most. Throw it away where it can never be found again. If after that your good fortune still does not alternate with setbacks, keep using the remedy I have prescribed."

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 438
paragraphs: Polycrates read the letter and thought Amasis gave good advice. He searched among his treasures for the one whose loss would grieve him most. He found it: a signet ring he wore, set with an emerald, the work of Theodoros of Samos. Having decided to throw this away, he manned a fifty-oared ship, went aboard, and ordered the crew to put out to sea. When they were far from the island, he took off the ring in full view of everyone and threw it into the sea. Then he sailed home and mourned his loss.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 439
paragraphs: Five or six days later, a fisherman caught a large, beautiful fish. He thought it deserved to be given as a present to Polycrates. He brought it to the palace door and asked to be admitted to Polycrates' presence. When this was granted, he offered the fish and said: "O king, when I caught this fish I did not think it right to take it to market, even though I live by my hands. It seemed worthy of you and your greatness. So I bring it as a gift." Polycrates, pleased with the speech, replied: "You have done very well, and I thank you twice—once for your words and once for the gift. I invite you to dinner." The fisherman went home, proud of the honor. When the servants cut open the fish, they found Polycrates' signet ring inside its belly. As soon as they saw it, they picked it up and brought it joyfully to Polycrates, telling him how it was found. Polycrates, struck by the realization that this was a divine sign, wrote down everything that had happened and sent the letter to Amasis in Egypt.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 440
paragraphs: Amasis read the letter and realized that it was impossible for one man to save another from the fate that was coming. Polycrates was destined to end badly, since he prospered in everything—even finding what he had thrown away. Amasis sent a herald to Samos to say that the guest-friendship between them was dissolved. He did this so that when a great and terrible disaster finally struck Polycrates, he would not be forced to grieve as he would for a friend.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 441
paragraphs: This was the Polycrates against whom the Spartans were making their expedition, invited by the Samians who later settled at Kydonia in Crete. Polycrates had secretly sent a message to Cambyses, who was preparing to march on Egypt, asking him to send a request for Samian troops. Cambyses gladly complied and sent to Samos requesting ships. Polycrates selected the citizens he most suspected of plotting against him, manned forty triremes with them, and sent them to Cambyses with instructions never to let these men return home.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 442
paragraphs: Some say these deported Samians never reached Egypt. When they got as far as Carpathos, they discussed the situation and decided not to sail any further. Others say they did reach Egypt, were put under guard, but escaped. As they sailed home, Polycrates engaged them with his fleet and won. But the returning exiles landed and fought him on shore. They were defeated in the land battle and then sailed to Sparta. Some say the returning force from Egypt actually defeated Polycrates, but I do not think this is correct. If they could beat Polycrates by themselves, they would have had no reason to invite the Spartans. Besides, a man who had so many hired mercenaries and native archers was unlikely to be beaten by a handful of returning Samians. Polycrates also shut his subjects' wives and children in the boat sheds, ready to burn them—sheds and all—if their menfolk went over to the returning exiles.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 443
paragraphs: When the Samians driven out by Polycrates reached Sparta, they appeared before the magistrates and made a long, urgent plea. At this first meeting, the officials replied that they had forgotten the beginning by the time the speech reached the end. At the second audience, the Samians came carrying a sack and simply said: "The sack needs flour." The officials said the word "sack" was unnecessary. But they resolved to help.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 444
paragraphs: The Spartans prepared a force and sailed against Samos. The Samians say it was to repay a debt, since the Samians had once helped Sparta with ships against the Messenians. But the Spartans say they did not go to help the Samians. They went to punish the Samians for stealing the mixing bowl they were sending to Croesus, and for stealing the corselet that Amasis had sent them as a gift. The Samians had seized the corselet the year before the bowl. It was made of linen, embroidered with many figures, and interwoven with gold and cotton threads. The most remarkable thing about it was that each thread, though thin, was made of three hundred and sixty visible strands. Its twin was the one Amasis dedicated to Athena at Lindos.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 445
paragraphs: The Corinthians also joined this expedition eagerly, because the Samians had wronged them as well. It happened a generation before this expedition, around the same time as the theft of the mixing bowl. Periander, son of Kypselos, had sent three hundred boys—sons of the leading men of Corcyra—to Alyattes at Sardis to be castrated. The Corinthians transporting the boys put in at Samos on the way. When the Samians learned why the boys were being taken to Sardis, they first taught the children to take sanctuary in the temple of Artemis. Then they refused to let anyone drag the suppliants from the temple. When the Corinthians tried to starve them out, the Samians invented a festival. Every night, while the children stayed in sanctuary, they organized choruses of young men and women who came carrying cakes of sesame and honey, so the Corcyrean boys could snatch food from them. This continued until the Corinthian guards gave up and left. The Samians then took the children back to Corcyra.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 446
paragraphs: If the Corinthians and Corcyreans had been on good terms after Periander's death, the Corinthians would not have joined the Samian expedition for this reason. But the two peoples had been enemies ever since the founding of the Corcyrean colony. The Corinthians held a grudge. Periander's motive for selecting the Corcyrean boys for castration was revenge, since the Corcyreans had first wronged him in a terrible way.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 447
paragraphs: After Periander killed his wife Melissa, a second misfortune struck him on top of the first. He had two sons by Melissa. One was seventeen, the other eighteen. Their mother's father, Procles, tyrant of Epidauros, invited them to stay with him and treated them kindly, as one would expect from a grandfather. When he sent them home, he said as they parted: "Boys, do you know who killed your mother?" The elder son paid no attention to this remark. But the younger, whose name was Lycophron, was so stricken by what he heard that when he reached Corinth he would not speak to his father—who was, after all, his mother's murderer. He would not talk to him or answer his questions. Finally, Periander grew furious and drove him from the house.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 448
paragraphs: After banishing the younger son, Periander questioned the elder about what their grandfather had said to them. The boy said Procles had received them warmly. But he did not remember the remark made at parting, since he had paid it no attention. Periander insisted that Procles must have said something and pressed him hard. The boy then remembered and told him. Periander, understanding and refusing to show any weakness, sent a message to the people who were sheltering the banished boy, forbidding them to take him in. Every time Lycophron was driven from one house, he was taken in by another—and driven from that one too when Periander threatened the hosts. Finally Periander issued a proclamation: anyone who sheltered Lycophron or even spoke to him would owe a fine to Apollo, in an amount he specified.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 449
paragraphs: After this proclamation, no one would take the boy in or talk to him. He himself did not even try, thinking it beneath him to beg. He wandered the porticos, sleeping rough. On the fourth day, Periander saw him—filthy and starving—and felt pity. He went to him and said: "My son, which is better—what you are suffering now, or inheriting my throne and all that I possess, if only you submit to your father? You are my son and prince of wealthy Corinth, yet you choose a vagrant's life, resisting and raging against the one person you should least oppose. If some misfortune occurred in our house that makes you suspicious of me, it fell on me too, and I bear it more than you, since I caused it. Now that you understand how much better it is to be envied than pitied, and what comes of being angry at your parents and those stronger than you—come home." Periander tried to win him over with these words. But the boy's only answer to his father was that Periander now owed the god a fine for speaking to him. Periander saw that the boy's stubbornness was hopeless and incurable. He sent him away by ship to Corcyra, which he also controlled. After sending him away, Periander made war on his father-in-law Procles, whom he held mainly responsible. He captured Epidauros and took Procles prisoner.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 450
paragraphs: As time went on and Periander was past his prime, he realized he could no longer manage the state by himself. He sent to Corcyra to summon Lycophron to take over the government. He passed over the elder son, who seemed slow-witted. Lycophron did not even dignify the messenger with a reply. Periander, who loved the young man dearly, sent his own daughter—Lycophron's sister—thinking she could persuade him. She came and said: "Brother, would you rather the tyranny fall to others and our father's wealth be plundered than come home and have them yourself? Come home. Stop punishing yourself. Pride is a dangerous possession. Do not cure one evil with another. Many people prefer what is fair to what is strictly just. Many have already lost their mother's estate while pursuing their father's rights. Tyranny is a slippery thing—many want it, and our father is old and past his prime. Do not hand what is yours to strangers." She used the most persuasive arguments her father had coached her with. But Lycophron answered that he would never come to Corinth as long as he knew his father was alive. She reported this. Periander sent a third time, through a herald, offering to move to Corcyra himself if Lycophron would return to Corinth and become tyrant. Lycophron agreed to these terms. Periander prepared to go to Corcyra, and Lycophron prepared to come to Corinth. But when the Corcyreans learned the whole story, they killed Lycophron to prevent Periander from coming to their island. That is why Periander took revenge on the Corcyreans.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 54
paragraphs: The Lacedaemonians arrived with a large force and began their siege of Samos. They attacked the wall and seized the tower that stands by the sea in the suburb of the city. But when Polycrates came up with a large body of men to relieve it, they were driven off. Meanwhile, at the upper tower on the ridge of the mountain, the foreign mercenaries and many of the Samians themselves came out to fight. They held their ground against the Lacedaemonians for a short while, then began to flee backwards, and the Lacedaemonians pursued and killed them.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 55
paragraphs: If all the Lacedaemonians present that day had been the equal of Archias and Lycopas, Samos would have been taken. For Archias and Lycopas alone rushed inside the wall together with the fleeing Samians, and being cut off from retreat were killed within the city of Samos. I myself spoke in Pitane—for that was the deme he belonged to—with the third in descent from this Archias: another Archias, son of Samios, son of Archias, who honoured the Samians above all other foreigners. He told me that his own father had been named Samios because Archias, his grandfather, had died a glorious death in Samos. And he said he honoured Samians because his grandfather had been granted a public funeral by them.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 56
paragraphs: When the Lacedaemonians had been besieging Samos for forty days and their operations were making no progress, they set out to return to the Peloponnese. There is a less credible story put about concerning these events: that Polycrates struck a quantity of a local coin in lead, gilded the coins over, and gave them to the Lacedaemonians, who accepted them and then set out to leave. This was the first expedition the Lacedaemonians—being Dorians—made into Asia.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 57
paragraphs: The Samians who had gone on the expedition against Polycrates also sailed away when the Lacedaemonians were about to abandon them, and came to Siphnos. They were short of money, and the Siphnians at that time were at the peak of their prosperity and had more wealth than any of the other islanders, since they had mines of gold and silver on their island. So rich were these mines that there is a treasury dedicated at Delphi from the tithe of their yield, furnished on a par with the wealthiest of those treasuries; and the people used to divide the yearly income from the mines among themselves. So when they were founding the treasury, they consulted the Oracle as to whether their present prosperity would last them a long time, and the Pythian prophetess gave them this reply:
“When in Siphnos the council-hall gleams white and the market-place is white of brow, then a wary man is needed to beware of an army of wood and a red-coloured herald.”
At that very time the market-place and the city hall of the Siphnians had been decorated with Parian marble.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 58
paragraphs: They could not understand this oracle either at the time or when the Samians arrived. For as soon as the Samians were putting in at Siphnos, they sent one of their ships bearing envoys to the city. In old times all ships were painted red, and this was what the Pythian prophetess had been foretelling to the Siphnians when she bade them beware of the “army of wood” and the “red-coloured herald.” The messengers came and asked the Siphnians to lend them ten talents. When they refused, the Samians began to ravage their lands. When the Siphnians heard of it, they came out at once to defend themselves, engaged in battle, and were defeated; many were cut off by the Samians and shut outside the city. The Samians then imposed on them a payment of a hundred talents.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 59
paragraphs: Then, by payment of money, they acquired from the men of Hermion the island of Hydrea, which lies near the coast of the Peloponnese, and they entrusted it to the Troezenians while they themselves settled at Kydonia in Crete. They had not sailed there for that purpose, but in order to drive the Zakynthians off the island. They remained there and prospered for five years—so much so that they were the builders of the temples now standing at Kydonia, including the house of Dictyna. In the sixth year, however, the Aeginetans together with the Cretans defeated them in a sea-battle and enslaved them. They cut off the prows of their ships, which were shaped like boars, and dedicated them in the temple of Athena on Aegina. The Aeginetans did this because they had a grudge against the Samians: for the Samians had first campaigned against Aegina in the reign of Amphicrates, and had inflicted much harm on the Aeginetans while suffering much harm in return. Such was the cause of this event.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 60
paragraphs: I have spoken at some length about the Samians because they have three works that are greater than any others ever constructed by Hellenes. First, a tunnel, open at both ends, dug through a mountain no less than one hundred and fifty fathoms high. The tunnel is seven furlongs long and eight feet high and wide, and throughout its whole length another channel has been cut twenty cubits deep and three feet wide, through which water is piped to the city from an abundant spring. The designer of this work was a Megarian, Eupalinos son of Naustrophos. That is one of the three. The second is a mole in the sea around the harbour, reaching down as much as twenty fathoms; its length is more than two furlongs. The third work they have accomplished is a temple larger than any other temple we know of. Its first designer was Rhoicos son of Philes, a native of Samos. For these reasons I have spoken at greater length of the Samians.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 61
paragraphs: Now while Cambyses son of Cyrus was spending a long time in Egypt and had gone out of his right mind, two brothers, Magians, rose up against him. One of them had been left behind by Cambyses as caretaker of his household. This man rose against him, realizing that the death of Smerdis was being kept secret, that only a few of the Persians knew of it, while the greater number believed without doubt that he was still alive. He therefore tried to seize the kingdom, and he formed his plan as follows. He had a brother—the one who, as I said, rose with him against Cambyses—and this man very closely resembled in appearance Smerdis son of Cyrus, whom Cambyses had killed, his own brother. He resembled Smerdis in form, and not only so, but he had the same name, Smerdis. Having persuaded this man that he would manage everything for him, the Magian Patizeithes brought him and seated him on the royal throne. Then he sent heralds to the various provinces, and among them one to the army in Egypt, to proclaim that from now on they were to obey Smerdis son of Cyrus instead of Cambyses.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 62
paragraphs: So the other heralds made this proclamation, and the one appointed to go to Egypt found Cambyses and his army at Agbatana in Syria. Standing in their midst, he began to proclaim what the Magian had commanded him. When Cambyses heard this from the herald, and supposed the herald was telling the truth and that he himself had been betrayed by Prexaspes—that is, that when Prexaspes had been sent to kill Smerdis he had not done so—Cambyses looked at Prexaspes and said: “Prexaspes, is this how you carried out the task I gave you?” Prexaspes replied: “Master, the story is not true that Smerdis your brother has risen against you, nor that you will have any dispute arising from him, great or small. For I myself, having done what you commanded, buried him with my own hands. If, therefore, the dead have risen to life again, then you may expect Astyages the Mede to rise against you too. But if things are as they were before, then there is no danger of any trouble springing up for you, at least from him. I think it would be best now for some men to pursue the herald and examine him, asking from whom he has come to proclaim to us that we are to obey Smerdis as king.”

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 63
paragraphs: When Prexaspes had spoken thus, Cambyses was pleased with his advice, and the herald was pursued at once and brought back. When he had returned, Prexaspes questioned him as follows: “Man, you say you have come as a messenger from Smerdis son of Cyrus. Now speak the truth and you may go in peace. I ask you: did Smerdis himself appear before your eyes and charge you to say this, or one of those who serve him?” He answered: “I have never yet seen Smerdis son of Cyrus, not since the day King Cambyses marched to Egypt. But the Magian whom Cambyses appointed as guardian of his household—he gave me this charge, saying that Smerdis son of Cyrus was the one who commanded me to say these things to you.” He spoke to them without adding any falsehood to his first statement, and Cambyses said: “Prexaspes, you have done what was commanded you like an honest man, and you have escaped blame. But which of the Persians can this be who has risen up against me and usurped the name of Smerdis?” Prexaspes replied: “I think, O king, I understand what has happened. The Magians have risen against you—namely Patizeithes, whom you left as caretaker of your household, and his brother Smerdis.”

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 64
paragraphs: Then Cambyses, when he heard the name Smerdis, at once grasped the true meaning of this report and of his dream. For in his sleep he had dreamed that someone reported to him that Smerdis was sitting on the royal throne with his head touching the heavens. Realizing that he had killed his brother without cause, he began to lament for Smerdis. And when he had lamented and grieved deeply over the whole disaster, he leapt onto his horse, intending to march his army as quickly as possible to Susa against the Magian. As he leapt onto the horse, the cap of his sword-sheath fell off, and the bare sword struck his thigh. Wounded in the same place where he had formerly struck Apis, the god of the Egyptians, and believing the blow to be mortal, Cambyses asked the name of the town. They said: “Agbatana.” Now even before this he had been told by the Oracle at the city of Buto that he would end his life in Agbatana. He had assumed he would die of old age in Agbatana in Media, his chief seat of power; but the oracle, it turned out, meant Agbatana in Syria. So when he now learned the name of the town by asking, and was struck with fear both by the disaster caused by the Magian and by the wound, he came to his senses. Understanding the meaning of the oracle, he said: “Here it is fated that Cambyses son of Cyrus shall end his life.”

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 65
paragraphs: That was all he said at the time. But about twenty days later he sent for the most distinguished of the Persians who were with him and spoke to them as follows: “Persians, I must now make known to you the thing I kept concealed beyond all others. While in Egypt I saw a vision in my sleep—would that I had never seen it. It seemed that a messenger came from home and reported to me that Smerdis was sitting on the royal throne and had touched the heavens with his head. Fearing I would be stripped of power by my brother, I acted quickly rather than wisely. For it seems no man can avert what is fated to happen. Fool that I was, I sent Prexaspes off to Susa to kill Smerdis. And once this great evil had been done, I lived in security, never considering the danger that some other man might one day rise up against me now that Smerdis had been removed. Missing the mark altogether of what was to happen, I both made myself the murderer of my brother—when there was no need—and have nonetheless been stripped of the kingdom. For it was Smerdis the Magian whom the divine power had foretold in the vision would rise up against me. So this deed has been done by me, and you must imagine that Smerdis son of Cyrus is no longer alive. In truth it is the Magians who are masters of your kingdom—the one I left as guardian of my household and his brother Smerdis. The man who above all others ought to have taken vengeance on my behalf for the dishonour I have suffered from the Magians has met an unholy death at the hands of his own nearest kin. And since he is no more, the next best thing I can do is to charge you, O Persians, with what I desire be done for me as I die.
