I lay this upon you, calling on the gods of the royal house to witness—on you, and most of all on those Achaemenids who are present here—that you do not allow the chief power to return to the Medes. If they have acquired it by craft, let them be deprived of it by craft in turn by you; if they have conquered it by force, then by force and a strong hand you must recover it. If you do this, may the earth bring forth her produce, and may your wives and your cattle be fruitful, while you remain free forever. But if you do not recover the power or attempt to recover it, I pray the opposite curses fall upon you, and moreover that every Persian meet an end to his life like the one that has come upon me.” As soon as Cambyses had finished speaking, he began to bewail and lament all his misfortunes.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 66
paragraphs: When the Persians saw that the king had begun to bewail himself, they tore the garments they wore and lamented without restraint. After this, when the bone had become diseased and the thigh had mortified, Cambyses son of Cyrus was carried off by the wound, having reigned in all seven years and five months, and being completely childless, with neither sons nor daughters. Meanwhile the Persians who were there scarcely believed that power was in the hands of the Magians. On the contrary, they were firmly convinced that Cambyses had said what he said about the death of Smerdis in order to deceive them—so that all the Persians would turn against Smerdis in war. So they were convinced that Smerdis son of Cyrus had been established as king. Prexaspes too strongly denied that he had killed Smerdis, since now that Cambyses was dead it was not safe for him to say he had destroyed the son of Cyrus with his own hand.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 67
paragraphs: So when Cambyses had ended his life, the Magian became king without any disturbance, usurping the place of his namesake Smerdis son of Cyrus. He reigned for the seven months still remaining for Cambyses to complete his eight years. During that time he performed acts of great benefit to all his subjects, so that after his death all the peoples in Asia—except the Persians themselves—mourned his loss. For the Magian sent messengers out to every nation he ruled, proclaiming exemption from military service and from tribute for three years.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 68
paragraphs: This proclamation, I say, he made as soon as he established himself on the throne. But in the eighth month his identity was discovered, and it came about in this way. There was a certain Otanes son of Pharnaspes, inferior to no Persian in birth or wealth. This Otanes was the first to suspect that the Magian was not Smerdis son of Cyrus but the person he really was, drawing his inference from these facts: that he never went out of the fortress, and that he did not summon any of the distinguished men among the Persians into his presence. Having formed this suspicion, he proceeded as follows. Cambyses had married Otanes' daughter, whose name was Phaidyme; and this same daughter the Magian was now keeping as his wife, living with her as with all the other wives of Cambyses. So Otanes sent a message to this daughter, asking who the man was beside whom she slept—whether Smerdis son of Cyrus or some other. She sent back word that she did not know, for she had never seen Smerdis son of Cyrus, nor did she know otherwise who the man was who lived with her. Otanes then sent a second time and said: “If you yourself do not know Smerdis son of Cyrus, then ask Atossa who this man is with whom both she and you live as wives. For she must surely know her own brother.”

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 69
paragraphs: To this his daughter replied: “I cannot speak with Atossa or see any of the other women who live here with me. For as soon as this man, whoever he is, succeeded to the kingdom, he separated us and placed us in different apartments by ourselves.” When Otanes heard this, the matter became clearer to him, and he sent another message in to her: “Daughter, it is right that you, nobly born as you are, should undertake whatever risk your father bids you take on. For if in truth this is not Smerdis son of Cyrus but the man I suppose, he ought not to escape with impunity for taking you to his bed or for holding the dominion of the Persians; he must pay the penalty. Now do as I say. When he sleeps beside you and you see he is soundly asleep, feel his ears. If he has ears, then believe you are living with Smerdis son of Cyrus; but if not, believe it is the Magian Smerdis.” Phaidyme sent back word that if she did this she would run a great risk. For if he happened not to have ears and she was caught feeling for them, she was quite sure he would put her to death. But nevertheless she would do it. So she undertook to do this for her father. Now as for this Magian Smerdis, his ears had been cut off by Cyrus son of Cambyses when he was king, for some grave offence. So Phaidyme, Otanes' daughter, carrying out everything she had undertaken for her father, when her turn came to go in to the Magian—for the wives of the Persians come in to them in regular turn—came and lay down beside him. When the Magian was in deep sleep, she felt his ears and perceived easily, not with difficulty, that her husband had no ears. As soon as it was day she sent word to her father of what had happened.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 70
paragraphs: Then Otanes took with him Aspathines and Gobryas, who were leading men among the Persians and his own most trusted friends, and told them the whole matter. They, as it then appeared, had suspicions themselves that this was so; and when Otanes laid the matter before them, they readily accepted his proposal. It was resolved among them that each should associate with himself the Persian he most trusted. So Otanes brought in Intaphrenes, Gobryas brought in Megabyzos, and Aspathines brought in Hydarnes. When they had thus become six, Darius son of Hystaspes arrived at Susa, coming from the land of Persia, of which his father was governor. Accordingly, when he came, the six Persians resolved to associate Darius with themselves as well.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 71
paragraphs: These seven, then, having come together, gave pledges of faith to one another and deliberated together. When it came Darius' turn to speak his mind, he addressed them as follows: “I thought I alone knew this—that it was the Magian who was reigning as king and that Smerdis son of Cyrus had ended his life. It is for this very reason that I have come with the earnest purpose of contriving the Magian's death. But since it turns out that you know of it as well, and not I alone, I think we should act at once and not put the matter off, for that is not the better way.” Otanes replied: “Son of Hystaspes, you are the scion of a noble stock, and you show yourself, it seems, in no way inferior to your father. But do not rush into this enterprise so thoughtlessly; take it up with more prudence. We must first grow more in number before undertaking the matter.” To this Darius answered: “Men here present, if you follow Otanes' way, know that you will perish miserably. For someone will carry word to the Magian, gaining some private advantage for himself. Your best course would have been to do this deed on your own risk alone. But since it seemed good to you to refer the matter to a greater number and you have told me of it, either we do the deed today, or be assured that if this present day passes, no other man shall forestall me as your accuser—I myself will tell these things to the Magian.”

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 72
paragraphs: To this Otanes, seeing Darius in violent haste, replied: “Since you compel us to hurry the matter and will not allow us to delay, come explain to us yourself how we shall enter the palace and lay hands on them. For there are guards set in various places, as you know probably as well as we do, if not by sight then by hearsay; how shall we pass through them?” Darius answered: “Otanes, there are many things that cannot be explained in words but only in deeds; and other things that can be explained in words but produce no famous deed. Know, however, that the guards that are set are not hard to pass. First, we being who we are, there is no one who will not let us by—partly out of respect for us, partly perhaps out of fear. And second, I myself have a very plausible pretext by which we may pass: I shall say I have just come from the land of Persia and wish to deliver a certain message to the king from my father. For where it is necessary for a lie to be told, let it be told—since both those who lie and those who always speak the truth are aiming at the same thing. Those lie whenever they are likely to gain something by convincing others with their lies; and these tell the truth in order to draw gain to themselves by the truth, and that things may be entrusted to them more readily. Thus, practising different ways, we all aim at the same goal. If, however, they were not likely to gain anything by it, the truth-teller would lie and the liar would tell the truth with equal indifference. So whichever of the door-keepers lets us pass of his own free will, for him it shall be the better afterwards. But whoever tries to oppose our passage, let him then and there be marked as our enemy; and after that let us push inside and set about our work.”

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 73
paragraphs: Then Gobryas said: “Friends, when will there be a better opportunity for us either to recover our rule—or, if we cannot get it back, to die? We who are Persians lie under the rule of a Mede, a Magian, and one whose ears have been cut off. All of you who stood beside Cambyses when he was sick surely remember what he laid upon the Persians as he was ending his life, if they should not attempt to win back the power. We did not accept it then, but supposed Cambyses had spoken only to deceive us. Now, therefore, I give my vote that we follow Darius' opinion, and that we do not depart from this assembly to go anywhere else but straight to attack the Magian.” So Gobryas spoke, and they all approved the proposal.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 74
paragraphs: Now while these were taking counsel together, by coincidence the following was happening. The Magians, taking counsel together, had resolved to join Prexaspes with themselves as a friend. They wished this both because he had suffered grievous wrong from Cambyses, who had killed his son with an arrow, and because he alone knew for certain of the death of Smerdis son of Cyrus, having killed him with his own hands; and finally because Prexaspes had great standing among the Persians. For these reasons they summoned him and tried to win him as their friend, binding him with pledge and oath that he would keep to himself and not reveal to any man the deception they had practised on the Persians, promising to give him countless rewards in return. After Prexaspes had agreed to this, the Magians, having persuaded him so far, proposed a second thing. They would summon all the Persians to come up to the wall of the palace, and they bade him go up on a tower and address them, declaring that they lived under the rule of Smerdis son of Cyrus and no other. They enjoined this because they believed he had the greatest credit among the Persians, and because he had frequently asserted that Smerdis son of Cyrus was still alive and had denied that he had killed him.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 75
paragraphs: When Prexaspes said he was ready to do this as well, the Magians summoned the Persians, had him go up on a tower, and bade him address them. Then he chose to forget what they had asked of him. Beginning with Achaemenes, he traced the descent of Cyrus on the father's side, and then, when he came down to Cyrus, at last he recounted what great benefits he had conferred on the Persians. Having gone through this recital, he went on to declare the truth: he said that previously he had kept it secret, since it had not been safe for him to tell what had been done, but at the present moment he was compelled to make it known. He went on to say how he had himself killed Smerdis son of Cyrus, forced to do so by Cambyses, and that it was the Magians who were now ruling. Then he called down many curses on the Persians if they did not win back the power and take vengeance on the Magians, and with that he let himself fall headlong from the tower. Thus Prexaspes ended his life, having been throughout his career a man of repute.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 76
paragraphs: Now the seven Persians, having resolved to lay hands at once on the Magians and not delay, made prayer to the gods and set out, knowing nothing of what had happened with Prexaspes. As they were on their way and halfway along their course, they heard what had happened with Prexaspes. At that they withdrew out of the way and considered among themselves again. Otanes and his supporters strongly urged that they delay and not set to work while things were in such an uproar, while Darius and his party urged that they go at once and carry out what had been resolved, without delay. While they were disputing, there appeared seven pairs of hawks pursuing two pairs of vultures, plucking out their feathers and tearing them. Seeing this, all seven approved Darius' opinion, and thereupon went to the royal palace, encouraged by the sight of the birds.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 77
paragraphs: When they appeared at the gates, things happened nearly as Darius had supposed. The guards, showing respect for men who were the chief among the Persians, and not suspecting anything of what was afoot, allowed them to pass inside under divine guidance, and no one asked them any question. When they had passed into the court, they met the eunuchs who carried messages in to the king. These inquired of them why they had come, and at the same time threatened the gate-keepers with punishment for having let them pass, and tried to stop the seven when they attempted to go further. Then the seven gave the word to one another, drew their daggers, and stabbed on the spot the men who tried to stop them; and they themselves ran on towards the men's chamber.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 78
paragraphs: Now the two Magians happened both of them to be there within, consulting about what Prexaspes had done. When they saw the eunuchs being attacked and crying aloud, they both ran back; and seeing what was happening, they turned to defend themselves. One of them got hold of his bow and arrows before being attacked; the other reached for his spear. Then they engaged in combat. The one who had taken up his bow and arrows found them of no use, since his enemies were close at hand and pressing hard; but the other defended himself with his spear and first struck Aspathines in the thigh, then Intaphrenes in the eye. Intaphrenes lost his eye from the wound, but not his life. So these two were wounded by one of the Magians. The other, when his bow and arrows proved useless, fled into a bedchamber opening off the men's chamber, intending to close the door; and with him two of the seven rushed in—Darius and Gobryas. When Gobryas was locked in combat with the Magian, Darius stood by at a loss what to do, because it was dark and he was afraid of striking Gobryas. Seeing him standing by idle, Gobryas asked why he did not use his hands, and Darius said: “Because I am afraid I may strike you.” Gobryas answered: “Thrust with your sword, even though it stab through us both.” So Darius was persuaded, thrust with his dagger, and happened to hit the Magian.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 79
paragraphs: So when they had killed the Magians and cut off their heads, they left behind those of their number who were wounded, both because these were unable to go and to take charge of the fortress. The other five, taking the heads of the Magians with them, ran with shouting and the clashing of arms and called on the other Persians to join them, telling what had been done and showing the heads. At the same time they killed every Magian who crossed their path. When the Persians heard what the seven had brought about and of the Magians' deception, they too decided to do the same, and drawing their daggers they killed every Magian they found. Had night not come on and stopped them, they would not have left a single Magian alive. This day the Persians celebrate in common more than any other day, and on it they keep a great festival which they call the Festival of the Slaughter of the Magians. On this day no Magian is permitted to appear out of doors, and the Magians keep themselves within their houses throughout that day.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 80
paragraphs: When the commotion had subsided and more than five days had passed, those who had risen against the Magians began to take counsel about the state in general. Speeches were made which some of the Hellenes do not believe were really spoken, but spoken they were nonetheless. Otanes urged that they should hand over the government to the whole body of the Persians, and his words were as follows: “In my view, no one of us should henceforth be sole ruler, for that is neither pleasant nor profitable. You saw how far the insolence of Cambyses went, and you have had a taste of the insolence of the Magian as well. How can the rule of one man be a well-ordered thing when the monarch may do whatever he desires without rendering any account of his acts? Even the best of men, if placed in such a position, would be driven by it to change his usual disposition. For insolence is bred in him by the good things he possesses, and envy is rooted in man from the beginning; and having these two, he has every vice. He commits many reckless wrongs, partly out of the insolence that comes with satiety, partly out of envy. And yet a despot at least ought to be free from envy, since he already has every sort of good thing. But his nature is just the opposite towards his subjects: he resents it that the nobles should survive and live, and delights in the basest of the citizens, and is more ready than any other man to listen to slanders. Worst of all, he is utterly inconsistent. If you admire him in moderation, he is offended that you pay him no great court; if you pay court extravagantly, he is offended with you for being a flatterer. And the most important thing is this: he disturbs the customs handed down by our fathers, he violates women, and he puts men to death without trial. The rule of many, on the other hand, has first the name that is the fairest of all—namely ‘Equality.' Second, the people do none of the things a monarch does: public offices are assigned by lot, the magistrates are compelled to render account of their actions, and all matters of deliberation are referred to the public assembly. I therefore give as my opinion that we let monarchy go and increase the power of the multitude. For in the many lies everything.”

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 81
paragraphs: This was the opinion Otanes expressed. But Megabyzos urged that they entrust matters to the rule of a few, saying: “What Otanes said against tyranny, let it be counted as said for me too. But in urging that we hand power to the multitude, he has missed the best counsel. For nothing is more senseless or insolent than a worthless crowd; and for men fleeing the insolence of a despot to fall into the insolence of an unrestrained populace is in no way to be borne. The despot, when he acts, acts knowing what he does, but the people do not even know. For how can they know—they who have neither been taught anything noble by others nor perceived anything of themselves—but push on matters with violent impulse and no understanding, like a raging torrent? Let those who are enemies of the Persians adopt democracy. But let us choose a company of the best men and attach the chief power to them; for among them we ourselves shall be counted, and it is likely that decisions taken by the best men will be the best.”

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 82
paragraphs: This was the opinion Megabyzos expressed. And third, Darius proceeded to give his opinion: “In what Megabyzos said about the multitude, it seems to me he spoke rightly, but in what he said about the rule of a few, not rightly. For there are three forms before us, and each supposed to be the best in its own kind—good popular government, rule of a few, and rule of one—and I say that this last is by far superior to the others. For nothing better can be found than the rule of an individual man of the best kind. Using the best judgment, he would be an irreproachable guardian of the multitude; and decisions against enemies would best be kept secret. In an oligarchy, on the other hand, it often happens that many, while practising virtue for the commonwealth, develop strong private enmities among themselves. For as each man desires to be leader himself and to prevail in counsel, they come to great enmities with one another, from which arise factions; out of the factions come bloodshed; and from bloodshed the rule of one man. Thus this very case shows by how much rule of one is the best. Again, when the people rule, it is impossible that corruption should not arise; and when corruption arises in the commonwealth, among the corrupt men there arise not enmities but strong bonds of friendship. For those acting corruptly to the injury of the commonwealth conspire secretly with one another. This continues until at last someone takes the leadership of the people and stops the course of such men. By this very act he is admired by the people, and being admired, he suddenly emerges as monarch. Thus he too furnishes an example that rule of one is the best thing. To sum it all up in one word: from where did the liberty we possess arise, and who gave it to us? Was it a gift of the people, or of an oligarchy, or of a monarch? I therefore hold the opinion that we, having been set free by one man, should preserve that form of rule; and in other respects also we should not overturn the customs of our fathers, which are well ordered, for that is not the better way.”

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 83
paragraphs: These three opinions had been proposed, and the other four men of the seven assented to the last. So when Otanes, who had wanted to give equality to the Persians, found his opinion defeated, he said to the assembled company: “Comrades, it is clear that one of us must become king, selected either by casting lots, or by entrusting the decision to the multitude of the Persians and taking whomever they choose, or by some other means. I shall not be a competitor with you, for I do not wish either to rule or to be ruled. On this condition I withdraw my claim to rule: that I shall not be ruled by any of you—neither I myself nor my descendants in time to come.” When he had said this, the six made an agreement with him on those terms, and he was no longer a competitor but withdrew from the assembly. Down to the present day this house alone of all the Persian houses remains free, and submits to rule only so far as it wills, not transgressing the laws of the Persians.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 84
paragraphs: The rest of the seven, however, continued to deliberate how they might set up a king in the most just manner. They resolved that, to Otanes and his descendants in succession, if the kingdom should come to any other of the seven, there should be given as special gifts a Median dress each year and all those presents that are reckoned among the Persians the most valuable. They determined to give him these things because he had been the first to propose the matter and had brought them together. These were the special gifts for Otanes. For all in common they also determined this: that any one of the seven who wished might enter the royal palace without being announced, unless the king happened to be sleeping with his wife; and that the king should not be permitted to marry into any other family, but only from those of the men who had revolted with him. Concerning the kingship itself they determined this: that whichever man's horse first neighed at sunrise in the suburb of the city while they were mounted, he should have the kingdom.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 85
paragraphs: Now Darius had a clever groom whose name was Oibares. To this man, after they had left their assembly, Darius said: “Oibares, we have resolved about the kingship as follows: that the man whose horse neighs first at sunrise, when we are mounted, shall be king. So if you have any cleverness, contrive that we may win this prize, and no one else.” Oibares replied: “My master, if it truly depends on this whether you be king or not, take heart on this score and keep your courage high, for no other shall be king before you—such are the charms I have at my command.” Then Darius said: “If you have any such trick, now is the time to devise it and not to put it off, for our contest is tomorrow.” Oibares, hearing this, did as follows. As night was falling, he took one of the mares—the one which Darius' horse most preferred—and led her into the suburb of the city and tied her up. Then he brought up Darius' horse, led him around her for some time—bringing him so close that he touched the mare—and finally let the horse mount her.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 86
paragraphs: At dawn the six came to the place as they had agreed, mounted on their horses. As they rode through the suburb of the city, when they came near the place where the mare had been tied up the night before, Darius' horse ran up to the spot and neighed. And just as the horse did this, there came lightning and thunder out of a clear sky. The occurrence of these signs to Darius sealed his claim, for they seemed to have happened by some divine design, and the others leapt down from their horses and did obeisance to Darius.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 87
paragraphs: Some say this was the contrivance of Oibares, but others say as follows—for the Persians tell the story both ways—that he touched the private parts of this mare with his hands and kept his hand hidden in his trousers; and when at sunrise the horses were about to be let go, this Oibares pulled out his hand and applied it to the nostrils of Darius' horse, and the horse, catching the smell, snorted and neighed.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 88
paragraphs: So Darius son of Hystaspes had been declared king, and throughout Asia all but the Arabians were his subjects, having been subdued first by Cyrus and then again by Cambyses. The Arabians, however, never submitted to the Persians as subjects, but had become guest-friends when they let Cambyses pass through to Egypt—for without the Arabians' consent, the Persians could not have invaded Egypt. Darius made the most noble marriages possible in the estimation of the Persians. He married two daughters of Cyrus: Atossa and Artystone. Atossa had previously been the wife of Cambyses her brother, and then of the Magian; Artystone was a virgin. Besides them he married the daughter of Smerdis son of Cyrus, whose name was Parmys; and he also took to wife the daughter of Otanes, the man who had exposed the Magian. Everything became filled with his power. And first he had a carving in stone made and set up, showing a man on horseback, and he wrote on it an inscription to this effect: “Darius son of Hystaspes, by the excellence of his horse,”—naming it—“and of his groom Oibares, obtained the kingdom of the Persians.”

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 89
paragraphs: Having so done in Persia, he established twenty provinces, which the Persians themselves call satrapies. Having set up the provinces and appointed rulers over them, he assigned tribute to be paid to him from them according to peoples, joining also to the chief peoples those who dwelt on their borders—or, passing beyond the immediate neighbours, assigning to various peoples those that lay more distant. He arranged the provinces and the yearly payment of tribute as follows: those who brought in silver were required to pay by the Babylonian talent, while those who brought in gold were to pay by the Euboïc talent. The Babylonian talent is equal to seventy-eight Euboïc pounds. For in the reigns of Cyrus and Cambyses, nothing had been fixed about tribute, but they used to bring gifts. Because of this assessment of tribute and other such measures, the Persians say that Darius was a shopkeeper, Cambyses a master, and Cyrus a father—the one because he handled all his affairs like a shopkeeper, the second because he was harsh and had little regard for anyone, and the third because he was gentle and arranged all things well for them.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 90
paragraphs: From the Ionians, the Magnesians of Asia, the Aiolians, Carians, Lykians, Milyans, and Pamphylians—for he appointed a single sum of tribute for all of these—there came in four hundred talents of silver. This was appointed the first division. From the Mysians, Lydians, Lasonians, Cabalians, and Hytennians there came in five hundred talents: this is the second division. From the Hellespontians who dwell on the right as one sails in, the Phrygians, the Thracians who dwell in Asia, the Paphlagonians, Mariandynoi, and Syrians, the tribute was three hundred and sixty talents: this is the third division. From the Cilicians, besides three hundred and sixty white horses—one for every day in the year—there came also five hundred talents of silver, of which one hundred and forty talents were spent on the cavalry guarding the Cilician land, while the remaining three hundred and sixty came in every year to Darius: this is the fourth division.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 91
paragraphs: From the division that begins at the city of Posideion—founded by Amphilochos son of Amphiaraos on the borders of the Cilicians and Syrians—and extends as far as Egypt, not including the territory of the Arabians (for this was exempt from payment), the amount was three hundred and fifty talents. This division comprises all of Phoenicia, Syria called Palestine, and Cyprus: this is the fifth division. From Egypt and the Libyans bordering on Egypt, and from Cyrene and Barca—these were ordered to belong to the Egyptian division—there came in seven hundred talents, not counting the money produced from the fish of Lake Moeris. Not counting this, I say, nor the grain contributed in addition by measure, seven hundred talents came in. As for the grain, they contribute by measure one hundred and twenty thousand bushels for the use of the Persians garrisoned at the “White Fortress” at Memphis and for their foreign mercenaries: this is the sixth division. The Sattagydai, Gandarians, Dadicans, and Aparytai, joined together, brought in one hundred and seventy talents: this is the seventh division. From Susa and the rest of the land of the Kissians came in three hundred: this is the eighth division.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 92
paragraphs: From Babylon and the rest of Assyria there came in a thousand talents of silver and five hundred boys for eunuchs: this is the ninth division. From Agbatana, the rest of Media, the Paricanians, and Orthocorybantians, four hundred and fifty talents: this is the tenth division. The Caspians, Pausicans, Pantimathoi, and Dareitai, contributing together, brought in two hundred talents: this is the eleventh division. From the Bactrians as far as the Aigloi the tribute was three hundred and sixty talents: this is the twelfth division.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 93
paragraphs: From Pactyïke, the Armenians, and the peoples bordering on them as far as the Euxine, four hundred talents: this is the thirteenth division. From the Sagartians, Sarangians, Thamanaians, Utians, Mycans, and those dwelling in the islands of the Erythraian Sea—where the king settles those called the “Removed”—from all these together a tribute of six hundred talents was produced: this is the fourteenth division. The Sacans and Caspians brought in two hundred and fifty talents: this is the fifteenth division. The Parthians, Chorasmians, Sogdians, and Areians: three hundred talents: this is the sixteenth division.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 94
paragraphs: The Paricanians and the Ethiopians in Asia brought in four hundred talents: this is the seventeenth division. To the Matienians, Saspeirians, and Alarodians a tribute of two hundred talents was assigned: this is the eighteenth division. To the Moschoi, Tibarenians, Macronians, Mossynoicoi, and Mares three hundred talents were ordered: this is the nineteenth division. The Indians are far more numerous than any other race of men we know, and they brought in a tribute larger than all the rest: three hundred and sixty talents of gold-dust. This is the twentieth division.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 95
paragraphs: Now if we compare Babylonian talents with Euboïc talents, the silver amounts to nine thousand eight hundred and eighty talents; and if we reckon gold at thirteen times the value of silver, weight for weight, the gold-dust amounts to four thousand six hundred and eighty Euboïc talents. When all these are added together, the total collected as yearly tribute for Darius amounts to fourteen thousand five hundred and sixty Euboïc talents. Sums less than these I pass over and do not mention.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 96
paragraphs: This was the tribute that came in to Darius from Asia and from a small part of Libya. But as time went on, other tribute came in as well from the islands and from those who dwell in Europe as far as Thessaly. The king stores this tribute in his treasury in the following way: he melts the metal down and pours it into earthenware jars; and when the jar is full, he breaks off the earthen jar from the metal. When he needs money, he cuts off as much as he requires on each occasion.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 97
paragraphs: These were the provinces and the assessments of tribute. I have not mentioned the Persian land as paying a contribution, for the Persians have their land to dwell in free from payment. The following peoples had no tribute fixed for them to pay but brought gifts instead: the Ethiopians bordering Egypt, whom Cambyses subdued when he marched against the Long-lived Ethiopians—those who dwell about Nysa, which is called “sacred,” and who celebrate festivals in honour of Dionysos. These Ethiopians and those who dwell near them use the same kind of seed as the Callantian Indians, and they have underground dwellings. The two peoples together brought every other year—and continue to bring down to my own time—two quart measures of unrefined gold, two hundred blocks of ebony, five Ethiopian boys, and twenty large elephant tusks. The Colchians too had placed themselves among those who brought gifts, along with their neighbours as far as the range of the Caucasus (for the Persian rule extends as far as those mountains, but those dwelling beyond Caucasus toward the North Wind regard the Persians no longer). These, I say, continued to bring, every four years, the gifts they had fixed for themselves, even down to my own day—namely a hundred boys and a hundred girls. Finally, the Arabians brought a thousand talents of frankincense every year. Such were the gifts these peoples brought to the king, apart from tribute.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 98
paragraphs: Now this great quantity of gold, from which the Indians bring in to the king the gold-dust that has been mentioned, they obtain in a manner I shall now describe. The part of the Indian land that lies towards the rising sun is sand. Of all the peoples in Asia we know or have any certain report of, the Indians dwell farthest towards the East and the sunrise, since the country east of the Indians is desert because of the sand. Now there are many tribes of Indians, and they do not all share a language. Some are pastoral, others not; some dwell in the swamps of the river and live on raw fish, which they catch by fishing from boats made of cane—each boat made from a single joint of cane. These Indians wear clothing made of rushes: they gather and cut the rushes from the river, weave them into a kind of mat, and put it on like a corslet.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 99
paragraphs: Other Indians, dwelling to the east of these, are pastoral and eat raw flesh. They are called Padaians, and they practise the following customs. Whenever any of their tribe falls ill, whether a woman or a man, if a man, his closest companions put him to death, saying that he is wasting away with disease and his flesh is being spoiled for them. Meanwhile he stoutly denies it and says he is not ill, but they do not agree with him; and after they have killed him they feast upon his flesh. If a woman falls ill, the women who are her closest friends treat her the same way as the men do in the other case. Indeed, even when a man reaches old age, they kill him and feast upon him; but very few of them reach old age, for they kill everyone who falls sick before he grows old.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 100
paragraphs: Other Indians, by contrast, have a manner of life as follows. They kill no living creature, they sow no crops, and it is not their custom to possess houses. They feed on herbs, and they have a grain the size of millet, in a husk, which grows of itself from the ground; this they gather and boil together with the husk, and make it their food. Whenever any of them falls sick, he goes out into the desert country and lies there, and none of them pays any attention either to the dead or to the sick.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 101
paragraphs: The sexual intercourse of all these Indians of whom I have spoken is carried on openly, like that of cattle, and they have all one colour of skin, resembling that of the Ethiopians. Moreover the seed they emit is not white, like that of other races, but black, like their skin; and the Ethiopians are similar in this respect. These tribes of Indians dwell further off than Persian power extends, toward the south wind, and they never became subjects of Darius.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 102
paragraphs: Others of the Indians are on the borders of the city of Caspatyros and the country of Pactyïke, dwelling to the north of the other Indians. Their manner of life is nearly the same as that of the Bactrians. These are the most warlike of the Indians, and it is they who make the expeditions for gold. For in the parts where they live the land is desert, on account of the sand; and in this desert and sandy tract ants are produced, smaller in size than dogs but larger than foxes. In fact some of them, caught here, are kept at the residence of the king of Persia. These ants build their dwellings underground and carry up the sand in the same manner as the ants in the land of the Hellenes, which they much resemble in form; and the sand they bring up contains gold. To obtain this sand the Indians make expeditions into the desert, each man having yoked together three camels—a female in the middle, with a male like a trace-horse to draw on each side. On the female he himself rides, having taken care that she be one taken for yoking from her young—the more recently born the better. For their female camels are not inferior to horses in speed, and they can carry much greater weights besides.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 103
paragraphs: As for the form of the camel, I shall not describe it here, since the Hellenes for whom I write are already familiar with it. But I will tell what is not commonly known: the camel has in its hind legs four thighs and four knees, and its organs of generation are between the hind legs, turned towards the tail.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 104
paragraphs: The Indians, I say, ride out to get the gold in the manner and with the kind of yoking I have described, timing it so they will be carrying off the gold at the hour of greatest heat—for the heat causes the ants to disappear underground. Now among these peoples the sun is hottest in the morning, not at midday as with others, but from sunrise to the time of closing the market; and during this time it produces far greater heat than at midday in Hellas, so that it is said they drench themselves in water then. Midday has roughly the same degree of heat for the Indians as for other men, while after midday their sun becomes like the morning sun of other men, and after that, as it moves further away, it produces still greater coolness, until at last at sunset it makes the air very cool indeed.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 105
paragraphs: When the Indians have arrived at the place with their bags, they fill them with sand and ride back as quickly as they can. For immediately the ants, as the Persians allege, perceive them by smell and begin to pursue; and this creature, they say, is swifter than any other, so that unless the Indians got a head start while the ants were gathering together, not one of them would escape. The male camels, being inferior in speed to the females, if they fall behind are even released from the female's side, one after another; but the females, remembering the young they left behind, show no slackness in their course. This is how the Indians obtain most of their gold, as the Persians say. There is, however, other gold in their land obtained by digging, but in smaller quantities.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 106
paragraphs: It seems that the extremities of the inhabited world have had the fairest things allotted to them by nature, just as it was the lot of Hellas to have its seasons tempered far more finely than other lands. For first, India is the most distant of inhabited lands towards the East, as I have said a little above; and in this land not only the animals, both birds and four-footed beasts, are much larger than in other places (except the horses, which are surpassed by the Median breed called Nessaian), but also gold is abundant there—some obtained by digging, some brought down by rivers, and some carried off as I have just described. And there the trees that grow wild produce wool that surpasses in beauty and quality that from sheep; and the Indians wear clothing obtained from these trees.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 107
paragraphs: Arabia is the furthest of inhabited lands in the direction of midday, and in it alone of all lands grow frankincense, myrrh, cassia, cinnamon, and gum-mastich. All of these except myrrh are difficult for the Arabians to obtain. Frankincense they collect by burning storax, which is brought to the Hellenes by the Phoenicians. By burning this, to produce smoke, they take the frankincense; for the trees that produce frankincense are guarded by winged serpents, small in size and of various colours, which keep watch in great numbers about each tree—of the same kind as those that attempt to invade Egypt—and they cannot be driven away from the trees by anything except the smoke of storax.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 108
paragraphs: The Arabians say that by this time all the world would have been filled with these serpents, if the same thing did not happen to them as I know happens to vipers. And it seems that Divine Providence, being wise—as was to be expected—has made all those animals prolific that are cowardly in spirit and good for food, so that they may not all be eaten up and their race fail, while those that are bold and harmful have small progeny. For example, because the hare is hunted by every beast and bird, as well as by man, it is extremely prolific. It is the only one of all beasts that becomes pregnant again before the first young are born, and carries in its womb some young already covered with fur and others still bare; while one is being shaped in the matrix, another is being conceived. That is how it is in this case. The lioness, on the other hand, the strongest and most courageous of creatures, produces only one cub, once in her life; for when she gives birth she casts out her womb together with her young. The cause is this: when the cub, while still in the mother, begins to move, having claws far sharper than any other beast he tears the womb, and as he grows larger he scratches ever more deeply. At last the time of birth approaches and there is no sound portion of it left.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 109
paragraphs: In just the same way, if vipers and the winged serpents of the Arabians were produced in the ordinary course of their nature, man would not be able to live upon the earth. But as it is, when they couple, and the male is in the act of generation—when he lets go his seed—the female seizes his neck, and fastening on it does not relax her hold until she has eaten through it. The male then dies in the manner I have described, while the female pays the penalty for the male in this way: the young, while still in the womb, take vengeance for their father by eating through their mother, and having eaten through her belly they make their way out for themselves. Other serpents, which are not harmful to man, produce eggs and hatch from them a very large number of offspring. Vipers are distributed over all the earth; but the winged ones are found in great numbers only in Arabia and nowhere else. That is why they appear so numerous.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 110
paragraphs: So frankincense is obtained in this way by the Arabians. Cassia they obtain as follows. They wrap cows'-hides and other kinds of skins around their whole body and face, leaving only their eyes exposed, and then go to gather cassia. This grows in a pool not very deep, around which and in which lodge, it seems, winged creatures much resembling bats, which squeak horribly and are fierce in fight. These they must keep away from their eyes while cutting the cassia.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 111
paragraphs: Cinnamon they gather in a still more marvellous way. Where it grows and what land produces it they cannot say, except that some claim—and it is a plausible account—that it grows in the regions where Dionysos was raised. They say that large birds carry those dried sticks which, from the Phoenicians, we have learned to call cinnamon; they carry them, I say, to nests made of clay plastered on sheer mountain cliffs that no man can climb. With regard to this the Arabians devise the following trick. They cut up the limbs of oxen and asses that have died, and of their other pack animals, into pieces as large as convenient, and carry them to these places; having laid them down not far from the nests, they withdraw to a distance. The birds fly down and carry the limbs of the pack animals off to their nests. But the nests are not able to bear the weight, so they break and fall to the ground; and the men come up and collect the cinnamon. Thus cinnamon is gathered, and comes from this nation to the rest of the world.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 112
paragraphs: Gum-mastich, which the Arabians call ladanon, comes in a still more extraordinary way. Though it is the most sweet-scented of all things, it is found in the most evil-scented thing, for it is found in the beards of he-goats, produced there like resin from wood. It is useful in making many perfumes, and the Arabians use it as incense more than anything else.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 113
paragraphs: Let this suffice for what we have to say about spices. From the land of Arabia there blows a scent of them wonderfully sweet. They also have two kinds of sheep worthy of admiration, not found in any other land. The one kind has a tail so long—no less than three cubits—that if they were allowed to drag it behind them, they would develop sores from the tails being worn against the ground. But as it is, every shepherd knows enough carpentry to make little carts, which they tie under the tails, fastening the tail of each animal to its own separate cart. The other kind of sheep has a broad tail, as much as a cubit in breadth.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 114
paragraphs: As one passes beyond the region of midday, the Ethiopian land extends furthest of all inhabited lands towards the sunset. It produces gold in abundance, huge elephants, all kinds of wild trees, and ebony; and men who are the tallest, the most beautiful, and the longest-lived of all men.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 115
paragraphs: These, then, are the extremities in Asia and Libya. But as to the extremities of Europe towards the West, I am not able to speak with certainty. I do not accept the tale that there is a river called Eridanos in barbarian speech, flowing into the sea that lies towards the north wind, from which amber is said to come; nor do I know of any real existence of “Tin Islands” from which tin comes to us. For first, the name Eridanos itself is Hellenic and not barbarian, and was invented by some poet; and second, though I took pains to discover it, I have not been able to hear from any eyewitness that there is a sea on the other side of Europe. However that may be, tin and amber certainly do come to us from the extremity of Europe.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 116
paragraphs: Again, towards the north of Europe there is evidently a far greater quantity of gold than in any other land. How it is obtained here again I cannot say for certain, but it is said to be stolen from griffins by the Arimaspians, a one-eyed race of men. I do not believe this tale either—that nature produces one-eyed men who in every other respect are like other men. However, it would seem that the extremities that bound the rest of the world on every side and enclose it in their midst possess the things we regard as the most beautiful and the most rare.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 117
paragraphs: There is a plain in Asia bounded by mountains on every side, and through the mountains there are five clefts. This plain once belonged to the Chorasmians and lies on the borders of the Chorasmians themselves, the Hyrcanians, Parthians, Sarangians, and Thamanaians; but ever since the Persians came to rule, it has belonged to the king. From this encircling mountain range of which I speak flows a great river called the Akes. In former times this river, divided into five streams and conducted through a separate cleft in the mountains to each separate nation, used to water the lands of the peoples just mentioned. But since they have come under the Persians, they have suffered as follows. The king has built up the clefts in the mountains and set gates at each cleft. Now that the water has been cut off from its outlet, the plain within the mountains has become a sea, because the river runs into it and has no outlet anywhere. Those, therefore, who in former times had depended on the water can no longer use it and are in great distress. For during winter they have rain from heaven like everyone else, but in summer they need the water when they sow millet and sesame seed. So when the water is not granted them, they come to the Persians together with their wives, and standing at the gates of the king's court they cry and howl; and the king orders that, for those who need it most, the gates leading to their land be opened. Then when their land has been satisfied with the water, these gates are closed again, and he orders the gates to be opened for others—namely, whichever of the rest has the greatest need. As I have heard, he exacts large sums of money for opening them, on top of the regular tribute.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 118
paragraphs: So stand these matters. But of the seven men who had risen against the Magian, it happened that one—Intaphrenes—was put to death immediately after their uprising, for an outrage I shall relate. He wished to enter the king's palace and confer with the king. For the law, in fact, was that those who had risen against the Magian were permitted to enter the king's presence without being announced, unless the king happened to be lying with his wife. Accordingly, Intaphrenes did not think any announcement necessary, but as he was one of the seven, he wished to go in. The gatekeeper and the messenger-bearer, however, tried to prevent him, saying the king was lying with his wife. But Intaphrenes, believing they were not telling the truth, drew his sword, cut off their ears and noses, and stringing these onto his horse's bridle, tied them around their necks and let them go.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 119
paragraphs: On this they showed themselves to the king and told him the reason they had suffered this. Darius, fearing that the six might have done this by common design, sent for each separately and tested his disposition, to see whether he approved of what had been done. When he was fully assured that Intaphrenes had not acted in combination with them, he seized Intaphrenes himself together with his sons and all his kinsmen, since he was much inclined to believe that Intaphrenes was plotting a revolt against him with the help of his relatives. Having seized them, he put them in bonds as men condemned to death. Then the wife of Intaphrenes came constantly to the doors of the king's court, weeping and lamenting; and by doing this continually in the same way she moved Darius to pity. So he sent a messenger to her with this word: “Woman, King Darius grants that you may save from death one of your kinsmen lying in bonds—whichever of them all you wish.” She, after considering, answered: “If in truth the king grants me the life of one, I choose my brother out of them all.” When Darius was told this, marvelling at her words, he sent a messenger with this question: “Woman, the king asks what was in your mind that you left your husband and your children to die and chose your brother to live, seeing that he is surely less close to you in blood than your children, and less dear to you than your husband.” She answered: “O king, if heaven wills, I might have another husband and other children, should I lose these. But another brother I could never have, seeing that my father and my mother are no longer alive. That was in my mind when I said those words.” Darius thought the woman had spoken well, and he released not only the brother she asked for but also her eldest son, because he was pleased with her; all the rest he killed. So one of the seven had perished at once, in the manner related.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 120
paragraphs: Now about the time of Cambyses' illness, this had come to pass. There was a certain Oroetes, a Persian, whom Cyrus had appointed governor of the province of Sardis. This man had set his heart on an unholy thing. Though he had never suffered any wrong from Polycrates the Samian, nor heard a single offensive word from him, nor even seen him, he desired to seize him and put him to death, for a reason of this kind, as most who tell the story say. While Oroetes and another Persian named Mitrobates, governor of the province of Daskyleion, were sitting at the door of the king's court, they passed from words to a quarrel. As they disputed their respective claims to distinction, Mitrobates taunted Oroetes and said: “Do you count yourself a man? You have never yet won the island of Samos for the king, though it lies close to your province and is so extraordinarily easy to take that a native of it rose up against the government with fifteen men-at-arms, seized the island, and is now its despot.” Some say that because he heard this and was stung by the reproach, he conceived the desire not so much to take vengeance on the man who said it, as to destroy Polycrates at all costs, since it was on account of him that he was spoken of ill.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 121
paragraphs: The lesser number of those who tell the tale, however, say that Oroetes sent a herald to Samos to ask for something—what it was is not mentioned—and Polycrates happened to be lying down in the men's chamber of his palace, with Anacreon of Teos present beside him. Somehow—whether by design, because he thought little of Oroetes' business, or by some chance occurrence—the envoy of Oroetes came into his presence and spoke with him, and Polycrates, who happened to be turned towards the wall, neither turned round at all nor gave any answer.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 122
paragraphs: The cause of Polycrates' death is told in these two different ways; we may believe whichever we please. Oroetes, who had his residence at the Magnesia situated on the river Maeander, sent Myrsos son of Gyges, a Lydian, to Samos bearing a message, having perceived Polycrates' designs. For Polycrates was the first of the Hellenes we know of who set his mind on command of the sea, apart from Minos the Cnossian and any other who may have ruled the sea before him. Of what we call the mortal race, Polycrates was the first, and he had great expectations of becoming ruler of Ionia and the islands. Oroetes, therefore, having perceived this design of his, sent him a message as follows: “Oroetes to Polycrates says this: I hear that you are making plans for great power, and that your wealth does not match your ambitions. Now, therefore, if you will do as I say, you will both do well for yourself and save me from destruction. For King Cambyses is planning my death, and this has been reported to me beyond all doubt. Take me and my wealth out of danger; keep a portion for yourself and let me keep a portion, and then, so far as wealth can bring it about, you shall be ruler of all Hellas. And if you do not believe what I say about the money, send someone you trust most, and I will show it to him.”

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 123
paragraphs: When Polycrates heard this he rejoiced and was ready to agree; and since, it seems, he had a great desire for wealth, he first sent Maiandrios son of Maiandrios, a native of Samos who was his secretary, to see it. This was the same man who, not long after these events, dedicated to the temple of Hera all the ornaments of the men's chamber in the palace of Polycrates—ornaments well worth seeing. Oroetes, having heard that the man sent to examine the treasure would soon arrive, did as follows: he filled eight chests with stones, except for a small space at the very top of each, and laid gold on top of the stones. Then he tied up the chests and kept them ready. So Maiandrios came, looked at them, and brought word back to Polycrates.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 124
paragraphs: And he, upon hearing this, prepared to set out there, though the diviners and his friends strongly dissuaded him, and in spite, moreover, of a vision his daughter had seen in her sleep, of this kind: it seemed to her that her father was raised up on high and was bathed by Zeus and anointed by the Sun. Having seen this vision, she used every effort to dissuade Polycrates from leaving his land to go to Oroetes; and as he was embarking on his fifty-oared galley, she accompanied his departure with words of prophecy. He threatened her that if he came back safe, she should remain unmarried for a long time; but she prayed it might be so, for she would rather, she said, be unmarried for a long time than be an orphan, having lost her father.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 125
paragraphs: Polycrates, however, disregarded every counsel and set sail for Oroetes, taking with him, besides many other friends, Demokedes son of Calliphon, a man of Croton who was a physician and practised his art better than anyone else of his time. When he arrived at Magnesia, Polycrates was miserably put to death in a manner unworthy both of himself and of his lofty ambitions. For apart from those who became despots of the Syracusans, none of the other Hellenic despots is worthy to be compared with Polycrates in magnificence. And when Oroetes had killed him in a way not fit to be told, he impaled his body. Of those who had come with him, he released all the Samians, bidding them be grateful to him for being free men; but all those in his company who were either allies or servants, he kept as slaves. Polycrates, then, being hung up, fulfilled his daughter's vision entirely: for he was bathed by Zeus whenever it rained, and anointed by the Sun as he gave off moisture from his body.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 126
paragraphs: To this end came the great prosperity of Polycrates, as Amasis king of Egypt had foretold. But not long afterwards retribution overtook Oroetes in turn for the murder of Polycrates. For after the death of Cambyses and the reign of the Magians, Oroetes remained at Sardis and rendered no service to the Persians, who had been deprived of their empire by the Medes. Moreover, during this time of disturbance he killed Mitrobates, the governor in Daskyleion who had reproached him about Polycrates, and he killed Cranaspes son of Mitrobates as well, both men of repute among the Persians. Besides various other outrages, once when a messenger had come to him from Darius, displeased with the message he brought, he killed him on his way back, having set men in ambush along the road; and after killing him, he made away with the bodies both of the man and of his horse.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 127
paragraphs: Darius accordingly, when he came to the throne, was eager to take vengeance on Oroetes for all his wrongdoings, especially for the murder of Mitrobates and his son. However, he did not think it wise to act openly and send an army against him, since his own affairs were still unsettled and he had only just come to the throne, while he heard that Oroetes' strength was great—he had a bodyguard of a thousand Persian spearmen and held the divisions of Phrygia, Lydia, and Ionia. So Darius contrived as follows. Having called together the Persians of highest repute, he said to them: “Persians, which of you will undertake to perform this matter for me by wisdom and not by force or tumult? For where wisdom will serve, there is no need of force. Which of you, I ask, will bring Oroetes to me alive or kill him? For he has never done the Persians any service, and has done them great harm. First he destroyed two of us, Mitrobates and his son; then he kills the men I sent to summon him, showing insolence not to be borne. So before he commits any further evil against the Persians, we must check him by death.”

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 128
paragraphs: Thus Darius asked, and thirty men undertook the task, each eager to do it himself. Darius stopped their contention and bade them cast lots. When they did so, Bagaios son of Artontes drew the lot out of them all. Having drawn the lot, Bagaios acted as follows: he wrote many papers dealing with various matters and set Darius' seal on them, and with these he went to Sardis. When he arrived there and came into Oroetes' presence, he took the covers off the papers one by one and gave them to the Royal Secretary to read—for all provincial governors have Royal Secretaries. Now Bagaios gave the papers in order to test the spearmen of the guard, to see whether they would accept the idea of revolting from Oroetes. When he saw that they paid great reverence to the papers and still greater reverence to the words read from them, he handed over another paper containing these words: “Persians, King Darius forbids you to serve as guards to Oroetes.” Hearing this, they lowered the points of their spears before him. Then Bagaios, seeing that they were obedient to the paper on this point, took courage and gave the last paper to the secretary. In it was written: “King Darius commands the Persians in Sardis to kill Oroetes.” So the spearmen of the guard, when they heard this, drew their swords and killed him on the spot. Thus retribution for the murder of Polycrates the Samian overtook Oroetes.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 129
paragraphs: After Oroetes' wealth had been carried up to Susa, it happened not long afterwards that King Darius, while hunting wild beasts, twisted his foot as he leapt off his horse—and twisted it, it seems, rather violently, for the ball of his ankle was knocked out of its socket. He had been accustomed to keep about him those Egyptians reputed foremost in the art of medicine, and he called on their services now. But by wrenching and forcing the foot they made things steadily worse. For seven days and seven nights Darius could not sleep from the pain he suffered. At last, on the eighth day, when he was in a wretched condition, someone who had earlier, while at Sardis, heard talk of the skill of Demokedes of Croton, reported this to Darius, and he ordered him to be brought into his presence at once. So having found him somewhere unnoticed among the slaves of Oroetes, they brought him forth into the midst, dragging fetters behind him and clothed in rags.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 130
paragraphs: When he was set in the midst of them, Darius asked him whether he understood the art; but he would not admit it, fearing that if he revealed what he was, he might lose forever the hope of returning to Hellas. It was clear to Darius, however, that he understood the art but was playing the ignorant, and he commanded those who had brought him to produce scourges and goads. Then he spoke out, saying that he did not understand the art precisely, but had kept company with a physician and had some slight knowledge of it. So when Darius had committed his case to him, by using Hellenic drugs and applying mild remedies after the former violent methods, he brought him to sleep and in a short time restored him completely, though the king had given up hope of being sound of foot again. On this Darius presented him with two pairs of golden fetters. Demokedes asked him whether he was deliberately giving him a double share of his suffering for making him well. Pleased with the remark, Darius sent him to visit his wives, and the eunuchs bringing him in told the women that this was the man who had restored the king's life. Each of them then plunged a cup into her gold-chest and gave Demokedes such an abundant gift that his servant, whose name was Skiton, following and picking up the coins that fell from the cups, gathered for himself a very large sum of gold.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 131
paragraphs: This Demokedes came from Croton, and became the associate of Polycrates in the following way. At Croton he lived in strife with his father, who had a harsh temper, and when he could no longer endure him he left and came to Aegina. Settling there, he surpassed in his first year all the other physicians, though he had no equipment and none of the instruments used in the art. In the next year the state of Aegina engaged him for the payment of one talent; in the third year he was engaged by the Athenians for a hundred pounds of silver; in the fourth by Polycrates for two talents. Thus he came to Samos. It was largely because of this man that the physicians of Croton got their reputation; for this event fell at the very time when the physicians of Croton began to be spoken of as the first in Hellas, while those of Cyrene were reputed second. About the same time the Argives had the reputation of being the finest musicians in Hellas.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 132
paragraphs: So Demokedes, having healed King Darius, was given a very great house in Susa and was made a table-companion of the king; and except for the one matter of returning to the land of the Hellenes, he had everything. First, regarding the Egyptian physicians who had tried to heal the king before him—when they were about to be impaled for proving inferior to a physician who was a Hellene, he begged their lives of the king and rescued them from death. Second, he rescued an Elean prophet who had accompanied Polycrates and had gone unnoticed among the slaves. In short, Demokedes stood very high in the king's favour.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 133
paragraphs: Not long after this another thing came to pass. Atossa, daughter of Cyrus and wife of Darius, had a tumour on her breast, which afterwards burst and began to spread further. So long as it was not large, she concealed it and told no one, because she was ashamed. But afterwards, when she was in a bad state, she sent for Demokedes and showed it to him. He said he would cure her, and made her swear that she would surely do in return whatever he asked of her; and he would ask, he said, nothing shameful.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 134
paragraphs: So when, by his treatment, he had made her well, then Atossa, instructed by Demokedes, spoke to Darius in his bedchamber with words something like these: “O king, though you have such great power, you sit still and do not win any new nation or dominion for the Persians. It is only fitting that a man both young and master of great wealth should perform some great deed, so the Persians may be sure that the man who rules them is indeed a man. It is expedient in two ways: both so that the Persians may know their ruler is a man, and so they may be worn down by war and have no leisure to plot against you. Now is the time to display some great deed, while you are still young; for as the body grows, the spirit too grows old with it, and is blunted for every kind of action.” So she spoke, according to Demokedes' instructions. He answered: “Woman, you have said all the very things I have in mind to do. For I have planned to yoke together a bridge from this continent to the other and make an expedition against the Scythians, and these designs will soon be fulfilled.” Then Atossa said: “Look now, hold off attacking the Scythians first, for they will be in your power whenever you wish. But make, I pray you, an expedition against Hellas; for I desire to have Lacedaemonian women, and Argive, and Athenian, and Corinthian, as my attendants, because I hear of them by report. And you have the man most fitted of all men to show you everything to do with Hellas and to be your guide—that man, I mean, who healed your foot.” Darius answered: “Woman, since it seems good to you that we should first test Hellas, I think it better to send first some Persians there, together with the man you mention, to investigate. When they have learned and seen, they may report each several thing to us; and then I will go against them with full knowledge of everything.”

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 135
paragraphs: So he said, and he proceeded to the deed as soon as he had spoken the word. For as soon as day dawned, he summoned fifteen Persians of repute and bade them travel the coasts of Hellas in the company of Demokedes, and take care not to let Demokedes escape from them, but bring him back at all costs. Having given them these orders, he next summoned Demokedes himself and asked him to act as guide for all of Hellas and show it to the Persians, and then return. He bade him take all his movable goods and carry them as gifts to his father and brothers, saying that he would give him many times as much in their place; and besides this, he said he would contribute to the gifts a merchant ship loaded with all sorts of goods, to sail with him. Darius, as it seems to me, promised these things with no crafty design. But Demokedes feared that Darius was testing him and did not rush to accept all that was offered; instead he said he would leave his own things where they were, so he might have them when he came back. He did, however, accept the merchant ship Darius promised him for the gifts to his brothers. So Darius, having given him these orders as well, sent them off to the sea.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 136
paragraphs: So these men, having gone down to Phoenicia and to the city of Sidon there, at once manned two triremes, and besides them loaded a large cargo ship with goods of every kind. Then when they had made everything ready they set sail for Hellas, and touching at various places they viewed the coastal regions and wrote a description, until at last, when they had seen most of the famous places, they arrived at Taras in Italy. There, out of goodwill toward Demokedes, Aristophilides the king of the Tarentines unfastened and removed the steering-oars of the Median ships, and also confined the Persians in prison, alleging they came as spies. While they were being dealt with this way, Demokedes went off and reached Croton. When he was safely in his own native place, Aristophilides set the Persians free and returned to them the parts of their ships he had taken off.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 137
paragraphs: The Persians, setting sail from there and pursuing Demokedes, reached Croton, and finding him in the market-place, laid hands on him. Some of the men of Croton, fearing Persian power, were willing to let him go; but others took hold of him and struck at the Persians with their staves, while the Persians pleaded: “Men of Croton, take care what you are doing. You are rescuing a man who was a slave of King Darius and ran away from him. How do you think King Darius will be content to receive such an insult? And how can this act be well for you, if you take him away from us? What city, do you think, shall we make an expedition against sooner than this, and what city shall we try to enslave before this?” Saying this, however, they did not persuade the men of Croton. Having had Demokedes rescued from them and the cargo ship they had brought with them seized, they set sail to return to Asia, and did not try to visit or investigate any more parts of Hellas, now that they were deprived of their guide. This, however, Demokedes gave them as a charge when they were putting out to sea: to tell Darius that Demokedes was betrothed to the daughter of Milon. For the wrestler Milon had a great name at the king's court; and I suppose that Demokedes pressed for this marriage, spending a great deal of money to bring it about, so that Darius might see that he was held in honour in his own country as well.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 138
paragraphs: The Persians, however, after putting out from Croton, were cast away with their ships in Iapygia. As they were being held there as slaves, Gillos, a Tarentine exile, rescued them and brought them back to King Darius. In return, Darius offered him whatever he desired; and Gillos chose the right to return to Taras, narrating first the story of his misfortune. In order not to disturb all Hellas—as would be the case if on his account a great expedition sailed to invade Italy—he said it was enough for him that the men of Cnidos should be the ones who brought him back, without any others. For he supposed that by their means, since they were friends of the Tarentines, his return from exile could most easily be arranged. Darius accordingly, having promised, carried it out: he sent a message to Cnidos and bade them bring Gillos back to Taras. The men of Cnidos obeyed Darius, but they could not persuade the Tarentines, and were not strong enough to use force. So these things turned out this way. These were the first Persians to come from Asia to Hellas, and for the reason stated, these were sent as spies.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 139
paragraphs: After this King Darius took Samos before any other city, whether of Hellenes or barbarians, for a cause that was as follows. When Cambyses son of Cyrus was marching against Egypt, many Hellenes arrived in Egypt—some, as one might expect, joining the campaign for profit, and some coming to see the land itself. Among these was Syloson son of Aiakes and brother of Polycrates, an exile from Samos. To this Syloson a fortunate chance occurred. He had taken and put on a flame-coloured mantle and was walking about the market-place in Memphis; and Darius, then one of Cambyses' spearmen and not yet held in any great esteem, seeing him, desired the mantle, and went up to him to offer to buy it. Then Syloson, seeing that Darius very greatly desired it, by some divine inspiration said: “I will not sell this for any sum, but I will give it to you for nothing, if, as it appears, you must have it at all costs.” Darius agreed to this and received the garment from him.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 140
paragraphs: Now Syloson supposed, without any doubt, that he had altogether lost this through easy simplicity. But in course of time, when Cambyses was dead, and the seven Persians had risen against the Magian, and Darius of the seven had obtained the kingdom, Syloson heard that the kingdom had come round to the very man to whom he had given the garment in Egypt at his request. Accordingly he went up to Susa and sat down at the entrance of the king's palace, saying he was a benefactor of Darius. When the doorkeeper heard this he reported it to the king, who marvelled and said: “Who of the Hellenes is my benefactor, to whom I am bound by gratitude? Seeing that I have had the kingdom only a short time and hardly any one of them has come up to our court as yet, I may almost say I have no debt owing to a Hellene. Nevertheless bring him in before me, that I may know what he means by saying these things.” Then the doorkeeper brought Syloson in; and when he was set before him, the interpreters asked him who he was and what he had done that he called himself the king's benefactor. Syloson told the whole story of the mantle and said that he was the man who had given it. To this Darius answered: “O most noble of men, you are the one who, when I had no power yet, gave me a gift—small perhaps, but the kindness counts with me as great as if I were now to receive some great thing from someone. Therefore I will give you gold and silver in abundance in return, that you may never regret having done a service to Darius son of Hystaspes.” Syloson replied: “To me, O king, give neither gold nor silver, but recover and give me my fatherland Samos, which now that my brother Polycrates has been killed by Oroetes is possessed by our slave. Give this to me without bloodshed or enslavement.”

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 141
paragraphs: Darius, hearing this, prepared to send an expedition with Otanes—one of the seven—as its commander, charging him to accomplish for Syloson everything he had requested. So Otanes went down to the sea-coast and began to prepare the expedition.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 142
paragraphs: Now Maiandrios son of Maiandrios was holding power over Samos, having received the government as a trust from Polycrates. Though he wished to show himself the most upright of men, he did not succeed. For when the death of Polycrates was reported to him, he acted as follows. First he founded an altar to Zeus the Liberator and marked out a sacred precinct around it—the one which still exists in the suburb of the city. Then, after doing this, he assembled all the citizens and spoke: “To me, as you know as well as I, has been entrusted the sceptre of Polycrates and all his power. Now I might make myself your ruler; but what I blame in my neighbour, I will refrain from doing myself, so far as I can.
