I did not approve of Polycrates acting as master of men who were not inferior to him, nor do I approve of anyone else who does such things. Polycrates has fulfilled his own appointed destiny; and I now hand the power over to the people, and proclaim equality among you. These privileges, however, I think it right to reserve for myself: that from Polycrates' wealth six talents be set aside and given to me as a special gift; and in addition I choose for myself and for my descendants in succession the priesthood of Zeus the Liberator, to whom I myself founded a temple, while I bestow liberty upon you.” So he offered this to the Samians; but one of them rose up and said: “No—you yourself are unworthy to be our ruler, being of mean birth and a pestilent fellow besides. Rather, take care to give an account of the money you have handled.”

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 143
paragraphs: So spoke a man of repute among the citizens, whose name was Telesarchos. Maiandrios, realizing that if he resigned power someone else would be set up as despot instead of himself, no longer intended to resign it at all. Instead, he withdrew to the fortress and sent for each man separately, pretending that he was going to give an account of the money; but he seized them and put them in bonds. These, then, had been imprisoned. After this Maiandrios was taken ill, and his brother, whose name was Lycaretos, expecting him to die, put all the prisoners to death so that he himself might more easily seize power over Samos. And all this happened because, as it appears, they did not choose to be free.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 144
paragraphs: So when the Persians arrived at Samos bringing Syloson back from exile, no one raised a hand against them; and moreover the party of Maiandrios and Maiandrios himself said that they were ready to withdraw from the island under a truce. Otanes, therefore, having agreed on these terms and made a treaty, had the most distinguished of the Persians seated on chairs in front of the fortress, where they were sitting.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 145
paragraphs: Now the despot Maiandrios had a brother who was somewhat mad; his name was Charilaos. For some offence this man had committed, he had been confined in an underground dungeon. At the time of which I speak, having heard what was happening, and putting his head out of the dungeon, he saw the Persians peacefully seated there and began to cry out, saying he wished to speak with Maiandrios. Maiandrios, hearing his voice, ordered him loosed and brought before him. As soon as he was brought, he began to abuse and revile his brother, trying to persuade him to attack the Persians. He said: “You basest of men, you put me in chains and thought me worthy of the underground dungeon—me, your own brother, who had done nothing worthy of bonds. Now you see the Persians casting you out of the land and making you homeless, and you dare take no revenge, though they are so very easy to overcome? But if you are truly afraid of them, give me your mercenaries and I will take vengeance on them for their coming here; and you I am willing to let go out of the island.”

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 146
paragraphs: So spoke Charilaos, and Maiandrios accepted what he said—not, I think, because he had reached such a pitch of folly as to suppose his own power would overcome the king's, but because he begrudged Syloson that he should receive the state without trouble and with no harm done to it. He therefore wished to provoke the Persians to anger and make the Samian power as feeble as possible before surrendering it, being well assured that the Persians, when they had suffered harm, were likely to be as bitter against the Samians as against those who had wronged them. He also knew he had a safe way of escape from the island whenever he wished, for he had had a secret passage made underground from the fortress to the sea. Maiandrios himself then sailed out from Samos; but Charilaos armed all the mercenaries, threw the gates wide, and sent them out upon the Persians, who were expecting no such thing but supposed everything had been arranged. The mercenaries, falling upon them, began to kill the Persians who had chairs carried out for them and were of most account. While these were thus engaged, the rest of the Persian force came to the rescue, and the mercenaries were hard pressed and forced to retire into the fortress.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 147
paragraphs: Then Otanes the Persian commander, seeing the Persians had suffered greatly, deliberately forgot the orders Darius had given him when he sent him out—not to kill any of the Samians nor to sell any into slavery, but to restore the island to Syloson free from all suffering. These orders, I say, he deliberately forgot, and gave the word to his army to slaughter everyone they caught, man or boy alike. So while some of the army were besieging the fortress, others were killing everyone who came their way, in sanctuary or out of sanctuary alike.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 148
paragraphs: Meanwhile Maiandrios had escaped from Samos and was sailing to Lacedaemon. When he arrived there, he had brought up to the city the things he had taken with him when he left, and acted as follows. First he would set out his cups of silver and gold; then, while his servants were cleaning them, he would engage in conversation with Cleomenes son of Anaxandrides, then king of Sparta, and would bring him home. When Cleomenes saw the cups he marvelled and was astonished at them, and Maiandrios would bid him take away as many of them as he wished. Maiandrios said this two or three times, but Cleomenes in this matter showed himself the most upright of men: not only did he think it wrong to take what was offered, but perceiving that Maiandrios would make gifts to other citizens and so obtain help for himself, he went to the Ephors and said it was better for Sparta that the Samian stranger should leave the Peloponnese, lest he might persuade either himself or some other Spartan to act basely. They accepted his counsel and expelled Maiandrios by proclamation.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 149
paragraphs: As for Samos, the Persians, after sweeping the population off it, delivered it to Syloson stripped of men. Afterwards, however, the commander Otanes even joined in resettling people there, moved by a vision in a dream and by a disease that seized him—a disease of his genital organs.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 150
paragraphs: After a naval force had thus gone against Samos, the Babylonians revolted, being exceedingly well prepared for it. For during the whole reign of the Magian and the rising of the seven—and throughout the attendant confusion—they had been preparing themselves for the siege of their city; and somehow it happened that they were not observed while doing so. When they at last openly revolted, they did as follows. After setting apart their mothers first, each man also set apart one woman for himself—whomever he chose of his own household—and they gathered all the rest together and killed them by suffocation. Each man set apart the one already mentioned to serve as bread-maker, and they suffocated the rest so that these might not consume their provisions.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 151
paragraphs: When Darius was informed of this, he gathered all his forces and marched against them. When he had brought his army up to Babylon, he began to besiege the city; but the Babylonians cared nothing for the siege. They would go up onto the battlements of the wall and show contempt for Darius and his army with gestures and words, and one of them uttered this saying: “Why, O Persians, do you remain sitting here, and do not depart? For only then shall you capture us—when mules bring forth young.” This was said by one of the Babylonians who never supposed a mule would bring forth young.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 152
paragraphs: So when a year and seven months had passed, Darius began to grow vexed, and his whole army with him, at their failure to conquer the Babylonians. And yet Darius had used every kind of device and every possible means against them; but not even so could he conquer them. Besides other devices, he had even tried the means by which Cyrus had conquered them, but the Babylonians were intensely on their guard and he could not take them.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 153
paragraphs: Then in the twentieth month a prodigy befell Zopyros, son of that Megabyzos who had been one of the seven men who killed the Magian. To this Zopyros, son of Megabyzos, a prodigy occurred: one of the mules that served as bearers of provisions for him gave birth. When this was reported to him, and Zopyros had himself seen the foal—for he did not believe the report—he charged those who had seen it to tell no one what had happened, and he considered with himself what to do. Bearing in mind the words of the Babylonian who had said at the start that when mules bore young the wall would be taken—remembering, I say, this ominous saying—it seemed to Zopyros that Babylon could be taken. For he thought that both the man had spoken and his mule had foaled by divine dispensation.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 154
paragraphs: Since it now seemed to him fated that Babylon should be captured, he went to Darius and asked whether he considered the capture of Babylon a matter of the very greatest moment. Hearing in reply that Darius did indeed consider it of great consequence, he then considered how he might be the man to take it, and how the achievement might be his own; for among the Persians great benefits are held to deserve a very high degree of honour. He concluded that he could conquer it by no other means than by maltreating himself and deserting to the Babylonian side. So, thinking little of himself, he maltreated his own body in a way that could not be cured. He cut off his nose and ears, shaved his hair round in an unseemly way, scourged himself, and so came before Darius.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 155
paragraphs: Darius was profoundly troubled when he saw the man of highest repute at his court in such a state. Leaping up from his seat, he cried aloud and asked who had done this to him, and for what deed. Zopyros replied: “No man exists, except yourself, with power enough to reduce me to this condition. No stranger, O king, has done this, but I myself to myself, reckoning it a very grievous thing that the Assyrians should mock the Persians.” Darius answered: “You most reckless of men, you gave the fairest name to the foulest deed when you said that on account of those besieged you had brought yourself into an incurable state. How, you senseless man, will the enemy surrender to us the sooner because you have mutilated yourself? Surely you were out of your mind when you did this to yourself.” Zopyros said: “If I had told you what I was about to do, you would not have permitted me; but as it is, I have done it on my own initiative. Now, therefore, unless something is wanting on your part, we shall take Babylon. For I shall go at once as a deserter to the wall, and I shall tell them I suffered this treatment at your hands; and I believe that once I convince them of this, I shall obtain command of part of their forces. You, on the tenth day after I enter the wall, take a thousand men from those troops whose loss would not concern you, and station them by the gate of the city called the Gate of Semiramis. Then on the seventh day after that tenth, station two thousand men, I pray you, at the gate called the Gate of the Ninevites. Then after this seventh day, let twenty days pass, and then lead another four thousand and place them at the gate called the Gate of the Chaldaeans. Let neither the former men nor these carry any weapons except daggers—that weapon they may have. Then, after the twentieth day, order the rest of the army to attack the wall all around, and station the Persians, I pray you, at the gates called the Gate of Belos and the Gate of Kissia. For I think that when I have displayed great feats of prowess, the Babylonians will entrust to me, among other things, the keys that draw the bolts of the gates. After that, it shall be the concern of myself and the Persians to do what must be done.”

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 156
paragraphs: Having given these orders he went off to the city gate, turning to look behind him as he went, as if he were truly a deserter. Those stationed in that part of the wall, seeing him from the towers, ran down, cracked open one wing of the gate, and asked who he was and why he had come. He addressed them and said he was Zopyros, and that he came as a deserter to them. The gate-keepers, on hearing this, led him to the public assembly of the Babylonians. Brought before it, he began to lament his fortunes, saying he had in fact suffered at his own hands, and that he had suffered this because he had counselled the king to withdraw his army, since there seemed to be no way of taking the city. “And now,” he went on, “I have come as a great good to you, O Babylonians, and as a great evil to Darius, his army, and the Persians. For he shall surely not escape with impunity for treating me this way; and I know all the courses of his plans.”

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 157
paragraphs: So he spoke; and the Babylonians, seeing the man of highest reputation among the Persians deprived of nose and ears and smeared with blood from scourging, assuredly supposing he spoke the truth and had come to help them, were ready to grant him what he asked—and he asked to be given command of a certain force. When he had obtained this from them, he did what he had agreed with Darius he would do. On the tenth day he led out the Babylonian army, surrounded the thousand men he had told Darius to station first at that place, and killed them. The Babylonians, seeing that his deeds matched his words, rejoiced greatly and were eager to serve him in everything. After the agreed number of days had passed, he again picked men from the Babylonians, led them out, and killed the two thousand men of Darius' troops. Seeing this deed too, the Babylonians all had Zopyros' name on their lips, and were loud in his praise. Then, after the agreed interval, he led them out to the appointed place, surrounded the four thousand, and killed them. When this too had been done, Zopyros was everything to the Babylonians, and he was appointed both commander of their army and guardian of their walls.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 158
paragraphs: But when Darius made his assault on every side of the wall, according to agreement, then Zopyros revealed all his stratagem. While the Babylonians were up on the wall defending themselves against the attacks of Darius' army, Zopyros opened the gates called the Gate of Kissia and the Gate of Belos and let the Persians inside the wall. Of the Babylonians, those who saw what was happening fled to the temple of Zeus Belos, while those who did not see remained each at his appointed post, until at last they too learned they had been betrayed.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 159
paragraphs: So Babylon was captured for the second time. When Darius had overcome the Babylonians, he first took away the wall around the city and pulled down all the gates—for when Cyrus had taken Babylon earlier, he had done neither of these things. Second, Darius impaled the leading men, some three thousand of them; but to the rest of the Babylonians he gave back their city to inhabit. To provide wives for the Babylonians, so their race might be propagated—since, as noted at the beginning, the Babylonians had suffocated their own wives out of concern for their food supply—Darius did as follows. He ordered the surrounding nations to bring women to Babylon, fixing a certain number for each nation, so that a total of fifty thousand women was gathered; and from these women the present-day Babylonians are descended.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 160
paragraphs: As for Zopyros, in Darius' judgment no Persian surpassed him in service, either of those who came after or of those who had gone before, except Cyrus alone—for no Persian has ever yet ventured to compare himself with Cyrus. Darius is said to have declared often that he would rather Zopyros were free from the injury he had done himself than have twenty Babylons added to his possessions on top of the one he already had. Moreover he gave him great honours: not only did he give him every year those gifts which the Persians count as the most honourable, but he also granted him Babylon to rule free of tribute for as long as he lived, and added many other gifts besides. The son of this Zopyros was Megabyzos, who was appointed commander in Egypt against the Athenians and their allies; and the son of this Megabyzos was Zopyros, who went over to Athens as a deserter from the Persians.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 1
paragraphs: After Babylon had been taken, Darius himself took the field against the Scythians. Now that Asia was flourishing in population and large revenues were being gathered, Darius formed the desire to take vengeance on the Scythians, because they had first invaded the Median land and defeated in battle those who opposed them—so they had been the original aggressors. The Scythians, in truth, as I have said before, had ruled over Upper Asia for twenty-eight years. They had invaded Asia in pursuit of the Cimmerians, and had deposed the Medes, who had ruled Asia before the Scythians came. Now when the Scythians had been away from their own land for twenty-eight years, as they were returning after so long, they were met by a contest no less severe than the one they had had with the Medes, for they found an army of no small size opposing them. The wives of the Scythians, because their husbands had been absent from them so long, had associated with the slaves.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 2
paragraphs: Now the Scythians put out the eyes of all their slaves because of the milk they drink, and they go about it as follows. They take blow-pipes of bone, just like flutes, and insert them into the vagina of the mare, and blow with their mouths, while others milk her while they blow. They say they do this because the mare's veins, being blown up, are filled, and so the udder is let down. When they have drawn the milk, they pour it into wooden hollowed-out vessels, and they station the blind slaves around the vessels and have them agitate the milk. What comes to the top they skim off, considering it the more valuable part, whereas what settles down they reckon inferior. For this reason the Scythians put out the eyes of all they catch; for they are not tillers of the soil, but nomads.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 3
paragraphs: From these slaves, I say, and from their wives, there had been born and bred up a generation of young men. Having learned the manner of their birth, they set out to oppose the Scythians as they returned from the Medes. First they cut off their land by digging a broad trench extending from the Tauric mountains to the Maeotian lake, at its widest point. Then afterwards, when the Scythians attempted to invade the land, they took up position against them and fought; and as they fought many times and the Scythians could gain no advantage in the fighting, one of them said: “What a thing is this we are doing, Scythians! We are fighting our own slaves, and not only are we growing fewer by being slain in battle, we are killing them too, and so shall have fewer to rule over in future. Now, therefore, it seems to me we should lay aside spears and bows, and each take his horse-whip and go up close to them. As long as they saw us with arms in our hands, they thought themselves our equals and of equal birth. But when they see we have whips instead of arms, they will realize they are our slaves; and acknowledging that, they will not stand to face our attack.”

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 4
paragraphs: When they heard this, the Scythians proceeded to do as he said; and the others, panic-stricken by what was happening, forgot their fighting and fled. Thus the Scythians had ruled over Asia, and thus, after being driven out again by the Medes, they returned to their own land. It was on this account that Darius wished to take vengeance on them, and was gathering together an army to march against them.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 5
paragraphs: Now the Scythians say their nation is the youngest of all peoples, and that this came about as follows. The first man ever to exist in this region, which was then desert, was one named Targitaos. Of this Targitaos they say—though I for my part do not believe it, but so they say—that his parents were Zeus and a daughter of the river Borysthenes. From some such origin as this, they report, Targitaos sprang, and from him were born three sons, Lipoxaïs, Arpoxaïs, and the youngest, Colaxaïs. In their reign there came down from heaven certain things wrought of gold—a plough, a yoke, a battle-axe, and a cup—and fell on the Scythian land. First the eldest saw them and came near, wanting to take them, but the gold blazed with fire at his approach. When he had gone away, the second approached, and again it did the same. So the gold repelled these two by blazing with fire. But when the third and youngest came up to it, the flame was quenched, and he carried the objects to his own house. The elder brothers, acknowledging the significance of the sign, handed the whole of the kingly power over to the youngest.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 6
paragraphs: From Lipoxaïs, they say, are descended those Scythians called the race of the Auchatai; from the middle brother Arpoxaïs, those called Catiaroi and Traspians; and from the youngest, the Royal tribe, called Paralatai. All together they are called Scolotoi, after the name of their king, they say; but the Hellenes gave them the name Scythians.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 7
paragraphs: Thus the Scythians say they came into being; and from their origin—that is, from the first king Targitaos—to the crossing over of Darius against them, they say the period is a thousand years and no more. This sacred gold is guarded by the kings with the greatest care, and they visit it every year with solemn sacrifices of propitiation. Moreover, if anyone goes to sleep while watching in the open air over this gold during the festival, the Scythians say he does not live out the year; and as compensation he is given as much land as he can ride around himself on his horse in one day. Since the land was large, Colaxaïs, they say, established three kingdoms for his sons, and made one of them larger than the rest—the one in which the gold is kept. As for the upper regions, which lie to the north of those who dwell above this land, they say one can neither see them nor pass further because of feathers which are poured down: both the earth and the air are full of feathers, and this is what shuts off the view.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 8
paragraphs: So the Scythians speak of themselves and of the region above them. But the Hellenes who dwell around the Pontus say the following. Heracles, driving the cattle of Geryones, came to this land, then desert, which the Scythians now inhabit; and Geryones, the tale says, dwelt away from the Pontic region, living in the island called by the Hellenes Erytheia, near Gadeira outside the Pillars of Heracles by the Ocean. As to the Ocean, they say indeed that it flows around the whole earth, beginning from the place of the sunrising, but they do not prove this by facts. From there Heracles came to the land now called Scythia, and since a storm came upon him together with icy cold, he drew his lion's skin over him and went to sleep. Meanwhile the mares harnessed to his chariot, as they were grazing, vanished by some miraculous chance.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 9
paragraphs: When Heracles awoke, he searched for them. Having gone over the whole land, at last he came to the region called Hylaia, and there he found in a cave a kind of twofold creature formed of the union of a maiden and a serpent, whose upper parts from the buttocks up were those of a woman, but whose lower parts were those of a snake. Seeing her and marvelling at her, he asked whether she had seen any mares straying anywhere; and she said she had them herself and would not give them up until he lay with her. So Heracles lay with her on condition of receiving them. Then she tried to put off returning the mares, wishing to keep Heracles with her as long as possible, while he for his part wished to get the mares and depart. At last she gave them back, saying: “These mares, when they wandered here, I saved for you, and you gave me a reward for saving them—for by you I have three sons. Tell me, then: what must I do with them when they have grown to manhood? Shall I settle them here, over which land I alone have power, or send them away to you?” She asked this of him, and he, they say, replied: “When you see the boys grown to men, do this, and you will not fail in right conduct. Whichever of them you see able to stretch this bow as I am doing now, and to be girded with this girdle, make him the settler of this land. But whichever of them fails in the tasks I prescribe, send him out of the land. If you do this, you will both have joy yourself and do what I have enjoined upon you.”

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 10
paragraphs: Upon this he drew one of his bows—for up to that time Heracles, they say, used to carry two—and showed her the girdle; then he handed over both the bow and the girdle, which had a golden cup at the end of its clasp. Having given them, he departed. She, when her sons had been born and grown to manhood, first gave them names: one she called Agathyrsos, the next Gelonos, and the youngest Skythes. Then, remembering the charge given to her, she did as commanded. Two of her sons, Agathyrsos and Gelonos, proving unable to accomplish the task set before them, were cast out of the land by their mother. But Skythes, the youngest, performed the task and remained in the land; and from Skythes, son of Heracles, are descended, they say, the succeeding kings of the Scythians. They say also that it is because of the cup that the Scythians still to this day wear cups attached to their girdles—and this is the one thing his mother contrived for Skythes. Such is the story told by the Hellenes who dwell around the Pontus.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 11
paragraphs: There is, however, another account, to which I am more inclined myself. It runs as follows. The nomadic Scythians dwelling in Asia, hard pressed in war by the Massagetai, left their abode and, crossing the river Araxes, came towards the Cimmerian land (for the land now occupied by the Scythians is said to have been in former times the land of the Cimmerians). The Cimmerians, as the Scythians were coming against them, took counsel together, seeing that a great host was coming to fight them; and it turned out their opinions were divided, both being vehemently maintained, but the better being that of their kings. The people's opinion was that they must depart and not run the risk of fighting against so many; but the kings' opinion was to fight for their land against those who came against them. Since neither would the people agree to their kings' counsel, nor the kings to the people's, the people planned to depart without fighting and surrender the land to the invaders, while the kings resolved to die and be laid in their own land, rather than flee with the mass of the people—considering the many good fortunes they had enjoyed, and the many evils likely to come if they fled from their native land. Having resolved thus, the kings divided themselves into two bands, and making their numbers equal, fought with one another. When these had all been killed by each other's hands, the people of the Cimmerians buried them by the bank of the river Tyras (where their burial-place can still be seen), and having buried them, they then made their way out from the land; and the Scythians, coming upon it, found the land deserted.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 12
paragraphs: And there are at the present day in the Scythian land Cimmerian walls and a Cimmerian ferry; there is also a region called Cimmeria, and the so-called Cimmerian Bosphorus. It is known, moreover, that the Cimmerians in their flight from the Scythians into Asia also made a settlement on the peninsula where the Hellenic city of Sinope now stands. And it is known too that the Scythians pursued them and invaded the land of Media, having lost their way; for while the Cimmerians kept along the sea in their flight, the Scythians pursued keeping the Caucasus on their right hand, until at last they invaded Media, turning their course inland. This, then, is another account, common both to Hellenes and barbarians.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 13
paragraphs: Aristeas, however, son of Caÿstrobios, a man of Proconnesos, said in the verses he composed that he came, possessed by Phoebus, to the land of the Issedonians, and that beyond the Issedonians dwelt the Arimaspians, a one-eyed race, and beyond them the gold-guarding griffins, and beyond them the Hyperboreans extending as far as the sea. All these except the Hyperboreans, beginning with the Arimaspians, were continually making war on their neighbours; and the Issedonians were gradually driven out of their country by the Arimaspians, and the Scythians by the Issedonians, and so the Cimmerians, who dwelt on the southern sea, being pressed by the Scythians, left their land. Thus Aristeas too disagrees with the Scythians' own account concerning this land.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 14
paragraphs: As for Aristeas, who composed this, I have already said whence he was; I will also tell the tale I heard about him in Proconnesos and Kyzicos. They say that Aristeas, who was inferior in birth to none of the citizens, entered a fuller's shop in Proconnesos and there died; and the fuller closed his workshop and went off to report the matter to the dead man's relatives. When the news had spread through the city that Aristeas was dead, a man of Kyzicos who had come from the town of Artake disputed with those who said so, and declared he had met him going towards Kyzicos and had spoken with him. While he was hotly arguing, the dead man's relatives came to the fuller's shop with the things proper for taking up the corpse for burial; and when the house was opened, Aristeas was not found there, either dead or alive. In the seventh year after this he appeared at Proconnesos and composed those verses the Hellenes now call the Arimaspeia; and having composed them he disappeared for the second time.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 15
paragraphs: So much is told by these cities. What follows, I know happened to the people of Metapontion in Italy two hundred and forty years after the second disappearance of Aristeas, as I found by piecing the evidence together at Proconnesos and Metapontion. The people of Metapontion say that Aristeas himself appeared in their land and bade them set up an altar of Apollo and place beside it a statue bearing the name of Aristeas of Proconnesos. He told them that to their land alone of all the Italiote cities Apollo had come, and that he—who was now Aristeas—had accompanied the god, being at that time a raven when he accompanied him. Having said this, he disappeared. The Metapontines say they sent to Delphi and asked the god what the apparition of the man meant; and the Pythian prophetess bade them obey the command of the apparition, telling them it would be better for them if they did. They accepted this answer and carried out the commands; and a statue bearing the name Aristeas now stands close beside the altar dedicated to Apollo, with laurel trees around it; and the altar is set up in the market-place. Let this suffice for what has been said about Aristeas.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 16
paragraphs: Now as for the land about which this account has begun, no one knows precisely what lies beyond it. I can hear of no one who claims to know as an eyewitness; and even Aristeas, the man I was mentioning just now, did not claim, though he was composing verse, that he went further than the Issedonians. What was beyond them he spoke of by hearsay, reporting that it was the Issedonians who said these things. So far, however, as I could get at certainty by hearsay, carrying inquiries as far as possible, all shall be told.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 17
paragraphs: Beginning with the trading station of the Borysthenites—for of all the places along the sea this is the central point of Scythia—beginning here, the first regions are occupied by the Callipidai, who are Hellenic Scythians; and above these is another people called the Alazonians. These last, and the Callipidai, in all other respects have the same customs as the Scythians, but they sow corn and use it for food, as well as onions, leeks, lentils, and millet. Above the Alazonians dwell Scythians who till the ground, and these sow their corn not for food but to sell.

Beyond them dwell the Neuroi; and beyond the Neuroi, towards the north wind, is a region without inhabitants so far as we know. These peoples are along the river Hypanis, to the west of the Borysthenes. After crossing the Borysthenes, the first region from the sea-coast is Hylaia, and beyond this, as one goes up the river, dwell agricultural Scythians, whom the Hellenes who live on the river Hypanis call Borysthenites (though they call themselves citizens of Olbia). These agricultural Scythians occupy the region extending eastwards for a three days' journey, reaching as far as a river called the Panticapes, and northwards for eleven days' sail up the Borysthenes. Immediately beyond these the desert begins and extends a great distance; and on the other side of the desert dwell the Androphagoi, a people apart, having no connection with the Scythians. Beyond them begins a region that is truly desert and has no race of men in it, so far as we know.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 19
paragraphs: The region to the east of these agricultural Scythians, once one has crossed the river Panticapes, is occupied by nomadic Scythians, who neither sow anything nor plough the earth; and the whole of this region is bare of trees except for Hylaia. These nomads occupy a country extending to the river Gerros, a distance of fourteen days' journey eastwards.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 20
paragraphs: Then, on the other side of the Gerros, we come to the parts called the Royal lands, and to those Scythians who are the bravest and most numerous, who count the other Scythians as their slaves. Their territory reaches southwards to the Tauric land, eastwards to the trench dug by those born of the blind slaves, and to the trading station called Cremnoi on the Maeotian lake; some parts of their country reach the river Tanaïs. Beyond the Royal Scythians, towards the north wind, dwell the Melanchlainoi, of a different race, not Scythian. The region beyond the Melanchlainoi is marshy and uninhabited, as far as we know.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 21
paragraphs: After one has crossed the river Tanaïs the country is no longer Scythia, but the first of the divisions belongs to the Sauromatai. Beginning at the corner of the Maeotian lake, they occupy land extending towards the north wind fifteen days' journey, entirely bare of trees, both cultivated and wild. Above them, holding the next division of land, dwell the Budinoi, who occupy a land wholly covered with forest of all kinds of trees.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 22
paragraphs: Then beyond the Budinoi, towards the north, is first a desert of seven days' journey; and after the desert, turning somewhat more towards the east wind, we come to land occupied by the Thyssagetai, a numerous people of a race separate from the others. These live by hunting. Bordering on them, settled in these same regions, are also men called Irycai, who likewise live by hunting, which they practise in the following way. The hunter climbs a tree and lies in wait for his game (trees are abundant in all this country); each has ready at hand a horse that has been trained to lie down on its belly to make itself low, and also a dog. When he sees the wild animal from the tree, he first shoots his arrow, then mounts his horse and pursues it, and the dog seizes hold of it. Above these, towards the east, dwell other Scythians, who have revolted from the Royal Scythians and have come to this region.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 23
paragraphs: As far as the country of these Scythians, the whole land described is level plain with deep soil. But after this point it is stony and rugged. When one has passed through a great extent of this rugged country, there dwell in the skirts of lofty mountains men who are said to be all bald-headed from their birth, male and female alike, with flat noses and large chins. They speak a language of their own, use the Scythian manner of dress, and live on the produce of trees. The tree whose fruit they live on is called the Pontic tree, and is about the size of a fig tree. It bears a fruit the size of a bean, containing a stone. When the fruit is ripe, they strain it through cloths, and there flows from it a thick black juice, which is called aschy. This they either lick up or drink mixed with milk, and from the lees—the solid part—they make cakes and use them for food; for they have few cattle, since the pastures there are not good. Each man has his dwelling under a tree, in winter covering the tree all round with close white felt cloth, and in summer leaving it uncovered. These people are injured by no one, for they are said to be sacred, and they possess no weapon of war. They are the ones who decide disputes among their neighbours; and besides this, any fugitive who takes refuge with them is injured by no one. They are called Argippaians.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 24
paragraphs: Now as far as these bald-headed men, there is abundant clear information about the land and about the nations on this side. Not only do certain of the Scythians go to them—from whom it is not difficult to get information—but also some of the Hellenes at the trading station of the Borysthenes and the other trading places on the Pontic coast. Those of the Scythians who go to them conduct their business through seven interpreters and in seven different languages.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 25
paragraphs: So far, I say, the land is known. But concerning the region north of the bald-headed men, no one can speak with certainty, for lofty, impassable mountains divide it off, and no one passes over them. These bald-headed men say, however—though I do not believe it—that the mountains are inhabited by men with goats' feet; and that after one has passed beyond them, others are found who sleep through six months of the year. This I do not accept as true at all. The country east of the bald-headed men, however, is known with certainty, being inhabited by the Issedonians. But what lies beyond both the bald-headed men and the Issedonians, towards the north wind, is unknown, except so far as we know it from the accounts given by these peoples just mentioned.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 26
paragraphs: The Issedonians are said to have these customs. When a man's father is dead, all the relatives bring cattle to the house, and having slaughtered them and cut up the flesh, they also cut up the dead body of their host's father, and mixing all the flesh together they set out a banquet. His skull, however, they strip of flesh, clean out, and then gild over; and after that they treat it as a sacred object and perform great sacrifices for the dead man every year. This each son does for his father, just as the Hellenes keep the day of memorial for the dead. In other respects, too, this people is said to live righteously, and their women have equal rights with the men.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 27
paragraphs: These too are known. But as to the region beyond them, it is the Issedonians who report that there are one-eyed men there and gold-guarding griffins; and the Scythians, having received this from them, report it in turn; and from the Scythians we—that is, the rest of mankind—have got our belief. We call them in Scythian Arimaspians, for the Scythians call the number one arima and the eye spu.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 28
paragraphs: This whole land I have described has such an exceedingly severe climate that for eight months of the year there is frost so hard as to be intolerable. During these months, if you pour out water you cannot make mud—you can only do so by lighting a fire. The sea is frozen, and the whole Cimmerian Bosphorus, so that the Scythians settled within the trench make expeditions and drive their wagons over into the country of the Sindians. So it continues to be winter for eight months, and even for the remaining four months it is cold in those parts. This winter is different in character from all the winters in other parts of the world. For in it there is no rain worth speaking of at the usual season for rain, whereas in summer it rains continually; and thunder does not come at the time it does in other countries, but is very frequent in summer. If thunder comes in winter, it is marvelled at as a prodigy; likewise if an earthquake occurs, whether in summer or winter, it is accounted a prodigy in Scythia. Horses can endure this winter, but neither mules nor asses can bear it at all—whereas in other countries, horses if they stand in frost lose their limbs by mortification, while asses and mules endure it.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 29
paragraphs: I think it is for this reason too that the hornless breed of oxen in that country grow no horns. There is a line of Homer in the Odyssey supporting my opinion, which runs:
“Also the Libyan land, where the sheep very quickly grow hornèd,”
for it is rightly said that in hot regions horns come quickly, whereas in extreme cold the animals either grow no horns at all, or hardly any.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 30
paragraphs: In that land, then, this happens because of the cold. But (since my history from the first has sought occasions for digression) I marvel that in the whole land of Elis mules cannot be bred, though that region is not cold, nor is there any other evident cause. The Eleians themselves say that because of some curse mules are not begotten in their land; but when the time approaches for the mares to conceive, they drive them into the neighbouring lands, and there in the land of their neighbours they let the jackasses mate with them until the mares are pregnant, and then they drive them back.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 31
paragraphs: As for the feathers the Scythians say fill the air, so that they can neither see nor pass through the further parts of the continent, my opinion is this. In the parts beyond this land it snows continually—though less in summer than in winter, as might be supposed. Now whoever has seen close at hand a thick snowfall knows what I mean without further explanation, for the snow is like feathers. On account of this wintry weather, such as I have described, the northern parts of this continent are uninhabitable. I think, therefore, that by “feathers” the Scythians and their neighbours mean the snow symbolically. This, then, has been said as far as the reports reach.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 32
paragraphs: About a Hyperborean people the Scythians report nothing, nor do any who dwell in this region, unless it be the Issedonians; but in my opinion these too say nothing, for if they did the Scythians would report it too, as they do about the one-eyed people. Hesiod, however, has spoken of Hyperboreans, and so has Homer in the poem Epigonoi—at least if Homer was really the composer of that epic.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 33
paragraphs: But much more about them is reported by the people of Delos than by any others. They say that sacred offerings bound up in wheat straw are carried from the land of the Hyperboreans and come to the Scythians, and from the Scythians the neighbouring nations in succession receive them and convey them westwards, finally as far as the Adriatic. From there they are sent on towards the south; the people of Dodona receive them first of all the Hellenes, and from these they come down to the Malian gulf and are passed over to Euboea, where city sends them on to city till they reach Carystos. After this Andros is skipped, for the Carystians are the ones who bring them to Tenos, and the Tenians to Delos. Thus, they say, these sacred offerings come to Delos. But at first, they say, the Hyperboreans sent two maidens bearing the sacred offerings, whose names, the Delians say, were Hyperoche and Laodike. With them, for their protection, the Hyperboreans sent five men of their nation to attend them—those who are now called Perphereës and receive great honour on Delos. But since the Hyperboreans found that those sent away did not come back, they were troubled at the thought of always having to send out and never receive back; so they carried the offerings, bound up in wheat straw, to the borders of their land, and laid a charge upon their neighbours, bidding them pass them on to another nation. These, they say, come to Delos by being passed on in this way. And I know of my own knowledge that a thing is done which resembles these offerings: the women of Thrace and Paionia, when they sacrifice to Artemis “the Queen,” never make their offerings without wheat straw.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 34
paragraphs: These I know do as I have said. For those maidens from the Hyperboreans, who died in Delos, both the girls and the boys of the Delians cut off their hair. The girls, before marriage, cut off a lock, and having wound it round a spindle lay it upon the tomb (the tomb is on the left hand as one enters the temple of Artemis, and an olive tree grows over it). All the boys of the Delians wind some of their hair about a green shoot of some tree and also place it upon the tomb.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 35
paragraphs: The maidens, I say, receive this honour from the dwellers in Delos. The same people say that Arge and Opis also, being maidens, came to Delos, passing from the Hyperboreans by the same nations mentioned, even before Hyperoche and Laodike. The latter, they say, came bearing for Eileithuia the tribute they had laid upon themselves for a speedy delivery in childbirth; but Arge and Opis came with the divinities themselves, and other honours have been assigned to them by the people of Delos. The women, they say, collect offerings for them, naming them by their names in the hymn which Olen, a man of Lycia, composed in their honour; and both the natives of the other islands and the Ionians have learnt from them to sing hymns naming Opis and Arge and taking up collections. This Olen came from Lycia and composed also the other ancient hymns sung on Delos. Moreover, they say that when the thighs of the victim are consumed on the altar, the ashes are thrown upon the tomb of Opis and Arge. Their tomb is behind the temple of Artemis, turned towards the east, close to the banqueting hall of the Keians.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 36
paragraphs: Let what has been said of the Hyperboreans suffice. For the tale of Abaris, who is reported to have been a Hyperborean, I do not tell—namely how he carried the arrow about all over the earth, eating no food. If, however, there really are Hyperboreans, it follows there are also Hypernotians; and I laugh when I see that, though many before this have drawn maps of the earth, no one has set the matter forth intelligently. They draw Ocean flowing around the earth, which is circular exactly as if drawn with compasses, and they make Asia equal in size to Europe. In a few words I shall state the size of each division and what its outline is like.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 37
paragraphs: The Persians inhabit Asia as far as the southern sea, called the Erythraian. Above these, towards the north wind, dwell the Medes; above the Medes the Saspeirians; and above the Saspeirians the Colchians, extending to the northern sea, into which the river Phasis runs. These four nations inhabit the territory from sea to sea.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 38
paragraphs: Westwards from them, two peninsulas stretch out from Asia into the sea, which I will describe. The first, on its northern side, begins from the Phasis and extends to the sea, running along the Pontus and Hellespont as far as Sigeion in the land of Troy; on its southern side the same peninsula stretches from the Myriandrian gulf, which lies near Phoenicia, towards the sea as far as the headland Triopion. In this peninsula dwell thirty races of men.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 39
paragraphs: This, then, is one of the peninsulas. The other, beginning from the land of the Persians, stretches to the Erythraian Sea, including Persia, next Assyria, and after Assyria Arabia. This ends—or rather is commonly supposed to end—at the Arabian gulf, into which Darius conducted a channel from the Nile. Along the line stretching from the land of the Persians to Phoenicia, the country is broad and the space abundant; but after Phoenicia this peninsula runs along the shore of our Sea, past Palestine, Syria, and Egypt, where it ends; and in it there are only three nations.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 40
paragraphs: These are the parts of Asia extending westwards from the Persian land. As for what lies beyond the Persians, Medes, Saspeirians, and Colchians, towards the east and the sunrise, on one side the Erythraian Sea runs along by them, and on the north both the Caspian Sea and the river Araxes, which flows towards the rising sun. Asia is inhabited as far as the Indian land; but from there onwards to the east it becomes desert, nor can any one say what kind of land it is.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 41
paragraphs: Such and so large is Asia. Libya is included in the second peninsula; for after Egypt, Libya begins at once. Around Egypt this peninsula is narrow, for from our Sea to the Erythraian Sea the distance there is ten myriads of fathoms, which would amount to a thousand furlongs; but after this narrow part, the portion of the peninsula called Libya happens to be extremely broad.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 42
paragraphs: I wonder at those who have divided the world into Libya, Asia, and Europe, since the difference between these is not small; for in length Europe extends alongside both, while in breadth it is clearly, to my mind, beyond all comparison larger. Libya furnishes proofs about itself that it is surrounded by sea, except where it borders on Asia; and this fact was first shown by Necos the king of the Egyptians, of all those of whom we have knowledge. When he had ceased digging the channel leading from the Nile to the Arabian gulf, he sent Phoenicians with ships, bidding them sail and return through the Pillars of Heracles into the northern sea, and so back to Egypt. The Phoenicians, accordingly, set out from the Erythraian Sea and sailed through the southern sea. Whenever autumn came on, they would put in to shore and sow the land, wherever in Libya they happened to be as they sailed, and then they waited for the harvest. Having reaped the grain, they sailed on; so that after two years had passed, in the third year they turned through the Pillars of Heracles and arrived again in Egypt. They reported a thing I cannot believe, though another man may: namely, that in sailing round Libya they had the sun on their right hand.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 43
paragraphs: Thus this country was first known to be what it is. After this, the Carthaginians make report of it. For as to Sataspes son of Teaspis the Achaemenid, he did not sail round Libya, though he was sent for this very purpose; rather, he was struck with fear by the length of the voyage and the desolation of the land, and so returned back without completing the task his mother had laid upon him. This man had outraged a daughter of Zopyros son of Megabyzos, a virgin. When he was about to be impaled by order of King Xerxes for this offence, Sataspes' mother, who was a sister of Darius, entreated for his life, saying she would herself impose on him a greater penalty than Xerxes would: he should be compelled, she said, to sail around Libya, until in sailing around it he came to the Arabian gulf. Xerxes having agreed to these terms, Sataspes went to Egypt and, obtaining a ship and crew from the Egyptians, sailed to the Pillars of Heracles. Having passed through them and rounded the promontory of Libya called Soloeis, he sailed on southwards. Then, after he had traversed much sea over many months, and ever more voyaging was required, he turned around and sailed back to Egypt. Having come from there into the presence of King Xerxes, he reported that at the furthest point he had reached, he was sailing past a dwarfish people who wore clothing made from the palm tree, and who, whenever his ship came to land, left their towns and fled into the mountains. When his men entered the towns, he said, they did no harm, but only took food from them. The reason, he said, why he had not completed the voyage round Libya was that the ship could sail no further and was stuck fast. Xerxes, however, did not believe he was speaking the truth, and since he had not performed the appointed task, impaled him, exacting the penalty pronounced before. A eunuch belonging to Sataspes ran off to Samos as soon as he heard his master was dead, carrying large sums of money. A man of Samos took possession of these—whose name I know, but I deliberately pass over without mention.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 44
paragraphs: Most of Asia was explored by Darius, who, wishing to know where the river Indus—the only river besides the Nile that produces crocodiles—runs out into the sea, sent with ships, besides others whom he trusted to speak the truth, Skylax also, a man of Caryanda. These men, starting from the city of Caspatyros and the land of Pactyïke, sailed down the river towards the east and the sunrise to the sea; and then sailing over the sea westwards, they came in the thirtieth month to the place from which the king of the Egyptians had sent out the Phoenicians mentioned earlier, to sail round Libya. After these men had made their voyage round the coast, Darius both subdued the Indians and made use of this sea. Thus Asia too, except for the parts towards the rising sun, has been found similar to Libya.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 45
paragraphs: As for Europe, it is clearly known by no one, either as regards the parts towards the rising sun or those towards the north, whether it is surrounded by sea; but in length it is known to stretch alongside both the other divisions. I am not able to understand for what reason to the earth, which is one, three different names have been given, derived from women, and why the river Nile of Egypt and the Phasis in Colchis were set as boundaries to divide it (or, as some say, the Maeotian river Tanaïs and the Cimmerian ferry). Nor can I find out who the persons were who made these boundaries, or why they gave them these names. Libya indeed is said by most of the Hellenes to have its name from Libya, a woman of that country, and Asia from the wife of Prometheus; but this last name is claimed by the Lydians, who say that Asia was called after Asias, son of Cotys, son of Manes—not from Asia wife of Prometheus—and they say the Asian tribe in Sardis gets its name from him too. As for Europe, however, neither is it known to any man whether it is surrounded by sea, nor does it appear whence it got this name or who gave it, unless we say that the land took its name from Europa the Tyrian woman; and in that case it would appear that before this it was nameless like the rest. She, however, clearly belongs to Asia and did not come to this land now called by the Hellenes Europe, but only from Phoenicia to Crete, and from Crete to Lycia. Let this suffice for what has been said about these matters; we will adopt the accounts commonly accepted.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 46
paragraphs: Now the region of the Euxine against which Darius was preparing to march contains, apart from the Scythian race, the most ignorant nations of all lands; for we can point to no people in the region of the Pontus distinguished for ability, nor do we know of any learned man who has arisen there, apart from the Scythian nation and Anacharsis. By the Scythians, one thing—the most important of all human matters—has been discovered more cleverly than by any other men we know; in other respects, I have no great admiration for them. That most important thing they have discovered is such that no one who has come to attack them can escape again; and if they do not wish to be found, it is impossible to catch them. For they who have no cities founded, no walls built, but carry their houses with them and are mounted archers, living not from the plough but from cattle, and whose dwellings are upon wagons—these are surely invincible and impossible to approach.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 47
paragraphs: They have worked this out because their land is suited to it and the rivers are their allies. First, the land is plain country, grassy and well watered, and the rivers flowing through it are not much fewer in number than the canals in Egypt. Of these, I will name those that are noteworthy and can be navigated from the sea: Ister with its five mouths; and after this, Tyras, Hypanis, Borysthenes, Panticapes, Hypakyris, Gerros, and Tanaïs. These flow as I shall now describe.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 48
paragraphs: The Ister, the greatest of all the rivers we know, flows always with equal volume in summer and in winter alike. It is the first of the Scythian rivers towards the west, and it has become the greatest of all rivers because other rivers flow into it. These are the ones that make it great. Five in number are those which flow through the Scythian land: the one the Scythians call Porata and the Hellenes Pyretos, and besides this, Tiarantos, Araros, Naparis, and Ordessos. The first-mentioned is a great river lying to the east, and there it joins its waters with the Ister. The second, Tiarantos, is more to the west and smaller. The Araros, Naparis, and Ordessos flow into the Ister running between these two.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 49
paragraphs: These are the native Scythian rivers that join to swell its stream, while from the Agathyrsians flows the Maris, which joins the Ister. From the summits of Haimos flow three other great rivers towards the north wind and fall into it: Atlas, Auras, and Tibisis. Through Thrace and the Thracian Crobyzians flow the rivers Athrys, Noes, and Artanes, running into the Ister; and from the Paionians and Mount Rhodope the river Kios, cutting through Haimos in the middle, also runs into it. From the Illyrians the river Angros flows northwards and runs out into the Triballian plain and into the river Brongos, and the Brongos flows into the Ister; thus the Ister receives both these great rivers. From the region above the Ombricans, the river Carpis and another river, the Alpis, also flow towards the north wind and run into it; for the Ister in fact flows through the whole of Europe, beginning in the land of the Celts, who after the Kynesians dwell furthest west of all the peoples of Europe. Flowing thus through all Europe, it falls into the sea alongside Scythia.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 50
paragraphs: So it is because these named rivers and many others join their waters together that the Ister becomes the greatest of rivers; for if we compare single streams, the Nile is superior in volume of water, since no river or spring flows into it to contribute to its volume. The Ister flows at an equal level always, both in summer and winter, for some such reason as this, I suppose. In winter it is at its natural size, or becomes only a little larger than usual, since this land receives very little rain in winter but constantly has snow; whereas in summer the snow that fell in winter, being abundant, melts and runs from all parts into the Ister. This snow, running into the river, helps to swell its volume, and with it also many violent showers of rain—for it rains during summer. Thus the waters mingling with the Ister are more copious in summer than in winter by roughly as much as the water the sun draws to himself in summer exceeds what he draws in winter. By the setting of these things against one another, a balance is produced, so that the river is seen to be of equal volume always.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 51
paragraphs: One, I say, of the rivers the Scythians have is the Ister; and after it the Tyras, which starts from the north and begins its course from a large lake that is the boundary between the land of the Scythians and that of the Neuroi. At its mouth are settled those Hellenes called the Tyritai.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 52
paragraphs: The third river is the Hypanis, which rises in Scythia and flows from a great lake around which graze white wild horses; this lake is rightly called “Mother of Hypanis.” From this the river Hypanis takes its rise, and for a distance of five days' sail it flows shallow and with sweet water still; but from that point on, for four days' sail towards the sea, it is very bitter, for the water of a bitter spring flows into it—so exceedingly bitter that, small as it is, it changes the water of the Hypanis by mingling with it, though the Hypanis is a river to which few are equal in greatness. This spring is on the border between the lands of the agricultural Scythians and the Alazonians, and its name, and the name of the place from which it flows, is in Scythian Exampaios, and in the Hellenic tongue Hierai Hodoi. The Tyras and the Hypanis approach one another in their windings in the land of the Alazonians, but after this each turns off and the space between them widens as they flow.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 53
paragraphs: Fourth is the river Borysthenes, which is both the largest of these after the Ister and also, in our opinion, the most serviceable, not only of the Scythian rivers but of all the rivers of the world besides, except only the Nile of Egypt—for no other river can be compared with the Nile. Of the rest, however, the Borysthenes is the most serviceable, since it provides the fairest and richest pastures for cattle; and fish which are by far the best and most numerous of any river; and the sweetest water to drink; and it flows with a clear stream, though others beside it are turbid; and along its banks crops grow better than anywhere else, while in parts not sown, grass grows deeper. Moreover, at its mouth salt forms of itself in abundance; and it produces huge spineless fish, which they call antacaioi, used for salting, as well as many other things worthy of wonder. As far as the region of the Gerrians, which is a forty days' voyage, the Borysthenes is known as flowing from the north wind; but beyond this, no one can tell through what nations it flows. It is certain, however, that it runs through desert to the land of the agricultural Scythians, for these Scythians dwell along its banks for a distance of ten days' sail. Of this river alone and of the Nile, I cannot tell where the sources are, nor, I think, can any of the Hellenes. When the Borysthenes comes near the sea in its course, the Hypanis mingles with it, running out into the same marsh; and the space between these two rivers, a kind of beak of land, is called the Point of Hippoles, and in it is placed a temple of the Mother. Opposite the temple, on the river Hypanis, the Borysthenites are settled.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 54
paragraphs: Such is the account of these rivers. After them there is a fifth river, called the Panticapes. This also flows both from the north and from a lake, and in the space between this river and the Borysthenes dwell the agricultural Scythians. It runs out into the region of Hylaia, and having passed by this, mingles with the Borysthenes.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 55
paragraphs: Sixth comes the river Hypakyris, which rises from a lake and flowing through the midst of the nomadic Scythians runs out into the sea by the city of Carkinitis, skirting on its right bank the region of Hylaia and the so-called Racecourse of Achilles.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 56
paragraphs: Seventh is the Gerros, which branches off from the Borysthenes near the point where the Borysthenes ceases to be known. It branches off, I say, in this region and has the same name the region itself bears, namely Gerros. As it flows to the sea, it forms the border between the country of the nomadic Scythians and that of the Royal Scythians, and runs out into the Hypakyris.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 57
paragraphs: The eighth is the river Tanaïs, which begins its course from a large lake and runs out into a still larger lake called Maeotis, which is the boundary between the Royal Scythians and the Sauromatai. Into this Tanaïs falls another river, whose name is Hyrgis.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 58
paragraphs: Such are the noteworthy rivers with which the Scythians are provided. As for cattle, the grass that grows in the land of Scythia is the most productive of bile of any grass we know; and you may judge that this is so by opening the bodies of the cattle.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 59
paragraphs: Such abundant supply have they of the most important things. As for the rest, their customs are as follows. The gods they propitiate by worship are these only: Hestia most of all, then Zeus and the Earth (supposing Earth is the wife of Zeus), and after these Apollo, Aphrodite Urania, Heracles, and Ares. All the Scythians have the worship of these established, and the so-called Royal Scythians also sacrifice to Poseidon. Hestia is called in Scythian Tabiti, and Zeus, most rightly named in my opinion, is called Papaios; Earth is called Api, Apollo Oitosyros, Aphrodite Urania Argimpasa, and Poseidon Thagimasidas. It is not their custom, however, to make images, altars, or temples to any except Ares, but to him they are accustomed to make them.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 60
paragraphs: They have the same manner of sacrifice established for all their religious rites, and it is performed thus. The victim stands with its fore-feet tied, and the sacrificing priest stands behind it; by pulling the end of the cord he throws the beast down. As the victim falls, he calls on the god to whom he is sacrificing, then at once throws a noose around its neck, inserts a small stick, twists it, and so strangles the animal, without either lighting a fire or making any first offering from the victim, or pouring any libation over it. When he has strangled it and flayed off the skin, he proceeds to boil it.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 61
paragraphs: Now since the land of Scythia is exceedingly ill-wooded, this contrivance has been invented for boiling the flesh. Having flayed the victims, they strip the flesh off the bones and put it into cauldrons (if they have any of native make, which much resemble Lesbian mixing-bowls except that they are much larger). Into these they put the flesh and boil it by lighting the bones of the victim beneath them. If, however, they have no cauldron at hand, they put all the flesh into the stomachs of the victims, add water, and light the bones beneath them; these blaze up beautifully, and the stomachs easily hold the flesh once stripped from the bones. Thus an ox is made to boil itself, and the other kinds of victims also boil themselves. When the flesh is boiled, the sacrificer takes a first offering of the flesh and vital organs and casts it before him. They sacrifice various kinds of cattle, but especially horses.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 62
paragraphs: To the other gods they sacrifice these kinds of beasts in this way; but to Ares as follows. In each district of the various governments they have a temple of Ares set up thus: bundles of brushwood are heaped up for about three furlongs in length and in breadth, though less in height; and on the top a level square is made, three of its sides sheer, but ascendable by the remaining side. Every year they pile on a hundred and fifty wagon-loads of brushwood, because it is constantly settling down on account of the weather. Upon this pile each people has an ancient iron sword set up, which is the sacred symbol of Ares. To this sword they bring yearly offerings of cattle and horses. In addition, beyond what they give to the other gods, they offer this sacrifice: of all the enemies they take captive in war, they sacrifice one man in every hundred—not in the same manner as they sacrifice cattle, but in a different way. First they pour wine over the men's heads; after that they cut their throats, so that the blood runs into a bowl; and then they carry this up to the top of the brushwood pile and pour the blood over the sword. This, I say, they carry up; and meanwhile below, beside the temple, they do thus: they cut off all the right arms of the slaughtered men, with the hands, and throw them up into the air; then, when they have finished offering the other victims, they go away. The arm lies wherever it chances to have fallen, and the corpse lies apart from it.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 63
paragraphs: Such are the sacrifices established among them; but of swine they make no use, nor indeed do they keep them at all in their land.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 64
paragraphs: Matters of war are arranged among them thus. When a Scythian kills his first man, he drinks some of his blood; and of all those he kills in the battle he brings the heads to the king—for if he has brought a head he shares in the spoil they have taken, but otherwise not. He takes off the skin of the head by cutting it round the ears, then taking hold of the scalp and shaking it off. Afterwards he scrapes off the flesh with the rib of an ox, and works the skin with his hands; and when he has thus tempered it, he keeps it as a napkin for wiping his hands, and hangs it from the bridle of the horse he rides, taking pride in it. For whoever has the most skins for wiping his hands is judged the bravest man. Many also make cloaks to wear from the skins they have stripped off, sewing them together like shepherds' skin-cloaks; and many take the skin, together with the finger-nails, from the right hands of their dead enemies and make them into covers for their quivers. For human skin, it seems, is both thick and glossy, more brilliantly white than any other skin. Many also take the skins from the whole bodies of men, stretch them on pieces of wood, and carry them about on their horses.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 65
paragraphs: Such are their established customs in these matters. To the skulls themselves—not of all enemies, but of their greatest—they do as follows. The man saws off everything below the eyebrows and cleans out the inside. If he is poor, he merely stretches ox-hide around it and uses it so; but if he is rich, besides stretching the ox-hide he gilds the inside, and uses it as a drinking-cup. They do this also if any of their own family has been at odds with them and the man prevails over his adversary in a trial before the king. When strangers whom he greatly esteems come to him, he sets these skulls before them and adds the comment that these, though his own kin, had made war on him, and he had got the better of them; and this they regard as a proof of manly virtue.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 66
paragraphs: Once every year each ruler of a district mixes in his own district a bowl of wine, from which those Scythians drink who have killed enemies; those who have not done so do not taste the wine, but sit apart dishonoured—and this is the greatest of disgraces among them. Those who have killed a very great number of men drink with two cups together at the same time.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 67
paragraphs: Diviners are many among the Scythians, and they divine with a number of willow rods in the following manner. They bring large bundles of rods, lay them on the ground, and unroll them; then, setting each rod by itself apart, they prophesy; and while speaking thus, they roll the rods together again, and after that place them in order a second time one by one. This manner of divination they have from their fathers. But the Enareës, or “man-women,” say that Aphrodite gave them the gift of divination, and they divine accordingly with the bark of the linden-tree. Having divided the linden-bark into three strips, the man twists them together in his fingers and untwists them again, and as he does this he utters the oracle.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 68
paragraphs: When the king of the Scythians is sick, he sends for three of the diviners—those most in repute—who divine in the manner described. They usually say something like this: that so-and-so has sworn falsely by the hearth of the king, naming one of the citizens, whoever it may happen to be. For it is the prevailing custom of the Scythians to swear by the hearth of the king when they wish to take the most solemn oath. The one whom they say has sworn falsely is brought in at once, held fast on both sides; and when he has come, the diviners charge him that their divination shows he has sworn falsely by the king's hearth, and that for this reason the king is suffering pain. He denies it and says he did not swear falsely, and complains indignantly. When he denies it, the king sends for other diviners twice as many in number, and if these also, by looking into their divination, pronounce him guilty of false swearing, they at once cut off the man's head, and the first diviners divide his goods among themselves by lot. But if the diviners who came later acquit him, other diviners come in, and then others after them. If the greater number acquit the man, the sentence is that the first diviners shall themselves be put to death.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 69
paragraphs: They put them to death accordingly in this way. First they fill a wagon with brushwood and yoke oxen to it. Then, having bound the feet of the diviners, tied their hands behind them, and gagged their mouths, they fasten them down in the middle of the brushwood, set fire to it, frighten the oxen, and let them go. Often the oxen are burned to death together with the diviners; often they escape after being scorched, when the pole to which they are fastened has burned through. The Scythians burn the diviners in this way for other causes too, calling them false prophets. When the king puts any to death, he does not leave their sons alive either; he kills all the males, but does no harm to the females.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 70
paragraphs: The Scythians make oaths to anyone thus. They pour wine into a great earthenware cup and mix with it the blood of those taking the oath together, either pricking with an awl or cutting with a dagger a little way into their body; and then they dip into the cup a sword, arrows, a battle-axe, and a javelin. Having done this, they invoke many curses on the breaker of the oath, and afterwards they drink it off, both those taking the oath and the most honoured of their company.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 71
paragraphs: The burial-place of the kings is in the land of the Gerrians, the point up to which the Borysthenes is navigable. In this place, when their king has died, they make a large square excavation in the earth; and when it is ready, they take up the corpse (the body having been covered over with wax, the belly ripped open and cleansed and then sewn together again after being filled with cut-up galingale, spices, parsley-seed, and anise), and they convey it in a wagon to another nation. Those who receive the corpse thus conveyed to them do the same as the Royal Scythians: they cut off part of their ear, shave their hair round about, cut themselves all over the arms, tear at their forehead and nose, and pass arrows through their left hand. From there they convey the corpse of the king in the wagon to another of the nations over whom they rule; and those to whom they had first come accompany them. When they have gone round to all, conveying the corpse, they are in the land of the Gerrians, who have their settlements furthest away of all the nations over whom they rule, and they have reached the spot where the burial place is. After this, having placed the corpse in the tomb upon a bed of leaves, they stick spears along either side of the corpse, stretch pieces of wood across them, and cover the space with matting. Then they strangle and bury in the remaining space of the tomb one of the king's concubines, his cup-bearer, his cook, his groom, his attendant, and his messenger, along with horses, a first portion of everything else, and cups of gold (for silver they do not use at all, nor yet bronze). Having done this, they all join together to pile up a great mound, vying with one another and zealously trying to make it as large as possible.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 72
paragraphs: Afterwards, when the year comes round again, they do as follows. They take the most capable of the remaining servants—these are native Scythians, for whoever the king himself commands serves him, and his servants are not bought for money. Of these attendants they strangle fifty, and also fifty of the finest horses; and when they have taken out their bowels and cleansed the belly, they fill it with chaff and sew it together again. Then they set the half of a wheel upon two stakes with the hollow side upwards, and the other half of the wheel upon two more stakes, and fix a number of these in this manner. After this they run thick stakes through the length of the horses as far as the necks and mount them on the wheels; the front pieces of wheel support the horses' shoulders, while those behind bear up their bellies, going by the side of the thighs; and both front and hind legs hang in the air. On the horses they put bridles and bits, stretching the bridles tight in front of them and tying them to pegs.
