And of the fifty young men who have been strangled they mount each on his horse, having first run a straight stake through each body along the spine up to the neck; a part of this stake projects below, and they fasten it into a socket made in the other stake that runs through the horse. Having set horsemen such as I have described in a circle round the tomb, they ride away.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 73
paragraphs: Thus they bury their kings. As for the other Scythians, when they die, their nearest relations carry them round laid in wagons to their friends in succession; and each of them, when he receives the body, entertains those who accompany it, and before the corpse they serve up about the same quantity of everything as before the others. Thus private persons are carried about for forty days, and then buried. After the burial, the Scythians purify themselves in the following way. They soap their heads and wash them well; and for their body, they set up three stakes leaning towards one another, and around these they stretch woollen felt coverings, and having closed them as tightly as possible, they throw red-hot stones into a basin placed in the middle of the stakes and the felt coverings.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 74
paragraphs: Now they have hemp growing in their land, which is very like flax except in thickness and height, for in these respects the hemp is much superior. It grows both of itself and with cultivation; and of it the Thracians even make garments that are very like those made of flaxen thread—so like, that one not specially familiar with it could not tell whether the garments were of flax or hemp, and one who had never before seen hemp cloth would suppose the garment was made of flax.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 75
paragraphs: The Scythians then take the seed of this hemp and creep under the felt coverings, and throw the seed upon the red-hot stones. It smoulders like incense and produces a vapour so thick that no vapour-bath in Hellas could surpass it; and the Scythians, delighted with the vapour-bath, howl like wolves. This is their substitute for washing, for they do not in fact wash their bodies at all with water. Their women, however, pound with a rough stone the wood of the cypress, cedar, and frankincense tree, pouring water in with it, and with the resulting thick paste they plaster their whole body and face. Not only does a sweet smell attach to them from this, but when they take off the plaster the next day, their skin is clean and shining.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 76
paragraphs: This nation too is very averse to adopting foreign customs, rejecting even those of other tribes among themselves, but especially those of the Hellenes—as the histories of Anacharsis and later of Skyles proved. As for Anacharsis, when he was returning to the abodes of the Scythians after having visited many lands and displayed in them much wisdom, he sailed through the Hellespont and put in to Kyzicos. Finding the people of Kyzicos celebrating a festival with great magnificence in honour of the Mother of the gods, Anacharsis vowed to the Mother that if he returned safe and sound to his own land, he would sacrifice to her with the same rites as he saw the men of Kyzicos perform, and also hold a night festival. So when he came to Scythia, he went down into the region called Hylaia (which runs along the racecourse of Achilles and happens to be quite full of all sorts of trees). Into this, I say, Anacharsis went down and proceeded to perform all the ceremonies of the festival in honour of the goddess, with a kettle-drum and with images hung about his person. One of the Scythians perceived him doing this and declared it to King Saulios; the king came himself, and when he saw Anacharsis doing this, shot him with an arrow and killed him. So at the present time, if one asks about Anacharsis, the Scythians say they do not know him—for this reason, that he had gone out of his own country to Hellas and adopted foreign customs. As I heard from Tymnes the steward of Ariapeithes, he was the paternal uncle of Idanthyrsos king of the Scythians, and the son of Gnuros son of Lycos son of Spargapeithes. If then Anacharsis was of this house, let him know he died by the hand of his brother, for Idanthyrsos was the son of Saulios, and it was Saulios who killed Anacharsis.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 77
paragraphs: I have, however, heard another story, told by the Peloponnesians: that Anacharsis was sent out by the king of the Scythians and so became a disciple of Hellas; and that when he returned, he said to the one who had sent him that the Hellenes were all busied about every kind of cleverness except the Lacedaemonians, and that these alone knew how to exchange speech sensibly. This story, however, has been invented without any ground by the Hellenes themselves; however that may be, the man was killed in the manner related above.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 78
paragraphs: So this man fared badly because of foreign customs and contact with the Hellenes. Many years afterwards, Skyles son of Ariapeithes suffered nearly the same fate. For Ariapeithes king of the Scythians had several sons, among them Skyles; and he was born of a woman of Istria, certainly not a native Scythian; and this mother taught him the language and letters of Hellas. Afterwards, in course of time, Ariapeithes was brought to his end by treachery at the hands of Spargapeithes king of the Agathyrsians, and Skyles succeeded to the kingdom. He took not only that but also his father's wife, whose name was Opoia; Opoia was a native Scythian, and from her Oricos had been born to Ariapeithes. Now when Skyles was king of the Scythians, he was by no means satisfied with the Scythian manner of life, but was far more inclined towards Hellenic ways because of the upbringing he had received. He used to do something like this: when he came with the Scythians in arms to the city of the Borysthenites (these Borysthenites say they are from Miletos)—when Skyles came to this city, he would leave his band in the suburbs and go himself within the walls and close the gates. Then he would lay aside his Scythian gear and put on Hellenic garments, and wearing them he would go about in the market-place with no guards or any other man accompanying him (and meanwhile the gates were watched, so that none of the Scythians might see him wearing this dress). In other respects too he adopted Hellenic manners of life, and he used to perform worship to the gods according to the customs of the Hellenes. Then, after staying a month or more, he would put on Scythian dress and depart. He did this many times, and he built for himself a house in Borysthenes and took a woman of the place as his wife.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 79
paragraphs: Since, however, it was fated that evil should befall him, it happened on an occasion like this. He conceived a desire to be initiated in the rites of Bacchus-Dionysos; and just as he was about to receive the initiation, a very great portent occurred. He had in the city of the Borysthenites a large and lavishly built house—which I mentioned a little before—with sphinxes and griffins of white stone placed around it. On this house Zeus let fall a thunderbolt, and the house was utterly burned down; but Skyles nonetheless completed his initiation. Now the Scythians make the rites of Bacchus a reproach against the Hellenes, for they say it is not fitting to invent a god like this, one who drives men to frenzy. So when Skyles had been initiated into the rites of Bacchus, one of the Borysthenites went off to the Scythians and said: “You Scythians laugh at us because we perform the rite of Bacchus and because the god seizes us; now this divinity has seized your king as well, and he is both joining in the rite of Bacchus and maddened by the god. If you disbelieve me, follow, and I will show you.” The chief men of the Scythians followed him, and the Borysthenite led them secretly into the town and placed them on a tower. So when Skyles passed by with the company of revellers, and the Scythians saw him joining in the rite of Bacchus, they were exceedingly grieved, and they went out and reported to the whole band what they had seen.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 80
paragraphs: After this, when Skyles was riding out again to his own abode, the Scythians took his brother Octamasades for their leader—a son of the daughter of Teres—and rose in revolt against Skyles. When he perceived what was being done against him and for what reason, he fled for refuge to Thrace. Octamasades, informed of this, marched upon Thrace. When he had come to the river Ister, the Thracians met him; and as they were about to engage in battle, Sitalkes sent a messenger to Octamasades with this word: “Why must we test one another in fight? You are my sister's son, and you hold my brother in your power. Give him back to me, and I will deliver to you your brother Skyles; and let neither of us put our armies in peril, neither you nor I.” Thus Sitalkes proposed through a herald; for a brother of Sitalkes was with Octamasades, having gone into exile for fear of him. Octamasades agreed; by giving up his own maternal uncle to Sitalkes, he received his brother Skyles in exchange. Sitalkes, when he received his brother, led him away as a prisoner, but Octamasades cut off Skyles' head there on the spot. So carefully do the Scythians guard their own customs, and such are the penalties they inflict on those who take foreign customs besides their own.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 81
paragraphs: How many the Scythians are I was not able to ascertain precisely, but I heard various reports of the number: reports both that they are very many and that they are few, at least as regards the true Scythians. Thus far, however, they gave me evidence for my own eyes. Between the river Borysthenes and the Hypanis there is a place called Exampaios, which I mentioned earlier, saying that there is in it a spring of bitter water whose waters flow in and make the river Hypanis undrinkable. In this place there stands a bronze bowl at least six times the size of the mixing-bowl at the entrance of the Pontus which Pausanias son of Cleombrotos dedicated; and for him who has never seen that, I will make the matter clear by saying that the bowl in Scythia easily holds six hundred amphors, and its thickness is six fingers. The natives of the place told me this bowl had been made of arrowheads; for their king, whose name was Ariantas, wishing to know how many the Scythians were, ordered every Scythian to bring him a single arrowhead from his own arrow, and threatened death to whoever should not bring one. So a great multitude of arrowheads was brought; and he resolved to make a memorial of them and leave it behind him. From these, they said, he made this bronze bowl and dedicated it in this place, Exampaios.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 82
paragraphs: This is what I heard about the number of the Scythians. Now this land has no marvellous things, except that it has rivers by far larger and more numerous than those of any other land. One thing, however, it has that is worthy of wonder besides the rivers and the greatness of the plain: a footprint of Heracles is pointed out in the rock by the bank of the river Tyras, which in shape is like the mark of a man's foot but in size is two cubits long. Such, then, is this; and I will now return to the history I was about to tell at first.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 83
paragraphs: While Darius was preparing to march against the Scythians and sending messengers to assign some of his subjects the furnishing of a land army, others the furnishing of ships, and others the bridging of the Thracian Bosphorus, Artabanos, son of Hystaspes and brother of Darius, urged him by no means to make the march against the Scythians, telling him how difficult the Scythians were to deal with. But since he did not persuade him, though he gave good counsel, he ceased to press. Darius, when all his preparations were complete, began to march his army forth from Susa.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 84
paragraphs: Then one of the Persians, Oiobazos, made a request of Darius: since he had three sons, all serving on the expedition, could one be left behind for him? Darius said that, since he was a friend and made a reasonable request, he would leave behind all the sons. Oiobazos was greatly rejoiced, supposing his sons had been released from service; but Darius commanded those in charge of such things to put all the sons of Oiobazos to death.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 85
paragraphs: These then were left behind, having been slain on the spot. Meanwhile Darius set out from Susa and arrived at the place on the Bosphorus where the bridge of ships had been made, in the territory of Chalcedon. There he embarked in a ship and sailed to the so-called Kyanean rocks, which the Hellenes say formerly moved back and forth; and taking his seat at the temple, he gazed out over the Pontus, which is a sight well worth seeing. Of all seas it is the most marvellous in its nature. Its length is eleven thousand one hundred furlongs, and its breadth, where widest, three thousand three hundred; and the mouth of this great sea is only four furlongs broad. The length of the mouth—that is, of the neck of water called the Bosphorus, where, as I said, the bridge of ships had been built—is not less than a hundred and twenty furlongs. The Bosphorus extends to the Propontis; and the Propontis, five hundred furlongs in breadth and one thousand four hundred in length, has its outlet into the Hellespont, which at its narrowest is only seven furlongs wide, though four hundred furlongs in length; and the Hellespont runs out into that expanse of sea called the Aegean.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 86
paragraphs: I have made these measurements as follows. A ship on average completes in a long day a distance of seventy thousand fathoms, and in a night sixty thousand. Now we know that from the mouth of the Sea to the river Phasis (where the Pontus is longest) is a voyage of nine days and eight nights, which amounts to one hundred and eleven myriads of fathoms—that is, eleven thousand one hundred furlongs. Then from the land of the Sindians to Themiskyra on the river Thermodon (where the Pontus is broadest) is a voyage of three days and two nights, amounting to thirty-three myriads of fathoms, or three thousand three hundred furlongs. This, then, is how I have measured the Pontus, the Bosphorus, and the Hellespont, and their nature is such as has been said. The Pontus also has a lake whose outlet is into it, a lake not much smaller than the Pontus itself; it is called Maeotis, and also “Mother of the Pontus.”

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 87
paragraphs: Darius, having gazed on the Pontus, sailed back to the bridge, of which Mandrocles a Samian had been chief constructor. Having gazed on the Bosphorus as well, he set up beside it two pillars of white stone with characters cut upon them—on one Assyrian, on the other Hellenic—giving the names of all the nations he was leading with him; and he was leading all over whom he ruled. The whole number of them, without the naval force, was reckoned at seventy myriads including cavalry; and ships had been gathered together to the number of six hundred. These pillars the Byzantians later conveyed to their city, after the events of which I speak, and used them for the altar of Artemis Orthosia, except for one stone which was left standing beside the temple of Dionysos in Byzantion, covered with Assyrian characters. Now the place on the Bosphorus where Darius made his bridge is, as I conclude, midway between Byzantion and the temple at the mouth of the Pontus.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 88
paragraphs: After this, Darius, being pleased with the floating bridge, rewarded its chief constructor, Mandrocles the Samian, with gifts tenfold. As an offering from these, Mandrocles had a painting made of figures presenting the whole scene of the bridge over the Bosphorus, with King Darius seated in a prominent chair and his army crossing over. He had this painted and dedicated it as an offering in the temple of Hera, with the following inscription:

“Having bridged the fish-abounding straits of the Bosphorus, to Hera Mandrocles dedicates this, a memorial of his work. A crown on himself he set, and he brought the Samians glory; and for Darius he performed all things according to his mind.”

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 89
paragraphs: This memorial was made of him who constructed the bridge; and Darius, after he had rewarded Mandrocles with gifts, crossed over into Europe, having first commanded the Ionians to sail into the Pontus as far as the river Ister, and when they reached the Ister, to wait for him there while bridging the river in the meantime. The chief of his naval force were the Ionians, the Aeolians, and the Hellespontians. So the fleet sailed between the Kyanean rocks and made straight for the Ister; and then they sailed up the river a two days' voyage from the sea and proceeded to bridge the neck, as it were, of the river, where the mouths of the Ister branch off. Darius meanwhile, having crossed the Bosphorus on the floating bridge, was advancing through Thrace; and when he came to the sources of the river Tearos, he encamped there for three days.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 90
paragraphs: Now the Tearos is said by those who dwell near it to be the best of all rivers, both in other healing qualities and especially for curing skin diseases in men and horses. Its springs are thirty-eight in number, all flowing from the same rock, some cold and others warm. The way to them is of equal length from the city of Heraion near Perinthos and from Apollonia on the Euxine Sea—two days' journey by each road. This Tearos runs into the river Contadesdos, the Contadesdos into the Agrianes, and the Agrianes into the Hebros, which flows into the sea by the city of Ainos.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 91
paragraphs: Darius, having come to this river and encamped there, was pleased with it and set up a pillar there also, with the following inscription: “The headwaters of the river Tearos give the best and fairest water of all rivers; and to them came, leading an army against the Scythians, the best and fairest of all men, Darius son of Hystaspes, king of the Persians and of all the Continent.” These were the words written there.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 92
paragraphs: Darius then set out from there and came to another river, whose name is Artescos, which flows through the land of the Odrysians. Having come to this river, he acted as follows. He marked out a place for his army and bade every man, as he passed out by it, place one stone in this appointed place. When the army had done so, he marched his army away, leaving behind great mounds of these stones.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 93
paragraphs: But before he came to the Ister, he conquered first the Getai, who believe in immortality. For the Thracians who occupy Salmydessos and are settled above the cities of Apollonia and Mesambria, called the Kyrmianai and the Nipsaioi, delivered themselves up to Darius without a fight. But the Getai, who are the bravest and most upright in their dealings of all the Thracians, having resorted to obstinacy, were forthwith subdued.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 94
paragraphs: Their belief in immortality is of this kind: they hold that they do not die, but that he who is killed goes to Salmoxis, a divinity (whom some of them call Gebeleizis). At intervals of four years they send one of their own people, chosen by lot, as a messenger to Salmoxis, charging him with such requests as they have to make on each occasion. They send him thus: certain men appointed for this hold three javelins, and others meanwhile take hold of the man being sent to Salmoxis, both by his hands and feet, and first they swing him up, then throw him into the air so that he falls upon the spear points. If he is pierced through and killed, they think the god is favourable to them; but if he is not killed, they find fault with the messenger himself, calling him a worthless man, and then, having faulted him, they send another. They give him the charge beforehand, while he is still alive. These same Thracians also shoot arrows up towards the sky when thunder and lightning come, and use threats against the god, believing that no other god exists except their own.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 95
paragraphs: This Salmoxis, I hear from the Hellenes who dwell about the Hellespont and the Pontus, was a man, and became a slave in Samos—a slave, in fact, of Pythagoras son of Mnesarchos. After becoming free, he gained great wealth and afterwards returned to his own land. Since the Thracians live hardly and are rather simple-minded, this Salmoxis, being acquainted with the Ionian way of life and with manners more cultivated than the Thracians were used to see—for he had associated with Hellenes, and not least with Pythagoras, who was no mean philosopher among them—prepared a banqueting hall, where he received and feasted the chief men of the tribe, instructing them meanwhile that neither he himself nor his guests nor their descendants in succession after them would die; but that they would come to a place where they would live forever and have all things good. While doing and saying these things, he was meanwhile making for himself a chamber under the ground. When his chamber was finished, he disappeared from among the Thracians and went down into the underground chamber, where he continued to live for three years. They grieved for his loss and mourned for him as dead. Then in the fourth year he appeared to the Thracians, and in this way what Salmoxis said became credible to them.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 96
paragraphs: Thus they say he did; but as to this matter and the underground chamber, I neither disbelieve it nor do I very firmly believe, but I think that this Salmoxis lived many years before Pythagoras. However, whether there ever lived such a man as Salmoxis, or whether he is simply a native deity of the Getai, let us bid farewell to him now.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 97
paragraphs: These people, then, with the manners I have described, were subdued by the Persians and accompanied the rest of the army. When Darius and with him the land army arrived at the Ister, then after all had crossed over, Darius commanded the Ionians to break up the floating bridge and to accompany him by land, together with the rest of the troops on the ships. As the Ionians were just about to break it up and do as he commanded, Coës son of Erxander, commander of the Mytilenians, said this to Darius, having first asked whether he was willing to hear an opinion from one who wished to offer it: “O king, since you are about to march into a land where no cultivated ground will be seen nor any inhabited town, let this bridge remain where it is, leaving as its guard the same men who constructed it. Then, if we find the Scythians and fare as we wish, we have a way of return; and even if we cannot find them, at least our way of return is secured. For that we should be defeated by the Scythians in battle I have never feared; rather, I fear that we may not be able to find them, and may suffer some disaster wandering about. Perhaps someone will say I am speaking for my own advantage, so that I may remain behind; but in truth, O king, I am offering you the opinion I found best for you, and I myself shall go with you and not be left behind.” With this opinion Darius was greatly pleased, and answered: “Friend from Lesbos, when I have returned safe to my house, be sure to appear before me, that I may requite your good counsel with good deeds.”

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 98
paragraphs: Having said this, and having tied sixty knots in a thong, he summoned the despots of the Ionians to speak with him and said: “Men of Ionia, know that I have abandoned the opinion I formerly declared regarding the bridge. Take this thong and do as I now say. As soon as you see me go forward against the Scythians, from that time begin and untie one knot each day. If within this time I am not back, and you find the days marked by the knots have gone by, sail away to your own lands. Until then, since our resolve has thus changed, guard the floating bridge, showing all diligence to keep it safe. Acting thus, you will do me a very acceptable service.” So said Darius, and he hastened on his march forward.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 99
paragraphs: Now in front of Scythia, in the direction towards the sea, lies Thrace; and where a bay is formed in this land, Scythia begins, into which the Ister runs out, the mouth of the river facing the south-east wind. Beginning at the Ister, I am about to describe the coast land of Scythia proper with regard to measurement. From the Ister begins the original land of Scythia, which lies towards the midday and the south wind, and extends as far as the city called Carkinitis. After this, the part that still lies on the coast of the same sea, a country which is mountainous and projects towards the Pontus, is occupied by the Tauric race, as far as the peninsula called the “Rugged Chersonese”; and this extends to the sea which lies towards the east wind. For two sides of the Scythian boundaries lie along the sea—one on the south, the other on the east—just as with Attica. The Tauroi, in truth, occupy a part of Scythia much resembling Attica; it is as if in Attica another race, not the Athenians, occupied the hill region of Sunion (supposing it to project more sharply at the point into the sea), the region cut off by a line from Thoricos to Anaphlystos. Such, if we may compare small things like this with great, is the shape of the Tauric land. For one who has not sailed along that part of the coast of Attica, I will make it clear by another comparison: it is as if in Iapygia another race, not the Iapygians, had cut off for themselves and were holding that extremity of the land bounded by a line beginning at the harbour of Brentesion and running to Taras. In mentioning these two similar cases, I am suggesting many other things as well to which the Tauric land has resemblance.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 100
paragraphs: After the Tauric land, Scythians come again at once, occupying the parts above the Tauroi and the coasts of the eastern sea—that is, the parts west of the Cimmerian Bosphorus and the Maeotian lake, as far as the river Tanaïs, which runs into the corner of this lake. In the upper parts, which extend inland, Scythia is bounded (as we know) first by the Agathyrsians, beginning from the Ister, then by the Neuroi, afterwards by the Androphagoi, and last by the Melanchlainoi.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 101
paragraphs: Scythia, then, looked upon as a four-sided figure with two of its sides bordered by the sea, has borders equal to one another in each direction—both the one extending inland and the one running along the sea. For from the Ister to the Borysthenes is ten days' journey, and from the Borysthenes to the Maeotian lake another ten; and the distance inland to the Melanchlainoi, who are settled above the Scythians, is twenty days' journey. Now I have reckoned the day's journey at two hundred furlongs; and by this reckoning the crosswise sides of Scythia would be four thousand furlongs in length, and the perpendiculars extending inland the same number. Such is the size of this land.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 102
paragraphs: Meanwhile the Scythians, having considered that they were not able by themselves to repel Darius' army in a pitched battle, proceeded to send messengers to their neighbours. Already the kings of these nations had come together and were taking counsel with one another, since so great an army was marching against them. Those who had come together were the kings of the Tauroi, Agathyrsians, Neuroi, Androphagoi, Melanchlainoi, Gelonians, Budinoi, and Sauromatai.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 103
paragraphs: Of these, the Tauroi have the following customs. They sacrifice to the “Maiden” both shipwrecked persons and those Hellenes they can capture by putting out to sea against them; and their manner of sacrifice is this: when they have made the first offering from the victim, they strike his head with a club. Some say they push the body down from the top of the cliff (for the temple is set on a cliff) and set the head up on a stake; but others, while agreeing about the heads, say the body is not pushed down from the cliff but buried in the earth. This divinity to whom they sacrifice, the Tauroi themselves say is Iphigeneia daughter of Agamemnon. Whatever enemies they capture they treat as follows: each man cuts off a head and carries it away to his house, then impales it on a long stake and sets it high above his house, usually above the chimney. They say these are suspended above as guards to preserve the whole house. This people makes its living by plunder and war.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 104
paragraphs: The Agathyrsians are the most luxurious of men and wear gold ornaments for the most part. They have promiscuous intercourse with their women, so that they may all be brothers to one another, and, all being nearly related, may feel no envy or malice among themselves. In their other customs they have come to resemble the Thracians.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 105
paragraphs: The Neuroi practise Scythian customs. One generation before Darius' expedition, it befell them that they were forced to quit their land entirely on account of serpents. For their land produced serpents in vast numbers, and still more fell upon them from the desert country beyond their borders, until, hard pressed, they left their own land and settled among the Budinoi. These men seem to be wizards; for it is said by the Scythians and by the Hellenes settled in the Scythian land that once every year each of the Neuroi becomes a wolf for a few days and then returns to his original form. For my part I do not believe them when they say this, but they say it nevertheless, and swear to it too.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 106
paragraphs: The Androphagoi have the most savage manners of all human beings, and they neither acknowledge any rule of right nor observe any customary law. They are nomads, and wear clothing like the Scythians, but they have a language of their own; and alone of all these nations they are man-eaters.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 107
paragraphs: The Melanchlainoi all wear black clothing, whence also comes their name; and they practise the customs of the Scythians.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 108
paragraphs: The Budinoi are a very great and numerous people, and they are all blue-eyed and fair of skin. In their land is built a city of wood called Gelonos, each side of its wall thirty furlongs in length and lofty as well, all made of wood. The houses are of wood too, and the temples; for there are in it temples of Hellenic gods furnished in Hellenic fashion with sacred images, altars, and shrines, all of wood. They keep festivals every other year to Dionysos and celebrate the rites of Bacchus; for the Gelonians are originally Hellenes, who migrated from the trading stations on the coast and settled among the Budinoi, and they speak partly the Scythian language and partly the Hellenic. The Budinoi, however, do not speak the same language as the Gelonians, nor is their manner of living the same.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 109
paragraphs: For the Budinoi are natives of the soil and a nomadic people, and alone of the nations in these parts feed on fir-cones; but the Gelonians are tillers of the ground, feed on grain, have gardens, and resemble the Budinoi neither in appearance nor in skin colour. However, by the Hellenes the Budinoi too are called Gelonians, though not rightly. Their land is all thickly overgrown with forests of all kinds of trees, and in the thickest forest there is a large and deep lake, surrounded by marshy ground and reeds. In this lake otters and beavers are caught, and certainly other wild animals with square-shaped faces; their fur is sewn as a fringe around their coats of skin, and the testicles are used by them for curing diseases of the womb.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 110
paragraphs: About the Sauromatai this tale is told. When the Hellenes had fought with the Amazons—now the Amazons are called by the Scythians Oiorpata, a name which in the Hellenic tongue means “slayers of men,” for they call “man” oior, and pata means “to slay”—then, the story goes, the Hellenes, having defeated them in the battle at the Thermodon, were sailing away, carrying with them in three ships as many Amazons as they had been able to take prisoner. These, out on the open sea, set upon the men and threw them out of the ships; but they knew nothing of ships, nor how to use rudders, sails, or oars, and after casting out the men they were driven about by wave and wind and came to that part of the Maeotian lake where Cremnoi stands. Cremnoi is in the land of the free Scythians. There the Amazons disembarked from their ships and made their way into the country; and having first met with a troop of horses feeding, they seized them, and mounted upon these they plundered the property of the Scythians.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 111
paragraphs: The Scythians meanwhile could not understand the matter, for they knew neither their speech nor their dress nor the race to which they belonged, but were amazed as to whence they had come, and thought they were men of a corresponding age. Finally they fought a battle against them; and after the battle the Scythians gained possession of the bodies of the dead, and thus discovered they were women. So they took counsel and resolved by no means to go on trying to kill them, but to send against them the youngest men from among themselves—judging the number so as to send just as many men as there were women. These were told to encamp near them and do whatever the women did; if the women came after them, they were not to fight, but to retire before them; and when the women stopped, they were to approach and encamp nearby. The Scythians adopted this plan because they wanted to have children born of them.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 112
paragraphs: The young men accordingly were sent out and did as commanded. When the Amazons perceived that they had not come to do them any harm, they let them alone, and the two camps approached nearer to one another every day. The young men, like the Amazons, had nothing but their arms and horses, and got their living the same way—by hunting and taking booty.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 113
paragraphs: Now the Amazons at midday used to scatter, either one by one or in pairs, going apart at some distance from each other to ease themselves; and the Scythians, having perceived this, did the same. One of the Scythians came near one of the Amazons who was off by herself, and she did not repulse him but allowed him to lie with her. She could not speak to him, for they did not understand one another's speech, but she made signs with her hand for him to come the next day to the same place and bring another with him, signifying that there should be two of them and she would bring another with her. So the young man, on his return, reported this to the others; and the next day he came himself to the place and brought another, and found the Amazon awaiting him with another in her company. Hearing of this, the rest of the young men in turn tamed for themselves the remaining Amazons.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 114
paragraphs: After this they joined their camps and lived together, each man having as his wife the one with whom he had first had dealings. The men could not learn the women's speech, but the women came to understand the men's. So when they understood one another, the men spoke to the Amazons thus: “We have parents and we have possessions. Let us, then, no longer lead this kind of life, but go to the main body of our people and dwell with them; we will have you as our wives and none others.” They replied: “We could not live with your women, for we and they have not the same customs. We shoot with bows, hurl javelins, and ride horses, but the works of women we never learnt. Your women, on the contrary, do none of these things we mentioned, but stay in the wagons and do the works of women, never going out to the chase or anywhere else. So we could not live in harmony with them. But if you wish to keep us as your wives and be thought honest men, go to your parents, obtain your share of the goods from them, and then let us go and dwell by ourselves.”

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 115
paragraphs: The young men agreed and did this. And when they had obtained their share of the goods and returned to the Amazons, the women said: “We are gripped by fear and trembling at the thought of dwelling in this place, since we have not only separated you from your fathers but also done great damage to your land. Since, then, you see fit to have us as your wives, do this together with us: let us depart from this land and cross the river Tanaïs and dwell there.”

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 116
paragraphs: The young men agreed to this also, and they crossed the Tanaïs and journeyed towards the rising sun for three days' journey from the Tanaïs, and also towards the north wind for three days' journey from the Maeotian lake. Having arrived at the place where they are now settled, they took up their abode there. From that time onward, the women of the Sauromatai practise their ancient way of living, going out regularly on horseback to the chase, both in the company of the men and apart from them, going regularly to war, and wearing the same dress as the men.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 117
paragraphs: The Sauromatai use the Scythian tongue, but have spoken it barbarously from the very first, since the Amazons did not learn it thoroughly well. As regards marriages, their rule is this: no maiden may marry until she has killed a man of the enemy; and some of them even grow old and die unmarried, because they cannot fulfil the requirement of the law.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 118
paragraphs: To the kings of these nations, mentioned in order, the Scythian messengers came, finding them gathered together, and spoke thus: that the Persian king, after subduing everything in the other continent, had laid a bridge over the neck of the Bosphorus and crossed over to this continent, and having crossed and subdued the Thracians, was now bridging the river Ister, wishing to bring all these regions also under his power. “Do not, then,” they said, “stand aloof and allow us to be destroyed, but let us be all of one mind and oppose the invader. If you do not do so, we on our part shall either be forced by necessity to leave our land, or we shall stay in it and make a treaty with the invader; for what else can we do if you are unwilling to help us? And afterwards, things will in no way be easier for you; for the Persian has come no less against you than against us, nor will it satisfy him to subdue us and keep his hands off you. We will mention strong evidence of the truth of what we say. If the Persian had been making this expedition against us alone, because he wished to take vengeance for our former lordship over him, he ought to have kept his hands off everyone else and come at once to invade our land, making it clear to all that he was marching to fight the Scythians and not the rest. But in fact, ever since he crossed over to this continent, he has compelled all who crossed his path to submit, and he now holds not only the other Thracians but also the Getai, our nearest neighbours.”

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 119
paragraphs: When the Scythians made this proposal, the kings who had come from the various nations took counsel together, and their opinions were divided. The kings of the Gelonians, Budinoi, and Sauromatai agreed among themselves and accepted the proposal that they should help the Scythians. But those of the Agathyrsians, Neuroi, Androphagoi, Melanchlainoi, and Tauroi answered the Scythians as follows: “If you had not been the first to wrong the Persians and begin the war, we should have thought you spoke justly in asking for what you now ask, and we should have yielded to your request and shared your fortunes. As it is, however, you invaded their land without us, and ruled the Persians for as long as God permitted; and now they in turn, since the same God stirs them up, are repaying you in kind. As for us, neither at that time did we do those men any wrong, nor shall we now attempt to wrong them unprovoked. If, however, the Persians come against our land too, and wrong us first, we too will refuse to submit; but until we see that, we shall remain by ourselves. For we hold the opinion that the Persians have come not against us, but against those who were the authors of the wrong.”

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 120
paragraphs: When the Scythians heard this answer reported, they planned not to fight a pitched battle openly, since these nations did not join them as allies, but to retire before the Persians and drive their cattle away from them, choking up with earth the wells and springs by which they passed and destroying the grass on the ground. For this they divided themselves into two bodies, and resolved that the Sauromatai should be joined with one of their divisions—namely that over which Scopasis was king—and that these should move on, if the Persians turned in that direction, straight towards the river Tanaïs, retreating before him along the shore of the Maeotian lake; and when the Persian marched back again, they were to come after and pursue him. This was one division of their kingdom, appointed to take the route described. The other two of the kingdoms—the large one of which Idanthyrsos was king, and the third of which Taxakis was king—were to join together into one, with the Gelonians and Budinoi added to them, and they too were to retire before the Persians one day's march in front of them, moving on out of their way and doing what had been planned. First they were to move straight for the countries that had refused alliance, so as to involve them in the war too; for though these had not voluntarily undertaken the war with the Persians, they were to be involved in it against their will. Afterwards, they were to return to their own land and attack the enemy, if it seemed good in council to do so.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 121
paragraphs: Having formed this plan, the Scythians went to meet Darius' army, sending the best of their horsemen ahead as scouts. But all the wagons in which their children and women lived they sent on, with all their cattle (leaving only enough to supply them with food), and ordered them to proceed continually towards the north wind. These, I say, were being sent on ahead.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 122
paragraphs: But when the scouts who went ahead of the Scythians discovered the Persians about three days' march from the Ister, the Scythians, having located them, continued to pitch their camp one day's march in front, destroying utterly whatever grew from the ground. When the Persians saw the Scythian horsemen appear, they came after them, following in their tracks, while the Scythians continually moved on. After this, since they had directed their march towards the first of the divisions, the Persians continued to pursue eastwards to the river Tanaïs; and when the Scythians crossed the Tanaïs, the Persians crossed after them and continued the pursuit, until they had passed right through the land of the Sauromatai and come to that of the Budinoi.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 123
paragraphs: Now so long as the Persians were passing through Scythia and the land of the Sauromatai, they had nothing to destroy, since the land was bare. But when they invaded the land of the Budinoi, they came upon the wooden wall, which the Budinoi had deserted and left wholly empty, and they destroyed it by fire. Having done this, they continued to follow further in the enemy's tracks, until they had passed through the whole of this land and arrived at the desert. This desert region is occupied by no men, and lies above the land of the Budinoi, extending for a seven days' journey. Above this desert dwell the Thyssagetai, and four large rivers flow from them through the land of the Maeotians and run into what is called the Maeotian lake—their names being Lycos, Oaros, Tanaïs, and Syrgis.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 124
paragraphs: When, therefore, Darius came to the desert region, he ceased from his course and halted his army by the river Oaros. Having done this, he began to build eight large fortifications at equal distances from one another, about sixty furlongs apart, whose ruins still existed down to my own time. While he was occupied with this, the Scythians whom he was pursuing went round by the upper parts and returned back to Scythia. Accordingly, since these had altogether disappeared and were no longer seen by the Persians, Darius left those fortifications half-finished, turned back himself, and began to go westwards, supposing that these were the whole body of the Scythians and that they were fleeing westwards.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 125
paragraphs: Marching his army as quickly as possible, when he came to Scythia he met with the two divisions of the Scythians together; and having fallen in with them, he continued to pursue, while they retired out of his way one day's journey ahead. As Darius did not cease to pursue, the Scythians, according to the plan they had made, continued to retire before him towards the land of those who had refused alliance—first towards the Melanchlainoi. When Scythians and Persians together had invaded and thrown these into disorder, the Scythians led the way to the country of the Androphagoi; and when these too had been disturbed, they proceeded to the land of the Neuroi. While the Neuroi were being thrown into disorder, the Scythians went on retiring before the enemy to the Agathyrsians. The Agathyrsians, however, seeing that their next neighbours were also fleeing from the Scythians and had been thrown into disorder, sent a herald before the Scythians invaded their land and proclaimed to the Scythians not to set foot within their borders, warning them that if they attempted to invade, they would first have to fight with them. The Agathyrsians, having given this warning, came out in arms to their frontiers, meaning to drive off those who were advancing against them. But the Melanchlainoi, Androphagoi, and Neuroi, when the Persians and Scythians together invaded them, did not resort to brave defence but forgot their former threat and fled in confusion ever further to the north, to the desert region. As for the Scythians, when the Agathyrsians had warned them off, they did not attempt to come against them any more, but led the Persians from the country of the Neuroi back to their own land.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 126
paragraphs: Since this went on a long time and did not cease, Darius sent a horseman to Idanthyrsos king of the Scythians and said: “You strangest of men, why do you keep fleeing when you might do one of two things? If you think yourself able to stand against my power, stop your wandering and fight. But if you acknowledge that you are too weak, then also cease your course and come to speech with your master, bringing him gifts of earth and water.”

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 127
paragraphs: To this, Idanthyrsos king of the Scythians made answer: “My case, Persian, stands thus. Never yet have I fled from fear of anyone, either in time past from any other man or now from you; nor have I now done anything different from what I was in the habit of doing in peacetime. And as to why I do not at once fight with you, I will declare that too. We have neither cities nor land sown with crops, about which we might fear their capture or ravaging, and so join battle with you more quickly. If, however, it should come to this quickly by all means, know that we have sepulchres in which our fathers are buried. Come, then, find these and try to destroy them, and you shall then know whether we will fight with you for the sepulchres or not. Before that, unless the impulse comes upon us, we shall not join battle with you. Let this suffice about fighting. As for masters, I acknowledge none over me but Zeus my ancestor, and Hestia the queen of the Scythians. To you, then, in place of gifts of earth and water, I shall send such things as it is fitting for you to receive; and in return for your saying you are my master, for that I say: woe betide you.” This is the proverbial “saying of the Scythians.”

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 128
paragraphs: The herald went off to report this to Darius; and the kings of the Scythians, having heard mention of subjection to a master, were filled with wrath. They therefore sent the division that was to be joined with the Sauromatai—the one Scopasis commanded—bidding them come to speech with the Ionians, namely those guarding the bridge of the Ister. Meanwhile those left behind resolved no longer to lead the Persians wandering about, but to attack them constantly as they were fetching provisions. So they watched Darius' soldiers as they gathered provisions and carried out their plan. The Scythian cavalry always routed that of the enemy; but the Persian horsemen, when they fled, fell back on the foot-soldiers, and these would come up to help; and meanwhile the Scythians, when they had driven in the cavalry, would turn back, fearing the foot-soldiers. The Scythians also used to make similar attacks by night.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 129
paragraphs: The thing which, strange to say, most helped the Persians and hindered the Scythians in their attacks on Darius' camp I will mention: the voice of the asses and the appearance of the mules. For Scythia produces neither ass nor mule, as I have stated before; nor is there at all in Scythian country either ass or mule, on account of the cold. The asses, therefore, by braying riotously, used to throw the Scythian cavalry into confusion; often, as the Scythians were in the middle of charging against the Persians, when the horses heard the asses' voices they turned back in confusion, filled with wonder, pricking up their ears, because they had never heard such a sound nor seen the creature before.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 130
paragraphs: So far, then, the Persians had the advantage for a small part of the war. But the Scythians, whenever they saw that the Persians were disquieted, in order that they might remain a longer time in Scythia and in remaining might suffer by being in want of everything, would leave some of their own cattle behind with the herdsmen, while they themselves rode off to another place; and the Persians would come upon the cattle and seize them, and having seized them they were elated at what they had done.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 131
paragraphs: Since this happened often, Darius at length began to be in straits. The kings of the Scythians, perceiving this, sent a herald bearing Darius gifts: a bird, a mouse, a frog, and five arrows. The Persians asked the bearer the meaning of the gifts; but he said he had been commanded only to give them and get away as quickly as possible, and he bade the Persians, if they had wisdom, to find out for themselves what the gifts were meant to express.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 132
paragraphs: Having heard this, the Persians took counsel with one another. Darius' opinion was that the Scythians were giving him both themselves and earth and water. He made this conjecture because a mouse is produced in the earth and feeds on the same earth's produce as a man, and a frog in the water, while a bird has a great resemblance to a horse; and, moreover, by giving the arrows they were delivering up their own might in battle. This was Darius' opinion. But Gobryas, one of the seven men who killed the Magian, was of the opposite view; he conjectured the gifts meant: “Unless you become birds and fly up into the heaven, O Persians, or become mice and sink down under the earth, or become frogs and leap into the lakes, you shall not return home, but shall be struck down by these arrows.”

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 133
paragraphs: So the Persians, I say, were trying to interpret the gifts. Meanwhile, the single Scythian division that had first been assigned to guard along the Maeotian lake and then to go to the Ister and come to speech with the Ionians, when they arrived at the bridge, spoke as follows: “Ionians, we have come bringing you freedom, if you are willing to listen to us. For we are informed that Darius gave you orders to guard the bridge for sixty days only, and then, if he had not come back within that time, to take yourselves off to your own land. Now, therefore, if you do as we say, you will be free from blame on his part and on ours. Stay the appointed days and then, after that, get yourselves away.” They, when the Ionians had engaged to do this, hastened back again by the quickest way.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 134
paragraphs: Meanwhile, after the arrival of the gifts to Darius, the Scythians who had been left behind had drawn themselves up against the Persians with both foot and horse, intending to engage in battle. Now when the Scythians had been arrayed for battle, a hare darted through them into the space between the two armies, and each company of them, as they saw the hare, began to chase it. When the Scythians were thus thrown into disorder and were raising loud cries, Darius asked what this clamour from the enemy was about; and hearing they were running after a hare, he said to those with whom he was accustomed to speak at other times: “These men hold us in very slight regard, and I now see that Gobryas spoke rightly about the Scythian gifts. Since I too now think this is how things stand, we need good counsel for our retreat homewards to be made safely.” To this Gobryas replied: “O king, even by report I was almost sure how hard these men are to deal with; and coming here I learnt it still more thoroughly, since I saw that they were mocking us. Now, therefore, my opinion is that as soon as night comes on we kindle the camp fires as we usually do at other times, and deceive with a false tale those of our men who are weakest to endure hardships; and that we tie up all the asses and take ourselves off, before either the Scythians make for the Ister to destroy the bridge, or the Ionians resolve on something that will be our ruin.”

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 135
paragraphs: Thus Gobryas counselled; and after this, when night came on, Darius acted on this opinion. Those of his men weakened by fatigue and whose loss was of least account he left behind in the camp, and the asses also tied up. He left behind the asses and the weaker men of his army for the following reasons: the asses, so that they might make a noise to be heard; and the men, really because of their weakness, but on the openly stated pretext that he was about to attack the Scythians with the effective part of the army and that they in the meantime were to defend the camp. Having given these instructions to those left behind, and having kindled camp fires, Darius hastened by the quickest way towards the Ister. The asses, no longer having the usual throng around them, cried out much more loudly for that reason; so the Scythians, hearing the asses, assumed without question that the Persians were still in their former place.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 136
paragraphs: But when day came, those left behind perceived that they had been betrayed by Darius, and they held out their hands in submission to the Scythians, explaining their situation. When the Scythians heard this, they joined together as quickly as possible—the two combined divisions of the Scythians, and the single division, along with the Sauromatai, Budinoi, and Gelonians—and began to pursue the Persians, heading straight for the Ister. But since the Persian army was mostly foot and was not familiar with the roads (the roads not being marked), while the Scythian army was made up of horsemen and knew the shortest cuts, they missed one another and the Scythians arrived at the bridge much before the Persians. Then, having learnt that the Persians had not yet arrived, they said to the Ionians who were in the ships: “Ionians, the days of your number are past, and you are not acting uprightly in continuing to wait. As you stayed before from fear, so now break up the passage as quickly as you can, and depart free and unhurt, feeling thankfulness both to the gods and to the Scythians; and as for the one who was formerly your master, we shall so convince him that he will never again march with an army against any nation.”

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 137
paragraphs: Upon this the Ionians took counsel together. Miltiades the Athenian, who was commander and despot of the men of the Chersonese on the Hellespont, was of the opinion that they should follow the Scythians' advice and set Ionia free. But Histiaios the Milesian was of the opposite opinion. For he said that at present it was by means of Darius that each of them was ruling as despot over a city; and if Darius' power were destroyed, neither could he himself continue to rule the Milesians, nor could any other of them rule any city—for each city would choose popular rather than despotic rule. When Histiaios declared his opinion thus, all at once turned to this opinion, whereas at first they had been adopting Miltiades'.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 138
paragraphs: Those who voted between the two opinions, and who were men of consequence in the king's eyes, were: first, the despots of the Hellespontians—Daphnis of Abydos, Hippoclos of Lampsacos, Herophantos of Parion, Metrodoros of Proconnesos, Aristagoras of Kyzicos, and Ariston of Byzantion—these were those from the Hellespont. From Ionia, Strattis of Chios, Aiakes of Samos, Laodamas of Phocaia, and Histiaios of Miletos, whose opinion had been proposed against Miltiades'. Of the Aeolians, the only man of consequence present was Aristagoras of Kyme.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 139
paragraphs: When these adopted Histiaios' opinion, they resolved to add to it deeds and words as follows: to break up that part of the bridge on the side facing Scythia—to break it up, I say, for a distance equal to the range of an arrow—both so they might seem to be doing something, though in fact they were doing nothing, and for fear the Scythians might make an attempt by force, wanting to cross the Ister by the bridge. And in breaking up that part of the bridge facing Scythia, they resolved to say they would do all the Scythians desired. Having added this to the opinion proposed, Histiaios then came forth from among them and answered the Scythians: “Scythians, you come bringing good news, and your haste is timely; and on your part you give us good guidance, while on ours we render you suitable service. For, as you see, we are breaking up the passage, and we will show all zeal in our desire to be free. While we are breaking up the bridge, it is fitting that you should be seeking those of whom you speak, and when you have found them, that you should take vengeance on them on behalf of us as well as of yourselves in the manner they deserve.”

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 140
paragraphs: The Scythians, believing for a second time that the Ionians were speaking the truth, turned back to search for the Persians, but missed their line of march through the land altogether. The Scythians themselves were the cause, since they had destroyed the pastures for horses in that region and choked the springs of water with earth; if they had not done this, they could have easily, if they wished, discovered the Persians. But as it was, by the very means they thought they had best taken their measures, they failed of success. The Scythians, on their part, kept passing through those parts of their own land where there was grass for the horses and springs of water, thinking that the Persians too were making their retreat through such country. The Persians, in fact, marched keeping carefully to the track they had made before, and so they found the passage of the river, though with difficulty. Arriving by night and finding the bridge broken up, they were brought to the extreme of fear, lest the Ionians should have deserted them.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 141
paragraphs: Now there was with Darius an Egyptian who had a voice louder than any other man on earth; and Darius ordered him to take his stand on the bank of the Ister and call out to Histiaios of Miletos. He proceeded to do so; and Histiaios, hearing the first call, brought out all the ships to carry the army over and put the bridge together again.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 142
paragraphs: Thus the Persians escaped, and the Scythians in their search missed the Persians a second time. The Scythians' judgment of the Ionians is this: if they are regarded as free men, they are the most worthless and cowardly of all men, but if regarded as slaves, they are the most devoted to their master and the least disposed to run away of all slaves. This is the reproach the Scythians cast against the Ionians.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 143
paragraphs: Darius then, marching through Thrace, arrived at Sestos in the Chersonese, and from there crossed over himself in his ships to Asia; but to command his army in Europe he left Megabazos a Persian—whom Darius once honoured by uttering this saying in the land of Persia. Darius was beginning to eat pomegranates, and at once, when he opened the first, his brother Artabanos asked him of what he would most wish to have as many as there were seeds in the pomegranate. Darius answered that he would wish to have men like Megabazos as many as that in number, rather than to have Hellas subject to him. In Persia, I say, he honoured him by uttering these words; and now he left him in command with eight myriads of his army.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 144
paragraphs: This Megabazos uttered one saying that left him an imperishable memory with the peoples of the Hellespont. Being once at Byzantion, he heard that the men of Chalcedon had settled in that region seventeen years before the Byzantians; and on hearing it he said that those of Chalcedon at that time must have been blind, for surely they would not have chosen the worse place when they might have settled in the better, had they not been blind. This Megabazos, then, was the one left in command at that time in the land of the Hellespontians, and he proceeded to subdue all who did not take the side of the Medes.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 145
paragraphs: He was doing this; and at the very same time a great expedition was also being mounted against Libya, for reasons I will explain after I have first told the following story. The descendants of the men who had sailed in the Argo had been driven from Lemnos by those Pelasgians who had carried off the Athenian women from Brauron. Expelled, they sailed to Lacedaemon, settled on Mount Taÿgetus, and kindled a fire there. When the Lacedaemonians saw it, they sent a messenger to ask who they were and where they came from. They answered the messenger's question by saying that they were Minyae, children of the heroes who had sailed in the Argo, for these heroes had put in at Lemnos and fathered the race from which they were descended. Having heard the story of the Minyae's descent, the Lacedaemonians sent a second time and asked why they had come into the country and why they were lighting a fire. They said that they had been cast out by the Pelasgians and had now come to the land of their fathers—for it was only just that this should be so—and that their request was to be allowed to live there with full civil rights and a portion of land allotted to them. The Lacedaemonians were willing to receive the Minyae on the terms they themselves proposed, moved above all by the fact that the sons of Tyndareus had sailed in the Argo. So they received the Minyae, gave them a share of land, distributed them among the tribes, and at once they took wives from Sparta and gave to other Spartans in marriage the women they had brought with them from Lemnos.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 146
paragraphs: But not long after, the Minyae began to behave arrogantly, demanding a share of the royal power and committing other impious acts. The Lacedaemonians therefore resolved to put them to death, seized them, and threw them into prison. Now the Lacedaemonians always execute their condemned at night, never by day. So when they were just about to kill them, the wives of the Minyae—who were native Spartans and daughters of the foremost citizens of Sparta—begged to be allowed to enter the prison and speak each with her own husband. They were let in, since no one suspected they would try any trick. Once inside, however, they handed over to their husbands all the clothes they were wearing and took their husbands' clothes in return. Thus the Minyae, dressed in women's clothing, walked out of the prison as women, and having escaped in this way they went back up to Mount Taÿgetus and settled there again.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 147
paragraphs: At that very same time Theras, son of Autesion, son of Tisamenus, son of Thersander, son of Polyneices, was preparing to leave Lacedaemon to found a settlement. This Theras was of the line of Cadmus, and was maternal uncle to the sons of Aristodemus, Eurysthenes and Procles. While these nephews were still children, Theras as their guardian held royal power in Sparta. But once his nephews had grown up and taken power into their own hands, Theras—resenting being ruled by others after he had tasted rule himself—declared that he would not remain in Lacedaemon but would sail away to his kinsmen. On the island now called Thera, formerly called Callista, there were descendants of Membliarus, son of Poikiles, a Phoenician. For Cadmus, son of Agenor, while searching for Europa, had put in at the island now called Thera; and whether because the country pleased him once he landed, or for some other reason, he left on this island, along with other Phoenicians, Membliarus, who was one of his own kinsmen. These men had occupied the island called Callista for eight generations before Theras came from Lacedaemon.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 148
paragraphs: To these men, as I said, Theras was preparing to go, taking people from the Spartan tribes with him, intending to settle alongside those who have been mentioned—not to drive them out, but on the contrary claiming them warmly as kinsmen. And when the Minyae, after escaping from prison, had settled again on Taÿgetus, and the Lacedaemonians were planning to put them to death, Theras begged them that no slaughter take place, engaging to lead the Minyae out of the land himself. The Lacedaemonians agreed, and he sailed off with three thirty-oared galleys to the descendants of Membliarus, taking only a few of the Minyae with him, not all of them. For the greater number turned toward the country of the Paroreatae and Caucones, drove them out of their land, divided themselves into six groups, and founded on their territory the following towns—Lepreum, Macistus, Phrixae, Pyrgus, Epium, Nudium—most of which the Eleans sacked within my own lifetime. Meanwhile the island got its name of Thera from Theras, who had led the settlement.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 149
paragraphs: And since his son said that he would not sail with him, Theras declared that he would leave him behind as a sheep among wolves; and from that saying the young man got the name Oiolycus, and this name prevailed over his former one. From Oiolycus was born Aegeus, from whom the Aegeidae are named, a powerful clan in Sparta. Because the children of this clan did not live to grow up, the men of the tribe, on the advice of an oracle, established a sanctuary to the Avenging Deities of Laius and Oedipus; and after this the same practice was kept up in Thera by the descendants of these men.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 150
paragraphs: Up to this point the Lacedaemonians agree in their account with the men of Thera; but what follows is reported by the Theraeans alone. Grinnus, son of Aesanius, a descendant of the Theras already mentioned, and king of the island of Thera, came to Delphi bringing a hecatomb from his state as an offering; and accompanying him, besides other citizens, was Battus, son of Polymnestus, who by descent belonged to the family of Euphemus of the Minyan race. Now when Grinnus, king of the Theraeans, was consulting the oracle about other matters, the Pythian priestess answered him by commanding him to found a city in Libya. He replied: “Lord, I am by now rather old and heavy to stir; but bid one of these younger men do it.” As he spoke he pointed toward Battus. So much for that occasion; but when they had gone home they were at a loss over the oracle's saying, having no knowledge of Libya—where on earth it was—and not daring to send a colony into the unknown.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 151
paragraphs: After this there was no rain in Thera for seven years, and in those years all the trees on the island withered up except one. When the Theraeans consulted the oracle, the Pythian priestess gave as the cause this matter of colonizing Libya. Having no remedy for their troubles, they sent messengers to Crete to find out whether any Cretan or any foreigner staying in Crete had ever been to Libya. These men, wandering about the country, came among other places to the city of Itanus, and there they met a murex-fisher named Corobius, who said he had been carried off course by winds and had reached Libya, and in Libya the island of Platea. They persuaded him with a payment of money and took him to Thera. From Thera, at first only a few men set sail to explore; and Corobius guided them to this same island of Platea. They left Corobius there with provisions for a certain number of months, and sailed back themselves as quickly as they could to report about the island to the people of Thera.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 152
paragraphs: But when these men stayed away longer than the time arranged, Corobius found himself out of provisions. After this, a Samian ship under the command of Colaeus, while sailing to Egypt, was carried off course and came to this same island of Platea. When the Samians heard Corobius's whole story, they left him enough food for a year. They themselves then put out from the island and tried to reach Egypt, but were carried off by a persistent east wind; and as the wind did not slacken, they passed through the Pillars of Heracles and came to Tartessus, guided by divine providence. This trading-post was at that time untouched by any Greek, so that when they returned home they made a greater profit on their cargo than any other Hellenes we have certain knowledge of, with the exception of Sostratus, son of Laodamas the Aeginetan—for with him no other man can compete. The Samians set aside six talents, a tenth of their gains, and had a bronze vessel made in the style of an Argolic mixing-bowl, with the heads of griffins projecting around it in a ring; this they dedicated in the temple of Hera, supporting it with three colossal bronze figures seven cubits tall, kneeling on their knees. Because of this deed above all a great friendship was formed between the Cyrenaeans and Theraeans and the Samians.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 153
paragraphs: Meanwhile the Theraeans who had left Corobius on the island reported on their return to Thera that they had colonized an island off the coast of Libya. The Theraeans then resolved to send one of every two brothers, chosen by lot, together with men taken from every district of the island, which are seven in number; and further that Battus should be their leader and king. In this way they dispatched two fifty-oared galleys to Platea.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 154
paragraphs: This is the account of the Theraeans; and for what follows the Theraeans are in agreement with the men of Cyrene—from this point onward, I say, since concerning Battus the Cyrenaeans tell a completely different story from the Theraeans. Theirs is this: In Crete there is a city called Oaxus, where a man named Etearchus became king. Having a daughter whose mother was dead, named Phronime, he nevertheless took another wife. This woman, coming into the household, decided to be a stepmother to Phronime in deed as well as in name, mistreating her and devising every possible injury against her. In the end she brought a charge of lewdness against her and convinced her husband that it was true. Persuaded by his wife, he devised an unholy plan against his daughter. There was in Oaxus a certain Themison, a merchant of Thera, whom Etearchus took in as a guest-friend and made swear that he would do whatever he was asked. Once he had sworn, Etearchus brought his daughter and handed her over, telling him to take her away and throw her into the sea. Themison was furious at the deceit practiced upon him in the matter of the oath, and dissolved his guest-friendship with Etearchus. He did as follows: he took the girl and sailed away, and when he had reached the open sea, to free himself from the oath he had sworn to Etearchus he tied ropes around her on each side, lowered her into the sea, and then drew her up again—and so came to Thera.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 155
paragraphs: After this, Polymnestus, a respected man among the Theraeans, took Phronime from him and kept her as his concubine. In time a son was born to him from her, a son with an impediment in his speech and a lisp. To him, both Theraeans and Cyrenaeans say, was given the name Battus, though I think some other name was given at first, and he was called Battus only after he came to Libya—taking this surname for himself from the oracle given to him at Delphi and from the rank he had obtained, for the Libyans call a king battos. For this reason, I think, the Pythian priestess, when she prophesied, addressed him so, using the Libyan word, because she knew he would become a king in Libya. When he had grown to manhood, he came to Delphi to inquire about his voice; and to his question the priestess answered:
“For a voice you came, O Battus; but lord Phoebus Apollo sends you out as a settler to sheep-rich Libya,”

as if she had said in Greek, “For a voice you came, O king.” He replied: “Lord, I came to you to inquire about my voice, but you answer me with something else that is impossible, bidding me go as a settler to Libya. With what resources, or with what force of men should I go?” For all he said, he did not persuade her to give him any other answer; and as she kept prophesying to him the same things as before, Battus left while she was still speaking and went back to Thera.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 156
paragraphs: After this, misfortune came upon both Battus himself and the other men of Thera. Not understanding what had befallen them, the Theraeans sent to Delphi to ask about the evils they were suffering. The Pythian priestess replied that if they joined with Battus in founding Cyrene in Libya, they would fare better. Then the Theraeans sent Battus off with two fifty-oared galleys. These men sailed to Libya and then came back again to Thera, not knowing what else to do. But the Theraeans pelted them with missiles as they tried to land, refused to let them put ashore, and ordered them to sail away again. Compelled, they sailed off and made a settlement on an island lying near the coast of Libya called, as was said before, Platea. This island is said to be about the same size as the present city of Cyrene.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 157
paragraphs: They lived there for two years; but as they had no prosperity, they left one of their number behind and all the rest sailed to Delphi. Reaching the oracle, they consulted it, saying that though they were living in Libya they were faring no better for it. To them the Pythian priestess made this reply:
“If you, who have not been there, know sheep-rich Libya better than I, who have been there, I marvel at your wisdom.”

Having heard this, Battus and his companions sailed back again; for in fact the god would not release them from the task of settlement until they had come to Libya itself. Arriving at the island and picking up the man they had left behind, they made a settlement in Libya proper, at a spot across from the island called Aziris, enclosed by lovely woods on two sides and with a river flowing along one side.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 158
paragraphs: They lived in this place for six years; but in the seventh year the Libyans persuaded them to leave, making the request and saying that they would lead them to a better region. So the Libyans led them from that place, starting them off in the evening; and so that the Hellenes might not see the fairest of all the regions as they passed through it, they led them past it by night, having timed it carefully for the hours of daylight. This region is called Irasa. Then having brought them to what is called the spring of Apollo, they said: “Hellenes, here is a fitting place for you to live, for here the sky is full of holes.”

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 159
paragraphs: During the lifetime of the first settler Battus, who reigned forty years, and of his son Arcesilaus, who reigned sixteen years, the Cyrenaeans continued to live there with the same numbers they had brought when they first set out for the colony; but in the time of the third king, called Battus the Fortunate, the Pythian priestess gave an oracle urging the Hellenes in general to sail and join the Cyrenaeans in settling Libya—for the Cyrenaeans were inviting them, with the promise of a division of land. The oracle she uttered was this:
“Whoever goes to the much-desired land, to Libya, after the land has been divided—I say he shall one day regret it.”

So great numbers gathered at Cyrene, and the Libyans who lived round about had much land cut away from their possessions.
