Therefore they, with their king whose name was Adicran—being deprived not only of their country but also treated with great insolence by the Cyrenaeans—sent to Egypt and gave themselves up to Apries, king of Egypt. He gathered a great army of Egyptians and sent it against Cyrene; but the Cyrenaeans marched out to the region of Irasa and the spring Theste, and there joined battle with the Egyptians and defeated them. For the Egyptians had not before tried the Hellenes in battle and so despised them, and they were slaughtered to the point that only a few returned back to Egypt. Because of this, and because they laid the blame on Apries, the Egyptians revolted against him.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 160
paragraphs: This Battus had a son named Arcesilaus who, on becoming king, quarreled with his own brothers until in the end they left for another region of Libya and, acting on their own initiative, founded the city that then and now is called Barca; and at the same time as they founded it, they induced the Libyans to revolt from the Cyrenaeans. After this, Arcesilaus led an expedition against those Libyans who had received his brothers and had also revolted from Cyrene. The Libyans, afraid of him, fled toward the eastern tribes of Libyans; and Arcesilaus pursued them as they fled, until in his pursuit he reached Leucon in Libya. There the Libyans resolved to make a stand. They joined battle and defeated the Cyrenaeans so decisively that seven thousand Cyrenaean hoplites fell on that field. After this disaster, Arcesilaus, being sick and having swallowed a potion, was strangled by his brother Haliarchus; and Haliarchus was killed by treachery by Arcesilaus's wife, whose name was Eryxo.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 161
paragraphs: Then Battus, son of Arcesilaus, succeeded to the kingdom. He was lame and unsound in his feet. The Cyrenaeans, in view of the misfortune that had befallen them, sent men to Delphi to ask what form of government they should adopt to live as well as possible; and the Pythian priestess told them to fetch a reformer of their constitution from Mantineia of the Arcadians. The Cyrenaeans made the request accordingly, and the Mantineians gave them the most respected man among their citizens, whose name was Demonax. When this Demonax had come to Cyrene and made careful inquiry into everything, he first caused them to form three tribes, distributing them as follows: one division he made of the Theraeans and their dependents, another of the Peloponnesians and Cretans, and a third of all the islanders. Secondly, for King Battus he set aside landed estates and priesthoods, but all the other powers the kings used to hold he assigned as public rights to the people.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 162
paragraphs: During this Battus's reign things continued in this way, but in the reign of his son Arcesilaus there was great disturbance about the offices of the state. For Arcesilaus, son of Battus the Lame and of Pheretime, declared that he would not allow things to remain as Demonax of Mantineia had arranged them, and demanded back the royal rights of his forefathers. After this he stirred up strife, was defeated, and went into exile to Samos, while his mother went to Salamis in Cyprus. At that time the ruler of Salamis was Euelthon—the same man who dedicated as an offering at Delphi the censer well worth seeing, which is placed in the treasury of the Corinthians. Pheretime came to him and asked him for an army to restore herself and her son to Cyrene. But Euelthon was ready to give her anything else rather than that. When she received what he gave her, she would say that this too was a fine gift, but finer still would be that other gift—an army—which she kept asking for. As she kept saying this about every gift he gave, finally Euelthon sent her a present of a golden spindle and distaff, with wool on it. When Pheretime said the same thing about this present too, Euelthon replied that such things are given as gifts to women, not armies.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 163
paragraphs: Meanwhile Arcesilaus, in Samos, was gathering everyone he could with a promise of dividing land; and while a great host was being assembled, he set off for Delphi to consult the oracle about his return from exile. The Pythian priestess gave him this answer: “For four named Battus and four named Arcesilaus—eight generations of men—Loxias grants you to be kings of Cyrene; beyond that he counsels you not even to attempt it. You, however, must keep quiet when you have come back to your land. If you find the furnace full of jars, do not heat the jars fiercely, but let them go with a fair wind; but if you heat the furnace fiercely, do not enter the place that is washed around by water—for if you do, you will die, both you and the bull that is fairest of all.”

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 164
paragraphs: Such was the answer the Pythian priestess gave to Arcesilaus. He, taking with him those in Samos, returned to Cyrene. Once he had seized power, he forgot the oracle's saying and set about exacting punishments from those of the opposing faction for having driven him out. Of these, some escaped the country altogether, but some Arcesilaus got into his hands and sent off to Cyprus to be put to death. These were driven off course to Cnidus, and the Cnidians rescued them and sent them away to Thera. Other Cyrenaeans, however, had taken refuge in a great tower belonging to a private citizen named Aglomachus, and Arcesilaus burned them alive by piling up brushwood around it. After the deed he realized that this was what the oracle had meant when the Pythian priestess forbade him, if he found the jars in the furnace, to heat them fiercely; and he deliberately kept away from the city of Cyrene, fearing the death foretold by the oracle and supposing that Cyrene was the place washed around by water. He had as wife a kinswoman of his own, the daughter of the king of Barca whose name was Alazeir. He went to him; and certain Barcans, together with some of the Cyrenaean exiles, noticing him walking in the marketplace, killed him, and killed his father-in-law Alazeir along with him. So Arcesilaus, whether willingly or unwillingly, by misreading the oracle fulfilled his own fate.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 165
paragraphs: Meanwhile his mother Pheretime, while her son Arcesilaus—having brought evil on himself—was living at Barca, held her son's royal power at Cyrene, exercising his other rights and also sitting in council. But when she heard that her son had been killed at Barca, she left and fled to Egypt. For she could count on services rendered by Arcesilaus to Cambyses, son of Cyrus—since it was this Arcesilaus who had given Cyrene over to Cambyses and imposed tribute upon himself. Pheretime, therefore, coming to Egypt, sat as a suppliant of Aryandes, begging him to help her, and giving as her reason that it was because of her son's leaning toward the Medes that he had been killed.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 166
paragraphs: This Aryandes had been appointed governor of the province of Egypt by Cambyses; and after the events here described he lost his life because he tried to measure himself against Darius. For having heard and seen that Darius wanted to leave behind him as a memorial something no other king had ever made, he imitated him—until at last he got his reward. For whereas Darius refined gold and made it as pure as possible, and had coins struck from it, Aryandes, being ruler of Egypt, did the same thing with silver; and even now the purest silver is what is called Aryandic. When Darius learned that he was doing this, he put him to death, bringing against him another charge—that of attempting rebellion.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 167
paragraphs: At the time of which I am speaking, however, this Aryandes had pity on Pheretime and gave her all the forces in Egypt, both land and sea, appointing Amasis, a Maraphian, to command the land-army and Badres, of the Pasargadae clan, to command the fleet. But before he sent off the army, Aryandes dispatched a herald to Barca and asked who it was that had killed Arcesilaus. The men of Barca all took it upon themselves, saying that they had previously suffered many great wrongs at his hands. Hearing this, Aryandes at last sent off the army with Pheretime. This charge, then, was the pretext; but in fact the army was being sent out, as I believe, to subdue Libya. For the Libyans are divided into many nations of many kinds, and few of them were subjects of the king, while the greater number paid no heed to Darius.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 168
paragraphs: The Libyans have their settlements as follows. Starting from Egypt, the first Libyans are the Adyrmachidae, who practice for the most part the same customs as the Egyptians, but wear clothing similar to that of the other Libyans. Their women wear a bronze ring on each leg and have long hair on their heads; when they catch their lice, each woman bites her own in retaliation and then throws them away. Of all the Libyans these are the only ones who do this; and they alone present their maidens to the king when they are about to be married, and whichever one of them pleases the king is deflowered by him. These Adyrmachidae extend along the coast from Egypt as far as the harbor called Plynus.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 169
paragraphs: Next after these come the Giligamae, who occupy the country westward as far as the island of Aphrodisias. Within this stretch lies, off the coast, the island of Platea, where the Cyrenaeans made their settlement; and on the coast of the mainland lie Port Menelaus and Aziris, where the Cyrenaeans used to live. From this point begins the silphium, which extends along the coast from the island of Platea as far as the entrance of the Syrtis. This nation practices customs closely resembling those of the rest.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 170
paragraphs: Next to the Giligamae on the west are the Asbystae. These live above Cyrene, and the Asbystae do not reach down to the sea, since the coastal region is occupied by the Cyrenaeans. Of all the Libyans these are the greatest drivers of four-horse chariots, and in most of their customs they try to imitate the Cyrenaeans.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 171
paragraphs: Next after the Asbystae to the west come the Auschisae. These live above Barca and reach down to the sea at Euesperides. In the middle of the Auschisae's territory live the Bacales, a small tribe, who reach down to the sea at the city of Taucheira in Barcan territory; these practice the same customs as those above Cyrene.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 172
paragraphs: Next after these Auschisae, moving westward, come the Nasamones, a numerous people, who in summer leave their flocks by the sea and go up to the region of Augila to gather the fruit of the date-palms, which grow there in great numbers, very large, and all fruit-bearing. They hunt the wingless locusts, dry them in the sun, grind them up, and then sprinkle them onto milk and drink it. Their custom is for each man to have many wives, and they share them in much the same way as the Massagetae—that is, they set up a staff in front of the door and so have intercourse. When a Nasamonian man marries his first wife, the custom is for the bride on the first night to go through the whole company of guests and have intercourse with them, and each man when he has lain with her gives a gift—whatever he has brought with him from his house. Their forms of oath and of divination are as follows. They swear by the men of their own people who are reported to have been most upright and brave, laying their hands on these men's tombs; and they practice divination by going to the burial mounds of their ancestors and lying down to sleep upon them after praying—and whatever thing the man sees in his dream, that he accepts. They also practice the exchange of pledges in this way: one gives the other to drink from his hand, and drinks himself from the other's hand; and if they have no liquid, they take dust from the ground and lick it.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 173
paragraphs: Bordering on the Nasamones is the country of the Psylli. These have utterly perished in the following way. The south wind blowing on them dried up all their water-cisterns, and their land became waterless, lying as it does wholly within the Syrtis. By common decision they took up arms and marched against the south wind—I report what the Libyans report—and when they had reached the sandy tract, the south wind blew and buried them in the sand. Having utterly perished, their land from that time onward has been held by the Nasamones.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 174
paragraphs: Above these, toward the south wind in the region of wild beasts, live the Garamantes, who flee from every man and avoid all company; they possess no weapon of war, nor do they know how to defend themselves against enemies.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 175
paragraphs: These live above the Nasamones; and next to the Nasamones, moving westward along the coast, come the Macae, who shave their hair to leave tufts—letting the middle strip grow long while shaving the sides close to the skin. For fighting they carry shields made of ostrich hide. The river Cinyps runs through their land out into the sea, flowing from a hill called the “Hill of the Charites.” This Hill of the Charites is thickly wooded, while the rest of Libya mentioned so far is bare of trees; the distance from the sea to the hill is two hundred furlongs.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 176
paragraphs: Next to these Macae are the Gindanes, whose women each wear a number of anklets made of the skins of animals, for the following reason, as is said: for every man who has had intercourse with her, a woman binds on an anklet; and the woman who has the most is considered the best, since she has been loved by the greatest number of men.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 177
paragraphs: On a peninsula projecting into the sea from the land of these Gindanes live the Lotus-eaters, who live entirely on the fruit of the lotus. The fruit of the lotus is in size like that of the mastich-tree, and in flavor resembles that of the date-palm. From this fruit the Lotus-eaters even make wine for themselves.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 178
paragraphs: Next after the Lotus-eaters along the coast are the Machlyes, who also use the lotus, but less than those just mentioned. These extend as far as a great river named the Triton, which runs out into a great lake called Tritonis, in which there is an island named Phla. About this island, the Lacedaemonians say, an oracle was given them to make a settlement.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 179
paragraphs: The following story is also told: that Jason, when he had completed the Argo beneath Mount Pelion, put in it a hecatomb and also a tripod of bronze, and sailed around the Peloponnese, wishing to come to Delphi. As he sailed and got near Malea, a north wind seized his ship and carried it off to Libya, and before he had caught sight of land he was already in the shoals of Lake Tritonis. As he was at a loss how to bring his ship out, the story goes that Triton appeared to him and told Jason to give him the tripod, saying he would show them the right course and let them go without harm. When Jason agreed, Triton showed them the passage out between the shoals and placed the tripod in his own temple, after first uttering a prophecy over the tripod and declaring to Jason and his crew the whole matter—namely, that whenever one of the descendants of those who had sailed with him in the Argo should carry off this tripod, then it was ordained by fate that a hundred cities of Hellenes would be founded around Lake Tritonis. On hearing this, the native Libyans hid the tripod.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 180
paragraphs: Next to these Machlyes are the Auseans. These and the Machlyes live around Lake Tritonis, with the river Triton as the boundary between them. The Machlyes grow their hair long at the back of the head, the Auseans at the front. At an annual festival of Athena, their maidens take their stand in two parties and fight one another with stones and clubs, saying that in doing so they are performing the rites handed down by their fathers to the divinity who sprang from that land, whom we call Athena; and the maidens who die of their wounds they call “false-maidens.” But before letting them begin the fight, they do this: all together they equip the maiden judged fairest on each occasion with a Corinthian helmet and full Hellenic armor, and then, placing her in a chariot, they conduct her around the lake. I cannot say what they used to equip the maidens with in the old days, before the Hellenes settled near them, but I suppose they used to equip them with Egyptian armor—for it is from Egypt, I say, that both the shield and the helmet have come to the Hellenes. They say, moreover, that Athena is the daughter of Poseidon and of Lake Tritonis, and that she had some cause of complaint against her father and therefore gave herself to Zeus, and Zeus made her his own daughter. Such is the story these people tell; and they have their intercourse with women in common, not marrying but mating like cattle. When a woman's child has grown large, the men hold a meeting within three months of that time, and whichever of the men the child most resembles, his son he is accounted to be.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 181
paragraphs: Those have now been mentioned who are nomad Libyans living along the coast; and above these, inland, is the part of Libya that has wild beasts, and above the wild-beast region stretches a raised belt of sand extending from Egyptian Thebes to the Pillars of Heracles. In this belt, at intervals of about ten days' journey, there are great lumps of salt forming hills, and from the middle of the salt on top of each hill there rises up a spring of cold, sweet water; and around the spring people live, at the furthest limit toward the desert, above the wild-beast region. First, at ten days' journey from Thebes, are the Ammonians, whose temple is derived from that of Theban Zeus—for the image of Zeus in Thebes too, as I have said before, has the head of a ram. They happen also to have another water from a spring, which in the early morning is warm; when the market fills, cooler; at noon it is quite cold, and then they water their gardens with it; but as the day declines it abates from its coldness, until, when the sun sets, the water is warm; and it continues to grow still hotter until midnight, when it boils and throws up bubbles; after midnight passes, it gradually cools again until daybreak. This spring is called the Fountain of the Sun.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 182
paragraphs: After the Ammonians, as you continue along the belt of sand, at another interval of ten days' journey there is a hill of salt like that of the Ammonians, and a spring of water, with people living around it; the name of this place is Augila. To it the Nasamones come year after year to gather the fruit of the date-palms.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 183
paragraphs: From Augila, at another distance of ten days' journey, there is another hill of salt and spring of water, with a great number of fruit-bearing date-palms, as in the other places; and people live here who are called the Garamantes, a very great nation, who carry earth to spread over the salt and then sow crops. From this point the shortest route is to the Lotus-eaters, for from them it is a thirty days' journey to the country of the Garamantes. Among them too are produced the cattle that graze backwards; and they graze backwards for this reason: they have horns that bend down forward, and so they walk backwards as they feed—for they cannot go forward, because their horns would drive into the ground in front of them. In no other respect do they differ from ordinary cattle, except in this and in the thickness and firmness of their hide. These Garamantes of whom I speak hunt the “Cave-dwelling” Ethiopians in their four-horse chariots, for the Cave-dwelling Ethiopians are the swiftest-footed of all people we hear tell of; and the Cave-dwellers feed on snakes and lizards and such creeping things, and they use a language unlike any other—in it they squeak just like bats.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 184
paragraphs: From the Garamantes, at another distance of ten days' journey, there is another hill of salt and spring of water, with people living around it called the Atarantes, who alone of all men we know are nameless: for while collectively they have the name Atarantes, no individual among them has any name given to him. These curse the sun when it is at its height, reviling it with every kind of foul name because it oppresses them with its burning heat—both themselves and their land. After this, at a distance of ten days' journey, there is another hill of salt and spring of water, with people living around it. Near this salt-hill is a mountain called Atlas, which is small in circumference and rounded on every side; and so exceedingly high is it said to be that its summits cannot be seen, for clouds never leave them either in summer or in winter. This mountain, the natives say, is the pillar of the sky. From this mountain these people get their name: they are called Atlanteans; and it is said that they neither eat anything that has life nor have any dreams.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 185
paragraphs: As far as these Atlanteans I can give in order the names of those settled in the belt of sand, but for parts beyond this I cannot. The belt, however, extends as far as the Pillars of Heracles and also beyond them; and in it there is a mine of salt at ten days' journey from the Atlanteans, with people living there—and all of them have their houses built of lumps of salt, since these parts of Libya that we have now reached have no rain, for if it rained, the walls being made of salt could not last. The salt dug there is both white and purple in color. Above the belt of sand, in the parts toward the south wind and the interior of Libya, the country is uninhabited, without water and without wild beasts, rainless and treeless, and there is no trace of moisture in it.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 186
paragraphs: I have said that from Egypt as far as Lake Tritonis there dwell Libyans who are nomads, eating flesh and drinking milk. These do not at all taste of the flesh of cows, for the same reason the Egyptians too abstain from it, nor do they keep swine. Moreover the women of the Cyrenaeans also think it wrong to eat cows' flesh, because of the Egyptian Isis, and they even keep fasts and celebrate festivals in her honor; and the women of Barca, in addition to not eating cow's flesh, also do not taste swine.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 187
paragraphs: So it is with these matters. But in the region west of Lake Tritonis the Libyans are no longer nomads, and they do not practice the same customs, nor do they do to their children anything like what the nomads do. For the nomad Libyans—whether all of them I cannot say for certain, but many of them—do the following. When their children are four years old, they burn with a greasy piece of sheep's wool the veins in the crowns of their heads, and some of them burn the veins of the temples, so that for the rest of their lives the cold humor may not run down from their heads and harm them. For this reason, they say, they are so healthy; for the Libyans are in truth the healthiest of all peoples we know of—whether for this reason or not I cannot say for certain, but the healthiest they certainly are. If, when they burn the children, a convulsion comes on, they have found a remedy: they pour the urine of a he-goat on them, and so save them. I report what the Libyans themselves report.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 188
paragraphs: The nomads' manner of sacrifice is this: they cut off a piece of the animal's ear as a first offering and throw it over the house, and having done this they twist its neck. They sacrifice only to the Sun and the Moon—that is, to these all the Libyans sacrifice; but those who live around Lake Tritonis sacrifice most of all to Athena, and after her to Triton and Poseidon.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 189
paragraphs: It would appear too that the Hellenes modeled the dress and aegis of the images of Athena after the Libyan women. For except that the Libyan women's clothing is of leather, and the tassels hanging from their aegis are not formed of serpents but of leather thongs, in every other respect Athena is dressed like them. Moreover, the name itself shows that the dress of the Pallas figures came from Libya, for the Libyan women wear over their other garments bare goatskins (aigeai) with tasseled fringes, colored with red madder, and from the name of these goatskins the Hellenes formed the name aegis. I think too that in these parts first arose the practice of crying aloud during sacred rites, for the Libyan women do this very well. The Hellenes also learned from the Libyans the yoking of four horses together.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 190
paragraphs: The nomads bury their dead in the same manner as the Hellenes, except for the Nasamones alone: these bury their bodies in a sitting position, taking care at the moment the man expires to place him sitting up and not let him die lying on his back. They have dwellings built of asphodel stems interwoven with rushes, made so that they can be carried about. Such are the customs followed by these tribes.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 191
paragraphs: West of the river Triton, next after the Auseans, come Libyans who are tillers of the soil and whose custom it is to have fixed dwellings; they are called the Maxyes. They grow their hair long on the right side of the head and cut it short on the left, and they smear their bodies with red ochre. They claim to be descended from the men who came from Troy.

This country and the rest of Libya toward the west are both much more frequented by wild beasts and far more thickly wooded than the country of the nomads. Whereas the eastern part of Libya, where the nomads live, is low-lying and sandy up to the river Triton, what lies west of it—the country of the tillers—is very mountainous, densely wooded, and full of wild beasts. For in the land of these people are found the monstrous serpent, the lion, the elephant, bears, venomous snakes, horned asses, and also the dog-headed men and the headless men with eyes in their chests—at least so say the Libyans about them—and the wild men and wild women, and a great multitude of other beasts that are not fabulous like these.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 192
paragraphs: In the land of the nomads, however, none of these creatures exists; but there are others, as follows: white-rump antelopes, gazelles, buffaloes, asses—not the horned kind but another sort that go without water (for in fact these never drink)—oryxes, whose horns are used to make the sides of the Phoenician lyre (this animal is about the size of an ox), small foxes, hyenas, porcupines, wild rams, wolves, jackals, panthers, boryes, land-crocodiles about three cubits long and very much like lizards, ostriches, and small snakes each with a single horn. These are the wild animals found in this country, besides those found elsewhere, except the stag and the wild boar; for Libya has no stags or wild boars at all. There are also in this country three kinds of mice: one called the “two-legged” mouse, another the zegeris (a Libyan word which in Greek means “hill”), and a third the “prickly” mouse. There are also weasels bred in the silphium, which are very like those of Tartessus. Such are the wild animals this land of the Libyans has, as far as we were able to learn by extending our inquiries as much as possible.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 193
paragraphs: Next to the Maxyan Libyans are the Zauekes, whose women drive their chariots for them in war.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 194
paragraphs: Next to these are the Gyzantes, among whom honey is made in great quantity by bees, but in much greater quantity still, it is said, by men who make it a trade. Be that as it may, these all smear themselves with red ochre and eat monkeys, which are bred in very great numbers on their mountains.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 195
paragraphs: Opposite these people, the Carthaginians say, lies an island called Cyrauis, two hundred furlongs long but narrow, which one can walk to from the mainland; and it is full of olives and vines. On it, they say, there is a pool from which the native girls, using birds' feathers smeared with pitch, bring up gold-dust out of the mud. Whether this is actually so I do not know, but I write what is reported; and nothing is impossible—for in Zacynthus too I myself saw pitch brought up out of a pool of water. There are several pools there, the largest measuring seventy feet each way and two fathoms deep. Into it they plunge a pole with a myrtle-branch tied to it, and with the myrtle-branch they bring up pitch, which has the smell of asphalt but is in other respects superior to the pitch of Pieria. They pour this into a pit dug near the pool; and when they have collected a large quantity, they pour it from the pit into jars; and whatever falls into the pool passes underground and reappears in the sea, about four furlongs away. So the report about the island lying near the coast of Libya is also probably true.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 196
paragraphs: The Carthaginians also say this: there is a place in Libya, and people living there, outside the Pillars of Heracles. When they come to them, they unload their merchandise from their ships, lay it out in order along the beach, and then go back aboard their ships and send up a smoke signal. The natives, seeing the smoke, come down to the sea and lay down gold as payment for the merchandise and then withdraw to a distance from the goods. The Carthaginians then come ashore and examine it; and if the gold seems to them a fair price for their merchandise, they take it up and go their way. But if not, they go back aboard their ships and wait; and the others come up and add more gold to what is already there, until the Carthaginians are satisfied. They say that neither side wrongs the other; for the Carthaginians do not touch the gold until it matches the value of their merchandise, nor do the natives touch the merchandise until the Carthaginians have taken the gold.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 197
paragraphs: These are the Libyan tribes we are able to name; and most of them neither now pay any heed to the king of the Medes, nor did they then. This much more I have to say about this land: it is occupied by four peoples and no more, so far as we know. Of these, two are natives of the soil and the other two not; for the Libyans and the Ethiopians are natives—the first dwelling in the northern parts of Libya, the second in the southern—while the Phoenicians and the Hellenes are newcomers.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 198
paragraphs: I think, moreover, that in quality of soil Libya does not greatly surpass Asia or Europe, except for the region of Cinyps—the name being shared with the river. This region is as good as the best of lands for producing Demeter's fruit, and it bears no resemblance at all to the rest of Libya; for it has black soil, is watered by springs, fears no drought, and is not harmed by drinking too much rain—for rain does fall in this part of Libya. The same measures of yield hold here as for the land of Babylon. That land too is good which the Euesperites occupy, for when it bears best it produces a hundredfold; but the region of Cinyps sometimes produces as much as three hundredfold.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 199
paragraphs: Moreover, the territory of Cyrene, which is the highest part of Libya occupied by nomads, contains within its borders three seasons of harvest, at which we may well marvel. First the parts along the sea-coast have their fruit ripe for reaping and grapes ready for the vintage; and when these have been gathered in, the parts lying above the coastal region, in the middle—what they call the hills—are ready to be gathered in; and as soon as this middle crop is gathered, the crop in the highest part of the country comes to perfection and is ripe. So by the time the first crop has been eaten and drunk up, the last is just coming in. In this way the harvest for the Cyrenaeans lasts eight months. So much for these matters.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 200
paragraphs: When the Persian forces sent by Aryandes from Egypt to help Pheretime had arrived at Barca, they laid siege to the city, proposing that the inhabitants hand over those guilty of the murder of Arcesilaus. But since all the people had shared in the guilt, they would not accept the terms. Then the Persians besieged Barca for nine months, digging underground passages leading to the wall and making vigorous assaults on it. The passages being dug were detected by a worker in bronze with a shield overlaid with bronze, who had devised a clever plan. Carrying the shield around inside the wall, he would apply it to the ground of the city; and whereas the other places where he applied it were silent, at those spots where digging was going on the bronze of the shield gave out a sound. The Barcaeans would then make a countermine there and kill the Persians who were tunneling. This was how the mines were detected, as I have said, and the attacks were repulsed by the men of Barca.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 201
paragraphs: As they continued to suffer hardship for a long time, and many were falling on both sides—but most of all on the Persian side—Amasis, commander of the land-army, devised the following scheme. Realizing that the Barcaeans could not be conquered by force but might be conquered by cunning, he dug by night a broad trench, laid over it timber of no great strength, and then brought earth and heaped it on top of the timber, leveling it with the rest of the ground. At daybreak he invited the Barcaeans to a parley; and they gladly consented, and in the end they agreed to make a treaty. The treaty was sworn over the hidden trench, to this effect: that so long as this earth remained as it was, the oath would remain firm; that the Barcaeans would agree to pay a reasonable tribute to the king; and that the Persians would do no further violence to the Barcaeans. After the oath, the Barcaeans, trusting these pledges, went out of their city themselves and allowed any of the enemy who wished to pass inside the walls, having opened all the gates. But the Persians first broke down the concealed bridge and then ran inside the city wall. And the reason they broke down the bridge they had made was so that they might keep their oath, since they had sworn to the Barcaeans that the oath would remain firm as long as the earth remained as it then was; once they had broken it down, the oath no longer held.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 202
paragraphs: Those Barcaeans most guilty of Arcesilaus's murder, when the Persians handed them over to her, Pheretime impaled in a ring around the wall; and she cut off the breasts of their wives and set these too around the wall in order. The rest of the people of Barca she ordered the Persians to carry off as spoil, except those who were of the house of Battus and who had had no share in the guilt of the murder; to these Pheretime gave the city in charge.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 203
paragraphs: So the Persians, having enslaved the rest of the Barcaeans, set out to return. When they appeared at the gates of the city of Cyrene, the Cyrenaeans let them pass through the town in order not to disregard some oracle. As the army was passing through, Badres, the fleet commander, urged that they take the city, but Amasis, commander of the land-army, would not consent, saying that they had been sent against no other Hellenic city except Barca. However, once they had passed through and were encamping on the hill of Zeus Lycaeus, they regretted not having seized Cyrene; and they tried again to get inside the city, but the Cyrenaeans would not let them. Then upon the Persians, though no one was fighting against them, there fell a sudden panic, and they ran away for about sixty furlongs before encamping. After the camp had been set there, a messenger from Aryandes came to it, summoning them back. So the Persians asked the Cyrenaeans to give them provisions for their march, and obtained them; and having received these, they set out for Egypt. After this the Libyans set upon them and, for the sake of their clothing and gear, killed those of them who from time to time were left or straggling behind, until at last they reached Egypt.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 204
paragraphs: This army of the Persians reached Euesperides, and this was their furthest point in Libya. The Barcaeans whom they had reduced to slavery they removed from Egypt and brought to the king, and King Darius gave them a village in the land of Bactria to make a settlement in. They gave this village the name of Barca, and it was still inhabited by them in my own time, in the land of Bactria.

chapters.title: Book IV — Melpomene, Chapter 205
paragraphs: Pheretime, however, did not end her life happily either. As soon as she had returned from Libya to Egypt, after taking her revenge on the Barcaeans, she died a terrible death, suddenly becoming full of worms while still alive—for, it seems, punishments inflicted by men that are too severe prove offensive to the gods. Such, and so great, was the punishment Pheretime, the wife of Battus, inflicted on the men of Barca.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 1
paragraphs: Meanwhile those of the Persians who had been left behind in Europe by Darius, under the command of Megabazus, had subdued first the people of Perinthus among the Hellespontians, since they refused to be subjects of Darius. These had in earlier days also been roughly handled by the Paeonians; for the Paeonians from the Strymon had been ordered by an oracle of their god to march against the Perinthians—and if, when encamped opposite them, the Perinthians should shout aloud and call to them by name, they were to attack; but if they did not shout to them, they were not to attack. This is what the Paeonians set out to do. When the Perinthians were encamped opposite them in the suburb of their city, a challenge was made and a single combat took place in three forms: man against man, horse against horse, and dog against dog. Then, as the Perinthians were getting the better of two of the three contests, in their exultation they raised the shout of paion; and the Paeonians guessed that this was the very thing the oracle had spoken of, and said to one another, “Surely the oracle is being fulfilled for us; now it is time to act.” So the Paeonians attacked the Perinthians when they had raised the shout of paion, and much the better of the fight, and left only a few of them alive.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 2
paragraphs: So much for what had been done to them in former times by the Paeonians; and on this occasion, although the Perinthians proved themselves brave men in defense of their freedom, the Persians and Megabazus got the better of them by sheer numbers. After Perinthus had been conquered, Megabazus marched his army through the length of Thrace, forcing every city and every tribe that lived there to submit to the king—for so he had been commanded by Darius, to subdue Thrace.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 3
paragraphs: Now the Thracian race is the most numerous in all the world, except for the Indians; and if it were ruled by one man, or united in common purpose, it would be irresistible in battle and by far the strongest of all nations, in my opinion. Since, however, this is impossible for them and can never come to pass among them, they are for that very reason weak. They have many names, belonging to their various tribes in different places; but they all follow customs that are nearly the same in every respect, except the Getae and Trausi and those who live above the Crestonians.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 4
paragraphs: Of these, I have already spoken of the practices of the Getae, who believe themselves to be immortal. The Trausi perform everything else in the same manner as the other Thracians, but in regard to those who are born and die among them they do as follows. When a child has been born, the nearest relatives sit around it and lament for all the evils whose measure he must now fill, since he has been born, enumerating the whole range of human ills; but when a man dies, they cover him up in the earth with sport and rejoicing, saying at the same time from how great evils he has escaped and that he is now in perfect bliss.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 5
paragraphs: Those who live above the Crestonians do as follows. Each man has many wives, and when any man of them dies, a great contest arises among his wives, with great efforts on the part of their friends, over which of them was most loved by their husband. She who is judged the winner and so honored is first praised by both men and women; then her throat is cut over the tomb by her nearest of kin, and afterwards she is buried together with her husband. The others are deeply grieved at it, for this is counted as the greatest reproach against them.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 6
paragraphs: Among the rest of the Thracians, the custom is to sell their children to be taken away out of the country. They do not keep watch over their maidens, but allow them to have intercourse with whatever men they please; but over their wives they keep very strict watch, and they buy their wives for great sums of money from the parents. To be tattooed is considered a mark of noble birth, and to be unmarked is a sign of low birth. Not to work is counted most honorable, and to be a tiller of the soil is above all else dishonorable. To live by war and plunder is the most honorable thing of all.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 7
paragraphs: These are their most striking customs; and of the gods they worship only Ares, Dionysus, and Artemis. Their kings, however, apart from the rest of the people, worship Hermes above all gods and swear by him alone; and they say that they are descended from Hermes.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 8
paragraphs: The manner of burial for the rich among them is this. For three days they display the corpse, and they slaughter all kinds of victims and feast, after first making lamentation. Then they perform the burial rites, either consuming the body with fire or covering it up in the earth without burning; and afterwards, when they have heaped up a mound, they hold games with every sort of contest, in which—reasonably enough—the greatest prizes are assigned to single combat. Such is the manner of burial among the Thracians.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 9
paragraphs: Of the region lying further north of this country, no one can say with certainty who the people are that live in it; but the parts immediately beyond the Ister are known to be uninhabited and vast in extent. The only people I can hear of who live beyond the Ister are those said to be called the Sigynnae, who dress in the Median fashion. Their horses, it is said, have shaggy hair all over their bodies, as long as five fingers; and they are small, flat-nosed, and too weak to carry men—but when yoked to chariots they are very spirited, which is why the natives drive chariots. The boundaries of this people extend, it is said, as far as the region near the Eneti, who live on the Adriatic; and people say that they are colonists from the Medes. In what way these came to be colonists from the Medes I for my part cannot conceive, but anything is possible in the long course of ages. However that may be, the Ligurians who live in the region inland above Massalia call traders sigynnae, and the Cypriots give the same name to spears.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 10
paragraphs: The Thracians say that the other side of the Ister is occupied by bees, and that on account of them one cannot pass through and go further. But to me it seems that when they speak so, they are saying what is not likely; for these creatures are known to be intolerant of cold, and to me it seems that the regions running up toward the pole are uninhabitable because of the cold climate. Such then are the tales reported about this country. However that may be, Megabazus was at this time bringing its coastal regions into subjection to the Persians.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 11
paragraphs: Meanwhile Darius, as soon as he had crossed the Hellespont and come to Sardis, remembered the service rendered to him by Histiaeus of Miletus and also the advice of Coës of Mytilene. Sending for them to come to Sardis, he offered them a choice of rewards. Histiaeus, being already tyrant of Miletus, did not ask for any additional government, but requested the district of Myrcinus belonging to the Edonians, wishing to found a city there. So Histiaeus chose this for himself; but Coës, not being a tyrant but a private citizen, asked to be made tyrant of Mytilene.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 12
paragraphs: After the desires of both had been fulfilled, they set off for what they had chosen. At this same time it happened that Darius saw something that made him want to order Megabazus to conquer the Paeonians and forcibly remove them from Europe into Asia. The matter was this. There were certain Paeonians named Pigres and Mantyes who, when Darius had crossed over into Asia, came to Sardis because they themselves wished to rule over the Paeonians, and with them they brought their sister, who was tall and beautiful. Then, having watched for a time when Darius was holding public audience in the suburb of the Lydian city, they dressed their sister up as well as they could and sent her off to fetch water, with a water-jar on her head, leading a horse after her by a bridle wound around her arm, and at the same time spinning flax. As the woman passed by him on her way out of the city, Darius took notice of the matter, for what the woman was doing was not Persian or Lydian fashion, nor indeed the manner of any people of Asia. So he sent some of his spearmen with orders to watch what the woman would do with the horse. They followed her; and having come to the river, she watered the horse, and having watered him and filled her jar with water, she came back along the same road, carrying the water on her head, leading the horse after her by the bridle round her arm, and at the same time turning the spindle.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 13
paragraphs: Darius, marveling both at what he heard from those he had sent to observe and at what he himself saw, bade them bring her into his presence. When she was brought, her brothers came with her, who had been watching all this from close by. So when Darius asked of what country she was, the young men said that they were Paeonians and that she was their sister; and he replied, “Who then are these Paeonians, and where on earth do they live?” and he asked them also what they wanted, that they had come to Sardis. They declared to him that they had come to give themselves up to him, and that Paeonia was a country on the river Strymon, that the Strymon was not far from the Hellespont, and finally that they were colonists from the Teucrians of Troy. All these things in turn they told him; and he asked whether all the women of that land were as industrious as their sister. They very readily replied to this also, saying that they were—for it was with precisely this in view that they had staged the whole thing.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 14
paragraphs: Then Darius wrote a letter to Megabazus, whom he had left to command his army in Thrace, ordering him to remove the Paeonians from their homeland and bring them to the king, both themselves and their children and their wives. A horseman at once set off to ride in haste bearing the message to the Hellespont; and having crossed over, he handed the paper to Megabazus. Having read it and obtained guides from Thrace, he set off to march upon Paeonia.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 15
paragraphs: The Paeonians, learning that the Persians were coming against them, gathered all their forces together and marched out toward the sea, supposing that when the Persians invaded them they would make their attack from that side. So the Paeonians were prepared, as I say, to drive off Megabazus's army when it came against them; but the Persians, hearing that the Paeonians had gathered their forces and were guarding the pass toward the sea, took guides and directed their course along the upper road; and passing unnoticed by the Paeonians, they fell upon the cities, which had been left without men, and finding them undefended easily took possession of them. When the Paeonians heard that their cities were in enemy hands, they at once dispersed, each tribe to its own place of habitation, and proceeded to hand themselves over to the Persians. So it was that these Paeonian tribes—the Siropaeones, the Paeoples, and all the others up to Lake Prasias—were removed from their homeland and taken to Asia.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 16
paragraphs: But those who lived around Mount Pangaeum and around the Doberes, Agrianes, and Odomantes, and around Lake Prasias itself, were not conquered at all by Megabazus. He did, however, try to remove even those who lived on the lake, whose dwellings were of this sort: a platform fastened together and resting on lofty piles stood in the middle of the lake's water, with a narrow approach from the mainland by a single bridge. The piles supporting the platform were no doubt originally set there by all the members of the community working together, but since then they continue to set them according to the following rule: every man who marries brings three piles for each wife from the mountain called Orbelus and sets them as supports—and each man takes many wives. Their dwellings are arranged like this: each man has his own hut on the platform to live in, with a trapdoor leading through the platform down to the lake; and they tie their infant children with a rope by the foot, for fear they should roll into the water. They feed their horses and beasts of burden on fish; and the fish are so plentiful that if a man opens the trapdoor and lowers an empty basket by a cord into the lake, after waiting only a short while he draws it up again full of fish. Of the fish there are two kinds, and they call them paprax and tilon.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 17
paragraphs: So those of the Paeonians who had been conquered were being taken to Asia. Meanwhile Megabazus, after conquering the Paeonians, sent as envoys to Macedonia seven Persians who, after himself, were the most respected men in the army. These were being sent to Amyntas to demand earth and water for King Darius. From Lake Prasias the way into Macedonia is very short: first, right by the lake, there is the mine from which, after this time, a talent of silver came in regularly every day to Alexander; and past the mine, when you have crossed the mountain called Dysorum, you are in Macedonia.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 18
paragraphs: These Persians, having been sent to Amyntas, came into his presence and proceeded to demand earth and water for King Darius. He was willing to give both, and he also invited them to be his guests; he prepared a magnificent dinner and received the Persians with friendly hospitality. When dinner was over and the Persians were drinking pledges to one another, they said: “Macedonian host, it is the custom among us Persians, when we hold a great dinner, to bring in also our concubines and lawful wives to sit beside us. Since, therefore, you have received us so readily and are now entertaining us magnificently as your guests, and since you are willing to give King Darius earth and water, consent to follow our custom.” Amyntas replied: “Persians, among us the custom is not so, but that men should be separate from women. Since, however, you, being our masters, make this additional request, this too shall be granted you.” With these words Amyntas sent for the women; and when they came at his summons, they sat down in a row opposite the Persians. Then the Persians, seeing comely women, spoke to Amyntas and said that what had been done was very poorly arranged—it would have been better for the women not to come at all than to come and not sit beside them, but sit opposite and be a torment to their eyes. So Amyntas, under compulsion, bade the women sit beside the Persians; and when the women obeyed, the Persians, being far gone in drink, began at once to touch their breasts, and some of them no doubt also tried to kiss them.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 19
paragraphs: Amyntas, seeing this, kept quiet—though he felt anger—because he was very much afraid of the Persians. But Alexander, son of Amyntas, who was present and saw this, being young and without experience of misfortune, was not able to hold back any longer. In his impatience he said to Amyntas: “Father, give in to what your age demands, and go away to rest, and do not persist any longer in the drinking; but I will stay here and provide our guests with everything needed.” At this Amyntas, understanding that Alexander intended some act of violence, said: “My son, I think I understand your words, as the heat of anger moves you—that you want to send me away and then commit some deed of violence. Therefore I ask you not to use violence against these men, lest it be our ruin; endure to look on at what is being done. As for my departure, however, in that I will do as you say.”

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 20
paragraphs: When Amyntas, having made this request of him, had departed, Alexander said to the Persians: “Guests, with these women you have every freedom to have intercourse with all, if you so desire, or with as many as you wish. You yourselves shall give the word on this; but now, since the hour is already approaching for you to go to bed, and I see that you have drunk well, let these women—if it pleases you—go away to bathe themselves, and when they have bathed, receive them back into your company.” Having said this, and the Persians readily agreeing, he dismissed the women, when they had gone out, to the women's chambers. Alexander himself then dressed up men equal in number to the women—smooth-faced men—in women's clothing, and giving them daggers led them into the banquet-room. As he led them in, he said to the Persians: “Persians, it seems to me that you have been entertained with a feast lacking nothing; for all the other things we had, and moreover such as we were able to devise and furnish, have been supplied to you; and now there is this especially as well, which is the chief thing of all—that we freely grant you also our mothers and our sisters, in order that you may fully perceive that you are honored by us with the treatment you deserve, and also that you may report to the king who sent you that a man of Hellas, a governor of the Macedonians under him, entertained you well at both board and bed.” With these words, Alexander had one of his Macedonians, disguised as a woman, sit beside each Persian; and when the Persians tried to lay hands on them, they slew them.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 21
paragraphs: So these men perished in this way, both they themselves and their whole train of servants; for carriages and servants and all the usual pomp of equipage had come with them, and all of it was made away with at the same time as they were. Afterwards, not long after, the Persians made a great search for these men, and Alexander halted the search by a clever stroke: by giving large sums of money and his own sister, whose name was Gygaea—by giving these things, I say, to Bubares, a Persian in command of those searching for the murdered men, Alexander halted their search.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 22
paragraphs: Thus the death of these Persians was kept hidden. And that these descendants of Perdiccas are Hellenes, as they themselves say, I happen to know for myself; and not only that, I will prove in the subsequent narrative that they are Hellenes. Moreover, the Hellanodicae, who manage the Olympic games, decided that they were so. For when Alexander wished to compete in the games and had gone down into the arena for this purpose, the Hellenes who were to run against him tried to exclude him, saying that the contest was not for barbarians to enter but for Hellenes. Since, however, Alexander proved that he was of Argos, he was judged a Hellene, and when he entered the foot-race his lot came out in a dead heat with the first.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 23
paragraphs: So that is how it happened with respect to these things. At the same time Megabazus had arrived at the Hellespont bringing with him the Paeonians, and from there, after crossing the straits, came to Sardis. Now Histiaeus the Milesian was already busy fortifying with a wall the place he had asked for and received from Darius as a reward for keeping safe the bridge of boats—this place being what is called Myrcinus, lying along the bank of the river Strymon. Megabazus, perceiving what Histiaeus was doing, as soon as he came to Sardis with the Paeonians said to Darius: “O king, what is this you have done, granting permission to a Hellene—a skillful and cunning one—to found a city in Thrace in a place where there is abundant forest for shipbuilding and a great supply of wood for oars and silver mines, and great numbers both of Hellenes and barbarians living round about, who, when they get a leader, will do whatever he orders, day and night. Stop this man from doing this, then, so that you are not caught up in a domestic war; stop him by sending for him in a courteous way, but once you have him in your hands, arrange that he shall never again return to the land of the Hellenes.”

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 24
paragraphs: With these words Megabazus easily persuaded Darius, who took him for a true prophet of what was likely to come to pass. Thereupon Darius sent a messenger to Myrcinus with this message: “Histiaeus, King Darius says this: Reflecting, I find that there is no one more sincerely well-disposed than you to me and my power; and this I know by deeds, not words. Now therefore, since I have it in mind to accomplish great matters, by all means come here to me, so that I may share them with you.” Trusting these words, and at the same time counting it a great thing to become a counselor of the king, Histiaeus came to Sardis; and when he had come, Darius spoke to him as follows: “Histiaeus, I sent for you for this reason: that when I had returned from the Scythians and you had gone out of my sight, never did I desire to see anything again so quickly as I then wished both to see you and to come to speech with you—since I perceived that the most valuable of all possessions is a friend who is a man of understanding and also sincerely well-disposed, both of which qualities I know exist in you, and of which I can bear witness in my own affairs. Now then—since you have done well to come here—this is what I propose to you: leave Miletus alone and your newly founded city in Thrace, and come with me to Susa; share whatever I have, eat at my table, and be my counselor.”

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 25
paragraphs: So Darius spoke; and having appointed Artaphrenes—his own brother and son of his father—to be governor of Sardis, he marched away to Susa taking Histiaeus with him, after first naming Otanes commander of those who lived along the coasts. This man's father, Sisamnes, who had been made one of the royal judges, King Cambyses had killed and flayed because he had judged a case unjustly for money. After tearing away the skin, he had cut leather thongs from it and stretched them across the seat where Sisamnes had used to sit to give judgment; and having stretched them in the seat, Cambyses appointed the son of the Sisamnes he had killed and flayed to be judge in his father's place, charging him to remember in what seat he was sitting to pass judgment.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 26
paragraphs: This Otanes, then, who was made to sit in that seat, had now become the successor of Megabazus in the command; and he conquered the Byzantians and Calchedonians, and conquered Antandrus in the land of Troas, and Lamponium; and having received ships from the Lesbians, he conquered Lemnos and Imbros, which were both at that time still inhabited by Pelasgians.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 27
paragraphs: Of these, the Lemnians fought well, and after defending themselves a long time were at last brought down. Over the survivors the Persians set as governor Lycaretus, the brother of that Maeandrius who had been king of Samos. This Lycaretus ruled in Lemnos until his death. And the cause of it was this: he went on enslaving and subjugating everyone, accusing some of having gone over to the Scythians and others of damaging Darius's army as it was coming back from Scythia.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 28
paragraphs: So much did Otanes accomplish when he was made commander. After this, for a short time, there was a lull in troubles; and then troubles began to fall a second time upon the Ionians, arising from Naxos and Miletus. For Naxos surpassed all the other islands in wealth, and Miletus at the same time had just then come to the very height of its prosperity and was the ornament of Ionia. Yet for two generations before these events it had suffered most violently from civil faction, until the Parians reformed it—for it was they whom, of all the Hellenes, the Milesians chose to be reformers of their state.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 29
paragraphs: The Parians reconciled the factions in the following way. Their best men came to Miletus, and seeing the Milesians in a disastrously ruined state, they said they wished to go over the country. While doing this and passing through the whole territory of Miletus, whenever in the desolation of the land they saw any field that was well cultivated, they wrote down the name of its owner. Then when they had gone through the whole land and found only a few such men, as soon as they returned to the city they called a general assembly and appointed to manage the state those whose fields they had found well cultivated—for they said they thought these men would care for public affairs as they had cared for their own; and the rest of the Milesians, who had before been divided by factions, they commanded to obey these men.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 30
paragraphs: So the Parians had reformed the Milesians. But at the time of which I speak, troubles began to come upon Ionia from these very states, in the following way. From Naxos certain men of the wealthier class were driven into exile by the people, and in their exile they came to Miletus. It happened that Miletus was then under the rule of Aristagoras, son of Molpagoras, who was both son-in-law and cousin of Histiaeus, son of Lysagoras, whom Darius was keeping at Susa. For Histiaeus was tyrant of Miletus, and it happened that he was at Susa at this time when the Naxians came, who had in former times been guest-friends of Histiaeus. When the Naxians arrived, they asked Aristagoras whether he would supply them with a force, so that they might return from exile to their own land. And he, thinking that if they returned to their state through his means he would be ruler of Naxos, but at the same time making a pretext of the guest-friendship with Histiaeus, made them this proposal: “I am not able to promise that I can supply you with force sufficient to bring you back from exile against the will of those Naxians who hold power in the state; for I hear that the Naxians have an army eight thousand shields strong and many warships. But I will use every effort to devise a way; and my plan is this. Artaphrenes happens to be my friend. Now Artaphrenes, you should know, is a son of Hystaspes and brother of King Darius; and he is ruler of all the coastal peoples of Asia, with a great army and many ships. He, I think, will do whatever we ask of him.” Hearing this, the Naxians turned the matter over to Aristagoras to manage as best he could, and they bade him promise gifts and the expenses of the expedition, saying that they would pay them; for they had every expectation that, once they appeared at Naxos, the Naxians would do all their bidding, and likewise the other islanders. For none of these islands, that is to say the Cyclades, was as yet subject to Darius.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 31
paragraphs: Aristagoras accordingly came to Sardis and said to Artaphrenes that Naxos was an island not large in size but beautiful nonetheless and fertile in soil, and near to Ionia, and that it had much wealth and many slaves. “Send out then an expedition against this land,” he said, “and restore it to those who are now exiles from it. If you do this, first I have ready for you large sums of money—apart from the expenses of the expedition, which it is only fair that we who conduct it should supply—and next, you will gain for the king not only Naxos itself but also the islands dependent on it, Paros and Andros and the others called the Cyclades; and setting out from these, you will easily attack Euboea, an island large and wealthy, as large indeed as Cyprus, and very easy to conquer. To subdue all these a hundred ships are enough.” Artaphrenes replied: “You bring good news to the royal house, and in all these matters you counsel well, except as to the number of the ships; for instead of a hundred, two hundred shall be made ready for you by the start of spring. It is right that the king himself also should join in approving this matter.”

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 32
paragraphs: So Aristagoras, hearing this, went back to Miletus greatly pleased; and meanwhile Artaphrenes, having sent to Susa and reported what Aristagoras had said, and Darius himself having joined in approving it, made ready two hundred triremes and a great host of Persians and their allies. He appointed as commander of these a Persian named Megabates, one of the Achaemenidae and cousin both to himself and to Darius—the same man to whose daughter Pausanias son of Cleombrotus the Lacedaemonian afterwards (if the story is true) became engaged, having conceived a desire to become tyrant of Hellas. Having appointed Megabates, I say, commander, Artaphrenes sent the armament off to Aristagoras.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 33
paragraphs: When Megabates had taken on the force along with the Naxian exiles, he sailed with the pretense of going to the Hellespont; but when he came to Chios, he directed his ships to Caucasa, to cross over from there to Naxos with a north wind. Then—since it was not fated that the Naxians should be destroyed by this expedition—the following thing happened. As Megabates was going round inspecting the watches set on the several ships, it chanced that on a ship from Myndus no one was on guard; and he, being very angry, ordered his spearmen to find out the captain of that ship, whose name was Scylax, and to bind him in an oar-hole of his ship in such a way that his head should be outside and his body within. When Scylax had been bound in this way, someone reported to Aristagoras that Megabates had bound his guest-friend of Myndus and was treating him with shameful outrage. Aristagoras came and asked the Persian to release him, and when he got nothing of what he was asking for, he went himself and set him free. On hearing this, Megabates was enormously angry and burst out in rage against Aristagoras. Aristagoras replied: “What have you to do with these matters? Did not Artaphrenes send you to obey me and sail wherever I should order? Why do you meddle with things that are not your concern?” So said Aristagoras; and the other, enraged at this, when night came on sent men by ship to Naxos to warn the Naxians of all the danger threatening them.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 34
paragraphs: For the Naxians had not at all expected that this expedition would come against them. But when they were informed of it, they at once brought inside the walls the property that was in the fields, provided themselves with food and drink as for a siege, and strengthened their wall. So these were making preparations as for war about to fall on them; and the others meanwhile, having brought their ships over from Chios to Naxos, found them well defended when they attacked, and besieged them for four months. When the money the Persians had brought with them had all been used up, and Aristagoras himself had spent much in addition, and the siege kept demanding ever more, they built walls for the Naxian exiles and went back to the mainland, having failed.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 35
paragraphs: So Aristagoras was not able to fulfill his promise to Artaphrenes; and at the same time he was hard pressed by the demand made on him for the expenses of the expedition, and he was afraid both because of the failure of the armament and because he had become an enemy of Megabates; and he supposed he would be stripped of his rule over Miletus. With all these fears, he began to plan revolt. For it happened that just at this time the man who had been marked on the head had come from Histiaeus in Susa, signifying that Aristagoras should revolt from the king. For Histiaeus, wishing to signify to Aristagoras that he should revolt, could find no safe way of doing so—since the roads were guarded—except by shaving the hair of the most trustworthy of his slaves, pricking marks into his head, and then waiting until the hair had grown again. As soon as it had grown, he sent him off to Miletus, giving him no other charge but this: that when he had reached Miletus he should bid Aristagoras shave off his hair and look at his head. The marks, as I have said, signified revolt. Histiaeus did this because he was deeply vexed at being detained at Susa. He had great hopes that if a revolt occurred, he would be let go to the coast; but if no change took place at Miletus, he had no expectation of ever returning there again.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 36
paragraphs: With this intention, then, Histiaeus was sending the messenger; and it happened that all these things came together upon Aristagoras at the same time. He took counsel with his partisans, declaring to them both his own opinion and the message from Histiaeus. All the rest expressed the same opinion, urging him to revolt; but Hecataeus the historian first urged that they should not undertake war with the king of the Persians, enumerating all the nations over whom Darius ruled and his power. When he could not persuade him, he counseled next that they should contrive to become masters of the sea. Now this, he continued, could not come to pass in any other way, so far as he could see, for he knew that the Milesians' own force was weak; but if the treasures should be taken that were in the temple at Branchidae, which Croesus the Lydian had dedicated as offerings, he had great hopes that they might become masters of the sea. By this means they would not only have wealth at their disposal themselves, but the enemy would not be able to carry the things off as plunder. These treasures were of great value, as I have shown in the first part of the history. This opinion did not prevail; but nevertheless it was resolved to revolt, and that one of them should sail to Myus to the force which had returned from Naxos and was now there, and try to seize the commanders sailing in the ships.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 37
paragraphs: So Iatragoras was sent for this purpose and seized by a trick Oliatus son of Ibanollis of Mylasa, and Histiaeus son of Tymnes of Termera, and Coës son of Erxander—to whom Darius had given Mytilene as a gift—and Aristagoras son of Heracleides of Cyme, and many others. And then Aristagoras openly revolted and devised every means he could to harm Darius. First he pretended to renounce the tyrant's power and gave Miletus political equality, in order that the Milesians might be willing to revolt with him; then he proceeded to do this same thing in the rest of Ionia as well. Some of the tyrants he drove out; but those whom he had taken from the ships that had sailed with him to Naxos he handed over, because he wished to do a favor to their cities, delivering each to the city from which he had come.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 38
paragraphs: Now the men of Mytilene, as soon as they got Coës into their hands, led him out and stoned him to death; but the men of Cyme let their tyrant go, and so too did most of the other cities. Thus were the tyrants deposed in the various cities; and Aristagoras the Milesian, having deposed the tyrants, bade each people appoint commanders in their several cities, and then himself set out as an envoy to Lacedaemon—for in truth it was necessary for him to find some powerful ally.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 39
paragraphs: At Sparta, Anaxandrides, son of Leon, was no longer alive as king, but had come to the end of his life; and Cleomenes, son of Anaxandrides, held the royal power, not having obtained it by merit but by right of birth. For Anaxandrides had as wife his own sister's daughter, whom he loved dearly, but no children were born to him by her. This being so, the Ephors summoned him before them and said: “If you will not take thought for yourself in time, yet we cannot allow this to happen—that the race of Eurysthenes should become extinct. Therefore set aside the wife you now have, since, as you know, she bears you no children, and marry another; and in doing so you will please the Spartans.” He answered that he would do neither of these two things, and that they were not giving him honorable counsel in advising him to send away the wife he had—who had done him no wrong—and take another into his house; in short, he would not follow their advice.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 40
paragraphs: At this the Ephors and the Senate deliberated together and put this proposal to Anaxandrides: “Since then we see that you are firmly attached to the wife you now have, agree to do this, and do not set yourself against it—lest the Spartans take some counsel concerning you otherwise than you would wish. We do not ask you to put away the wife you have; rather, continue to give her everything you give her now, and at the same time take into your house another wife besides this one, to bear you children.” When they spoke to him in this way, Anaxandrides consented, and so he had two wives—a thing by no means in keeping with Spartan custom.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 41
paragraphs: Not much time had passed when the wife who had come in afterwards bore the Cleomenes we spoke of; and just as she was bringing to the light an heir to the Spartan kingdom, the former wife, who had been childless up to that point, by some chance conceived, happening to do so at just that moment. She was in truth with child, but the kinsfolk of the wife who had come in afterwards, when they heard about it, cried out against her, saying that she was making an empty boast and meant to pass off another's child as her own. Since they made a great show of indignation, and as the time drew near, the Ephors, being skeptical, sat around and watched the woman during the birth of her child; and she bore Dorieus, and then immediately conceived Leonidas and after him Cleombrotus—indeed, some even say that Cleombrotus and Leonidas were twins. The wife, however, who had borne Cleomenes and had come in after the first, daughter of Prinetades the son of Demarmenus, bore no more children.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 42
paragraphs: Now Cleomenes, it is said, was not quite in his right mind but on the verge of madness, while Dorieus was first of all his age-mates and felt sure he would obtain the kingdom by merit. With this opinion in mind, when Anaxandrides died and the Lacedaemonians, following custom, placed the eldest, Cleomenes, on the throne, Dorieus, indignant and not thinking it fit that he should be a subject of Cleomenes, asked the Spartans for a band of followers and led them out to found a colony—without either consulting the oracle at Delphi about what land to settle in, or doing any of the things customarily done. Vexed as he was, he sailed off with his ships to Libya, with Theraeans as his guides. On reaching Cinyps, he made a settlement in the fairest spot of all Libya, along the banks of the river; but in the third year he was driven out of it by the Macae, the Libyans, and the Carthaginians, and returned to the Peloponnese.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 43
paragraphs: Then Antichares, a man of Eleon, gave him counsel out of the oracles of Laius, to make a settlement at Heraclea in Sicily, saying that the whole land of Eryx belonged to the Heraclidae, since Heracles himself had won it. On hearing this, Dorieus went at once to Delphi to ask the oracle whether he would be able to conquer the land he was setting out for; and the Pythian priestess replied that he would conquer it. Dorieus therefore took with him the force he had led before to Libya, and sailed along the coast of Italy.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 44
paragraphs: At this time the Sybarites say that they and their king Telys were about to make an expedition against Croton, and the Crotoniats, being exceedingly alarmed, asked Dorieus to help them and obtained their request. So Dorieus joined them in an expedition against Sybaris and helped them take the city. This is what the Sybarites say of the doings of Dorieus and his followers; but the Crotoniats say that no stranger helped them in the war against the Sybarites, except Callias alone, a diviner of Elis and one of the descendants of Iamus, and he in the following way: he ran away, they say, from Telys the tyrant of the Sybarites, when the sacrifices did not prove favorable as he was sacrificing for the expedition against Croton, and so came to them.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 45
paragraphs: Such, I say, are the tales these two sides tell, and each produces as evidence the following facts.
