The Sybarites point to a sacred enclosure and temple beside the dried-up bed of the Crathis, which they say that Dorieus, after he had helped take the city, set up to Athena surnamed “of the Crathis”; and besides, they consider the very death of Dorieus to be very strong evidence, thinking that he perished because he had acted contrary to the oracle given him—for if he had not turned aside along the way and had kept on doing what he had been sent to do, he would have conquered the land of Eryx, and having conquered it would have become its possessor, and he and his army would not have perished. The Crotoniats, on the other hand, declare that many things were granted in the territory of Croton as special gifts to Callias the Elean, of which the descendants of Callias were still in possession down to my time, while nothing was granted to Dorieus or to his descendants. But if Dorieus had indeed helped in the war against Sybaris, they say, many times as much as was given to Callias would have been given to him. These are the proofs the two sides produce, and we may agree with whichever we find more credible.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 46
paragraphs: There sailed with Dorieus other Spartans too, as joint-founders of the colony—namely Thessalus, Paraebates, Celeas, and Euryleon; and when they reached Sicily with their whole force, they were defeated in battle by the Phoenicians and the men of Egesta and were killed—Euryleon alone of the joint-founders surviving this disaster. This man, having collected the survivors of the expedition, seized Minoa, the colony of Selinus, and helped to free the Selinuntines from their tyrant Peithagoras. After he had deposed him, he himself laid claim to the tyranny in Selinus and became sole ruler there, though only for a short time; for the Selinuntines rose in revolt against him and killed him, though he had fled for refuge to the altar of Zeus Agoraeus.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 47
paragraphs: Accompanying Dorieus and dying with him was also Philip, son of Butacides, a man of Croton, who, having been betrothed to the daughter of Telys the Sybarite, had become an exile from Croton; then, disappointed of the marriage, he sailed off to Cyrene, and from there set out and accompanied Dorieus with a trireme of his own, supplying the expenses of the crew himself. This man had been a victor at the Olympic games and was the most beautiful of the Hellenes of his time; and because of his beauty he received from the men of Egesta what no one else ever received from them—they established a hero-shrine over his tomb and still propitiate him with sacrifices.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 48
paragraphs: So in this way Dorieus ended his life. But if he had endured to be a subject of Cleomenes and had stayed in Sparta, he would have been king of Lacedaemon; for Cleomenes reigned no very long time, and died leaving no son to succeed him but only a daughter, whose name was Gorgo.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 49
paragraphs: However, Aristagoras the tyrant of Miletus arrived at Sparta while Cleomenes was reigning, and so it was with him that he came to speech. The Lacedaemonians say that he had with him a bronze tablet engraved with a map of the whole earth, with all the sea and all the rivers. When he came to speech with Cleomenes he said: “Do not marvel, Cleomenes, at my earnestness in coming here; for the case is this. That the sons of the Ionians should be slaves instead of free is a reproach and a grief most of all indeed to ourselves, but to you above all others, inasmuch as you are the leaders of Hellas. Now therefore I entreat you by the gods of Hellas to rescue from slavery the Ionians, who are your own kinsmen. You may easily achieve this, for the barbarians are not brave in battle, whereas you have reached the very height of valor in matters of war; and their fighting is of this sort—with bows and a short spear, and they go into battle wearing trousers and caps on their heads. So they are easily conquered. Then again, those who occupy that continent have good things in such quantities as all the other nations of the world put together do not possess: first gold, then silver and bronze, embroidered garments, beasts of burden, and slaves—all of which you could have for yourselves if you so desired. The nations moreover are arranged one after another as I shall show: the Ionians here; next to them the Lydians, who not only live in a fertile land but are also exceedingly rich in gold and silver,”—as he said this he pointed to the map of the earth he carried with him engraved on the tablet—“and here next to the Lydians,” Aristagoras went on, “are the Eastern Phrygians, who have the greatest number of sheep and cattle of any people I know, and also the most abundant crops. Next to the Phrygians are the Cappadocians, whom we call Syrians; and bordering them are the Cilicians, coming down to this sea, in which lies the island of Cyprus here; and these pay five hundred talents to the king as their yearly tribute. Next to these Cilicians are the Armenians, whom you see here, and these too have great numbers of sheep and cattle. Next to the Armenians are the Matieni, occupying this country here; and next to them is the land of Cissia here, in which, along the banks of this river Choaspes, is situated the city of Susa, where the Great King has his residence and where the money is laid up in treasuries. Once you have taken this city, you may then confidently enter into a contest with Zeus himself in the matter of wealth. No—can it really be that you feel obliged to take on the risk of battles against the Messenians and Arcadians and Argives, who are a match for you, for the sake of land that is not much in extent nor very fertile, and for boundaries that are merely small, though these peoples have no gold or silver at all, which are what makes a man eager to fight and die? Can this be so? Will you not now choose another course, when it is possible for you easily to have rule over all Asia?” So Aristagoras spoke, and Cleomenes answered him: “Milesian guest-friend, I defer my answer to you until the day after tomorrow.”

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 50
paragraphs: So far they went at that time; and when the appointed day arrived for the answer, and they had come to the place agreed upon, Cleomenes asked Aristagoras how many days' journey it was from the Ionian sea to the residence of the king. Now Aristagoras, who in other respects acted cleverly and deceived him well, in this point made a mistake: for whereas he should not have told him the truth, at least if he wished to bring the Spartans out to Asia, he in fact said that it was a journey up from the sea of three months. The other cut short the rest of Aristagoras's account of the way and said: “Milesian guest-friend, get yourself out of Sparta before the sun sets; for you speak a word that sounds not well in Lacedaemonian ears, wanting to take them on a three months' journey from the sea.”

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 51
paragraphs: Cleomenes, having said this, went off to his house. But Aristagoras took the suppliant's branch and went to the house of Cleomenes; and having entered as a suppliant, he asked Cleomenes to send away the child and listen to him—for Cleomenes's daughter was standing beside him, whose name was Gorgo, and she happened to be his only child, being now eight or nine years old. Cleomenes, however, told him to say what he wanted and not to hold back on the child's account. Then Aristagoras proceeded to promise him money, beginning with ten talents, if he would accomplish what he was asking for; and when Cleomenes refused, Aristagoras went on increasing the sums offered, until at last he had promised fifty talents, and at that moment the child cried out: “Father, the stranger will corrupt you if you do not leave him and go.” Cleomenes, pleased by the child's advice, went off into another room, and Aristagoras left Sparta altogether, and had no further opportunity to explain about the road up from the sea to the king's residence.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 52
paragraphs: As to this road, the truth is as follows. Everywhere there are royal stages and excellent rest-houses, and the whole road runs through inhabited and safe country. Through Lydia and Phrygia there extend twenty stages, amounting to ninety-four and a half leagues; and after Phrygia comes the river Halys, at which there is a gate that one must pass through in order to cross the river, and a strong guard-post is established there. Then, after crossing into Cappadocia, it is twenty-eight stages, being one hundred and four leagues, by this road to the borders of Cilicia; and on the Cilician frontier you pass through two separate gates and go by two separate guard-posts. After passing these, it is three stages, amounting to fifteen and a half leagues, to journey through Cilicia; and the boundary of Cilicia and Armenia is a navigable river called the Euphrates. In Armenia the number of stages with rest-houses is fifteen, and the number of leagues fifty-six and a half, and there is a guard-post on the way. From Armenia, when one enters the land of Matiene, there are thirty-four stages, amounting to one hundred and thirty-seven leagues; and through this land flow four navigable rivers, which cannot be crossed except by ferries—first the Tigris, then a second and a third, both called by the same name, though they are not the same river nor do they flow from the same region (the first of them flows from the Armenian land and the other from that of the Matieni), and the fourth of these rivers is called the Gyndes, the same river that Cyrus once divided into three hundred and sixty channels. Passing thence into the Cissian land, there are eleven stages, forty-two and a half leagues, to the river Choaspes, which is also navigable; and on this is built the city of Susa. The total number of stages comes to one hundred and eleven.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 53
paragraphs: This is the number of stages with rest-houses as one goes up from Sardis to Susa. If the royal road has been correctly measured in leagues, and if the league is equal to thirty furlongs (as it undoubtedly is), the number of furlongs from Sardis to what is called the palace of Memnon is thirteen thousand five hundred, the number of leagues being four hundred and fifty. So if one travels one hundred and fifty furlongs a day, exactly ninety days are spent on the journey.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 54
paragraphs: So when Aristagoras the Milesian told Cleomenes the Lacedaemonian that the journey up from the sea to the residence of the king was one of three months, he spoke correctly; but if anyone demands a still more exact statement than this, I will give him that also: for we ought to reckon in addition the length of the road from Ephesus to Sardis. I say, then, that the total number of furlongs from the Hellenic sea to Susa (for by that name the city of Memnon is known) is fourteen thousand and forty, since the number of furlongs from Ephesus to Sardis is five hundred and forty; and so the three months' journey is lengthened by three days added.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 55
paragraphs: Aristagoras, driven out of Sparta, proceeded to Athens—which had been set free from the rule of tyrants in the way I shall tell. When Hipparchus, son of Peisistratus and brother of the tyrant Hippias, had been slain by Aristogeiton and Harmodius—men who were by descent Gephyraeans—after seeing a vision in a dream that plainly signified it to him, the Athenians continued to be ruled by a tyranny for four years after this, no less than before—indeed, even more harshly.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 56
paragraphs: The vision in Hipparchus's dream was this. On the night before the Panathenaea, it seemed to Hipparchus that a man came and stood by him, tall and of fair form, and riddling spoke these verses to him:
“With enduring soul, as a lion, endure unendurable evil: no man who does wrong shall escape the appointed judgment.”

As soon as it was day, he publicly communicated these verses to the interpreters of dreams; but afterwards he dismissed the vision from his mind and began to take part in that procession in which he lost his life.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 57
paragraphs: Now the Gephyraeans, to whom the murderers of Hipparchus belonged, by their own account were originally descended from Eretria; but as I find by carrying inquiries back, they were Phoenicians of the company that came with Cadmus to the land now called Boeotia, and they lived in the district of Tanagra, which had been allotted to them in that land. Then, after the Cadmeians had first been driven out by the Argives, these Gephyraeans in turn were driven out by the Boeotians and made their way to Athens. The Athenians received them on certain fixed conditions to be citizens of their state, laying down rules that they should be excluded from a number of things not worth mentioning here.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 58
paragraphs: Now these Phoenicians who came with Cadmus, of whom the Gephyraeans were a part, brought with them into the land of Boeotia, when they settled there, many arts, and especially letters, which did not exist, it seems to me, among the Hellenes before this time. At first they introduced the letters used by the Phoenician race generally; but in time, as they changed their speech, they also changed the form of the letters. In most of the places where they lived, the Ionians were the Hellenic people living nearest them; and these, having received the letters by the Phoenicians' instruction, altered their form slightly and so made use of them, and in doing so they called them “phoenicians,” as was only fair, since the Phoenicians had introduced them into Hellas. The Ionians too from ancient times call paper “skins,” because formerly, when paper was scarce, they used goat- and sheep-skins; and even in my own day many of the barbarians write on such skins.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 59
paragraphs: I myself once saw Cadmean characters in the temple of Ismenian Apollo at Thebes of the Boeotians, engraved on certain tripods, and for the most part resembling the Ionic letters. One of these tripods has the inscription:
“Me Amphitryon offered on returning from the Teleboan land.” This inscription would be of an age contemporary with Laius, son of Labdacus, son of Polydorus, son of Cadmus.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 60
paragraphs: Another tripod speaks thus in hexameter verse:
“Me Scaeus offered to you, far-darting Apollo, victor in the boxing contest, a gift most fair in your honor.”

This Scaeus would be the son of Hippocoön (if indeed it was really he who offered it, and not another of the same name as the son of Hippocoön), being of an age contemporary with Oedipus, son of Laius.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 61
paragraphs: And the third tripod, also in hexameter verse, says:
“Me Laodamas offered to you, fair-aiming Apollo, being king, out of his wealth, as a gift most fair in your honor.”

It was in the reign of this very Laodamas, son of Eteocles, that the Cadmeians were driven out by the Argives and went off to join the Encheleans; and the Gephyraeans, left behind then, were afterwards forced by the Boeotians to withdraw to Athens. Moreover, they have temples established in Athens in which the other Athenians have no part; and among other distinctive shrines, they have especially a temple of Demeter Achaia and a celebration of her mysteries.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 62
paragraphs: I have now told of the vision Hipparchus saw in his dream, and also the descent of the Gephyraeans, to whom the murderers of Hipparchus belonged; and in addition to this I must take up and continue the story I was about to tell at first—how the Athenians were freed from their tyrants. While Hippias was tyrant and was dealing harshly with the Athenians because of the death of Hipparchus, the Alcmaeonidae, who were of Athenian race and were fugitives from the sons of Peisistratus, failed in an attempt made together with the other Athenian exiles to return by force; and when they tried to return and set Athens free, they met with a great disaster, after having fortified Leipsydrium, which lies above Paeonia. These Alcmaeonidae, still devising every means against the sons of Peisistratus, accepted the contract to build and complete the temple at Delphi—that which now exists but did not as yet at that time. Being already both wealthy and of old repute, they completed the temple in a manner more splendid than the contract required, particularly in this: that having agreed to make the temple of common limestone, they built the front portions of it in Parian marble.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 63
paragraphs: Then, as the Athenians say, these men, settled at Delphi, persuaded the Pythian priestess by gifts of money that whenever men of the Spartans should come to consult the oracle, whether privately or publicly, she should propose to them to set Athens free. The Lacedaemonians, since the same utterance was delivered to them on all occasions, sent Anchimolius son of Aster, a man of repute among their citizens, with an army to drive the sons of Peisistratus out of Athens—even though these were very closely connected with them by guest-friendship; for they held that the concerns of the god should be preferred to those of men. This force they sent by sea in ships. Anchimolius, having put in to shore at Phalerum, disembarked his army; but the sons of Peisistratus, having learned of this beforehand, called in an auxiliary force from Thessaly, for they had made an alliance with the Thessalians, and the Thessalians at their request sent by public resolution a body of a thousand horse and also their king Cineas, a man of Conium. With these as allies, the sons of Peisistratus devised the following: they cut down the trees in the plain of Phalerum and made this district fit for horsemen to ride over, and then they sent the cavalry to attack the enemy's camp; and falling upon it, they killed (among many other Lacedaemonians) Anchimolius himself, and the survivors they shut up in their ships. Such was the outcome of the first expedition from Lacedaemon; and the burial-place of Anchimolius is at Alopece in Attica, near the temple of Heracles at Cynosarges.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 64
paragraphs: After this the Lacedaemonians equipped a larger expedition and sent it against Athens, appointing as commander of the army their king Cleomenes son of Anaxandrides, and sending it this time not by sea but by land. With these, when they had invaded the land of Attica, the Thessalian cavalry first engaged in battle; and in no long time they were routed—more than forty of their men fell, and the survivors departed without more ado and went straight back to Thessaly. Cleomenes then came to the city together with those Athenians who wished to be free, and began to besiege the tyrants shut up in the Pelasgian wall.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 65
paragraphs: The Lacedaemonians would never have captured the sons of Peisistratus at all—for they had no intention of mounting a long blockade, and the others were well supplied with food and drink, so that they would have gone back to Sparta after only a few days' siege—had not something happened at this very moment which was unfortunate for one side and helpful to the other. The children of the sons of Peisistratus were captured while being secretly smuggled out of the country; and when this happened, all their plans were thrown into confusion, and they surrendered, receiving back their children on the terms the Athenians wanted: namely, that they should depart out of Attica within five days. After this they left the country and went to Sigeum on the Scamander, having ruled over the Athenians as a family for thirty-six years. These too were originally Pylians and sons of Neleus, descended from the same ancestors as the house of Codrus and Melanthus, who had earlier become kings of Athens though they had come from abroad. Hence too Hippocrates had given his son the name Peisistratus as a memorial, calling him after Peisistratus the son of Nestor.

So the Athenians were freed from their tyrants. And the deeds and sufferings worth narrating that they did or endured after liberation, up to the time when Ionia revolted from Darius and Aristagoras the Milesian came to Athens to ask for their help—these I will set forth first before going further.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 66
paragraphs: Athens, which even before that time was great, then, once it had been freed from tyrants, became gradually greater still; and in it two men exercised power—Cleisthenes, a descendant of Alcmaeon, the same man who is reported to have bribed the Pythian priestess, and Isagoras, son of Tisander, of a family highly reputed, though of his original descent I am unable to say; his kinsmen, however, sacrifice to the Carian Zeus. These men came into party strife over power; and when Cleisthenes was being worsted in the struggle, he made common cause with the people. After this he caused the Athenians to be divided into ten tribes, who were formerly in four; and he changed the names that they had been known by after the sons of Ion—Geleon, Aegicoreus, Argades, and Hoples—and invented for them names taken from other heroes, all native Athenians except Ajax, whom he added as a neighbor and ally, though he was no Athenian.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 67
paragraphs: In these matters it seems to me that this Cleisthenes was imitating his mother's father, Cleisthenes the tyrant of Sicyon. For when that Cleisthenes went to war with Argos, he first put a stop in Sicyon to the contests of rhapsodes, which were concerned with the poems of Homer, because Argives and Argos are praised in them almost everywhere. Secondly, since there was (as there still is) in the very marketplace of the Sicyonians a hero-shrine of Adrastus, son of Talaus, Cleisthenes conceived a desire to cast him out of the land because he was an Argive. So he came to Delphi and consulted the oracle as to whether he should cast Adrastus out; and the Pythian priestess answered that Adrastus was king of the Sicyonians, whereas he was a stoner of them. Since the god did not permit him to do this, he went away home and considered means by which Adrastus might be brought to leave of his own accord; and when he thought he had discovered them, he sent to Thebes in Boeotia and said that he wished to introduce Melanippus, son of Astacus, into his city, and the Thebans gave him leave. So Cleisthenes introduced Melanippus into his city, appointed a sacred enclosure for him within the precincts of the city hall itself, and established him there in the strongest position. Cleisthenes introduced Melanippus (for I must report this too) because he was the greatest enemy of Adrastus, having killed both his brother Mecisteus and his son-in-law Tydeus. Once he had appointed the sacred enclosure for him, Cleisthenes took away the sacrifices and festivals of Adrastus and gave them to Melanippus. Now the Sicyonians had been accustomed to honor Adrastus with very great honors; for this land was formerly the land of Polybus, and Adrastus was the son of Polybus's daughter, and Polybus, dying without sons, gave his kingdom to Adrastus. The Sicyonians accordingly gave other honors to Adrastus, but especially, with reference to his sufferings, they honored him with tragic choruses, paying this honor not to Dionysus but to Adrastus. Cleisthenes, however, gave the choruses back to Dionysus, and the other rites besides these he gave to Melanippus.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 68
paragraphs: Thus he dealt with Adrastus. He also changed the names of the Dorian tribes, so that the Sicyonians might not have the same tribes as the Argives—in which he showed great contempt for the Sicyonians, for the names he gave them were taken from the names of a pig and an ass, altering only the endings, except in the case of his own tribe, to which he gave a name derived from his own rule. These last, then, were called Archelai (“rulers of the people”); the others of one tribe were called Hyatai (“pig-men”), another Oneatai (“ass-men”), and the remaining tribe Choireatai (“swine-men”). These tribe-names were used by the Sicyonians not only in the reign of Cleisthenes but also for sixty years after his death. Then, however, they reconsidered the matter and changed them to Hylleis, Pamphyli, and Dymanatae, adding a fourth to these, to which they gave the name Aegialeis, after Aegialeus the son of Adrastus.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 69
paragraphs: This is what the Cleisthenes of Sicyon had done; and the Athenian Cleisthenes, who was his daughter's son and named after him, I suppose despising the Ionians as his namesake had despised the Dorians, imitated him so that the Athenians might not have the same tribes as the Ionians. For at this time, when he added to his own party the whole body of the Athenian common people—whom before he had despised—he changed the names of the tribes and made them greater in number than they had been; he made in fact ten tribe-rulers instead of four, and in tens also he distributed the demes among the tribes. Having added the common people to his party, he was far superior to his opponents.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 70
paragraphs: Then Isagoras, as he was being worsted in his turn, contrived a plan against him: he called in Cleomenes the Lacedaemonian to help him, who had been his guest-friend since the siege of the sons of Peisistratus; moreover Cleomenes was accused of being intimate with Isagoras's wife. First, then, Cleomenes sent a herald to Athens demanding the expulsion of Cleisthenes and with him many other Athenians, calling them “the accursed.” This message he sent at Isagoras's prompting; for the Alcmaeonidae and their party were accused of the murder to which this referred, while he and his friends had had no part in it.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 71
paragraphs: Now those of the Athenians who were “under the curse” got this name as follows. There was a certain Cylon among the Athenians, a man who had been victorious at the Olympic games. He behaved arrogantly, wishing to make himself tyrant; and having formed for himself an association of men of his own age, he tried to seize the Acropolis. Not being able to take it, he sat as a suppliant before the image of the goddess. These men were taken from their place as suppliants by the presidents of the naucraries, who at that time administered affairs at Athens, on the condition that they should be liable to any penalty short of death; and the Alcmaeonidae were accused of having put them to death. This had happened before the time of Peisistratus.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 72
paragraphs: Now when Cleomenes sent demanding the expulsion of Cleisthenes and of those under the curse, Cleisthenes himself secretly withdrew. But even so Cleomenes thereafter appeared in Athens with no very large force, and on arriving he expelled as accursed seven hundred Athenian families whose names Isagoras had suggested to him. Having done this, he next tried to dissolve the Council, and put the offices of state into the hands of three hundred men who were Isagoras's partisans. The Council, however, opposed him and refused to submit; so Cleomenes, together with Isagoras and his partisans, seized the Acropolis. Then the rest of the Athenians joined together by common consent and besieged them for two days; and on the third day all those among them who were Lacedaemonians left the country under a truce. Thus was accomplished for Cleomenes the ominous saying that had been uttered to him: for when he had gone up onto the Acropolis with the intention of seizing it, he was going into the sanctuary of the goddess to address her in prayer, but the priestess rose from her seat before he had passed through the door and said, “Lacedaemonian stranger, go back, and do not enter the temple, for it is not lawful for Dorians to pass inside here.” He said: “Woman, I am not a Dorian but an Achaean.” So, paying no attention to the ominous utterance, he made his attempt, and then was expelled again along with the Lacedaemonians; but the rest of the men the Athenians put in bonds to be executed, among them Timesitheus of Delphi, of whom I could tell of very great deeds of strength and courage.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 73
paragraphs: These men, having thus been placed in bonds, were put to death; and the Athenians after this sent for Cleisthenes to return, and also for the seven hundred families that had been driven out by Cleomenes. They then sent envoys to Sardis, desiring to make an alliance with the Persians, for they were well aware that the Lacedaemonians and Cleomenes had been made their utter enemies. When these envoys reached Sardis and were saying what they had been instructed to say, Artaphrenes son of Hystaspes, governor of Sardis, asked who these men were who were requesting to be allies of the Persians, and where on earth they lived; and having heard this from the envoys, he summed up his answer to them thus: that if the Athenians were willing to give earth and water to Darius, he was willing to make alliance with them, but if not, he bade them begone. The envoys, taking it upon themselves, said that they were willing to do so, because they desired to make the alliance.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 74
paragraphs: When these envoys returned to their own land, they were severely censured. Meanwhile Cleomenes, believing that he had been outrageously treated by the Athenians in both word and deed, was gathering an army from the whole of the Peloponnese, not declaring the purpose for which he was gathering it, but wishing to take vengeance on the people of Athens and intending to make Isagoras tyrant—for he too had come out of the Acropolis along with Cleomenes. Cleomenes, then, with a large army entered Eleusis, while at the same time the Boeotians, by arrangement with him, captured Oenoe and Hysiae, the demes lying on the extreme borders of Attica, and the Chalcidians on the other side invaded and began to ravage various districts of Attica. The Athenians, though attacked on more sides than one, resolved to deal with the Boeotians and Chalcidians later, and drew themselves up against the Peloponnesians at Eleusis.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 75
paragraphs: Just as the armies were about to join battle, the Corinthians first, reflecting among themselves that they were not acting rightly, changed their minds and went away; and after that Demaratus son of Ariston, who was king of the Spartans along with Cleomenes, did the same, though he had joined with him in leading the army out from Lacedaemon and had not up to this point been at variance with Cleomenes. Because of this dissension a law was laid down at Sparta that it should not be permitted, when an army went out, for both kings to go with it—for up to this time both used to go—and that as one of the kings was released from service, so one of the sons of Tyndareus too should be left behind; for before this, both of these were called on for help and went with the armies.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 76
paragraphs: At this time then, at Eleusis, the rest of the allies, seeing that the kings of the Lacedaemonians did not agree and that the Corinthians had deserted their place in the ranks, themselves also left and hurried away. This was the fourth time the Dorians had come to Attica: twice they had invaded to make war upon it, and twice they had come to help the mass of the Athenian people—first when they founded Megara at the same time (this expedition may rightly be put in the reign of Codrus as king of the Athenians); the second and third times when they came on expeditions from Sparta to drive out the sons of Peisistratus; and the fourth time on this occasion, when Cleomenes at the head of the Peloponnesians invaded Eleusis. So this was the fourth Dorian invasion of Athens.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 77
paragraphs: This army having thus been inglorously broken up, the Athenians after that, wishing to avenge themselves, marched first against the Chalcidians; and the Boeotians came to the Euripus to help the Chalcidians. Seeing the reinforcements, the Athenians resolved first to attack the Boeotians before the Chalcidians. They engaged the Boeotians in battle, and had much the better of them; after killing very many, they took seven hundred of them captive. On this same day the Athenians crossed over into Euboea and engaged the Chalcidians as well; and having conquered these too, they left four thousand allotment-holders on the land belonging to the “Breeders of Horses”—for the wealthier Chalcidians were called Hippobotae, the Breeders of Horses. As many of them as they took captive they kept in confinement together with the captured Boeotians, bound in fetters; and then after a time they let them go, having fixed their ransom at two minae apiece. But the fetters in which they had been bound they hung up on the Acropolis; and these were still there in my time, hanging on walls that had been scorched with fire by the Mede, just opposite the sanctuary that faces west. The tenth part of the ransom they dedicated as an offering, and made of it a bronze four-horse chariot, which stands on the left hand as you enter the Propylaea in the Acropolis, and on it is the following inscription:

“Matched in the deeds of war with the tribes of Boeotia and Chalcis, the sons of Athens prevailed, conquered and tamed them in fight: in chains of iron and darkness they quenched their insolent spirit, and to Athena present these, a tithe of the ransom they paid.”

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 78
paragraphs: So the Athenians grew in power. And it is clear, not from a single case but from every angle, that Equality is an excellent thing: for while the Athenians were ruled by tyrants, they were no better in war than any of those who lived around them, but once they had got rid of tyrants they became by far the first. This proves that when they were held down they were willfully slack, because they were working for a master; whereas, once they had been set free, each one was eager to achieve something for himself.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 79
paragraphs: So were these faring. The Thebans after this sent to the god, wishing to be avenged on the Athenians. The Pythian priestess, however, said that vengeance was not possible for them by their own strength alone, but told them to report the matter to the “many-voiced” and ask help of those who were “nearest” to them. When those sent to consult the oracle returned, they called a general assembly and reported it; and when the Thebans heard them say that they were to ask help of those who were nearest, they said: “Surely those who live nearest to us are the men of Tanagra, Coroneia, and Thespiae; and these always fight zealously on our side and endure the war with us to the end. What need is there to ask of them? Rather, perhaps, that is not the meaning of the oracle.”

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 80
paragraphs: While they were discussing it thus, at length one of them perceived “what the oracle means to tell us. Asopus is said to have had two daughters born to him, Thebe and Aegina; and as these are sisters, I think the god has given us as his answer that we should ask the men of Aegina to become our helpers.” Since there seemed to be no better opinion expressed than this, they at once sent and asked the men of Aegina to help them, calling upon them in accordance with the oracle; and the Aeginetans, when the request was made, said that they were sending them the sons of Aeacus as helpers.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 81
paragraphs: After this the Thebans, having made an attempt with the alliance of the sons of Aeacus and having been roughly handled by the Athenians, sent again and gave them back the sons of Aeacus and asked them for men. So the Aeginetans, exalted by great prosperity and recalling an ancient grudge against the Athenians, at the Thebans' request began a war against the Athenians without notice. For while the Athenians were intent on the Boeotians, the Aeginetans sailed against them to Attica with warships and devastated Phalerum and many other demes in the rest of the coastal region; and by so doing they deeply stirred the Athenians' resentment.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 82
paragraphs: Now the grudge that was already owed by the Aeginetans to the Athenians arose from the following beginning. The land of the Epidaurians was yielding its inhabitants no produce; and concerning this calamity the Epidaurians went to Delphi to inquire, and the Pythian priestess bade them set up images of Damia and Auxesia, saying that when they had set these up, they would meet with better fortune. The Epidaurians then asked further whether they should make the images of bronze or of stone; and the priestess told them to use neither, but to make them of the wood of a cultivated olive-tree. The Epidaurians accordingly asked the Athenians to allow them to cut an olive-tree for themselves, since they thought that Athenian olives were the most sacred—indeed, some say that at that time there were no olives in any part of the earth except at Athens. The Athenians said they would allow it on condition that the Epidaurians should every year bring due offerings to Athena Polias and to Erechtheus. The Epidaurians, having agreed to these terms, obtained what they had asked; they made images out of these olive-trees and set them up, and their land bore fruit, and they continued to fulfill toward the Athenians what they had agreed.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 83
paragraphs: During this time, and also before this, the Aeginetans were subjects of the Epidaurians, and among other things they were accustomed to cross over to Epidaurus to have their private lawsuits settled. After this time, however, they built ships for themselves and revolted from the Epidaurians out of willfulness. Being at odds with them, they kept on doing them damage, since in fact they had command of the sea; and especially they stole from them these very images of Damia and Auxesia, bringing them and setting them up in the interior of their own country at a place called Oea, which is about twenty furlongs from their city. Having set them up in this place, they worshipped them with sacrifices and with choruses of women accompanied by scurrilous jesting, ten men being appointed for each of the deities to provide the choruses. The choruses spoke evil of no man, but only of the women of the place. The Epidaurians too had the same rites; and they also have rites which may not be divulged.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 84
paragraphs: Once these images had been stolen, the Epidaurians no longer continued to fulfill toward the Athenians what they had agreed. The Athenians accordingly sent and expressed their displeasure to the Epidaurians; and these declared that they were doing no wrong, for during the time they had the images in their country they had continued to fulfill what was agreed, but since they had been deprived of them, it was not just for them to make the offerings any longer; and they bade them demand the offerings from the Aeginetans, who had the images. So the Athenians sent to Aegina and demanded the images back; but the Aeginetans said they had nothing to do with the Athenians.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 85
paragraphs: The Athenians then report that those citizens whom the state sent after this demand were dispatched in one single trireme; and having come to Aegina, they tried to tear the images up from their pedestals (claiming that they were made of wood belonging to the Athenians), in order to carry them back with them. But being unable to get hold of them in this way (say the Athenians), they threw ropes around them and began pulling, when suddenly, as they pulled, thunder came on and an earthquake along with the thunder; and the crew of the trireme who were pulling were driven out of their wits by these things, and being in this state they killed one another as if they were enemies, until at last only one of the whole number was left; and he returned alone to Phalerum.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 86
paragraphs: Thus the Athenians say it came about. But the Aeginetans say that it was not with a single ship that the Athenians came; for a single ship, and even a few more than one, they could easily have repelled even if they had had no ships of their own. Rather, they say, the Athenians sailed against their country with a large fleet, and the Aeginetans gave way before them and did not fight a sea-battle. They cannot, however, declare for certain whether they yielded in this way because they admitted they were not strong enough to fight the battle at sea, or because they intended to do something of the kind they actually did. The Athenians then, they say, since no one met them in fight, disembarked from their ships and made for the images; but being unable to tear them up from their pedestals, at last they threw ropes around them and began to pull—until the images, as they were being pulled, both did the same thing (and here they report something which I cannot believe, though another man may): they say the images fell on their knees before them, and that they have remained in that position ever since. The Athenians, they say, were doing this; and meanwhile they themselves (so the Aeginetans say), having been informed that the Athenians were about to make an expedition against them, had brought in the Argives to help them; and just as the Athenians had disembarked on Aeginetan land, the Argives had come to their rescue—and having crossed unnoticed from Epidaurus to the island, they fell upon the Athenians before these had heard anything of the matter, cutting them off secretly from the way back to their ships. And it was at this moment that the thunder and the earthquake came upon them.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 87
paragraphs: This is the report given by both the Argives and the Aeginetans, and it is admitted by the Athenians too that only one man of them survived and came back to Attica. Only, the Argives say this one man survived destruction wrought by them upon the army of Athens, while the Athenians say that the divine power was the destroyer. Even this one man, however, did not remain alive but perished, they say, in the following way. When he returned to Athens he reported the disaster that had happened; and the wives of the men who had gone on the expedition to Aegina, hearing it and being very indignant that he alone of all had survived, crowded around this man and proceeded to stab him with the pins of their mantles, each of them asking where her husband was. So he was killed; and to the Athenians the deed of the women seemed far more terrible even than the disaster itself. Not knowing, it is said, how to punish the women in any other way, they changed their fashion of dress to that of Ionia—for before this the Athenian women wore Dorian dress, very like that of Corinth—they changed it therefore to the linen tunic, so that they might have no use for pins.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 88
paragraphs: In truth, however, this style of dress is not originally Ionian but Carian, for the old Hellenic fashion of dress for women was everywhere the same as that which we now call Dorian. Moreover, with reference to these events, it is said that the Argives and Aeginetans made it a custom among themselves in both countries to have the pins made half as large again as the size then established in use, and that their women should offer pins especially in the temple of these goddesses, and also that they should bring neither Athenian pottery nor anything else of Athenian make to the temple, but that it should be the custom henceforth to drink there from pitchers made in their own lands.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 89
paragraphs: From this time onward the Argive and Aeginetan women, because of the quarrel with the Athenians, continued to wear pins larger than before, and still do so even to my day; and the origin of the Athenians' enmity toward the Aeginetans came about in the way described. So at this time, when the Thebans invoked them, the Aeginetans readily came to the aid of the Boeotians, calling to mind what had happened concerning the images. The Aeginetans then were laying waste, as I have said, the coastal regions of Attica; and when the Athenians resolved to make an expedition against the Aeginetans, an oracle came to them from Delphi bidding them wait for thirty years, reckoned from the time of the wrong done by the Aeginetans, and in the thirty-first year appoint a sacred enclosure for Aeacus and then begin the war against the Aeginetans, and they would succeed as they desired. But if they made an expedition against them immediately, they would in the meantime suffer very much evil and also inflict very much, but at last would subdue them. When the Athenians heard the report of this, they appointed a sacred enclosure for Aeacus—the one now established close to the marketplace—but they could not bear to hear that they must wait for thirty years, after they had suffered injuries from the Aeginetans.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 90
paragraphs: While they were preparing to take vengeance, a matter arose from the Lacedaemonians that hindered them. For the Lacedaemonians, having learned of what the Alcmaeonidae had contrived with regard to the Pythian priestess, and of what the Pythian priestess had contrived against themselves and the sons of Peisistratus, were doubly grieved—not only because they had driven into exile men who were their guest-friends, but also because, after having done this, no gratitude was shown to them by the Athenians. Moreover, in addition, they were urged on by oracles that said they would suffer many injuries from the Athenians—oracles they had not been aware of before, but had come to know since Cleomenes had brought them to Sparta. Cleomenes had, in fact, obtained from the Athenian Acropolis those oracles which the sons of Peisistratus had possessed before and had left behind in the temple when they were driven out; and Cleomenes recovered them after they had been left behind.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 91
paragraphs: At this time, then, when the Lacedaemonians had recovered the oracles and saw that the Athenians were growing in power and were by no means willing to submit to them, and perceiving that the Athenian race, now that it was free, was becoming a match for their own—whereas when held down by tyrants it had been weak and ready to be ruled—perceiving, I say, all these things, they sent for Hippias son of Peisistratus to come from Sigeum on the Hellespont, to which the family of Peisistratus had fled for refuge. When Hippias had come at the summons, the Spartans also sent for envoys to come from their other allies, and spoke to them as follows: “Allies, we are conscious within ourselves that we have not acted rightly. For, incited by counterfeit oracles, we drove into exile men who were most closely united with us as guest-friends and who had undertaken to make Athens subject to us; then, after doing this, we handed over the state to a thankless populace, which, as soon as it had raised its head—having been freed by us—drove out us and our king with wanton outrage; and now, puffed up with pride, it is growing in power, so that the neighbors of these people have already learned this—first the Boeotians and Chalcidians—and perhaps others will learn it afterwards: that they made a mistake. Since, then, we erred in what has been described, we will now try, together with you, to take vengeance on them; for this is why we sent for Hippias, whom you see here, and for you to come from your cities, so that with common counsel and common force we might bring him to Athens and restore to him what we formerly took away.”

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 92
paragraphs: So they spoke; but the majority of the allies did not approve of their words. The rest kept silent, but the Corinthian Socles spoke as follows: “Surely now the heavens shall be beneath the earth, and the earth raised up high above the heavens; men shall have their dwelling in the sea, and fishes that habitation which men had before—seeing that you, Lacedaemonians, are doing away with free governments and are preparing to bring tyranny back into our cities, than which there is nothing more unjust or more murderous among men. For if this really seems good to you—that cities should be ruled by tyrants—then you yourselves first set up a tyrant in your own state, and then try to establish them for others. As it is, you are acting unfairly toward your allies, seeing that you have had no experience of tyrants yourselves and take the greatest care at Sparta that such a thing may never come to pass. Yet had you had experience of it, as we have had, you would be able to contribute juster opinions about it than you do now. For the established order of the Corinthian state was this: the government was an oligarchy, and the oligarchs, who were called the Bacchiadae, controlled the state and intermarried among themselves. One of these men, named Amphion, had a daughter born to him who was lame, and her name was Labda. Since none of the Bacchiadae was willing to marry her, she was taken to wife by Aëtion son of Echecrates, of the deme of Petra, but by descent a Lapith and of the race of Caeneus. Neither from her nor from any other wife were children born to him, so he set out to Delphi to inquire about offspring; and as he entered, the priestess addressed him immediately with these lines:
“‘Much to be honored are you, yet no one honors you. Labda conceives, and a rolling boulder will she bear, which shall fall down upon the heads of kings, and bring chastisement to Corinth.’

This answer given to Aëtion was somehow reported to the Bacchiadae, to whom a previous oracle delivered at Corinth had not been intelligible—an oracle that referred to the same thing as Aëtion's and ran thus:

“‘An eagle conceives in the rocks, and shall bear a ravening lion, strong and fierce to devour, who shall loosen the knees of many. Ponder this well in your minds, I bid you, Corinthians, whose dwelling lies about fair Peirene's spring and in craggy Corinth.’

This oracle, I say, having come before to the Bacchiadae, was obscure; but when afterwards they heard the one given to Aëtion, at once they understood the earlier one also, that it was in accord with Aëtion's; and understanding this second one as well, they kept quiet, intending to destroy the offspring that would be born to Aëtion. As soon, then, as his wife had borne the child, they sent ten of their own number to the deme where Aëtion lived, to kill the child. When these men had come to Petra and passed into the courtyard of Aëtion's house, they asked for the child; and Labda, knowing nothing of the purpose for which they had come and supposing them to be asking for the child out of friendly feeling for its father, brought it and placed it in the hands of one of them. They had, it seems, resolved along the way that whichever of them first received the child should dash it on the ground. However, when Labda brought and gave it, it happened by divine providence that the child smiled at the man who received it; and when he noticed this, a feeling of compassion prevented him from killing it, and in this compassion he handed it to the next man, and he to the third. Thus it passed through the hands of all ten, each handing it on, since none of them could bring himself to destroy its life. So they gave the child back to its mother and went out; and standing by the doors, they abused and reproached one another, laying blame especially on the one who had first received the child, because he had not done what had been decided. At last, after some time, they resolved to go in again and all take a share in the murder. But from the offspring of Aëtion it was fated that evils should spring up for Corinth. For Labda had been listening to all this as she stood close by the door; and fearing that they might change their minds and take the child a second time and kill it, she took it and hid it in the place that seemed to her least likely to be discovered—a corn-chest—knowing that if they returned and began to search, they were likely to examine everything. And this is just what happened. When they had come, and their search had failed to find it, they thought it best to return and say to those who had sent them that they had done everything they had been charged with. So they went away and said this; and afterwards the son of Aëtion grew up, and because he had escaped this danger, he was given the surname Cypselus, derived from the corn-chest (cypsele). When Cypselus had come to manhood and was seeking a divination, a two-edged answer was given to him at Delphi; trusting in it, he made an attempt upon Corinth and took possession of it. The answer was this:
“‘Happy indeed is the lot of this man who enters my dwelling, offspring of Aëtion; he shall rule in famous Corinth—Cypselus, he and his sons, but his children's children no longer.’

Such was the oracle. And Cypselus, when he became tyrant, was a man of this character: many of the Corinthians he drove into exile, many he deprived of their wealth, and very many more of their lives. And when he had reigned thirty years and brought his life to a prosperous end, his son Periander became his successor in the tyranny. Now Periander at first was milder than his father; but after he had corresponded through messengers with Thrasybulus, tyrant of Miletus, he became far more murderous even than Cypselus. For he sent a messenger to Thrasybulus to ask what arrangement of affairs was safest for him to make in order to govern his state best. Thrasybulus led the messenger who had come from Periander out of the city and went into a field of growing corn; as he passed through the crop, asking and asking again about the reason for his coming from Corinth, he kept cutting off the heads of any ears of corn he saw standing higher than the rest, and as he cut them off he threw them away, until he had destroyed in this way the finest and richest part of the crop. So having passed through the place and suggested not a single word of counsel, he dismissed the messenger. When the messenger returned to Corinth, Periander was eager to hear the counsel he had been given; but the messenger said that Thrasybulus had given him no counsel at all, and added that he marveled at Periander for sending him to such a man, who was out of his senses and a destroyer of his own goods—relating at the same time what he had seen Thrasybulus do. So Periander, understanding what had been done and perceiving that Thrasybulus was counseling him to put to death the most eminent men among his subjects, from that moment began to display every kind of evil treatment toward the citizens of the state. Whatever Cypselus had left undone in killing and banishing, Periander completed. In a single day he stripped all the wives of the Corinthians of their clothing on account of his own wife Melissa. For he had sent messengers to the Thesprotians on the river Acheron to consult the oracle of the dead about a deposit left with him by a guest-friend; and Melissa appeared and said that she would not tell in what place the deposit was laid, for she was cold and had no clothes, since those he had buried with her were of no use to her, not having been burned. As evidence that she was speaking the truth, she said, he should recall that he had put his loaves into a cold oven. When the report of this was brought back to Periander, the token convinced him, because he had had intercourse with Melissa after she was dead; and immediately upon receiving the message, he proclaimed that all the wives of the Corinthians should come out to the temple of Hera. They came as to a festival, in their finest adornment; and he, having stationed the spearmen of his guard in ambush, stripped them all alike—free women and their attendants—and gathering all their clothes together in a pit, he set them on fire, praying at the same time to Melissa. After he had done this and sent a second time, the apparition of Melissa told him the place where he had laid the deposit entrusted to him by his guest-friend.

“Such a thing, Lacedaemonians, you must know, is tyranny, and such are its deeds; and we Corinthians marveled greatly at first when we saw that you were sending for Hippias, and now we marvel still more because you say these things. And we adjure you, calling upon the gods of Hellas, not to establish tyrannies in the cities. If, however, you will not desist from your purpose but try to restore Hippias contrary to what is just, know that the Corinthians at least do not give their consent to what you are doing.”

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 93
paragraphs: Socles, the envoy of Corinth, spoke thus; and Hippias made answer to him, calling to witness the same gods as Socles had, that assuredly the Corinthians, more than any others, would one day regret the loss of the sons of Peisistratus, when the appointed days came for them to be troubled by the Athenians. Thus Hippias made answer, being better acquainted with the oracles than any other man. But the rest of the allies, who for a time had restrained themselves and kept silence, when they heard Socles speak freely, all gave voice to what they felt, and adopted the opinion of the Corinthian envoy, adjuring the Lacedaemonians not to do any violence to a Hellenic city.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 94
paragraphs: Thus was this matter brought to an end. Hippias, being dismissed from there, was offered Anthemus by Amyntas king of the Macedonians, and Iolcus by the Thessalians. He, however, accepted neither of these, but retired again to Sigeum—a city Peisistratus had taken by force of arms from the Mytilenians, and having taken it had appointed his own natural son Hegesistratus, born of an Argive woman, to be tyrant of it. But Hegesistratus did not keep possession of what he had received from Peisistratus without a struggle; for the Mytilenians and Athenians waged war for a long time, with their strongholds at Achilleum and Sigeum respectively—the one side demanding that the place be restored to them, while the Athenians refused to admit this demand and proved by argument that the Aeolians had no better claim to the territory of Ilium than they themselves had and the rest of the Hellenes who had helped Menelaus exact vengeance for the rape of Helen.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 95
paragraphs: While they were waging this war, among many other things of various kinds that happened in the battles, once when a fight took place and the Athenians were winning, Alcaeus the poet, taking to flight, escaped himself, but the Athenians retained possession of his arms and hung them up on the walls of the temple of Athena at Sigeum. About this Alcaeus composed a song and sent it to Mytilene, reporting his misfortune in it to a certain Melanippus, who was his friend. Finally Periander son of Cypselus made peace between the Athenians and the Mytilenians, for they referred the matter to him as arbitrator; and he made peace between them on the condition that each should continue to occupy the territory they then held.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 96
paragraphs: Sigeum, then, had in this way come under Athenian rule. When Hippias had returned to Asia from Lacedaemon, he set everything in motion, stirring up enmity between the Athenians and Artaphrenes, and using every means to secure that Athens should come under his own rule and that of Darius. While Hippias was so engaged, the Athenians, hearing of these things, sent envoys to Sardis and tried to prevent the Persians from following the suggestions of the exiled Athenians. Artaphrenes, however, commanded them, if they wished to be preserved from ruin, to receive Hippias back. This proposal the Athenians were by no means disposed to accept when it was reported to them; and since they did not accept it, it at once became the common opinion among them that they were enemies of the Persians.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 97
paragraphs: While they held these thoughts and had been set at enmity with the Persians, at this very time Aristagoras the Milesian, ordered away from Sparta by Cleomenes the Lacedaemonian, arrived in Athens; for this was the most powerful city besides Sparta. Aristagoras came forward before the popular assembly and said the same things he had said at Sparta about the wealth in Asia and about the Persian manner of fighting—how they used neither shield nor spear and were easy to overcome. Thus he spoke, and he added that the Milesians were colonists from the Athenians and that it was only reasonable for the Athenians to rescue them, since they had such great power; and there was nothing he did not promise, being very pressing in his request, until at last he persuaded them. For it seems that it is easier to deceive many than one, since, though he was not able by himself to deceive Cleomenes the Lacedaemonian, he did just that to thirty thousand Athenians. Being persuaded, the Athenians voted a resolution to send twenty ships to help the Ionians, and appointed to command them Melanthius, one of their citizens, who was highly regarded in all things. These ships proved to be the beginning of evils for the Hellenes and the barbarians.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 98
paragraphs: Aristagoras sailed on ahead and came to Miletus; and then, having devised a plan from which no advantage was likely to come for the Ionians (nor indeed was he doing what he did with that in view, but in order to vex King Darius), he sent a man to Phrygia to the Paeonians who had been taken captive by Megabazus from the river Strymon, and who were living in a district and village of Phrygia apart by themselves. When the messenger came to the Paeonians, he spoke these words: “Paeonians, Aristagoras the tyrant of Miletus has sent me to offer you salvation, if you are willing to do as he says. For now all Ionia has revolted from the king, and you have an opportunity to get safely back to your own land. To reach the sea will be your concern; after that it will from that point on be ours.” The Paeonians, hearing this, welcomed the proposal most gladly, and taking their wives and children with them, began a flight to the sea—though some of them were afraid and remained where they were. Having come to the coast, the Paeonians crossed over to Chios; and when they were already in Chios, a large body of Persian horsemen arrived in their track in pursuit of the Paeonians. These, not overtaking them, sent over to Chios and demanded that the Paeonians return. The Paeonians, however, did not accept the proposal, but the Chians ferried them from Chios to Lesbos, and the Lesbians brought them to Doriscus, and from there they proceeded by land and came to Paeonia.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 99
paragraphs: Aristagoras meanwhile, when the Athenians had arrived with twenty ships, bringing also five triremes of the Eretrians (who joined the expedition not for the sake of the Athenians but of the Milesians themselves, to repay a debt they owed—for the Milesians in former times had borne with the Eretrians the whole burden of that war which they had fought with the Chalcidians, when the Chalcidians on their side were helped by the Samians against the Eretrians and Milesians)—when these, I say, had arrived and the other allies were on the spot, Aristagoras proceeded to march on Sardis. On this march he did not go himself, but remained at Miletus and appointed others to command the Milesians, namely his brother Charopinus and a certain Hermophantus from among the other citizens.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 100
paragraphs: With this force, then, the Ionians came to Ephesus, and leaving their ships at Coressus in the territory of Ephesus, they themselves went up in a large body, taking Ephesians as guides on their march. They marched along the river Cayster, and then, arriving after crossing the range of Tmolus, they took Sardis without any resistance, all except the citadel; the citadel Artaphrenes himself saved from capture, having with him a considerable force.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 101
paragraphs: From plundering the city after they had taken it, they were prevented by this: the houses in Sardis were mostly built of reeds, and even those of them that were of brick had their roofs thatched with reeds. One of these houses was set on fire by a soldier, and the fire, spreading from house to house, began to take the whole town. As the town burned, the Lydians and all the Persians in the city, cut off from escape since the fire prevailed around them on every side and they had no way out, gathered together in the marketplace and along the river Pactolus—which brings them down gold-dust from Tmolus, flowing through the middle of their marketplace, and then empties into the river Hermus, which in turn empties into the sea. To this Pactolus, I say, and to the marketplace the Lydians and Persians gathered, and were compelled to defend themselves. Then the Ionians, seeing some of the enemy standing on their defense and others in great numbers coming up to attack, were struck with fear and withdrew to the mountain called Tmolus, and at nightfall went off to their ships.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 102
paragraphs: Sardis was then destroyed by fire, and with it the temple of the native goddess Cybebe—which the Persians later gave as a reason for burning, in return, the temples in the land of the Hellenes. At the time in question, however, the Persians who occupied districts within the river Halys, informed beforehand of this movement, were gathering to come to the aid of the Lydians; and as it happened, they found when they arrived that the Ionians were no longer in Sardis. But they followed closely in their tracks and caught up with them at Ephesus; and the Ionians did stand against them in battle order, but when they joined battle they had much the worse of it. Besides other men of note whom the Persians killed, Eualcides also fell, commander of the Eretrians, a man who had won wreaths in athletic contests and was much celebrated by Simonides of Ceos; and those of the Ionians who survived the battle dispersed to their various cities.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 103
paragraphs: So they fought at that time; and after the battle the Athenians abandoned the Ionians, and when Aristagoras urgently called upon them by messengers for help, they said they would not help him. The Ionians, however, though deprived of the Athenian alliance, no less continued to prepare for the war with the king, so great were the offenses they had already committed against Darius. They also sailed to the Hellespont and brought under their power Byzantium and all the other cities there; and then having sailed out of the Hellespont, they gained in addition most of Caria as an ally—for even Caunus, which before had been unwilling to be their ally, now, after they had burned Sardis, was added to them too.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 104
paragraphs: The Cypriots too, except for those of Amathus, were added voluntarily to their alliance; for these also had revolted from the Medes in the following way. There was a certain Onesilus, younger brother of Gorgus king of Salamis, and son of Chersis, the son of Siromus, the son of Euelthon. This man, too, had often in the past advised Gorgus to revolt from the king, and now, when he heard that the Ionians had revolted, he pressed him hard and tried to urge him to it. When he could not persuade Gorgus, Onesilus watched for a time when Gorgus had gone out of the city of Salamis, and then together with the men of his own faction he shut him out of the gates. Gorgus, robbed of the city, took refuge with the Medes, and Onesilus became ruler of Salamis and tried to persuade all the men of Cyprus to join him in revolt. Most he persuaded; but since those of Amathus were not willing to do as he wished, he sat down before their city and besieged it.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 105
paragraphs: While Onesilus was besieging Amathus, it was reported to King Darius that Sardis had been captured and burned by the Athenians and the Ionians together, and that the leader of the conspiracy for bringing these things about was the Milesian Aristagoras. It is said that when he was first informed of this, he paid no heed to the Ionians, because he knew that they at any rate would not escape unpunished for their revolt, but he asked who the Athenians were; and when he had been told, he asked for his bow, and having received it and set an arrow on the string, he shot it up toward the heavens, and as he shot into the air he said: “Zeus, grant me to take vengeance on the Athenians!” Having so said, he charged one of his attendants to say to him, whenever dinner was set before the king, always three times: “Master, remember the Athenians.”

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 106
paragraphs: Having given this charge, he summoned into his presence Histiaeus the Milesian, whom Darius had by now been keeping with him for a long time, and said: “I am informed, Histiaeus, that your deputy, to whom you entrusted the government of Miletus, has rebelled against me; for he has brought men against me from the other continent, and persuaded the Ionians too—who shall pay the penalty to me for what they have done—to go along with them, and so has robbed me of Sardis. Now then, how do you think that this is well? And how was anything of this kind done without your counsel? Take care lest you afterwards find reason to blame yourself for this.” Histiaeus replied: “O king, what kind of speech is this you have uttered, saying that I counseled a matter from which any vexation, great or small, was likely to arise for you? What have I to seek, in addition to what I already have, that I should do such things; and of what am I in need? For I have everything that you have, and I am thought worthy by you to hear all your counsels. No—if my deputy is in fact acting in any such way as you say, be assured that he has done it entirely on his own account. I, for my part, do not even admit the report to be true, that the Milesians and my deputy are acting in any rebellious fashion against your power. But if they are indeed doing anything of the kind, and if what you have heard, O king, is the truth, then see what a thing you did in removing me from the seacoast; for it seems that the Ionians, once I was out of their sight, did what they had long desired to do—whereas if I had been in Ionia, not a city would have made the least movement. Now, therefore, let me set out as quickly as possible to go to Ionia, so that I may arrange all these matters for you as they were before, and deliver into your hands this deputy of Miletus who contrived these things. And when I have done this to your satisfaction, I swear by the gods of the royal house that I will not take off the tunic I wear when I go down to Ionia until I have made Sardinia tributary to you, the largest of all islands.”

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 107
paragraphs: With these words Histiaeus tried to deceive the king; and Darius was persuaded and let him go, charging him, when he had accomplished what he had promised, to return again to him at Susa.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 108
paragraphs: Meanwhile, while the news about Sardis was going up to the king, and while Darius, after doing what he did with the bow, was coming to speech with Histiaeus, and Histiaeus, having been let go by Darius, was making his way to the coast—during all this time the following events were taking place. As Onesilus of Salamis was besieging those of Amathus, it was reported to him that Artybius, a Persian, bringing with him on ships a large Persian army, was expected soon to arrive in Cyprus. On receiving this news, Onesilus sent heralds to various places in Ionia to summon the Ionians to his aid; and they took counsel together and came without delay with a large force. The Ionians arrived in Cyprus just at the time when the Persians, having crossed over from Cilicia in ships, were proceeding by land to attack Salamis, while the Phoenicians with the ships were sailing around the headland called the “Keys of Cyprus.”

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 109
paragraphs: This being the case, the tyrants of Cyprus called together the commanders of the Ionians and said: “Ionians, we of Cyprus give you a choice: which enemy would you rather fight, the Persians or the Phoenicians? If you would rather array yourselves on land and try yourselves against the Persians in battle, it is time for you to disembark from your ships and draw up on land, and for us to embark in your ships to fight the Phoenicians. But if, on the other hand, you would rather try yourselves against the Phoenicians—whichever of these two you choose, you must try to ensure, so far as it rests with you, that both Ionia and Cyprus shall be free.” To this the Ionians replied: “We were sent out by the common authority of the Ionians to guard the sea, and not to hand our ships over to the Cyprians and fight on land ourselves against the Persians. We therefore will try to do good service in the post to which we were assigned; and you must call to mind all the evils you suffered from the Medes when you were their slaves, and prove yourselves brave men.”

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 110
paragraphs: The Ionians made answer in these words. Afterwards, when the Persians had come to the plain of Salamis, the kings of the Cyprians drew up their battle order, choosing the best of the troops of Salamis and Soli to face the Persians, and setting the other Cyprians against the rest of the enemy's forces; and against Artybius, the commander of the Persians, Onesilus took up his place in the line by his own free choice.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 111
paragraphs: Now Artybius was riding a horse that had been trained to rear up against a hoplite. Onesilus, on being informed of this, and having a shield-bearer by race a Carian who was of very good repute as a soldier and full of courage besides, said to this man: “I am informed that the horse of Artybius rears upright and works both with his hooves and his mouth against anyone he is brought to attack. Consider the matter, then, and tell me at once which of the two you would rather watch for and strike, the horse or Artybius himself.” His attendant replied: “O king, I am ready to do both or either of these, and in every case to do what you appoint for me; but I will tell you the way I think most suitable for your condition. I say it is right that one who is a king and commander should fight with a king and commander; for if you kill the enemy's commander, it turns to great glory for you; and again, if he kills you—which heaven forbid—even death, when it is at the hands of a worthy foe, is only half to be lamented. As for us who are under your command, it is fitting that we fight with the others under his command and with his horse. And of the horse's tricks have no fear at all, for I promise you that after this at least he shall never stand against any man again.” So he spoke; and shortly afterwards the opposing forces joined battle both on land and with their ships.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 112
paragraphs: On that day the Ionians for their part greatly distinguished themselves and overcame the Phoenicians, and of them the Samians were best. Meanwhile on land, when the armies met, they came to close quarters and fought; and as regards the two commanders, what happened was this: when Artybius came riding on his horse to fight with Onesilus, Onesilus, as he had arranged with his shield-bearer, struck at Artybius himself when he came to fight with him; and when the horse set its hooves against Onesilus's shield, then the Carian struck with a curved blade and cut off the horse's feet.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 113
paragraphs: So Artybius, the commander of the Persians, fell there on the spot together with his horse. While the others too were still fighting, Stesenor, the tyrant of Curium, deserted them, having with him a large force of men—these Curians are said to be colonists from Argos—and when the Curians had deserted, forthwith also the war-chariots of the men of Salamis did the same as the Curians. When these things happened, the Persians had the advantage over the Cyprians; and after their army had been routed, many others fell, and among them Onesilus son of Chersis, the man who had brought about the revolt of the Cyprians, and also the king of the Solians, Aristocyprus son of Philocyprus—that Philocyprus whom Solon the Athenian, when he came to Cyprus, praised in verse above all other tyrants.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 114
paragraphs: The men of Amathus then cut off the head of Onesilus, because he had besieged them, and having brought it to Amathus, hung it over the gate of the city. As the head hung there, once it had become hollow, a swarm of bees entered it and filled it with honeycomb. When this had come to pass, the Amathusians consulted an oracle about the head, and they received an answer bidding them take it down and bury it, and sacrifice yearly to Onesilus as a hero; and if they did this, things would go better for them.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 115
paragraphs: The Amathusians accordingly continued to do so even to my time. But the Ionians who had fought the sea-fight in Cyprus, when they perceived that the fortunes of Onesilos were ruined and that the cities of the Cyprians were besieged, except Salamis, and that this city had been delivered over by the Salaminians to Gorgos the former king,--as soon as they perceived this, the Ionians sailed away back to Ionia. Now of the cities in Cyprus Soloi held out for the longest time under the siege; and the Persians took it in the fifth month by undermining the wall round.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 116
paragraphs: The Cyprians then, after they had made themselves free for one year, had again been reduced to slavery afresh: and meanwhile Daurises, who was married to a daughter of Dareios, and Hymaies and Otanes, who were also Persian commanders and were married also to daughters of Dareios, after they had pursued those Ionians who had made the expedition to Sardis and defeating them in battle had driven them by force to their ships,--after this distributed the cities amongst themselves and proceeded to sack them.
